approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Very long approach: Chewuch River trail nearly to Remmel Lake, then a climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin
Loose rock and grainy granite in places; rockfall from parties above
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat

approach_variants.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
camps: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier or snowfield crossing near West Fury toward the saddle carries crevasse and moat hazard
Traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury is required just to reach the saddle
Steep brushy off-trail travel in the Access Creek drainage
Extreme remoteness, no quick bailout; any injury means multi-day self-rescue
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Loose rock on some approach pinnacles
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a saddle between two named summits and you reach it by having crossed both summits of Fury. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. Arrival: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the northwest ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. Nothing marks the foot of the southwest face; what you navigate by is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. What going too far looks like: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

approach_variants.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Bacon Creek Road (off SR-20 near Marblemount)

approach_variants.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Long off-trail ridge sequence over Porkbelly, Mystery and Pioneer ridges and Crowder's northeast ridge with no tread
Steep, brushy, sometimes cliffy off-trail terrain
No independent descent; leaving the range means a long off-trail drainage exit
Class 3 south side above Pickell Pass, downclimbed on return
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Extreme remoteness, any injury means multi-day self-rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Pickell Pass the south side of Swiss is climbed directly, and the test is that you are going up rather than along. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

How to know you are at Pickell Pass rather than another saddle on the same ridge system: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's northeast ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

Why this side may be the better choice, as a planning fact rather than a landmark: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

approach_variants.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
approach_variants.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the moat between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the south peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

approach_variants.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
approach_variants.notes:
FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the washed-out Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
approach_variants.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the south peak.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; steep cross-country through timber and over downed logs
Rock gully with downsloping slabs and loose gravel near the summit, rockfall from parties above
Loose talus and scree in the gullies with class 3-4 moves and exposure near the crest
Lingering snow in forest and basin firms or ices the gullies early season
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water above the lower forest
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Climb until the forest opens. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A meadow basin below the west ridge and gully complex, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

From the basin, trend south and southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col and basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat. That col is the aiming point, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the broad west ridge, or the shallow gully just north of it, to the summit shoulder.

The last section is the one that confirms you are on the summit line rather than a neighbouring gully: a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall, over downsloping slabs and loose gravel. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft

approachLogistics.trailhead: Unmarked SR-20 pullout about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass

approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: Unmarked pullout on SR-20 found only by distance from the Blue Lake trailhead; walk along the road shoulder
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water on the route
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col in a single push
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass and looking straight across the valley at Silver Star Mountain. There is no numbered Forest Service trail here — the whole thing is an established boot path.

Scramble down the embankment past cairns. The first stretch is loose, scree-covered talus before it settles into a proper path. Cross Early Winters Creek on one of the logs; the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season.

On the far bank the path winds through forest for about a quarter of a mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly. At about 6,460 ft the angle relents at a broad flat bench — big enough for a dozen tents and the obvious rest stop.

Above the bench the path climbs and traverses loose scree gullies before a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. That is roughly 3,700 ft above the creek. That last scree is worse on the way down than the way up.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — logs shift, and the ford is cold and swift in early season
extremely unstable ball-bearing scree over slab on the final stretch to the col — this is the section that kicks rocks onto whoever is below, so travel close together
loose talus on the initial drop from the highway
very large gain for a day trip; most parties camp
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the destination and the route starts essentially straight off it. Burgundy Col is a narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and once you are stood in it the first pitch is directly above and visually obvious — the North Face rises immediately from the col rather than requiring any traverse along the base. If you have to walk any distance from the notch to find a start, you are at the wrong notch. Confirmation from the col: the Silver Star Glacier lies below on the far (east) side, so a col that drops onto a glacier behind you is the right one.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
approach_variants.notes:
The usual way this is done. Walk the same line from the milepost 166 pullout — down the loose talus embankment, across Early Winters Creek on logs, through the forest and then steeply up between the two small creeks — and stop at the broad flat bench at about 6,460 ft, which holds a dozen or more tents and is the natural halfway point. There is usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby.

Next morning you carry only what you need for the col and the route, which makes the loose scree above the bench substantially less unpleasant. Reckon on the bench being the last flat ground and the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: the direct-looking gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
loose scree over slab on the traverse into the col
no reliable water above the bench
rockfall onto parties below on the final approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, the route to the col climbs and traverses scree gullies with cairns on the final stretch. Aim for the narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on your left and Paisano Pinnacle on your right; the first pitch of the North Face rises directly out of it. Do not take the obvious direct gully that appears to lead straight to the col — it is loose and exposed. The path goes up the gully above camp and then makes a rising traverse right beneath the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: Long approach through an old burn: little shade, overgrown wet tread
No climbers' trail to the base; navigate by the gully dividing the peak from the tower
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
No-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, so retreat is slow
Shorter-looking Canadian approach is an illegal border crossing and patrolled
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approach_variants.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Trailhead published under several names; long extra drive
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up into the gully, and start on the left wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Longest valley approach; trail follows the Chewuch River
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches

Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat

approach_variants.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply right from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the north side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct, snow-free
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and right of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, on snow
approach_variants.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Apr, ice and mixed
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing in high water; cable car or ford
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
Steep brushy timber, slide alder and a loose divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir below the wall
Deep moat at the toe of the buttress late season
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Remote and committing, several days from help
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. The alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is shorter, but the cross-border stretch can be heavy bushwhacking, so the long trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: International border crossing on foot
Overgrown, unmaintained tread; heavy bushwhacking on the cross-border stretch
Same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall below the buttress
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Cross-border rescue complications; remote and committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

approach_variants.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
approach_variants.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The notch is the gap in the crest at the foot of the West Ridge proper, and the couloir below it is the obvious continuous snow line splitting the left-hand edge of the south face. Navigate to the notch, not to the first gully you reach — several lines start off the same snowfield and only this one tops out at the crest. You are at the base of the climbing when you step through the notch onto the ridge crest; from there the route to the summit runs to climber's right.

approach_variants.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
approach_variants.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cat Scratch is not the snow couloir, and that mix-up is the usual reason parties lose time here: it is the parallel rock gully system just west (climber's left) of the couloir, and it tops out at the same notch. Several parallel gullies in that system look alike from below — the correct one finishes at the notch itself rather than on the ridge either side of it, so pick your line by where it ends on the skyline, not by which entrance looks easiest from the basin.

approach_variants.name: Up the gully to its own ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the pullout near milepost 166, hike the gully below the wall for about an hour and follow a narrow ledge back right to the start, a prominent left-arching wide corner. The direct way, and the most practical when the gully is in shape.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, especially with parties above or after rain
Full-day south-facing sun and heat in summer
Loose and deteriorating rock on pitches 1, 2 and 6
Loose chockstones in the first corner above the start
Highway gated shut through winter, so the wall is unreachable by car for months

approach_variants.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: Retreat from the lower pitches means reversing or rappelling a different route
Loose, deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Not all belays are rigged for rappel; find the stations before you need them
Rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
Rockfall in the approach gully and exposed easy-fifth step
Full-day south-facing sun; lower pitches seep into early summer in wet years
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are looking for a two-bolt anchor sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge below a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse left along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

approach_variants.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: Escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose, deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rigged for rappel; plan the descent before leaving the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material
Seepage on the lower pitches into early summer in wet years
Full-day south-facing sun; loose talus in the approach gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse left — further than from the centre line — until you find the two-bolt anchor set on the ledge directly below a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the talus fan toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for cannot be seen from below. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with two options off it, a left-hand line past a chockstone that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered from the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

approach_variants.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
approach_variants.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
approach_variants.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the boulder at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
North and west faces are cliffy; going straight up from High Pass does not work
Short fourth-class step to the true north summit
Steep snow and moat on the snow finger in early season (June-early July)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a broad saddle on the south side at about 7,650 ft, and the way you get to it is a snow finger rather than a slope. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a snow finger and its moat, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

The saddle is where the route leaves the basin. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

The negative marker is the most important thing on this peak and it is about aspect: Berge's north and west faces are cliffy. Parties must stay on the south-west side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

The route-finding rule lower down is a descending traverse, which feels wrong and is right: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

The last obstacle has an elevation and a character: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with slanted slabs and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

The summit is not one point. The true, north summit needs a short fourth-class step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)

approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go; this approach passes beneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on the Buck Creek approach
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
Exposed scrambling to gain the narrow 7,840 ft notch in the ridge crest
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft on the final climb
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, lengthening the drive-in to Trinity
Remote country, 15+ miles round trip, usually multi-day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The High Pass approach delivers you to the wrong side of the mountain on purpose, and the rule is that you must keep going around. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. The climb is on the south-west side. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

The arrival is the same place for every approach to this peak: the broad saddle on Berge's south side at about 7,650 ft, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

The approach-specific marker on the High Pass line is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

The 7,840 ft notch is the link between the two sides and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

And the same summit warning applies: the true summit is the north one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Leroy Creek crossing on a log or by rock-hopping, awkward when running high early season
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse; bergschrund at the base of the face
Cornice at the top of the face; pieces have released across parties' tracks
Frequent rockfall as the face warms; very poor rock quality across this group of peaks
Easy to descend a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line

bivy.name: Upper Ice Lake
bivy.notes: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.
bivy.water: The lake, which can still be partly frozen early in the season
bivy.permit: Also in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, with the same free self-issued permit; the standard guidance is to pitch on the pumice and keep off the meadows
bivy.capacity: Open pumice flats with room for several parties, at the south end of the lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs; a log jam may stand in for a missing log
Very long walk in on a trail through terrain burned by the 2015 Wolverine Fire
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side; crevasse crossing on the Entiat Glacier
Cornice at the top of the face; wet snow sluffing
Frequent rockfall from bordering buttresses as the face warms; variable ice conditions
Poor rock quality throughout; exposure on the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its foot rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

approach_variants.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds; helmet from the talus upward
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
Huge cliffs on the approach; the start of the gully lies about 100 ft left of them
Whiteout route-finding on the winter approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

approach_variants.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall very likely with a documented fatal history
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully; helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant
Private property on the walking approach is closed to climbers; no-parking signs on the road
Chockstone and moat problems; verglas on rock in cold shoulder seasons
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The gully is the obvious one on the south side, and the test is that it forces you out left. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

The confirmation is the chockstone, and it comes early. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' left out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

What the rock should feel like: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

And the negative test against its neighbours: the big west face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, ford Canyon Creek - there is no bridge, and it runs high and hazardous in spring and early summer, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the start
crevasses and steep neve on the Jerry Glacier both ways
loose blocks on the crest - the rock on this mountain pulls off freely
sustained exposure with rappels needed to reverse the steps
a long committing position with a multi-hour retreat to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route is the crest, and the test is that you never leave it. From camp climb to the level step on the southeast ridge at about 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That step is the start: the ridge above it is the route, and everything you climb from there should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

The negative marker is the one that matters here, because the wrong turn is the popular one. From the same shoulder the South Face route turns west and makes a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, aiming for snow patches and a boulder with slings on it under a cliff band. If you are walking sideways on scree with a wall above you and your feet in a moat, you have joined the south face and left this route behind. There is no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on the Direct.

The positive test is the shape of the ground under your hands: the crest gives continuous scrambling with occasional steps rather than a traverse across a face, and the exposure is symmetrical. When the crest throws up a step you cannot scramble, the answer is a short pitch on the crest or a brief turn on its flank, not a traverse that takes you a rope length or more away from it.

A cross-check high on the route: near 8,600 ft the South Face rejoins the crest by way of a scree band beside a snow patch. If you are already on the crest well below that and stay on it, you and a South Face party will meet there having climbed two different mountains' worth of ground.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of the basin from the meadows camp
no water above the lakes or meadows
wind-exposed camps
loose ground on the climb back to the shoulder
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both camps feed the same starting point - the level step on the southeast ridge between about 7,000 and 7,200 ft. From the lakes, cross the notch to the south and climb out of Crater Creek Basin to it; from the meadows, climb straight up to it.

Recognise the step by the ground going flat. The ridge eases into a level shoulder before rearing up again, and that flat is where the climbing starts. If the angle has not relented, you are still below it.

From there, stay on the crest. The moment the ground under you becomes a sidehill traverse on scree rather than a ridge with air on both sides, you have drifted onto the South Face's line beneath the cliff band. Turn back to the crest rather than continuing, because the two routes do not rejoin until near 8,600 ft.

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is not approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the west side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the talus, Liberty Crack is the obvious continuous vertical crack that passes to the right of the huge roof high on the wall — the roof is the Lithuanian Lip, and it is the single feature that identifies the line even in flat light. Do not scramble straight up beneath it. The standard entry traverses in from the left for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to reach the ledges directly under the true first-pitch crack; there is also a fourth-class alternative that goes up the right-hand side of the block at the base. Parties that head straight up the fall line from the talus end up on the neighbouring East Face lines rather than on Liberty Crack — the East Face here holds a whole cluster of routes within a few rope lengths of each other, so pick the line by the roof above you, not by whichever crack is nearest.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
approach_variants.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identifier is still the big roof — Liberty Crack is the continuous crack running past the right side of the Lithuanian Lip. What changes is the last few metres: a deep moat opens where the snow pulls away from the base of the wall, and getting from snow into the rock can mean a committing step across or a short stemming move down and back up out of the gap. Scout along the base rather than dropping into the first moat you meet; parties have found the moat mellowing out within about thirty feet of where they first reached it.

approach_variants.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin

bivy.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
bivy.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
bivy.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
