bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

approachLogistics.trailhead: PCT North Trailhead (Snoqualmie Pass, I-90 Exit 52)

approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
hazards: Wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun; early-season snow needs an axe, crampons if firm
Heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
No reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
Ridge unsafe when wet and unsafe without rock gear
Exposed, unprotected summit step with low-5th moves
Loose rock and scree, especially dangerous on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear right at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
hazards: Exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
Early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
Unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
Slide alder low down
Exposed, unprotected summit step with low-5th moves; ridge unsafe when wet
Loose rock and scree, especially dangerous on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Perfect Pass is the arrival, and you know it because the ground stops and the glacier starts. From the pass, getting down onto the Challenger Glacier at about 7,000-7,200 ft can involve roughly 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The exact entry point moves year to year with crevasse conditions, so do not look for a particular spot; look for the lowest place you can step from rock onto continuous ice.

Arrival at the climbing, which is not the same thing as arrival at the glacier: the technical climbing on this route is 50 ft long and it is the last 50 ft. Above the bergschrund the glacier steepens into a snow arete, then a clean 3rd-class scramble runs out at the base of a short, well-protected 5.5-5.7 pitch. That pitch is the route. If you are roping up anywhere lower than the foot of a single unbroken 50 ft wall with a rappel anchor visible at its top, you have roped up too early.

The moat is the marker you will meet first, and in fog it is the one that matters. Just below the summit rocks a moat has been reported up to about 5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to hunt a snow bridge. Reaching an uncrossable gap where the snow has pulled away from the summit rock means you are at the base, not lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing east along the crest away from the summit block puts you on the connecting ridge toward Poltergeist Pinnacle and Crooked Thumb, which is a different day entirely.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The impasse is the checkpoint, not the base, and confusing the two is the common error in cloud. It is a notch in the ridge guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 step to regain the crest beyond.

Beyond it, the test is the same as on the other approach: Perfect Pass, then step onto ice, then keep going until the walking stops at a 50 ft rock wall. Nothing on this route is technical until that wall.

A named whiteout trap on this line: on the snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, parties in fog have headed for Whatcom Peak's summit wall instead of the pass. If the ground in front of you is steepening into a wall rather than levelling into a saddle, you are aimed at the wrong feature. Perfect Pass is a saddle with running water; Whatcom's wall has neither.

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
camps: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
approach_variants.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face and one is the Royal Creek drainage
Boot path leaving the ridge trail northward leads to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake; route-finding is entirely your own
Loose, dirty Class 3 gully through the cliff band, unreliable holds in both directions
Off-trail talus and brush with slippery grass and dense alder low on the face
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: Make sure you are in the right drainage before you climb — several little bowls look like this face, and the one to your east is Royal Creek. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top. Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

approach_variants.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about five hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

approach_variants.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: About 500 ft descent from the Rock-Crescent col to Crescent Lake that must be regained on the way out
Snow persisting on the col and above ~5,000 ft on Rock Lake side into late spring
Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face
Loose, dirty Class 3 gullies through the cliff band above the lake
Off-trail talus and brush above the lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage
Long day made longer by the added distance; water unreliable above Crescent Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Crescent Lake is the common starting point, and on this side you arrive at it from above. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Nisqually Glacier crossing through heavily crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above, dangerous in poor visibility
The Fan gully carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard
Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it; centre and east of the Turtle are raked by ice and rock
Firm alpine ice in two steps in the Kautz chute, bare and hard late season; thin or rotten ice late
Crevasse navigation on the upper Nisqually and Kautz glaciers; bergschrund at the chute base
Descent by multiple rappels through the ice chute, typically two to five
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts below Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be losing height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park

bivy.name: Upper Castle
bivy.notes: Where most parties camp, at about 9,400 to 9,500 ft, and where the Comet Falls way in joins. Wind-exposed.
bivy.water: Running water close by from about mid-June; otherwise melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: Large rock rings behind old windbreaks

bivy.name: Camp Hazard
bivy.notes: On the climber's left of the Turtle Snowfield at about 10,800 ft: three large rock rings below the Kautz Ice Cliff, and the highest regular camp on the route. It shortens summit day. The original Camp Hazard, nearer 11,000 ft, sits in the fall line of ice from the cliff and is not used.

bivy.name: Rock Step bivy sites
bivy.notes: A few small sites by the notch above the Rock Step, right beside the morning rappel. Little room, and under the same ice cliff as Camp Hazard.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration

approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail near Van Trump Park
Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent; save a track
Starts about 1,700 ft lower, so a steeper carry; avoids the Nisqually crossing
Serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard; keep to climber's left on the Turtle
Firm alpine ice in two steps in the Kautz chute, bare and hard late season; bergschrund at the chute base
Crevasses on the Van Trump remnant and upper glaciers; descent by multiple rappels through the chute
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then down a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road
approach_variants.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
approach_variants.season: spring; snow cover strongly preferred
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for roughly a rope length, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
approach_variants.season: winter/spring, on skis
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.

approach_variants.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
camps: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
approach_variants.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater, easy to lose in fog
Wide Duckabush River ford above Duckabush Camp, thigh-deep and swift early season or after rain
Fallen timber and standing dead snags in the burned sections of the lower valley
Steep loose switchbacks on Big Hump, hard on tired legs
Extremely remote, rescue likely takes a day or more
approach_variants.baseFinding: The turnoff is unmarked — no sign, cairns at best — and getting it right is the whole navigation problem on this route. Above Duckabush Camp, watch for a small feeder creek coming in from climber's-left and follow it up out of the valley. It leads into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of the summit, and that amphitheater is the base: once you are standing in it the climbing is easy Class 2 heather and talus straight up to the summit ridge, so the hard part is behind you. The maintained trail runs on past the turnoff toward the pass, so if you find yourself gaining the pass or arriving at Marmot Lake you have walked past the creek and should drop back down the trail. Snow fills the amphitheater and the slopes above into summer and cornices build on the summit ridge into late June, so carry an axe and treat the crest as possibly unsupported. Water is dependable at the creek and scarce once you leave it — fill up before you start climbing.

approach_variants.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin

approachLogistics.trailhead: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)

approach_variants.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June; stay back from the eastern lip
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open basin ground that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on slopes either side of the col
Approach corridor closed since the fire, so access is not currently available
Turning the wrong way off the saddle commits you to a different peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From First Divide, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake. That lake is the marker for this whole variant — it is the only standing water in the basin and it sits directly below the two summit humps of Steel, so if you are in an open basin with no lake in it you are in the wrong one. From the lake, drop southwest to the saddle between those humps; the saddle is the base of the climb, and from it you turn north along the summit ridge for the final easy Class 2 stretch to the high point. The direction of that turn is the thing to get right. Duckabush lies beyond the same col to the southwest and reads as the higher, more striking mountain from below, so a party that turns the wrong way off the saddle ends up committed to a different peak. The early-summer cornice and unconsolidated-snow caution applies just as strongly on this side: the crest holds snow late and it is not always attached to the rock beneath it, so stay back from the eastern lip.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass; about 1.75 miles of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route starts AT the top of the notch, on the Concord (south) side — not below it. Stand on the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord col and turn to face Concord Tower: the first pitch is the crack system running up that wall to a large ledge holding a few small trees, and that ledge is the pitch-one belay and is visible from the notch. The mistake to avoid is dropping 30 feet down the Liberty Bell side to the tree with the ledge running left into a blocky chimney — that is the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, the other tower, and parties heading for opposite summits share this saddle all day. If your first pitch tops out on a treed ledge you are on Concord; if it starts by walking a small ledge leftward into a chimney you are on Liberty Bell.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through late Jun
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the start — it is still the crack system on the Concord wall rising directly from the crest of the notch to the treed ledge. What snow does is fill the notch, so the col reads as a smooth saddle and the base of the first pitch can sit above a moat. Look up at the tower on the south side of the col for the treed ledge to confirm you are on the right wall before committing.

approach_variants.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
camps: Mountaineer Creek basin (beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers)
The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or long walk-around is needed
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the complete North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to not mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

approach_variants.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass

bivy.name: Goat Pass
bivy.notes: The camp for the southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek — a longer, higher-gain walk in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop because the Cascadian Couloir descent drops back the same way. A planned camp with plenty of flat ground, though water becomes a carry once the snow patches are gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns early to mid season; Ingalls Creek is the reliable source, below the pass
bivy.capacity: Numerous good bivy sites on the pass

bivy.name: The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
bivy.notes: The classic place to split the complete ridge, reached by the snow-filled gully (usually climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) above the Stuart Glacier. This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, but only two spots are actually comfortable and a party of three or more will be spread out. Wind-scoured and fully exposed, with no water above it, so the summit day starts with everything you carried.
bivy.water: None reliable — seasonal snow patches only, and nothing at all once they melt out
bivy.capacity: Two genuinely good bivy spots, plus a number of mediocre ones nearby

approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through summer
About 2,000 ft of descent on the way in that must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass; approach consistently underestimated
Traverse under the Stuart Glacier with route-finding rather than tread
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the west, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

approach_variants.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
camps: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
Chilliwack River crossing by hand-operated cable car or a ford
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack is the riskier option
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the broad toe of the ridge, and you find it by walking south off the pass until the path dies. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is stay on the crest rather than follow any marked line.

So the fog test is a handrail test, and it is the best kind: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

Arrival at the start: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

What the upper ridge is like, because it decides whether you come back this way: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

And the other thing this ridge is: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told not to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

approach_variants.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

approach_variants.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
Whatcom Glacier loop back to the pass needs glacier travel gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive at Whatcom Pass, the base test is identical: leave the maintained trail, head directly south on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

The one thing this side changes, and it is a logistics fact rather than a navigation one: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

How you know you are at the pass and not at a camp below it: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.

approach_variants.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs about four miles and roughly two thousand one hundred feet to Lower Crater Lake; the upper lake lies off to the south-south-west and is not on the way. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route leaves the trail at the lake - there is no tread beyond it. From the lake basin the south-east ridge rises to the north-west toward a col at about 8,000 ft. The ridge is the route and the test is symmetry: once established you should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

If the ground closes in and you are climbing a confined, extremely loose chute, you have slipped off the crest onto a flanking gully. Those gullies are the other route's ground, gained from the next drainage north, and they are notably worse rock than the crest.

At the col near 8,000 ft the summit is along the crest, not directly above. A small separate peak stands west of the ridge saddle and is routinely mistaken for the top; the true high point is the eastern one and reaching it is a tedious traverse over talus and large boulders past several intervening bumps.

So the confirmation is effort, not elevation: if you arrived at a summit within a few minutes of gaining the crest and did not cross bouldery bumps to get there, you are on the wrong high point and should look east along the ridge.

approach_variants.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
approach_variants.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the lake the crest is gained by a loose gully, and the gully is unpleasant enough that its quality is the confirmation. Parties commonly exit it about half-way up onto the parallel rib, which holds more solid rock, and return to it higher; the rib is a refuge beside the gully rather than a separate line, so keep the gully in sight.

If the chute you are in is solid and enjoyable, it is probably not the one - several chutes rise out of this basin and the route's own is notorious.

At the top the saddle is on the crest, and the summit is east of it. A small peak stands just west of the saddle; a summit reached in a few minutes by turning left out of the gully is that lower point, not the top.

The true high point costs a traverse over talus and large boulders past intervening bumps. Arriving without that traverse means you are in the wrong place. Coming from this side the ridge is joined further west than the south-east ridge joins it, which is exactly why this mistake is easier to make on this approach than on the other one.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the far side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy ramp about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
approach_variants.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.

approach_variants.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The hardest thing to find on this approach is the path itself, and it is found at a firepit. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ends at a small clearing with an old firepit. The climbers' path leaves on the left near that clearing, unsigned and steep from its first step. Fix the spot in your mind on the way in - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

The second decision is a cairned fork near 5,200 ft. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; stay right and uphill on the climbers' path. If you are losing height toward water, you have taken the fisherman's trail.

Expect to lose the tread on the ridge and not to panic about it. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. When in doubt, stay on the crest.

The climb proper starts above the lake meadows. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A rock wall lines the east side of that outlet; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

Rope up before stepping onto the snow, not part-way across. If you are trying to climb a rock wall beside the outlet stream, you have missed the turn around its end.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
approach_variants.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever camp you use, the climb starts at the head of the lake's outlet stream. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A rock wall runs along the east side of it - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of that wall with a single class 3 step. Forcing the wall directly is the wrong answer and is how parties get stopped here.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

The arrival test is the notch, not the angle. You should step down into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the left, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts where the camp ends: from Perfect Pass, head north and up onto the broad south snowfield. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a conspicuous col in the summit ridge above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

So the aiming point is a notch in a skyline, and in cloud the substitute for it is this: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow runs out against rock. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

Confirm above: the final stretch along the crest is short, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

The variation that is not an error: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the northeast of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

The impasse, which is the other thing you have to find on this approach: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.

approach_variants.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
camps: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
approach_variants.notes:
An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant is defined by what it avoids, and that is the test: if you have crossed the impasse, you are not on it. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

Arrival is the same arrival: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

What you trade for it, and why the choice is a conditions call rather than a preference: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
approach_variants.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base of the actual climb when the climbers' path fades out in a large meandering gully at the bottom of a broad debris and deposition fan, with the couloir narrowing above it — roughly 4,000-4,300 ft. The path ending is the marker; there is no cairn or sign.

Above that, two features tell you the route is going right.

The Hourglass, near 5,800 ft, is a narrow rock and snow constriction and the crux of getting to the summit block: a couple of exposed 3rd-to-4th class moves in summer, or a steep 35-45 degree snow neck in spring which can be a thin snow bridge and which opens a moat at its base as it melts.

Higher, at the top of the snow, there is a notch with a large rock in it. Climb around that rock to the right to reach the scree gully beyond. The general rule reported by parties who lose the thread here is: when in doubt, go right.

Cairns exist most of the way, but several of them are misleading. Treat a cairn as a hint and the terrain as the authority. The final roughly 200 vertical feet to the true south summit is class 4 with real exposure.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow ascent
approach_variants.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
approach_variants.season: Apr-May, snow
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The deposition fan at the foot of the couloir is still the mark, but under snow the fan and the couloir merge visually. Read it by width: the base is where the open fan narrows into a defined couloir line, several hundred feet of which you then climb before exiting onto its west side and continuing up toward the spur.

The Hourglass around 5,800 ft is the feature to inspect from below. In spring it is a steep snow neck at 35-45 degrees and is sometimes a thin snow bridge — a moat at its base is the sign it is going.

The notch with the large rock at the top of the snow is still passed on the right.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
approach_variants.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The couloir is visible from the lake and that is the point of approaching from this side. From the water, look south-west at the peak: the route is the obvious north-facing snow line that splits the summit block itself. Pick it out before you start moving, because from underneath the flanking gullies all look alike.

The positive test is where the line ends. It must top out on the summit block, not on the ridge beside it. A couloir that finishes at a notch with more mountain above it and to one side is one of the flanking gullies and not the route.
