The second test is aspect. This is the north side: it should be the shaded flank, holding firmer snow than anything around it in the morning and going soft late. If the snow you are standing on is in early sun, you have come round onto an eastern or western flank.

The third test is continuity. The route is a single continuous line from the basin to the top of the block. If the snow you are following breaks into disconnected patches with rock steps between them, you are either too late in the season for it or on a different feature.

And check the mountain. There is a similarly named peak elsewhere in the range that is reached from an entirely different valley and has nothing to do with this one. The confirmation here is that the lake lies immediately north-east of your peak and the summit stands directly across it from you.

approach_variants.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
approach_variants.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The fixed point on this side is the lake, and everything above it is read off the peak itself. The lake sits immediately north-east of the summit, so from the water the mountain stands to the south-west and the route faces you.

The route is the continuous north-facing snow line cleaving the summit block. It must finish on the block. A gully that tops out on the ridge to either side of the summit is a flanking line, not the route.

Use shade as the confirmation: the north side holds shadow while the basin around it is lit, and the snow in it stays firm longest in the morning.

Because the approach from this side is unmarked, fix your line into the basin on the way in. There is no tread to follow back out, and the basin has no obvious exit when seen from above.

approach_variants.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
approach_variants.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lone Tree Pass cannot be picked out from directly beneath it, and that is the single most useful thing to know about this approach. Look at the mountain from the valley before you start — from the highway at Darrington — and fix where the pass sits relative to the shoulder, because once you are traversing inside the forest between 4,500 and 4,700 ft there is nothing to aim at. The confirmation from inside the trees is the ground itself: you are traversing, not climbing, and the correct entry is where that traversing forest opens into a broad snow couloir. A narrow gully or a steep timbered rib is not it.

For the upper half, the landmark is White Benchmark, Point 6357 — a blocky tower that works as a lighthouse for the whole rising traverse to High Pass. Keep it in view and aim at it; the broad gully up to the pass is right there. If you have run out of the rising traverse without a blocky tower above you, you are low and short of the pass.

The climbing itself starts at High Pass, where you cross onto the glacier. Snow travel of up to about thirty-five degrees leads to the summit snow ridge. The final marker is at the very top: by midsummer the bergschrund and moat below the summit rock often force a short section of fifth-class rock or a delicate roped step across a snow bridge, so the route does not simply walk out on snow.

approach_variants.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
approach_variants.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
approach_variants.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window
approach_variants.baseFinding: This variation rejoins the same upper ground, so the markers are unchanged: White Benchmark (Point 6357) for the traverse to High Pass, and High Pass itself as the step onto the glacier. The specific trap here is timing rather than terrain — if you are fighting slide alder rather than walking on snow, the line is out of condition and the standard Niederprum trail is the better choice that day.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered ten or eleven miles and about 6,000 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the west side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns or tread above Prusik Pass: serious route-finding over talus and heather
Steep talus and scree up to the Druid Plateau, loose underfoot
Snow lingering on the cross-country section into July; verglas on shaded ground
Final fifteen feet are an exposed, holdless friction slab, harder to downclimb than climb
No shelter on open high ground: sun, lightning and afternoon storms
Very long approach (30+ miles round trip, 7,300+ ft gain) so nearly everyone camps
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit block is a separate object and the plateau is not the top. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct block that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

So the test is: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the western slopes to the foot of the block.

Which side of the block, and this is the part that matters in cloud: the way up is a ramp on the block's south side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

What the right ground feels like: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

Staging check below the plateau: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their west side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail at all
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain; landmarks of the other approach do not apply
Steep gully below the plateau can hold snow into July; verglas on shaded ground
Exposed, holdless friction ramp on the summit block, harder to downclimb
No shelter on high ground: lightning and afternoon storms
Loose talus and scree on the slopes; benches can cliff out on descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge on the Druid Plateau, so the base test is identical and the arrival test is not. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are not on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

What still holds: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its western slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its south side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

The north-side-specific warning: the ground below the basin has cliff bands in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

And a route-choice note: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are two trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads north. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading west, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn left, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the left path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The handrail is elevation plus one named feature. Follow the scramble gully on the right side of the rounded spur upward until the spur runs into the summit formation at about 6,400 ft. That contact point — where broken spur ground ends against continuous rock — is where the approach stops and the climb starts.

From there the line is the obvious gully on the upper left, to the left of the South Buttress. If the buttress is on your left you have gone too far right; the buttress should be to your right as you enter the gully.

One recorded refinement inside that gully, which is around a hundred yards long: stay right at first and cross left higher up, scrambling on rock, rather than taking the centre — the middle holds the loose rock and the steeper steps.

One to two pitches of the southwest face above the gully reach the ridge crest, and most parties rope up for that even though it is graded fourth class. From the crest it is a short scramble to the top.

What is not here, and the absence is worth saying: there is no famous single wrong gully at Cathedral Rock. The published hazard is rockfall and loose rock, stated repeatedly and in plain terms. The genuinely wrong-start stories on this peak are all from the Northeast Buttress, a different route on the other side, so do not import them.

approach_variants.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
approach_variants.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pond you gain the same summit gully, but from below and on the south side rather than by traversing in from the pass. Climb to the ledge above the pond and follow it to the foot of the gully system.

The identification is unchanged: you want the gully to the left of the South Buttress, entered where the spur ground dies against the continuous summit rock near 6,400 ft. Coming from the pond you meet that rock from underneath, so the check is that the buttress stands to your right as you turn up into the gully.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
camps: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
approach_variants.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep
hazards: Spider Gap: permanent snow slope that can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season; axe and crampons
Whiteout or morning refreeze makes crampons necessary
Descending the steep first 100 ft north of the gap
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cloudy Pass is the staging point, not the base: the climbing starts where the boot path leaves the meadows and gains the southwest ridge, with the summit about 1,500 ft above the pass.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

approachLogistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)

approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative reaching Cloudy Pass from the Trinity Trailhead by way of Buck Creek Pass. One of the three ways in; it is a multi-day trip rather than a variation on the standard day.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep
hazards: Long multi-day approach over Buck Creek Pass
Ice axe and traction advised near the Lyman Glacier basin even in August
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek from Holden Village

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass

approach_variants.notes: Reaches Lower Lyman Lake and Cloudy Pass from Holden Village, which is itself reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a vehicle shuttle. The longest of the three and the one with the most fixed logistics.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep
hazards: Long approach reliant on ferry and shuttle logistics from Holden
Valley walk up Railroad Creek, then meadows to Cloudy Pass
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log; trail destroyed by an old avalanche swath near 4,500 ft
Open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Dome Glacier
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cairned cross-country traverse to the glacier is easy to lose in cloud
Cornices on the upper ridge; remote, multi-day approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with cairns and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately north of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is correct and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass

bivy.name: Dome-Dana col
bivy.notes: A high perch around 7,300 ft used by parties who want to shorten summit day or who are linking the Ptarmigan Traverse. It puts you above the traverse and its route-finding, with the upper Dome Glacier — which parties describe as mellow — immediately above. The trade is no running water and full exposure; the ridge camp lower down is the more common choice, and pushing this high is generally judged not to save enough time to be worth it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness
bivy.capacity: Small; two parties have camped there at once

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
Crevasses on the Dome Glacier and a bergschrund below the notch
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cornices on the upper ridge
Remote terrain, long evacuation if injured
Camp at the Dome-Dana col has snowmelt water only
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

approach_variants.notes:
The White Chuck River Trail was destroyed by a 2003 flood and has no road or trail access, so this approach is no longer usable; reach Kennedy Ridge from White Pass on the PCT instead. The old line ran from the White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing, which is your water, to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail on Glacier Ridge about two thirds of a mile beyond the creek. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Road access on the White Chuck side has long-running problems and the river trail is gone, so this way in is likely unusable
Unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
Loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
Very long PCT approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
camps: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
approach_variants.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Twenty-mile-plus approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Possibly unstable old rappel slings at the Rabbit Ears
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

name: Standard Route (Northeast summit via South Gully and East Ridge)

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of this climb is a fork, and the fork is marked by a rock formation called the Thumb. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to Mount Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to Inner Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

The fog test that does not need the Thumb, and it is the better one, is the shape of the gully you end up in. From the broad couloir, veer right into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled defile. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

Second test, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

What going too far looks like, and it is the recorded way this route goes wrong: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the southwest summit, which has no easy connection across to the true northeast high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

Safety note that is part of the route-finding: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Crystal Pass the base of the climb is directly below you rather than above you, which is the one real advantage of this side. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the right (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

The test is still the Thumb and the defile, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that narrows to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the right side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

The fog test for that northeast line is which side of the crest you are on. Stay on the crest's right-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

What going too far looks like: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the southwest summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the northeast top.

Honest limit: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August over a buried climbers' path
Steep, slick descent off Grand Pass in wet weather or lingering snow
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the ridge connecting the three summits
Obstruction Point Road is narrow, one-lane gravel and closes for most of the year
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Cameron Pass and the test is the direction you turn out of it: the ridge you climb rises to the east. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. Second test, and it is the one that matters most here: the ridge is a sequence of false summits. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. Third test, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. Carry a map and count your summits.

approach_variants.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

approach_variants.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with chest-high berry bushes and log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears, with several unbridged creek branches
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
No reliable water above the basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical once you are at Cameron Pass: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is west of the summit whatever the route title says. The extra test this side needs is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. What going too far looks like: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin

bivy.name: Cameron Basin

approach_variants.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Closed Dosewallips road adds a long walk or bike ride up the washed-out roadbed, many extra miles
Multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
Minimal to no cell coverage; long distance from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical at the pass: the ridge rises east out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. The test this side needs is about which valley you are in, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet; an overnight stay needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. A short way up, stay left where the Maynard Burn Way branches off; it is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp, about 4 miles in, is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The notch below the divide holds 35-40 degree snow and an axe is worth carrying outside late season
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow basalt that breaks away readily, with rockfall funnelled by the gullies above the col
A Class 4 step on poor rock over steep runout dirt that must be reversed on descent — one party graded a move on the downclimb at 5.8
A reported moat over 30 ft deep below the gully late in the season
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer, and a 35-40 degree snow slope below the Royal-Deception notch
Remote terrain — a solo traveller died in a fall near the peak's south end in July 2022
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is the lower left corner of the Mystery Glacier, and the thing that marks it is a lake you cannot mistake for anything else: a jade-green moraine-bounded lake sits at the glacier's base. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its lower left corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

The test for the glacier crossing is a diagonal: you enter at the lower left and exit at the upper right, at a col at about 6,700 ft on the peak's east side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

Second test, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach open snow about 200 ft south of the col, then climb those slopes staying south of the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

Third test, and it is the commitment point: a short class 4 step on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a notch near 7,500 ft. Trend climber's left on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

What confirms you are through: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and the rock gets markedly better than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.

approach_variants.name: Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
approach_variants.notes:
The other side, and the one that suits a party already camped at Home Lake for Fricaba or Warrior. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, Trail #833.2 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Shelter at about 6.4 miles and 4,890 ft, then the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake at roughly 9.3 miles and 5,308-5,330 ft. From camp, climbers' paths lead up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, and from there the route traverses and descends west into upper Deception Basin.

This is the same basin the Royal Basin parties drop into, reached from the opposite end. It is the approach a high-route party is already on, and one detailed account describes exiting this way over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips and Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels — a valid variant exit, distinct from reversing the ascent.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose scree traverses between Constance Pass and Deception Basin
All the summit-block hazards of the standard variant, including the reversible Class 4 step
Steep snow lingering on the Constance Pass and Deception Basin traverse into July
Long committing backcountry travel far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical once you are in Deception Basin, and the shared test is the good one: the jade-green moraine-bounded lake at the foot of the Mystery Glacier. Get on the ice at its lower left corner and cross diagonally to the col at about 6,700 ft at its upper right, on the peak's east side.

The extra test this side needs is at Constance Pass, because you arrive at Deception Basin along its length rather than dropping into its head. Leave the maintained trail at the pass and work west and down into the upper basin. Loose scree on the descent is normal here. If you are contouring without losing height you have not committed to the basin; if you are climbing again you have crossed it and are heading for the Fricaba-Hal Foss ridge instead.

Above the col the tests are the same: open snow about 200 ft south of the col, climbed staying south of the blocky rock band; then a short Class 4 step approached climber's left to a notch near 7,500 ft; then a clean Class 3 gully on markedly better rock to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
camps: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Chilliwack cable-car crossing and Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
About 1,000 ft descending traverse across snow and talus to the buttress, to be regained on the return
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; crevasse fall risk
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully; natural anchors only
False summit and exposed ridge crest: route-finding risk in fog or whiteout
Fast-moving fog and fickle weather; 2-3 days of travel each way
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is a saddle inside the buttress, at about 6,100 ft, and you get there by losing height first. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse east across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

So the test in cloud is the shape of the ground, not the view: you go down and east for a thousand feet, then up a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

What going too far looks like: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

Confirm on the climb: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed after the Luna Fire; check the park's fire-closure list for current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

approach_variants.notes: From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, about half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder lower down and farther downstream
Risk of falling into holes hidden in the brush and of separating from a partner
No trail and no cairns; disorienting on the way back down
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower; false summit and exposed ridge crest in fog
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In this drainage the navigation rule is about height, not direction, and it is the one thing that makes the day work. The creek must be forded in places, and fords get harder the lower and farther downstream you are. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

Arrival, which is unambiguous even with no visibility: above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

From there the base test is the same one the northern approach uses: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A real risk peculiar to this approach, recorded because it has happened: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

approach_variants.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir

bivy.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
bivy.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
bivy.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

approach_variants.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep, trail-less forest with two cliffbands and no marked line; the weaknesses are hard to spot from above on the way down
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir to the col: helmets and a tight party
Crevasse and moat hazard on the Hagan Glacier ice apron, even in summer; rope and crampons
Snow into midsummer and steep heather around the Hidden Lake tarn camp
Several summits on one massif: route-finding errors and wrong-col mistakes are easy
Afternoon thunderstorms
Remote, trail-less ground far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: A broad scree-and-talus couloir, topping out at a col at the southwest end of the crags. From the open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank, one broad couloir of loose scree and talus leads up to a col near the southwest end of the line of Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. That col is the base of the climbing, and the slabs above it on the south side go at Class 3 to the top. Hagan is a massif of several crags rather than a single peak, so which col you reach matters: if the notch you have gained sits in the middle of the crags with towers rising on both sides of you, it is not this one — keep working to the southwest end of the line. Note carefully where the couloir meets the heather benches before you leave them, because it is also the way down and it is far harder to identify from above.

approach_variants.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
camps: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
approach_variants.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard from lower Blum Lake to the 6,831 ft pass; the rope goes on before the traverse
The Blum climbers' path off the Baker River Trail is faint and brushy, marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif: easy to commit to the wrong gap or summit
Loose scree and talus on the south-side slabs and couloir
Afternoon thunderstorms
Remote, trail-less ground far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: The pass sits between the south and middle peaks, and it is the south peak you climb. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's north side to a notch on its upper east side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead (about 4,240 ft) at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, FR 9737. A free self-issue Alpine Lakes wilderness permit is filled out at the register.

There are two forks and they are easily run together. The first comes at roughly a quarter to half a mile, where the old mine-road grade splits: bear right onto Ingalls Way #1390. Straight on is Esmeralda Basin #1394, a different valley. The second fork is higher, around 5,600 ft and roughly a mile and a half in: right climbs to Longs Pass, which is a viewpoint and the way toward Ingalls Creek and Stuart's south side, not a way to this climb. Stay left.

From there the trail traverses steadily to Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group come into view all at once. Continue about another mile to Lake Ingalls, roughly 6,400-6,480 ft and about 4 miles from the car. This is the last water.

From the lake, work up and climber's-left on Class 2-3 slabs, talus and boulders. Stay with the cairned line. Parties who leave it for a more direct-looking line get cliffed out; one party downclimbed past a waterfall to escape.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the slabs above the lake are clear; snow lingers below the notch into early summer
hazards: Cliffing out on the slabs above and beside the lake if you leave the cairned line for a direct one
Loose talus and scree in the approach gully with parties above
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed ridge — start early
A 60 m rope does not reach on the descent rappels, roughly fifteen feet short; carry a 70 m or doubles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is visible from the lakeshore: the cleft between the North and South peaks, with a single pointed spire sitting in it. That spire is the Dogtooth. Aim just left of it and let it draw you up the slabs.

At the Dogtooth, go right for the traditional approach gully. The last gully is scree. If the gully you are in is green and lush it is the wrong one and it will carry you too high — traverse right out of it onto clean scree.

Arrival is physical: a short section of Class 4 up a crack of roughly forty feet at the top of the gully lands you on a ledge. That ledge is where the rope comes out. Pitch one is the low-angle slab above it, taking the large crack system up the middle.

Touch test at the start: the rock here is green serpentine, an odd slick band quite unlike the surrounding granite, sitting just up from the Dogtooth crag. Large hexes work in it where cams skate. Confirmation higher up — the pitch-three ledge carries two big bolts and there are three more at the top.

Negative marker, and this is the one that matters. This route climbs the south ridge of the north peak, and the North peak (7,662 ft) is the true summit. The South peak (7,640 ft) is a separate Class 3 scramble that starts from the same notch. If you reached the notch, dropped about fifty feet down its west side and scrambled easy gullies back to a top without ever roping up, you climbed the South peak. That is not this route and not the high point.

Second marker: finishing the technical pitches does not put you on the summit. There is a few hundred feet of walking left to tag the actual high point, so a summit that arrives the instant the climbing ends is the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Ingalls Pass. Just past the pass the trail splits and the right-hand branch is signed Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2. It drops into Headlight Basin, crosses Headlight Creek, and holds the established campsites and the reliable water. The main #1390 stays high along the rim of the basin and is the more direct line to the lake.

The two rejoin at a signed junction less than a quarter mile below Lake Ingalls, so this costs you a descent and a re-ascent in exchange for a legal camp and running water. Parties climbing the same day generally take the high line; parties camping take the low one.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this is the branch to take if you are sleeping out, since camping at Lake Ingalls is prohibited
hazards: Headlight Creek crossing
Braided use paths through the basin camps — stay on durable ground, this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness
Extra descent and re-ascent on the way out with a full pack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This branch does not change where the climbing starts — it rejoins the standard line at the signed junction below the lake, and from there the Dogtooth, the scree gully and the forty-foot Class 4 crack onto the belay ledge are exactly as on the high route.

What it does change is your starting view. Coming up out of Headlight Basin you meet the lake from below rather than from the pass, so you will not have had the long look across at the peak that the high traverse gives you. Walk to the lake outlet and pick out the notch and the Dogtooth spire from there before starting up the slabs, rather than trying to identify them mid-scramble.

approach_variants.name: Blanca Lake Trail to Virgin Lake, then the south-ridge climbers' path
approach_variants.notes: From the Blanca Lake trailhead at the end of the North Fork road, follow the lake trail north into the wilderness. It climbs immediately in a long series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining most of the day's easy elevation over the first three miles to a ridge crest — muddy, rooty and icy in wet or early-season conditions. From the ridge the trail runs on through meadows to Virgin Lake, the trail's high point before it drops about six hundred feet to the big lake, and a good overnight camp and the last easy reliable water before the off-trail climbing. This is where the single most common navigation error happens.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Early season adds snow on the ridge and makes the glacier variant the safer of the two.
hazards: The unsigned turnoff at Virgin Lake is the commonest error on this peak
Route-finding on the faint ridge path, which is easy to lose in brush
Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block with real exposure
Dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse late in the season
A long single push with a likely after-dark return unless camped at the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: At Virgin Lake, do not continue downhill on the main tread — that goes to the big turquoise lake below and away from the peak. Instead pick up the faint, unsigned climbers' path leaving the lake into the woods toward the ridge. It gains the peak's south ridge and follows it northeast, staying on the ridge's east side to get round minor gendarmes, levels out around fifty-three hundred feet, crosses to the west side around fifty-eight hundred, then climbs steep heather and scree working around cliff bands. The technical ground starts at a notch beside a subsidiary point, reached across a boulder field — the notch is the first place the ridge is blocked by a rock step you cannot walk around, and above it the rock turns loose and pebbly for the scramble to the summit ridge. Negative markers: if you are on obvious maintained tread descending toward a turquoise, silty lake, you took the main trail at Virgin Lake and are heading away from the peak; if you are roped up on a glacier, you are on the alternative line rather than this one.

approach_variants.name: Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake basin
approach_variants.notes: The alternative line onto the upper mountain, and several parties pair it with the ridge path — one for the way up, one for the way down. From Virgin Lake, take the main tread down into the basin, cross or skirt the lake's south shore on logs and boulders (poles help), then work up the boulder field and heather slopes above the north shore to the glacier toe. Stay on the glacier's east side; the west-side ice is noticeably steeper.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Best when the glacier is snow-covered enough to bridge but firm enough to travel; midday summer slush makes it slow and sliding.
hazards: Crevasses on the Columbia Glacier — low-angle but real, especially where snow is soft
Soft, sliding midday slush in summer
Wading or log-crossing the lake outlet stream
Loose, crumbly rock on the lateral moraine and at the glacier exit
Camping is banned within half a mile of the big lake, so plan the overnight around Virgin Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the rock is the glacier's exit, and it is a specific and short one: about fifty feet of ledgy, somewhat loose third-class ground taking you off the ice onto rock, after which you traverse right toward the peak's southwest side and join the ridge line higher up. The test is the exit itself — a short ledgy step, not a long climb; if you are looking at hundreds of feet of rock rising straight off the ice, you are at the wrong point on the glacier's edge. Once on rock, the pebbly, loose 'kitty litter' ground and two narrow catwalks leading toward the summit block confirm you are on the standard line. Negative marker: if you are still gaining height on ice with cliffs above you and the summit off to the side, you have gone too far up the glacier past the exit.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's left of the cliff bands.
