Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-early Oct
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the far end of the meadows, watch for an unsigned path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream and pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the southeast and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad north-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's left (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head south toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad north-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the left (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a north-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
camps: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
approach_variants.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
Bergschrund at the head of the Eel, hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly rock on the final class 3 summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus about 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
Long committing approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is Flypaper Pass, and the test is which things are on which side of it. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between Mount Anderson on the east and Echo Rock (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

The approach test, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse above the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

Second test, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older published figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — those descriptions are old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

What going too far looks like: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.

approach_variants.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west

bivy.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is the last water on the route: the snow finger to Flypaper Pass and everything on the Eel above it has none, so fill here or plan to melt. Exposed to wind, with no built shelter.
bivy.water: the tarn when melted out; often still frozen in spring, so melt snow
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
bivy.capacity: a few tents on open ground near the tarn

approach_variants.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a trail the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
hazards: Long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
40-45 degree firm or icy snow finger at Flypaper Pass
Crevasses on the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund at its head, hardest late season
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly rock on the final summit scramble
Arriving at Anderson Pass from the west: shelter and climbers' path lie behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage on either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical to the Dosewallips variant above, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when Mount Anderson is on one side of the notch and Echo Rock on the other.

The extra test this side needs is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves north off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
approach_variants.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 16 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: Thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col; conditions change between seasons
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk and refreezing snow on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz bushwhacking above the col
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on the open ridge, saddle and col
Extreme remoteness: an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or helicopter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you south — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

The confirming test is a number and a duration: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

Second test, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you drop down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the Christie Glacier. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a moat forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

What waits at the col, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

approach_variants.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Closed road adds 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike to reach Whiskey Bend
Long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical to the Quinault variant once you are at Low Divide, and that shared test is a good one: from lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft; then down loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

The extra test this side needs is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route leaves maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: Southeast-facing snow chute is an avalanche funnel, sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
Very popular trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on the route; carry all you need
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision point on this mountain is a signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, and a sign is the best fog marker there is because it does not depend on visibility beyond arm's length. At that junction the winter climbing route breaks right, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the left one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

Second test, higher: the summer trail threads a narrow notch and then crosses west-facing slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

Honest limit, and it is seasonal rather than navigational: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: The 3,900 ft merge with the upper trail is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
Southeast-facing snow chute above timberline is an avalanche funnel, prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
No water on the upper route
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first test is the merge at about 3,900 ft, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take downhill to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

The decision point is the same signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the winter climbing route breaks right up the chute, the summer trail switchbacks left. Take the left.

And the same confirmations above it: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and the right-hand branch out of it. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

The confirming test is that the ground stops switchbacking. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

The test for whether you should be there at all, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
approach_variants.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant ends at camp, not at climbing. The confirmation you are at Glacier Meadows rather than somewhere short of it is the washout ladder and fixed rope just below it — if you have not climbed a ladder, you are still below.

From the meadows a way trail runs about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine, a narrow exposed catwalk with loose rock underfoot, then follows the crest roughly another 0.2 mile before dropping onto the toe of the Blue Glacier. The drop onto the ice is where you rope up; nothing before it is glacier travel.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-mid Aug for straightforward glacier travel
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because the true summit is not visible from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is east of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the left, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

name: Standard Scramble (Putvin Trail / Lake of the Angels approach)

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.notes: This is the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stand at Lake of the Angels and the cirque itself tells you which way to go: Mount Stone is on your right, another peak is on your left, and Mount Skokomish is straight ahead. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

The turn is around the right-hand side of the lake, on a way trail heading west to the ridge. Then take a broad gully southwest and up toward the saddle just north of point 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud.

Second test, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours south and southwest across scree, grass and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn. The tarn is the confirmation. Turn right and start climbing when you are above the large tarn — that is the trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

Third test, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around left to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has three summit horns and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

A directional warning: contouring too far right (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut west over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: This is not the standard approach, but it is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — near the area burned by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base on this side is the open basin and saddle beneath the south peak at about 5,500 ft, and the test for it is underfoot: the footing turns to loose, rotten rock from there up. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. The test for the approach itself is the root ladder, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then descends off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. The limit of this approach: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. The standard route is on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

name: South Route via Lake of the Angels

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
camps: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, slick when wet and worse descending
Rock headwall mid-trail needing hand-over-hand moves, sometimes a fixed handline
Little to no reliable water on the lower trail
Snow lingering on shaded steps and in the basin above the lake into summer
Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels; fog common and parties lose the route
Loose rock on the summit block with rockfall onto parties below
Ambiguous Class 3/4 crux and exposed unprotected summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is a notch in Mount Stone's west ridge, and the test for it is a turn you make before a gate. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward St. Peter's Gate — the obvious notch above the basin. Just before the gate, turn sharply left and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. Second test, at the notch: turn right and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short low class 3 chimney to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. Third test, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. What the route's own timing says: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. Fog warning specific to this mountain: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lena Lake Trailhead (Hamma Hamma Road, FR-25)

approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Long off-trail route over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes near St. Peter's Gate
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
Fog on the upper mountain; parties have lost the route
Very long approach with limited bail options
Loose rock on the summit block and an ambiguous Class 3/4 crux
Exposed unprotected summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from the east you arrive at St. Peter's Gate itself, which is the high point of the traverse at about 5,950 ft and an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. From the gate there are two ways onto the peak and they are different climbs. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go through the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the west ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. So the fog test for this variant is which side of the gate you end up on: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. Above the notch the tests are identical to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 chimney to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a groove on the left that bends right to the true south summit.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Multi-day approach by boat and abandoned, brushy trail; steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Several unmarked routes on a 1,400 ft wall; identification is by position under the summit only
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall, worst once sun hits the face
Dirt- and moss-filled cracks mid-route and teetering blocks near the top
No cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

approach_variants.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September
hazards: The described line crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides, one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face; loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Retreat from anywhere on the trip is measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

From that view, drop a plumb line from the summit. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the rockfall line rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

Negative marker: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass
approach_variants.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: About 27 miles of high walking on the crest to Castle Pass before any off-trail travel
Harts Pass road usually opens only in July
Cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side, then the glacier at the wall's foot
Rockfall on the lower wall and loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Awkward bergschrund or moat; no cell coverage and a multi-day retreat

approach_variants.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
approach_variants.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail; the path is often lost
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 4,440 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: South Fork Slate Creek road end (over Harts Pass)

approach_variants.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

approach_variants.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
approach_variants.notes: Up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips.
hazards: Long approach up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side
Slide alder and downed timber on the unmaintained Mill Creek approach
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Full lightning exposure; very remote with a long, difficult evacuation

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
camps: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir; a fatal accident on record
Loose Class 3-4 rock in the gully, with parties above and below
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse and buried creek channels
Couloir can be melted out to rock in late season
Short glacier crossing on the Taboo Glacier, firm snow or ice early season
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

approach_variants.name: Torment Basin climbers' path

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely contested — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade River Road at the river bridge, about a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead

approach_variants.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
approach_variants.season: midsummer once brush is passable
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach, so less current information on conditions
Loose crumbly rock on the climb and rockfall onto parties below
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
Biting insects on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

name: Raven Ridge Standard Route (Libby Lake Gully-Ridge)

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The gully above the lake is the route and it is the worst ground of the day - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the rib that parallels it, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

If the ground you are climbing is pleasant, you are not in the right gully. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

The critical negative marker is on the ridge, not on the approach: a small peak stands just west of the saddle, and it is not the summit. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble eastward along the ridge. If you topped out of the gully and went left to a summit within a few minutes, you are on the lower point west of the saddle.

The positive test at the top is the walk. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.

approach_variants.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
approach_variants.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is where the maintained trail ends at the lake and the ridge above it begins. The south-east ridge rises from the lake basin toward a col at about 8,000 ft - the ridge is the handrail and it should have ground falling away on both sides once you are established on it.

If you find yourself in a confined, very loose chute, you have dropped off the crest into one of the gullies on its flank. That is the other route's ground, approached from the other drainage, and it is not where this line goes.

At the col, the summit is the high point along the crest and it is not the first bump. The ridge here carries several intervening high points, and a small peak stands west of the ridge saddle that is regularly mistaken for the top. The true summit is the eastern high point; if you have gone west from a saddle and arrived quickly, you are on the wrong one.

The practical cross-check is talus. Reaching the true summit involves a tedious out-and-back over talus and large boulders rather than a quick step up from wherever you gained the crest.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route is entered at a col, and there are two cols in a row - getting the order right is the navigation. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the first glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow. Cross over the first col, then descend the second, larger glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right - eastward - across it. The col you want is at about 7,640 ft and it sits between this peak and its larger neighbour to the west. A bergschrund guards it and can be hard to cross late in the season, sometimes needing a short rappel to get down onto or across it. The schrund is the confirmation as much as the obstacle: a col reached without one is likely the first col, not the second. The positive test at the col is where you go next: contour on an easy snowfield round to the peak's south side and climb a loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge. If you are still on the north or shaded side of the crest with the face above you, you have not contoured far enough round. The most important negative marker is about which mountain you are on. The summit lies just under a mile east of its better-known neighbour along the connecting ridge. If you have topped out on the summit block immediately above the first col you crossed, you are on the neighbour, not on this peak. Keep going east. There is also a direct alternative from the col: an exposed class 3+ ridge taken straight from the saddle instead of the gully. Both finish on the same crest; the gully is the standard and the loose rock in it is the main hazard on the climb.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
approach_variants.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Either camp feeds the same line: traverse the upper basins near 7,000 ft to gain the first glacier, cross its col, descend the second glacier to about 7,200 ft, and traverse east to the 7,640 ft col between this peak and its neighbour.

Count the cols. The first is crossed and the second is the destination, with a bergschrund on it. Standing at a col with a large icefield behind you and the summit block immediately above is the first col and the neighbouring peak, not this one.

From the correct col, contour round on easy snow to the peak's south side and find the loose gully. A route that climbs directly out of the col on exposed class 3+ crest is the direct variant rather than the standard, so choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

If you camped at the lake, budget the extra height gain into the morning; if you camped on the ridge, budget the wind into the night.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other.
