The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
approach_variants.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through Jun
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe easier to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col between the two Mox summits is the whole navigation, and the trap is that there are two summits. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

At the col, check which tower you are under. This route is on the eastern summit, which is the harder and higher of the pair. If the peak above you is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, you are facing the western summit and have turned the wrong way out of the saddle.

The sequence above the col is a ladder of specific shapes, in order, and it is how you know you are right: a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief descent to a small flat area. The flat spot after a downclimb is the confirmation - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

From that flat area, locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. If you are uncoiling a rope at the col itself, you are hundreds of feet too low.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From either camp the route meets at the same place: the saddle between the two Mox summits, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

The high camp's own marker is that it sits on rock outcrops at the glacier's edge at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

At the saddle, the summit you want is the eastern one - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

The confirmation sequence is the same ladder: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short downclimb to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: In the basin, The Scoop starts to the right of the West Face and the Tempest and to the left of Rikki Tikki Tavi. The confirmation is not at the ground but three pitches up: the first three pitches, to about 5.10a, lead to launch ledge, the platform sitting directly below the namesake Scoop corner. If the ledge you reach after three pitches has no large corner system rising above it, you are not on The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble to the wall.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cairns mark the base of the correct gully and stop there. Leftmost is the test. From the basin, The Scoop is right of the West Face and Tempest and left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; Launch Ledge, three pitches up with the Scoop corner above it, is what confirms the line.

approach_variants.name: Road walk from the pullout to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes: From Randle, head south and follow the main forest road roughly nineteen miles, then turn off at the signed meadows turning and follow the next road under three miles before turning again onto the last one. That final road is rough and wants high clearance; follow it about two miles until the rock appears, then carry on to the large pullout where the climbers' trail is obvious. From the pullout, simply walk up the road toward the wall and onto its base. There is no cell service on the approach or at the crag.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia studded with cobbles and knobs that can pop loose without warning
Rough gravel approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service on the approach or at the crag
The formation's base wraps a long way; the toe is a specific point, not a general area
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go to the lowest toe of the West Face — the point where the wall's base comes down closest to the road, rather than anywhere along its higher flanks. The start is a short prow, and the test is bolts you can count: two of them, low, on the prow, within reach from the ground. Confirm from the pitches above — the first climbs a short face onto clean ramps to a ledge belay, and the second traverses across a saddle to a chain anchor, which is a distinctive shape for a second pitch and not something a neighbouring line does. Negative marker: if you are under a long face with no bolts within reach of the ground and the only protection on offer is slinging the embedded cobbles and knobs, you are on one of the older knob-slinging lines rather than this bolted one.

approach_variants.name: Around the East Face and through the Gap
approach_variants.notes: The other way onto this side of the formation, and the one to use if you are coming from routes on the far side. From the same pullout, take the climbers' trail around the east face of the rock — this trail traverses the whole formation — and pass through the deep gully that splits it, then drop down to the left onto the West Face's base. It is longer than walking up the road but it links the two sides without returning to the car.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia with loose cobbles and knobs
The traverse round the formation is on climbers' trail with loose ground below the walls
Rough approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service anywhere on the approach or at the crag
approach_variants.baseFinding: Having dropped down and left out of the walk-through gully, keep descending along the base until you reach the lowest toe of the West Face — the far low point of the wall, not the first rock you meet after the gap. The start is a short prow carrying two bolts within reach of the ground. Confirm above: a short face to clean ramps and a ledge belay, then a traverse across a saddle to a chain anchor. Negative markers: if the deep walk-through gully is still behind and above you and you have not dropped down and left, you are on the flank rather than at the foot of the face; if you are looking at a long unbolted face where knobs are the only protection, you are on an older line.

approach_variants.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
approach_variants.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur. A longer alternative reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail, used mainly for through-hikes or when this side is inaccessible.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
hazards: The turn off the highway is on a blind curve with fast traffic
The ridge trail narrows to a knife edge with steep rock-filled gullies dropping away on both sides
The crest is exposed to weather with no shelter along it
The lower trail climbs steeply through burn with little shade or water
approach_variants.baseFinding: A '9' nailed to a tree is the marker, and the knife edge is the confirmation. Walking west along Nason Ridge Trail #1583, the crest pinches down to a ten-foot-wide knife edge with steep, rock-filled gullies falling away to the highway on the south and into the river drainage on the north — that narrowing is Ninemile Saddle, and a sign carrying the numeral 9 is fixed to a tree there. It is the only labelled feature on this stretch of ridge. A few hundred yards past the saddle the trail forks: the Nason Ridge trail drops left toward Merritt Lake, and the lookout trail stays right and climbs the last traverse to the staffed lookout on the summit. The negative marker is simple: if you are losing height off the crest toward Merritt Lake and no building has come into view, you took the left fork and should go back to the junction just past the narrow section with the numbered tree.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek over Andrews Pass
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
approach_variants.notes: Hike the Andrews Creek trail up the valley and over Andrews Pass to Upper Cathedral Lake, then scramble up to Cathedral Pass and along to the base of the north ridge. It is the shorter of the two ways in and the usual one for a climbing trip.
hazards: Loose rock along the ridge
Exposure on the steeper steps
Afternoon thunderstorms typical in summer
Long backpack over Andrews Pass to Upper Cathedral Lake, far from help
Route-finding along the ridge from Cathedral Pass to the base

approach_variants.name: Chewuch River trail from Thirtymile

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

approach_variants.notes: Start at the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road and follow the Chewuch River trail up the valley, then climb to Cathedral Pass. It is longer than the Andrews Creek line but on a steady, well-used trail, and many parties walk in one way and out the other.
hazards: Loose rock along the ridge
Exposure on the steeper steps
Afternoon thunderstorms typical in summer
Longer walk-in up the Chewuch River trail before the climb to Cathedral Pass
Route-finding along the ridge from Cathedral Pass to the base

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake and the west-side boot path
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
approach_variants.notes: The whole peak is a backpack with a short walk-up bolted onto the end of it. Nearly every party camps at or near Upper Cathedral Lake, around 7,380 ft, and climbs from there. The lake is reached most directly from the Andrews Creek Trailhead at the end of the pavement on Forest Road 51, going in over Andrews Pass and along the Boundary Trail; the Chewuch River option out of Thirtymile is considerably longer and joins the same ground near Cathedral Pass. Once at the lake nothing about the climb is committing: it is grass, scree and boulder from the trail to the top, with the occasional short step where hands come out. Most parties tag Cathedral Peak the same day, and the two are linked by a connecting gully rather than a return to the lake between them.
approach_variants.season: Early July to late September
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes and summit plateau
Snow lingering in the access gullies and upper basin into July
High, cold creek crossings on the approach during runoff
Open, treeless plateau with no shelter from afternoon storms
Long day's walk or more from the nearest road
approach_variants.baseFinding: From Upper Cathedral Lake the trail runs southeast and rounds the low toe of Amphitheater's west ridge. Roughly half a mile along, at about 7,200 ft, a beaten boot path breaks off uphill and climbs grass and scree to the northeast. That boot path is the start of the climb, and it is the only prepared thing you will see between the lake and the top. If the trail is still contouring level, you have not reached it; if the trail begins to lose elevation steadily and the ridge above you falls back behind your shoulder, you have walked past it. The path leads into an open bowl at about 8,000 ft rimmed with broken rock, the amphitheater the mountain is named for, and once you are standing in that bowl you are on the route. Two things fool parties here. In early season a steep snow gully rises straight out of the lake basin toward the ridge crest, and it does work, but it is a harder and icier start than the boot path and it is not the standard line. And the summit mass is shaped like a T with several plateau rises on it, so the first high point you reach after leaving the bowl is often not the highest. Keep walking the plateau until the ground stops rising. The check on the other side is the rock: the dramatic spires standing north of the lake belong to Cathedral Peak, and if you are climbing toward them you are on the wrong mountain.

approach_variants.name: Chewuch River trail from Thirtymile

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
bivy.notes: This sits a short way off the main line to Cathedral Pass and works well as a base if Remmel Mountain is on the list alongside Cathedral and Amphitheater. The meadow ground is soft and easily damaged, so pull back onto the timber edge rather than pitching in the open grass. There is a signed spur from near the guard station running up toward the Cathedral basin, which makes this a workable alternative if the lakes above are full or posted closed. Being lower and more sheltered, it is a considerably kinder camp in bad weather than anything at the pass.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake plus the creeks draining the meadows. Along with Upper Cathedral, the other place on the approach where you can count on filling.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit, no quota. The cabin at Spanish Camp is a Forest Service administrative structure, not a public shelter, and should not be treated as available lodging.
bivy.capacity: Broad grassy meadows with room for multiple parties, but the sites are dispersed rather than developed and horse parties use this area heavily

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

bivy.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
bivy.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of Chewuch road, FR 51)

approach_variants.notes: Start at the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road and follow the Chewuch River trail up the valley past the Tungsten Creek junction, then climb to Cathedral Pass and drop to Upper Cathedral Lake. It is longer than the Andrews Creek line but on a steady, well-used trail, and many parties walk in one way and out the other as a loop.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes and summit plateau
Snow lingering in the access gullies and upper basin into July
Stream crossings can be hazardous in high early-season runoff
Open, treeless plateau with no shelter from afternoon storms
Considerably longer walk-in from Thirtymile, far from the road

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: Everything turns on one feature and it is misdescribed by its own name. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it feels more like a sloping ledge than a gully. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting down to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

The bench is where you rope up. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You cannot see the Walrus Glacier until you are committed to it. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the left, southern margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

Negative marker, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the south basin route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

approach_variants.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
hazards: Mowich Lake road has no public access since April 2025; this start is unavailable
Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp; site camp outside the serac fall line
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier; verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Crevasse fall crossing the Mowich or Winthrop glaciers; avalanche-prone approach slopes on the Mowich/Carbon side
Committing, remote position with a carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop
approach_variants.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
approach_variants.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers; crossing the Carbon
Long committing traverse with no quick exit; much longer approach
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Bergschrund and upper mixed ground; verglassed rock and water ice late season
Carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop through large crevasses
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: Boat crossing of Ross Lake needed; a long multi-day approach with a retreat measured in days
Abandoned, brushy Freezeout Creek trail; tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft
Steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the walk
Awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

approach_variants.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed
Very remote, multi-day approach with no quick rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Wildfires close this road and parts of the northern wilderness in some summers, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: Very long high walk of about 27 miles, a 3-5 day trip with no shortcut
Harts Pass road is single lane, steep and exposed; usually opens only in July; wildfire can close it
Snow lingering on north-facing traverses into August; sparse water along the crest
Wind and cold on the open crest, far from the car if weather turns
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face; descent by the east ridge and snow finger

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
approach_variants.hours: Half a day from Boston Basin camp
approach_variants.notes:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; July and August are the most settled, and snow can linger around camp into July
hazards: Rockfall off the ridge and the tower is the primary hazard
Weather that builds fast, with afternoon thunderstorms usual
A very small, exposed tower top that many parties choose not to stand on
Approach terrain shared with Forbidden's West Ridge descent, so parties may be above you in the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The formation is the easy part: the aiguille is conspicuous on entering Boston Basin and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

The base is the notch to the right of the north ridge — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

Count the pitches, because the count is the route: three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling to the base of a tower, and then one 40-ft pitch to its top. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

The most important thing to know about the top is that it is not the top. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

Tell it from the south ridge by which side you walked round. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass to Cache Col
approach_variants.notes: Drive Cascade River Road out of Marblemount to its end and take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail up its open switchbacks to the pass. That trail is the last graded tread on the whole traverse and the pass is the last easy water; everything south of it is unmarked cross-country travel over glaciers and talus. Most parties set a car shuttle to the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle side, or reverse the trip out over the pass when the southern road is washed out.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September, once the Cache Glacier snow has consolidated and the cornice on the far lip of Cache Col has dropped
hazards: The north lip of Cache Col is commonly corniced into mid-summer and is a hazard on the way out as much as the way in
Permanent, steep snow on the Cache Glacier — axe and crampons rather than optional
No tread, no markers and no signage anywhere past the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cascade Pass itself is the reference, and the test is which way you leave it. The maintained trail arrives at a broad saddle and then continues east, dropping in switchbacks toward Pelton Basin and the Stehekin side; if you are losing height on good graded tread with a valley opening ahead of you, you have walked past the start of the traverse. The traverse leaves the pass on the opposite bearing: turn south, step off the tread onto heather and talus, and aim for the obvious apron of permanent snow hanging under the ridge above you. That snow is the Cache Glacier and the notch at its head is Cache Col. The proof is underfoot within a few minutes — no cut trail at all, only boot-scuffed talus and occasional cairns — and overhead, with the snow directly above you rather than across a valley. If you are still walking on benched trail ten minutes after the pass, you are on the wrong side of it.

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike and Fourth Creek Pass to an Ingalls Creek camp, then straight up the south side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Beverly Turnpike trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 off the North Fork Teanaway Road, at about 0.5 mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391. Taking the Bean Creek fork here is a commonly reported mistake, so read the sign.

At about 2.8 miles, at a faint fork in a grove of trees, turn right onto Trail #1218, the Fourth Creek Trail; about 0.3 mile later you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to roughly 6 miles and 4,200 ft, ford Ingalls Creek, and camp at the Fourth Creek confluence. Day one is about 6 miles and 2,000 ft.

From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile, then cut sharply left and north and climb straight upslope. Expect roughly 300 vertical feet of tangled forest and then close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above that — progress can drop to a few hundred feet an hour.

At about 5,200 ft the brush relents. Climb the left side of a large drainage gully to about 6,600 ft, then the gully itself.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The brush is the reason: it is impassably wet in early season and the gully may hold snow in the shoulders
hazards: Close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above 300 ft of jackstraw forest — the defining feature of the day
An Ingalls Creek ford that can be cold and swift early, and ice-covered in the shoulders
Loose blocks low on the route
Possible snow in the gully in the shoulder seasons — carry axe and crampons if in doubt
The descent rappels a chockstone gully where ropes are reported to hang up on the chockstone
A heavily worn sling anchor above that chockstone: inspect and back it up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two tests, one at the gully fork and one at the wall, and you need both.

First, the fork at about 7,100 ft. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the left branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

Second, the wall itself, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are two short left-facing corners side by side. The route starts in the rightmost and larger of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

What the climbing should feel like, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is not evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A separate feature worth not confusing with the start: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and the approach description on this route describes it as though it were the route. It is not the base of the 5.6 face climb, and a party navigating to it will end up on the scramble.

approach_variants.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

The off-trail departure is not well defined; plan it from current maps and imagery before you go.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The lake is the anchor and the route is read from it. The lake sits immediately north-east of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

Leave the lake basin and gain the broad basin and slopes on the peak's south side, aiming for the low point on the summit ridge rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

The ground confirms itself as you gain height: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. Note your ascent line, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

The finish is the test that you chose the right side. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short exposed class 3 scramble. If the ground above you is a steep continuous snow line splitting the summit block, you have come round onto the north side and are under the couloir route, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
approach_variants.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pass the travel is east and downhill to the lake, so the arrival marker is water at about 4,170 ft with the peak standing to the south-west of it.

From the lake, the south slopes are gained by going round the peak, not up the side facing you. The face you can see from the lake is the northern one. The route is on the opposite flank - the broad basin and slopes above the lake basin on the south side, taken toward the low point on the summit ridge.

The negative marker is the snow line. If you are looking up at a continuous couloir splitting the summit block and are tempted by it, that is the north couloir route and not this one. It is a snow climb with a different season and different equipment.

The positive markers on the route are underfoot: loose talus and heather benches on a steep grade, with no cairns, followed by an exposed class 3 scramble off the ridge to the top. Note your ascent line for the descent, because nothing here is marked.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is the same day out as the Southwest Ridge route on this peak and the two describe substantially the same ground. From the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,600 ft, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col. Tepeh Towers are passed along this same traverse. From the col, follow the ridge line along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where the standard sequence is a rappel of about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier, then a traverse high and left across it toward Austera. This is meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado, and it is worth saying plainly: this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak, despite the catalog filing several of these objectives out of the same area. Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête, not a free-standing summit, and it is the most accessible top in that group — which is exactly why parties end up on the wrong one.
approach_variants.season: Aug is the usual window; the timing is set by the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers being safely negotiable rather than by the rock
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glacier traverses
A moat at the rappel point that has to work in both directions
Loose rock on the final summit tower
Rime or verglas on the final chimney even in summer
Exposed climbing on the closing pitches above a remote glacier, with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft that you rappel into, not walk through. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

Get there by counting, not by sighting Austera. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your left through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the second break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

Above the glacier traverse the climbing is short and countable: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a sub-summit, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the right on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

The false summit is the real hazard on this peak, and it is the test that matters. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. The true summit is reached only after crossing a narrow, often snowy ridge between two blocks and climbing a short chimney or a few feet of low fifth beyond it. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The moat beside the rappel point is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

approach_variants.name: Azurite Pass, the 7,400 ft shoulder and the west-face traverse
camps: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
approach_variants.notes: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully; stay out of each other's fall line
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Two or three short snow runnels to cross on the west-face traverse
Many similar ribs and gullies; turning up too late puts you on the southwest face
Exposed class 3 on the traverse and summit gully
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Turn up too late and you meet the southwest face — that is the error to watch for. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the last gully to the south and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.

approach_variants.name: Harts Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail south

bivy.name: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
bivy.notes: This is the natural first night on the eastern approach to Azurite Pass and it breaks a walk that is otherwise too long to enjoy. From the trailhead near two thousand seven hundred feet the trail follows the West Fork Methow past Trout Creek and Brush Creek toward Jet Creek, and the camp sits partway along at about four thousand three hundred and fifty feet. Two warnings are worth taking seriously. The lower trail is overgrown and faint in places, though the tread improves as it climbs. And the brush on the banks of Jet Creek becomes extremely dense with no clear path through it at all, which is the section that costs parties hours and tempers. From here it is a sustained climb of well over two thousand feet to Azurite Pass and the peaks beyond, so leave early. Anyone weighing the two approaches should know they are about the same length and about equally neglected — pick by which side of the mountains you are driving from, not by hoping one has a better trail.
bivy.water: Creek water close at hand, reliable through the season. This is the last comfortable water before the long climb to the pass, so fill completely here.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed national forest camping — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the West Fork Methow trailhead. Fires only in an existing ring and only outside a burn ban, which by August usually means not at all.
bivy.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.

bivy.name: Azurite Pass
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

bivy.name: River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
bivy.notes: These are the staging camps for the eastern approach and the comfortable answer to the night before. From Winthrop the drive runs west on SR 20 and then up the Lost River Road through Mazama to the end of the pavement, continuing a mile and a half or so on the gravel of the Harts Pass road. The West Fork Methow trailhead sits close by at around two thousand seven hundred feet, at a wooden fence just off a short spur. Being low and in timber, they are usable well before and after the high country is in condition, and they are far enough down the road that none of the Harts Pass driving difficulties apply. They also make a sensible base for a party that wants a look at the trail before committing to it, which on this side is worth doing — the West Fork Methow tread is badly overgrown and in poor repair, and the brush on the banks of the upper creeks is dense enough that the trail effectively disappears.
bivy.water: The river is right there. Treat these as basic sites and assume you will filter rather than find a working spigot.
bivy.permit: No permit and no reservation, just a nightly fee paid on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a campsite, only to park at a trailhead. These are outside any wilderness, so none of the Pasayten self-issue paperwork applies.
bivy.capacity: Two small forested Forest Service campgrounds a short distance apart along the West Fork Methow, roughly eight to nine miles up the road from Mazama. Both are first come, first served only — there is no way to reserve and you must arrive in person to claim and pay for a site. Each is modest, so a summer weekend is a gamble.

approach_variants.notes: Start high at Harts Pass and follow the Pacific Crest Trail south to Horse Heaven Camp, where the old Mill Creek trail climbs to Azurite Pass. It avoids the lower West Fork Methow trail, which has been brushy and slow past its first few miles.
hazards: Long approach on the Pacific Crest Trail with a sustained climb to Azurite Pass
Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Exposed class 3 on the west-face traverse and summit gully
Route-finding among ribs and gullies on the upper slopes
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek and Mill Creek from SR-20

bivy.name: Azurite Pass
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

approach_variants.notes: From the Canyon Creek trailhead on SR-20, follow Canyon Creek to the Mill Creek trail and up past the old Azurite Mine to the west slopes of the peak or on to Azurite Pass. The Mill Creek trail is badly overgrown in places and route-finding through alder is slow, so most parties prefer the east-side starts.
hazards: Mill Creek trail badly overgrown, with slow alder route-finding
Long approach; Azurite Pass under snow into July in a normal year
Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Exposed class 3 on the west-face traverse and summit gully
Afternoon thunderstorms; no shelter near the pass
