approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek fisherman's trail to the foot of the slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, hike the Waptus River Trail about nine miles to Waptus Lake. The hiker bridge over Spinola Creek near the lake has washed out, so cross at the nearby horse ford, reached from the Waptus Pass Trail. Where the trail joins the PCT, head southbound (west).

Shortly before the PCT crosses the Waptus River, leave the trail and head northwest toward a faint shoulder and bench through flat, easy forest. Pick up a fisherman's trail on the southwest side of that bench and follow it toward Shovel Creek, then up and over the bench past an informal campsite with a giant cairn, where it starts to climb the shoulder on the east side of Shovel Creek.

Before long the trail leaves the forest straight onto talus. Easy talus walking brings you to Shovel Creek; cross where convenient.

Roughly 13 miles to the base, five to six hours. Most parties camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge.
approach_variants.season: July to September; documented ascents cluster in August
hazards: About 2,000 ft of unprotected friction slab, mostly climbed unroped
Rock quality deteriorating markedly on the final three summit-block pitches
No water on the slab — carry the whole climbing day's supply
A long, remote approach with no confirmed cell coverage
The Shovel Lake descent alternative involves loose dirt high, brush and cliff bands low, and heavy route-finding
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Crossing Shovel Creek off the talus puts you at the foot of the Mega Slab — that is the arrival, and it is a creek crossing rather than a judgement. The slab drops from the peak's southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft all the way to Shovel Creek at about 3,700 ft, so there is no ambiguity about which piece of rock it is: it is the enormous unbroken sheet above you, one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in North America.

Which line on the slab is the real question here, and for this route the answer is a single word: lowest. Infinite Beauty begins at the lowest part of the slab, on a shallow rib. Walk the base downhill until it stops going down, and start on the rib there.

How that distinguishes it from its neighbour: Timeless Treasure climbs the middle of the slab. So if you have walked out along the base looking for a nicer-looking start, you are on Timeless Treasure. The lowest point is the whole distinction and it is decidable by walking downhill rather than by looking.

What the rock should feel like, as confirmation: clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone with minimal breaks, and roughly 2,000 ft of sustained fourth class. Approach shoes or trail runners friction well on it and most of the slab is climbed unroped. If you are pulling into cracks or dodging vegetation, you are off the clean sheet.

And where the route ends its own identity: after about 2,000 ft the line naturally angles right and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-fifth moves up overlaps trending up and right to the southeast shoulder. Easy scrambling then leads to the summit block, where the rock quality noticeably deteriorates over the final three pitches.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek track to the middle of the slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and the PCT about nine miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly eleven to twelve flat miles in all. The hiker bridge where the Waptus River Trail crosses the river below Waptus Lake is gone, so cross at the horse ford a quarter mile upstream.

From camp, an old, faint, unmaintained track parallels Shovel Creek through forest to a bench around 3,400 ft, then talus-hops to the base of the Mega Slab at roughly 3,700 ft.

About 19.3 km one way and 4,697 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: A long, remote approach with no confirmed reliable cell coverage
Loose rock and heavy route-finding on the Shovel Lake descent
No water on the slab itself
Deteriorating rock on the shared summit-block pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same slab, different place on it: this route takes the middle. Once you have crossed Shovel Creek off the talus and are standing under the Mega Slab, walk along the base to its middle and start there. The slab runs from about 3,700 ft at the creek to the southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft, so the middle is a real and findable place along a very long base.

The discriminator against its neighbour is a single step: Infinite Beauty starts at the lowest point of the slab, on a shallow rib. If you are at the bottom end of the base, you are on Infinite Beauty. Walk up along the base until you are in the middle of the sheet.

What the rock should feel like: perfect stone, mostly fourth class with occasional low-fifth moves higher up. If it is broken or vegetated you have drifted off the clean centre of the slab.

Where the two routes merge, and why that matters to the finding: both finish on the same three-pitch 5.6+ summit block. So being on the correct route matters for the first 2,000 ft and stops mattering above the shoulder. If you are already on the summit block and unsure which line you climbed, the question no longer has a practical answer.

A practical note that is part of the finding here: most parties either reverse the slab, which is easy and secure, or descend toward Shovel Lake. Reversing is the recommended option precisely because you already know that ground.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, staying west of the creek longer than the West Face line, then over the Half Moon col into the south basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the west side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, but stay on the trail, on the right or west side of the creek, longer than the west face line does. Do not cross the creek where that route splits off.

Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin. Roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base, with 2.5-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the route-finding through boulder fields. Noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Talus hopping and route-finding through boulder fields for 2 miles
A lot of large loose rock on the route, making rappelling it inadvisable
An exposed unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old bolt if tagging the true summit
A steep, loose upper gully on the shared descent
Snow lingering in the approach basin and the gullies near the top of the route in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Cut left, east, toward the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon. That col drops and traverses you into the south-facing basin directly below Big Kangaroo's south wall.

Arrival at the route itself is visual and unambiguous when you can see the wall: the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splits the face. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

So the order of finds is: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

The negative test against the west face, which is the commonest error from this car: the west face route crosses Early Winters Creek after only half a mile, at the edge of the talus field, and takes a broad shallow west-facing gully with a chockstone in it. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

And against the other south-face lines, which share this basin: Kearney-Thomas crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Going down under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then traverses right across overlaps to its own start ledge. Skinny Start is about 30 metres right of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

Descent is not down this route, and the reason matters: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which is a few hundred feet higher, and descend the gully from there.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout, south along Early Winters Creek about 2 miles, then cross and take the left fork at the high Y-junction
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, roughly milepost 163, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face.

Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season. Seven pitches.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A Y-junction where the wrong fork puts you on different ground
2.5 to 5 hours of approach with unreliable water late season
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Three routes starting within about 30 metres on the same wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high Y-junction in the approach gully is the decision point, and this route takes the left fork. That is a countable, binary choice on the ground, and every south-face route on this peak depends on it.

So the sequence is: roughly two miles south along the creek, then cross, then up a prominent gully to a Y, then left. Crossing after half a mile instead of two puts you on the West Face approach, on the other side of the mountain, in a broad shallow gully with a chockstone in it.

Arrival at the wall: the base of the south face. The Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splitting the face is the reference feature here, because two other routes are measured from this one and from that ramp.

How the south face starts sort out, in order, and the one measurement that separates them: Skinny Start is about 30 metres right of the standard Kearney-Thomas start. Going down under starts from the Beckey-Tate base and traverses right across overlaps to its own ledge. The central ramp is Beckey-Tate. So: if you have walked thirty metres right of where you meant to be, you are on Skinny Start.

Water is unreliable late season. Carry it from the creek before crossing, since the crossing is the last of it.

Descent: as with the neighbouring Beckey-Tate line, scramble to the notch just north of the true summit and follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully, left fork at the Y, then 30 metres right of Kearney-Thomas
approach_variants.notes:
Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas and Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the left fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the south face.

Three pitches, established in 2012.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A 30-metre offset from a neighbouring start as the only positional marker
A reported failure to find the expected rappel anchor on the standard descent
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Unreliable water late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is about 30 metres right of the standard Kearney-Thomas start. Thirty metres is the whole margin, which means you must find Kearney-Thomas first and then pace it out.

How to anchor yourself on this wall: the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splits the face and is the feature everything else is described against. Kearney-Thomas is the standard south-face start; this route is thirty metres right of it; Going Down Under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and traverses right across overlaps to its own ledge.

So the negative test is directional and short: if you are left of Kearney-Thomas you are heading toward the central ramp and Beckey-Tate. Thirty metres is roughly forty paces along the base; if you have walked a hundred, you have overshot.

A warning about the descent that should change what you carry, and it comes from a party who actually hit it: the intended descent follows the Beckey-Tate line, scrambling to the notch north of the summit and then the loose gully back to the Hairpin. At least one party was unable to find a rappel anchor along the top of that suggested descent and instead had to change into rock shoes and make a high traverse to a saddle before descending. Budget extra time and be prepared to build your own anchors.

approach_variants.name: The gated Middle Fork road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Dingford Creek trailhead gate and walk — or mountain-bike, which is the sensible choice — the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about seven miles.

The boot path for the Hardscrabble Lakes leaves roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers' path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake.

About 20 km and 5,300 ft, and very light foot traffic — do not expect a reliable boot path throughout.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The east face and buttress above lower Hardscrabble Lake are steep and cliffy — stay on the inlet-side path
A long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the final stretch
Very light foot traffic, so no dependable boot path
Early-season snow in the gully to the col
A multi-mile road walk out at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The trail departure is marked by a fallen log across the road from it, and it is half a mile short of the Horse Camp. Those two facts together are what make it findable, because the boot path itself is unmarked. If you have reached the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, you have gone about half a mile too far.

The rule that keeps you alive on the way to the lakes: climbing past the lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, stay close to the inlet. Straying left leads into cliff bands, and the east face and buttress above the lower lake drop directly into the water in steep walls. Inlet on your side, cliffs away to the left.

From upper Hardscrabble Lake, the sequence is short and countable: climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Gully, col, granite slab, ridge. If you top the gully and are not looking at an open slab of granite, you are at the wrong col.

What this route is not: the East buttress is a ten-pitch technical line on the same side of the mountain, reached from the lower lake rather than the upper one. If you are roping up, you are on the buttress and not on this route.

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek Trail to Myrtle Lake, then off-trail past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Dingford Creek trailhead gate via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road / FSR 56, about eighteen miles from North Bend, with the last several miles rough gravel and high clearance recommended.

Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 miles to the Hester Lake Trail junction, then continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake, about two miles more.

From Myrtle Lake the maintained trail ends. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking start here and failed attempts from losing the line are common.

About 9.7 km and 5,280 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September, best once the gullies and couloir have melted out
hazards: No maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake, and any boot path stays faint
Steep gullies and chutes above Big Snow Lake holding snow or ice well into summer
Crumbly, mossy rock in the chutes
Remote, seldom-visited terrain with real self-rescue implications
Rough gravel road access with high clearance recommended
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Three lakes in order are the whole navigation, and they are the only things on this route that cloud cannot take away: Myrtle, then Big Snow, then Snowflake. Leave the maintained trail at Myrtle Lake. Climb steep, increasingly brushy ground to Big Snow Lake. Then traverse right around Snowflake Lake. If you have not passed a lake in the last while, you are off the line.

Where the climbing begins: above Snowflake Lake, ascend gullies and chutes — a snow couloir early in the season — on the mountain's northwest flank to the upper rock fields. The transition from brush and heather to rock fields is the arrival at the climbing proper, and it is a change underfoot rather than a view.

What the final ground is: class 2-3 scrambling across the upper rock fields to the summit. If you find yourself needing a rope, you have wandered into steeper ground than this route takes.

The honest warning, which is the most useful sentence here: there is no maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake and light foot traffic keeps any boot path faint. Parties fail on this peak by losing the line rather than by finding the climbing hard. Carry a track, and treat the lake sequence as the route.

approach_variants.name: As for the South Ridge to Wing Lake, then the hogsback moraine wide right to the low point in the Northeast Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, the right fork at the signed junction toward Heather Pass, then the unmarked climbers' path north across two talus fields to Lewis Lake and up roughly 1,000 ft more to a camp at Wing Lake at about 6,900 ft.

Five pitches, first climbed in September 1973.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct, best Jun-Sep
hazards: A permanent snowfield or mini-glacier below the col persisting into September
Unstable ground on a direct line to the notch; the wide-right moraine line is the stable one
A descent by the South Ridge's loose cairned gully, found from above
The same unmarked off-trail approach stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp, ascend snow toward the low point in the northeast ridge. The route-finding rule is the useful part and it is counterintuitive: following the Hogsback moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch is reported to stay on more stable ground than a direct line.

So you deliberately go wide and then come back, and the handrail is a moraine, which is a ridge of rubble you can keep under your feet without seeing anything. If you are on snow with no moraine beside you, you have taken the direct line and you are on the looser ground.

A small permanent snowfield or mini-glacier can persist below the col into September, so expect snow under the notch even late in the year. That persistence is itself a confirmation: this is the shaded side.

Arrival: the low point of the ridge, a notch. Five pitches follow.

The discriminator against the South Ridge, which leaves the same camp at Wing Lake: that route goes around the right, north, side of the lake and up an obvious talus and snow gully into the couloir just south of the summit, exiting climber's-right to the south col. South col and a couloir means the other route; northeast notch and a moraine means this one.

And the descent is the South Ridge's, which you will have to find from above: from the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a downclimb to get below the initial band of rock, then continue south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully, described by multiple parties as tedious and choss-prone, back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake.

approach_variants.name: Shellrock Basin camp and the traverse to the east-face col
camps: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
approach_variants.notes: Blackcap is a leg of a multi-day traverse rather than an objective on its own, and the walk in is measured in days, not hours. The usual staging is a camp in Shellrock Basin just below and east of Shellrock Pass, reached over Rolo Pass from Fred's Lake after a long valley approach up the Middle Fork Pasayten. From camp the peak is a half-day round trip on easy ground. Water is at the basin and in upper Eureka Creek and there is none on the mountain. An eastern line exists off the Monument Creek trail into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, but the Shellrock side is the travelled one and the one with a recognisable start.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten in runoff
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a col, and getting to it is the only route-finding on the day. Leave the trail at Shellrock Pass itself and traverse south-southwest across the open grassy and rocky basin, keeping below the cliff bands the whole way. That traverse ends at the foot of a talus slope. Work the left, eastern edge of that talus southward until the cliff band above you finally runs out; the saddle at the end of it, directly beneath Blackcap's east face, is where the climbing starts. The confirmation is the rock itself and it is the clearest single marker on this peak: Blackcap's summit cap is near-black hornfels and shale sitting abruptly on top of much paler rock, and the colour boundary is visible from the col and is under your hands within a few minutes of leaving it. If everything around you is still light-coloured after several hundred feet of scree, you are on the wrong flank. Two ways to know you have overshot. Following the trail over Shellrock Pass and down its far side takes you away from the peak altogether. Continuing south past the end of the cliff band instead of turning up drops you toward the Monument basin. In early season a steep snowfield sits below the pass on this traverse and is normally bypassed on its left; carry an axe if it is still there.

approach_variants.name: Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass

bivy.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
bivy.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

bivy.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
bivy.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
bivy.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

approach_variants.notes: From the Robinson Creek trailhead on the Lost River road, climb over Robinson Pass and descend into the Middle Fork Pasayten, joining the standard line up to Freds Lake and over Rolo Pass into Shellrock Basin. It starts much lower than Slate Pass but works when the upper Harts Pass road is not an option, and suits loop trips.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten in runoff
Multi-day approach over Robinson Pass, with the return regaining the pass
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap basin
approach_variants.notes: Follow the Monument Creek trail toward Butte Pass, and a few miles short of the pass leave it where Monument Creek bends west into the basin between Monument Peak and Blackcap. The lower basin is slow going, but its upper part is open and pleasant, and the peak is climbed from there.
hazards: Slow going in the lower Monument-Blackcap basin
Loose scree and talus on the climb; descending is worse
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Exposed 5th-class ridge toward Monument Peak; avoid it as a route
Avalanche and cornice terrain on winter approaches
Long, remote approach with no quick escape

approach_variants.name: Holden Village via the Lake Chelan ferry, then Holden Lake and Holden Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Getting to the trailhead is part of the trip and it runs on someone else's timetable: drive to Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry up the lake to the Lucerne landing, then the roughly thirteen-mile bus up to Holden Village at about 3,300 ft. Reservations and a look at the ferry and bus schedules come before anything else in the planning.

From Holden, walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail west about a mile to the signed Holden Lake Trail junction and bear right. That trail climbs steadily about four miles through forest and brush, with small side-creek crossings for water, to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft, in a cirque directly beneath Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and the last easy water.

Past the lake outlet the tread fades. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus, which is real bushwhacking and route-finding especially with high water early in the season, then climb a hillside traverse north-west to Holden Pass at 6,360 ft — the standard high camp and the last reliable water before the glacier. That is roughly five miles and three thousand feet from the village.

It is worth going in July in most years: later the glacier breaks up and the problem becomes getting off the ice and onto the rock at all.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best early to mid July
hazards: wet, slabby class 3 with a waterfall running through it below the glacier
loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin — keep out of the fall line of parties above
icefall above the slabs
moat at the top of the glacier, which widens through the season
slide alder and vague route-finding past Holden Lake, worst with high water
black flies between about 3,000 and 4,000 ft, mosquitoes from the lake upward
the trip is gated by the ferry and bus schedule, so a delay is not recoverable on the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Holden Pass a use trail — which may be under snow — climbs north and west toward the ridge. After several hundred feet of gain you reach a large ledge at about 6,700 ft, often snow-covered. That ledge is the first checkpoint; if you are still on the pass or on undifferentiated slope, you have not gained it.

The unmistakable marker for the start of the climbing is water. Above the ledge is a set of low-angle slabs with a waterfall running down them, draining the Mary Green Glacier — the 'waterfall slabs'. Running water on slabby rock at around 7,000 to 7,300 ft is the confirmation you are in the right place; there is nothing else like it on this side of the peak.

The route up them is class 3 and the rule is to start high and to the right, skirting the waterfall rather than climbing through it. That is the test that separates the right line from the wrong one: if water is running over the rock you are on, and the holds are wet and mossy, you are too far left and too low — traverse right and up before committing. Topping the slabs puts you on the northern edge of the glacier.

On the glacier itself, bear west along its north (climber's right) edge, then traverse south-west along the base of the north-east ridge to the glacier's upper corner, where the moat is usually a single step across onto rock.

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then past the Soviet buttress and across the pocket glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard one for this side of the peak and is shared with the route next door: Lake Chelan ferry to Lucerne, village bus to Holden, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 west up the valley to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft, then leave the trail and climb the rock-and-heather terraces on the west side of the drainage to camp near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak.

The first-ascent party did not use it — ferry and road closures that year forced them into a roughly 32-mile one-way approach from the west up the Suiattle, including about ten miles of mountain biking, then the PCT to Suiattle Pass, Cloudy Pass and cross-country to the col. That was a workaround, not the route's approach, and it should not be copied unless the boat is out again.

From the top of the col to the first climbing is about an hour and a half of talus and scree.

The route is roughly 2,200 ft with about 1,600 ft of independent ground, sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, and it joins the route next door for the last 600 ft to the summit block.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the first ascent was in early September
hazards: Loose, sparsely protected and often lichen-covered rock on a long sustained buttress
A near-vertical 600 ft wall with significant overhangs directly above the bivy ledge, passed only by a small left-trending ledge system
Very few bail options once above the lower ledge, on a wall with no fixed gear
A rising traverse up the toe of a pocket glacier just to reach the rock, in approach shoes for most parties
Total dependence on the Lake Chelan boat and the Holden bus, both closed since the December 2025 flood
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You reach this route by crossing snow, and its neighbour by not crossing any. That is the cleanest test on this wall. From the col, traverse north-east past the Soviet Route's buttress — about an hour and a half, some of it excellent scree — and then make a rising traverse up the toe of a small pocket glacier. If you got to rock without touching snow or ice, you stopped one buttress short and you are at the Soviet.

The exact point you gain rock: a few dozen yards uphill and left of the lowest point of the buttress, off the top of that pocket-glacier traverse. Not at the toe, and not on the right side.

The confirmation is instant and it is the strongest thing on this page: you are making near-vertical 5.8-5.9 moves immediately, from the first pitch. There is no easing-in. If the climbing above where you stepped onto rock is scrambly, or a chimney, or 5.7, you are on the Soviet buttress instead — that route starts with a narrow chimney 60 ft above its own toe and is a full grade easier out of the blocks.

Left to right across the wall, facing it from the west: Oregonian, Soviet, Cascadian. This is the left-hand (northern) one, which is why the instruction is always "keep walking".

The mid-route checkpoint, which matters because the first ascent bivied there: seven pitches of moderate ground with harder moves, often loose, sparsely protected and lichenous but on the crest of the buttress, lead to a lower ledge flat enough to sleep on. Above it a near-vertical wall with several significant overhangs rises for more than 600 ft, and the way through is a small ledge system traversing left to regain the crest — that pitch has the best rock on the climb. A party staring up at overhangs and thinking about rappelling is in the right place and looking at the wrong feature.

Where it stops being its own route: the last 600 ft are shared with the Soviet, and the two lines converge at a pinnacle around 8,700 ft before continuing to the Southwest Summit. Meeting another route's ground high up is expected here, not a sign you have wandered.

approach_variants.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
approach_variants.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
approach_variants.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
hazards: Icefall traversed on the approach; crevasse and serac fall, and the crossing is described as frightening
Crumbly red rock band across the whole face at mid-height is the source of rockfall
Extreme remoteness; an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed is very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground compound the difficulty
Narrow season window depending on a bridged icefall and residual snow in the summit gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: The sequence is countable from bottom to top and it is the best thing this route has: easier cliffs, then a small glacier, then left up it to an icefall, then right through the icefall to the rock. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one. The rope-up point is a ledge system near the second prominent tree, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible. The mid-route confirmation is a colour and it crosses the whole face: a prominent, crumbly red stratum at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting. Between those two, follow the prominent central rib essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-ft notch is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit. And the negative test is the whole peak: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.notes: Reach the Stehekin valley by boat and the valley shuttle, or on foot over Cascade Pass, then walk or bike the washed-out upper valley road to the Park Creek trailhead. The Park Creek trail climbs toward Park Creek Pass, and the face sits at the head of the valley below the pass. Much less walking than Thunder Creek once you are in the valley.
hazards: Icefall traversed above the small glacier; crevasse and serac fall
Crumbly red rock band across the face at mid-height is the source of rockfall
Extreme remoteness; an incident on this face is very hard to get help for
Boat and shuttle schedules; a missed connection can cost a day
Washed-out upper valley road before the Park Creek trailhead

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col, then the connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft at about mile 21.7 of Cascade River Road, the unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and slide alder into Boston Basin, roughly 3.2 miles and 3,100 ft. Most parties camp at high camp near 6,400 ft; the low camp near 5,300 ft works for slower groups. Sahale Glacier Camp on the other side of the ridge serves the same objective for parties coming over Cascade Pass.

An alpine start is standard. Rope up the Quien Sabe Glacier — the big crevasses are low on the glacier and the direct line through them runs to about 45 degrees and is very exposed, so most parties take the left side and traverse in beneath Sharkfin Tower. Later in the season, end-run the bergschrund below the col by traversing climber's right, then cut back up-left above it to gain the Sahale-Boston Col at about 8,200 ft.

From the col the route follows the connecting ridge toward Boston: flat at first, then widening onto loose rock, staying generally right and on the crest.

The difficulty here is the rock quality, not the grade. This peak has a real fatality history and the descent — three rappels off fixed slings down the southeast side — should not be treated casually.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasses on the Quien Sabe, with a potentially poorly bridged bergschrund below the col that worsens through the season
Notoriously loose and rotten rock, with rockfall onto and within the party
Essentially unprotectable class 4 with real exposure on the knife-edge section
A short but exposed snow traverse on the col that wants axe and crampons
Aging natural rappel anchors on the descent — slung horns and blocks, not bolts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the Sahale-Boston Col at about 8,200 ft, and the col is the one thing on this route that is hard to mistake: it is the saddle shared with the Sahale trade route, so it carries traffic and it has ground falling away on both sides. If you gained a high point rather than a saddle, you are not there.

The approach test is the bergschrund. Later in the season the way onto the col is to traverse climber's right to end-run the schrund and then cut back up-left above it. A party that walked onto the col without meeting a schrund has almost certainly come up in early-season conditions — fine, but it means the position cannot be confirmed that way and the ridge itself has to do it.

The countable sequence on the ridge, and the false summit is the point of it: the crest steepens, widens, and then narrows to a knife edge — that is where the route becomes genuinely exposed. At the high point of that ridge a false summit stands in front of you. You do not climb it. Make the class 4 downclimbing moves and follow the cairned line along the cliff edge to the right (east) around it. After about 100 ft of that bypass the Boston Glacier and the true summit pyramid come into view for the first time.

The strongest negative test is the last one, and it works in fog: you cross about 200 ft of glacier above a bergschrund immediately before the final summit block. If you are scrambling loose rock to a high point and you have not crossed snow above a schrund in the last few minutes, that high point is the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The last feature before the top is a small ledge on the left just short of the summit block, sometimes with a moat at it; above that it is class 3 on loose rock to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block; parties above can knock rocks down
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season; axe needed
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
Loose scree on the upper slopes
approach_variants.baseFinding: Hemlock Pass is where the trail stops climbing. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

approach_variants.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
approach_variants.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits left (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: Gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring
Loose scree, centre and left markedly worse than the right
Gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow requiring axe and crampons
Exposed, loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The thumbtack is the landmark you walk past, and the gully is the one immediately beyond it. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

What the gully is, in other words: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

The footing test tells you where to be within it: climb favouring the far climbers' right side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

Where it delivers you: the gully tops out on the Bryant-Chair connecting ridge, not on a summit. From there you work south over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

And the last step changes character with the snow, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the north — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

approach_variants.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
camps: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
approach_variants.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
hazards: Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail: hot, exposed, with blowdown
No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on a fully sun-exposed ridge
Hard snowfields at High Pass where crampons are worth having
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height; steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle are sketchy when wet
Loose, rubbly schist on the summit crest; a fatal fall is on record
Short Class 3-4 step near a rock horn just below the summit
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in late summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about height, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, stay high. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and cross a river. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

Summit warning, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: parties do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the north horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley

approachLogistics.trailhead: Little Giant Trailhead (Chiwawa River Road, Trail #1518)

approach_variants.notes: Ford the Chiwawa River at the Little Giant trailhead, climb steeply over Little Giant Pass and drop into the Napeequa valley. Go upvalley, then leave the trail at Louis Creek and climb its brushy left side past a waterfall into the basin around 6,400 ft on the peak's southwest side. The river ford can be deep and swift in early summer.
hazards: Fording the Chiwawa River at the trailhead; it can be deep and swift in early summer
Steep climb over Little Giant Pass into the Napeequa valley
Leaving the trail at Louis Creek: brushy slope beside a waterfall, off-trail
Loose, slabby schist on the upper scramble slopes
Short Class 3-4 step near a rock horn just below the summit
Lingering snowfields into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in late summer

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the unmarked path past Lewis Lake to Wing Lake
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area and Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 157.5 at about 4,850 ft, a 40-car lot with a privy. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the Lake Ann below Mount Shuksan on the Mount Baker Highway; the two are about 80 km apart and share a name.

Follow the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass; the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann. Climb through meadows to Heather Pass at about 2.6 miles and 6,100 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus and boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake at about 3.5-4 miles and 5,700 ft, with timbered campsites on the north side and water. This off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake at about 5 miles and 6,900 ft, the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct, best Jun-Sep
hazards: An unmarked off-trail stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake, the approach's main route-finding challenge, worse with cairns buried by snow
Cliff bands directly below the south col if you climb the gully straight up rather than angling right
An exposed cairned ledge traverse below the summit block
A short class 4 step at the summit
Two lakes in Washington named Lake Ann; this route uses the Rainy Pass one
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two lakes in sequence are the approach's spine, and they are water features, which is why this approach is survivable when the cairns are buried. Lewis Lake first, then about twelve hundred feet of climbing, then Wing Lake. If you have reached only one lake you are not at camp.

From Wing Lake, go around the right, north, side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus and snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit. Climb that gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping out at the south col on the crest of the south ridge. The south col is the true start of the climbing.

So the one instruction that keeps you out of trouble is the exit from the gully: angle right near the top. Going straight up puts you under cliff bands below the col.

Arrival at the col: a gap on a ridge crest with the summit pyramid to the north of you. Above it the route is cairned class 3 along the ridge, then a loose gully just west of the crest (stay right where it forks) up to the summit pyramid, then a cairned class 2 ledge system traversing below the summit block, exposed near its end, and finally A short class 4 step of about 15 ft to the true summit.

So the sequence above the col is: cairned ridge, the loose west-side gully, the ledge system, and the short, exposed finish to the summit. A boulder is slung at that step for an optional short rappel or hand line; a 30 m rope is more than enough, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in.

The discriminator against the peak's northeast ridge, which leaves the same camp: that route ascends snow toward the low point in the northeast ridge, following the Hogsback Moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch. Both routes cross moraine above the lake, so that alone tells you nothing; a notch on the northeast side instead of the south col means you are on the other route.

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek Trail to Hart Lake, then the terraces to the North Star-Bonanza col
approach_variants.notes: From Holden Village follow Railroad Creek Trail #1256 west up the valley about 3.5 miles to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft. The Holden Lake Trail branches off partway along and is not your turn — stay on the main valley trail the whole way. Hart Lake is the last easy water and the last straightforward walking. Leave the maintained trail at the lake and fill up, because the ground above holds very little water. Climb out of the lake basin onto the rock-and-heather terraces on the true left (west) side of the drainage, staying left of the waterfalls and cliff bands that come down off the west-facing buttress. Open forest gives way to heather benches and then blocky, loose ground — roughly 3,000 ft of gain, two and a half to three hours, and genuinely routefinding-heavy. There is no trail above Hart Lake. Camp is the flat ground near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak, with snowmelt and tarns for water. The wall above this camp is one of the largest in the Cascades and carries three routes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Aug into Sep, when the rock is driest
hazards: Rockfall from loose reddish rock bands, worst below the summit headwall
Almost no weather escape high on the route on a wall this size
A long descent traverse over a gendarmed ridge followed by two 200 ft rappels off anchors that are not fixed
Route-finding on the terraces above Hart Lake, which has no trail and is loose and brushy enough to be a crux of its own
Extreme remoteness and very few repeat ascents, so nothing about conditions can be inferred from recent traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the Soviet is a chimney, and it is not at the lowest point of the buttress. From camp cross the talus basin to the foot of the buttress — a little under an hour of walking on loose blocks with no trail. The climb starts about 60 ft above the lowest point of the toe, where a narrow chimney takes the first pitch at 5.7. Narrow chimney, 5.7, roughly a rope length: that is the confirmation. If your first pitch is a face, or if it is harder than 5.7, you are not on it.

Left to right across this wall, facing it from the west, the three routes are: Oregonian, Soviet, Cascadian. Learn that before you leave camp. The Soviet is the middle one, and the two neighbours identify themselves at the base by things you can see in poor light.

How to know you have not gone too far left: the Oregonian is reached by walking past this buttress to the north and crossing the toe of a small pocket glacier. If you have put crampons on, or stepped onto snow to reach rock, you have walked past the Soviet.

How to know you have not gone too far right: the Cascadian starts on white slabs beside a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and its opening pitch is an easy 5.4 scramble leading to an obvious large open book. Easy slabby ground and a big corner above means you are one route right of here.

The route-finding key is high, not low, and it is worth knowing from the ground: around half height a sloping ramp cuts diagonally across the buttress crest from east to west. That ramp is the whole line — it bypasses two headwalls that block anything direct. Below it there is a cave-like alcove used as a belay by both the first-ascent party and later parties, which is the one comfortable stance on the climb and a reliable position check.

What the rock tells you: it is meta-granitic and mostly good, with bands of loose red rock. Below the summit headwall the rock turns visibly redder and looser. Favour solid grey stone where the line allows — where you are on red rock, you are where the route is at its worst, not where you are off it.

The descent is not a reverse. From the Southwest Peak you traverse the north-east ridge to the West Peak over gendarmes with one short rappel, then make two roughly 200 ft rappels down slabs on the north-west side. Anchors there have historically been improvised — a nut and a piton on one recorded descent — so carry cord and rack for them and a rope long enough for 200 ft raps.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then 5-10 minutes around the north face to the splitter flake
approach_variants.notes: From the SR-20 pullout at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and opposite Silver Star, a boot path drops through talus into forest, passes a register box, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft. The trail climbs east, roughly 2,200 ft, to a flat bench and campsite at about 6,460 ft, the halfway point and a common high camp, then works up through loose scree gullies and a final cairned stretch of unstable scree-over-slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft. Roughly 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Unstable cairned scree-over-slab on the final stretch to Burgundy Col, the approach's main hazard in both directions
Loose rock and sometimes steep snow on the walk around the base of the north face
Anchors on the descent are a mix of slung boulders and horns with fixed bolts; watch for old webbing
Ledges on the face that catch a pulled rope
Reliable water only at Early Winters Creek; seasonal water near the Bench and an unreliable trickle near the col
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Action Potential does not start at the col. From Burgundy Col, scramble down and around the base of Burgundy's north face for about 5 to 10 minutes until you are below a clean splitter flake. That flake is the route start.

So the three things to check are a direction, a duration and a feature: down and around the north face, five to ten minutes, and a clean splitter flake. Clean is the operative word on a peak where most of the rock is not.

The order along the base, which is what makes this one placeable: this route sits just beyond Ultramega OK's start. Ultramega OK is only about 15 FT climber's-right of this route, at a twin-crack system marked by obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up. So: if you are looking at two cracks with loose blocks sixty feet above you, keep going about 15 ft.

And if you have not walked at all, you are on the north face: that line starts with 4th-class scrambling straight above the col, which is also where the last rappel of the standard descent lands. The North Face start at the near end, twin cracks with loose blocks five to ten minutes along, and the splitter flake about 15 ft beyond them.

Early in the season the walk along the base may be snow rather than scree, sometimes steep enough to want an axe into midsummer. That does not change the count; it changes the footing.

Descent is the north face's, which returns you to Burgundy Col: five double-rope rappels from the summit area, ending with a final 60 m to the col, 5-10 minutes from this route's start.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
approach_variants.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the bergschrund at the toe of the face, on the Boston Glacier, and the position test is directional: from the col you traverse south across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

The entry move is a zig-zag and it is the positive test: work climber's left of the bergschrund, then back right into the centre of the lower face, and then straight up. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

What you are climbing confirms it: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

The finish is the other countable point, and getting it wrong costs time at the worst moment: continue straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse to the left. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

And the approach itself is the strongest negative test against this peak's other route: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. If you walked past an old mine in a basin at 7,000 ft, you are on the southwest route.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork ford and the north-side gully
approach_variants.notes: Do not follow the maintained trail out of the road-end lot. Walk roughly 300 ft upstream and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to its true-right bank; in early summer this runs thigh-deep and cold, so scout upstream for a braided section or a log rather than forcing the main channel. Everything above is trailless: a boulder field, a brushy gully, timber, and open talus, with nearly all the day's gain packed into the last two miles. There is no water once you leave the river apart from occasional snowmelt trickles near the pass.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Cold, pushy river ford at the very start
Sustained salmonberry and black currant bushwhack in the lower gully
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Firm, sustained snow ramp below the pass — genuine self-arrest terrain
Moat between snow and rock near the top of the ramp
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two things have to be identified, and both are easy to get wrong. The first is the gully entrance: from the far bank climb the boulder and talus field straight above the river for about 400 vertical feet until a rock band stops you. That band is the signal — do not try to force it, and do not drift right. Angle left (west) off the boulders into the steep gully choked with salmonberry and black currant, follow it into timber near 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until they run out onto open talus. The second is the notch. Work up and climber's-left toward the low saddle beside Point 5,841 — the gap separating Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediately west — keeping to talus and boulders to stay off the steepest snow, with the heather and cedar benches giving the easiest going. The last couple of hundred vertical feet to that notch is the snow ramp itself, and near its top a moat often forces a short traverse beneath the snow edge to reach solid rock. From the notch a short class 3-4 step heading east begins the summit block. The neighbouring northwest gully holds harder, class 4 ground and is not the way up.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the west-side basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the end of FR-5606 at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,940 ft, take North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. The lower trail is outside the wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal on the first several miles and many parties use one on a 20-mile round trip.

The first six miles follow the river on a gentle forested grade, straight through old burn. The river is the last reliable water — everything above is dry — so fill before leaving the valley. Expect to work over, under and around blowdown, and to lose the tread briefly among downed timber; Grouse Creek is crossed on a log inside one of the worst of those stretches.

A signed spur to Fern Lake splits off at about mile 6.1 — stay on #1437. Around mile 7 near 5,800 ft the trail bends sharply east and switchbacks about half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 junction near 6,600 ft. That junction is a useful timing landmark: the summit is roughly a mile from it.

Leave the trail there and head east through sparse forest and then talus toward the peak's west and south-west flank. A camp flat sits around 7,100 ft in the open basin.
approach_variants.season: Late May-Sep. In late May and June this is effectively a snow climb — the gully to the saddle holds 40-50 degree snow and wants an axe and crampons. By August it dries into loose Class 3 talus
hazards: A gully that is loose top to bottom in summer and 40-50 degree snow through June, with the whole party in the fall line
An exposed, sometimes-corniced summit ridge traverse of roughly 500 ft with genuine consequence
A short unrated technical step between the middle summit and the true south summit that many parties decline
Constant loose rock on the traverse below the summit ridge, so parties must not stack up
A dry, long approach through burn with heavy blowdown, and no water above the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a gully that leads to a gap between two summits, and the gap is what you navigate to — not the peak. From the basin camp, contour onto the peak's western slopes and work south below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree until you are underneath the broad gully leading to the notch between the north and middle summits, at about 8,300 ft. Every party uses that same notch whichever flank they approached from, so it is the one landmark this mountain has.

The gully is broad, not a cleft, and it faces north-west. Early season it is moderately steep snow up to about 40 degrees; later it is loose Class 2 talus and scree the whole way. If the feature above you is a narrow slot, or if it is not the widest weakness on that stretch of face, you are under the wrong one.

The confirmation is what happens at the top of it: you arrive on a saddle with summits on both sides of you. From there the ground is a ridge scramble along or just east of the crest. If you top out of a gully onto a single continuous slope rather than a gap, you are not there.

The negative marker is about the summit and it decides whether your day is over: the ridge from the saddle leads to the middle summit, which is non-technical and where most scramblers stop. The true summit is the slightly higher south one, and reaching it takes a short exposed step — described historically as a vertical chimney onto a foot-wide summit ridge, unrated and treated by every account as the crux. If you have walked to a top without meeting a hard move, you are on the middle summit.

The thing that sends parties here from the north side, worth knowing so you recognise it if you meet them: when the north ridge holds snow and verglas, parties abandon it and drop onto the east and south-east slopes below the summit ridge to finish — this route's ground. That is a documented retreat, not an error.

Stow crampons at the top of the gully if the rock above is dry. The exposure on the ridge is real and the moves near the top run Class 3 and arguably Class 4.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Lake to Lake Caroline and Windy Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Eightmile Lake Trailhead, reached off Icicle Creek Road and Eightmile Road. Start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (#1552). At about 2.8 miles, just past Little Eightmile Lake, a junction appears — go right onto the Eightmile-Trout Creek Trail (#1554), signed for Lake Caroline.

That trail switchbacks up through a recovering burn. At roughly 5.5 miles it crosses the ridgeline and drops to Lake Caroline, then continues past Little Lake Caroline. From Little Lake Caroline it is about another 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass; Mount Stuart, Dragontail and Colchuck Lake come into view as you gain the pass.

Leave the maintained trail at about 6,850 ft and walk cross-country to the east. Camp spots and the last reliable water appear a little further on, around 7,100 ft. From there climb north-northeast to the broad col on the peak's west side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the snowfield below Windy Pass has gone; Jun trips normally still find snow on the traverse
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the class 3-4 ground from the col upward
Rockfall onto your own party — the standard advice is to keep the group tight rather than strung out
A snowfield below Windy Pass that persists into mid-summer; an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
A summit block only about the size of a table, with gusts reported over 30 mph
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts at the broad col on the west side, but the col is not the part people get wrong — the gully is.

Working east from the col you pass a run of tooth-like gendarmes. Do not commit to a chimney or gully while you are still among them: stay low, on the south side while you pass the western spires, then cross onto the north face and keep traversing low rather than climbing.

The gully you want only presents itself once you are on the north side and the end of the summit formation is in sight ahead of you. From there a class 3 gully opens directly above you and leads to a notch. Standing in that notch you can see down the far side of the mountain — that view through is the confirmation. From the notch it is easy scrambling straight up the crest with one short corkscrew move to a summit block no bigger than a dinner table.

Two errors are on record and they are opposite. If the ground is pushing you into fourth-class moves, or the summit formation still runs on ahead of you, you took a gully too early. If you find yourself climbing a cliffy step out of a notch, you walked past the correct gully and are forcing the first notch you came to.

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes, Pinnacle Saddle and the scree traverse east to the Castle-Pinnacle col
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, or at the year-round Narada Falls lot when that road is snowed in. Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft to the saddle at about 5,920 ft.

From the saddle, do not climb Pinnacle. Traverse east across Pinnacle's south-facing scree and boulder field, holding roughly 6,000-6,200 ft, about another half mile of cross-country travel to the col between Pinnacle and The Castle.

From the col, scramble onto Castle's south rib, make a short class-3 traverse onto the east flank, and follow the crack-chimney system up and right to a notch beside a natural rock horn. A brief exposed class 3-4 scramble along the summit crest reaches the true summit.

Stevens Canyon Road is gated and closed by snow roughly mid-October to late May or early June.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for dry rock; the line is scrambled into June and October with snow on the approach
hazards: Exposed, largely unprotected class 3-4 terrain along the summit ridge crest
A short 5th-class pitch with sparse natural protection
Loose volcanic rock on the approach scree traverse and off-route
Residual snow and ice on the shaded traverse into early summer
Rapid afternoon thunderstorm development typical of this range in summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two saddles, and you want the second one. That is the whole approach problem and it is countable.

The maintained trail ends at Pinnacle Saddle at about 5,920 ft — the notch between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak. That is not your objective. From there you leave the trail and contour east across Pinnacle's south scree at 6,000-6,200 ft to a second col, the one between Pinnacle and The Castle. The Castle's base is there.

Three ways to be wrong, and each is a different peak. Start climbing at the first saddle and you are on pinnacle. Go west from the first saddle and you are heading for Plummer. Stop short on the traverse and you are on Pinnacle's south face rather than at the col.

The base of the climbing is one feature and it is a hole, not a face: an obvious crack-chimney system on the southeast and east flank, gained after a short class-3 traverse off the south rib. If you are on open face with no continuous crack to follow, you are off it — the easy-5th line is in the chimney.

Confirmation at the top of the pitch, and it is worth finding deliberately on the way up because you will want it on the way down: the chimney ends at a notch beside a natural rock horn. That horn is the rappel anchor. Carry your own webbing rather than trusting tat left there.

The last negative, and it costs people the summit: the notch is not the top. The true summit is the northernmost block, reached by a short exposed scramble along the crest from the notch. If you have topped out of the chimney and stopped, you are one airy scramble short.
