approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: Old burn on the Andrews Creek trail: no shade, brushy tread; a full long day to Upper Cathedral Lake
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending than ascending; second step-across never has snow
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; ducks and cairns are the only markers
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month at 8,600 ft
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you leave the trail, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by texture, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

Negative marker: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin

approach_variants.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Longer valley walk on the Chewuch trail
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Continuing north along the crest leads toward The Pope and the Canadian border, which is not lawful to cross
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead you start from. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Some trailheads also require a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approach_variants.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.
hazards: Very remote, multi-day approach with no easy rescue access
Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
Continuing north along the crest leads toward the Canadian border

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Rock Trail to the pass, then a rising traverse under the east face
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Cle Elum, take SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake for about 14.8 miles, then gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and the short NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit.

The trail climbs through old growth to Nosh Nosh Wahtum, formerly Squaw Lake, at about 4,850 ft and 2.5 miles, then opens into meadow with Cathedral Rock ahead. At about 4 miles you reach Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft and the PCT junction.

Walk north on the PCT for a couple of minutes, then cut across the meadow to a stand of trees. Parties cache the gear they do not need on the climb there. From the trees, start a rising traverse under the east face, past the meadows, and then across a loose talus slope with the northeast buttress in sight.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The northeast side is shaded and dries slowly, so give it time after rain and expect approach snow into July
hazards: Loose, fractured andesite throughout — poor and unpredictable protection on every technical route on this peak
A short steep snowfield with loose and sharp rock below it, crossed by parties in approach shoes
The moat at the top of the snow
Rockfall down the gully systems from parties, wind and thaw
Descent route-finding on the shattered south and southwest flanks, where many plausible gullies cliff out
Summer convection over the Cascade crest, on an exposed tower with no cell coverage and a remote trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the top of a short, steep snowfield, and that snowfield is the arrival test. Crossing the loose talus under the east face you come to it; it is short but steep enough that parties in approach shoes have picked their way up it holding stones for security. Reaching the top of that snow patch is reaching the start of the climbing.

And here is the mistake parties actually make at that point, which is the most useful thing to know about this route: at the top of the snow it is natural to exit right onto ledges and start up from there. That is wrong. A party that does it finds the ground harder than the fourth class the description promises, wanders left, right and up, and comes back down. The correct start is to exit back left into the moat at the top of the snow, where the terrain is much easier.

So the test is a difficulty test: if your first moves off the snow feel harder than fourth class, you are on the wrong side of the snowfield. Go back and take the moat on the left.

What should follow: easy ground you can simul-climb, then a ledge system that traverses rightward toward the crest of the buttress. The buttress runs about seven pitches and 900 ft, 5.7, grade III. A route that is sustained from the first pitch is not it.

And one thing to settle before you leave the trees: this peak is descended by the south side, not by reversing the buttress. Note where you came up.

approach_variants.name: Source Lake and the WNW gully into the east-face basin
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot (about 3,100 ft) via I-90 exit 52. A cat track leaves the end of the lot and runs up the valley just left of the stream; the Snow Lake trail forks at roughly 1.5 miles — take the left/west branch toward Source Lake. About half a mile along that branch, look for a fairly narrow rocky gully heading west-northwest starting around 4,200 ft. Depending on the season it holds snow, with water running down it. Climb the gully. Around 4,800 ft you reach a small cliff; work through the notch there, then cross the basin beyond on climbers' path or snow, heading southwest straight at Chair's east face.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; an axe is useful in shoulder-season snow
hazards: snow and running water in the approach gully around 4,200 ft
loose scree on the final stretch to the wall
rockfall in the basin below the face
the descent gully off the summit drops east to a notch in the southeast ridge - do not confuse it with the approach gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Go past the Thumb Tack. The Thumb Tack is a freestanding rock sitting in the middle of the basin and it is a waypoint, not the base — parties that stop and rack up there are several hundred feet low and one bench short of the wall. From the Thumb Tack, continue up the basin to the foot of the east face proper, around 5,500 ft.

The other confusion at that rock is directional: if you turned sharply right at the Thumb Tack and started scrambling heather and ledges toward a divide, you are on the Northeast Buttress approach, not the East Face. For the East Face you keep going straight up the basin with the wall filling the view ahead.

You are at the base when the basin runs out against a continuous face rising directly above you and the ground underfoot changes from basin talus to loose scree banked against rock.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then the snow traverse south beneath Burgundy's east face onto the Silver Star Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, a steep faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek. Cross the creek and follow the climber's path and talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col, roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. Stay climber's-left toward the obvious col notch where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down.

A snow patch at or near the col is the last dependable water and is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A snow and glacier traverse that can be firm or icy in the morning; carry an axe through midsummer
The last dependable water is a snow patch at the col which is unreliable by late summer
Rope-snag hazard in the chimney and offwidth pitches on the rappel descent
Fixed anchors that should be visually checked at each station; this is not a bolted sport descent
A re-ascent of 200-300 ft back to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Burgundy Col, drop a short snow and rock step and traverse south beneath Burgundy Spire's East Face, across a small snowy rib, onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, and around to Chianti Spire's obvious east side at about 7,900 ft. Under an hour from a col or bench camp.

So the sequence of surfaces is the handrail, and you can feel each one underfoot: rock step down, snow traverse, a rib, then glacier. If you have not crossed onto glacier you have not gone far enough.

The route on the face, and this is where the two east-face lines are told apart: Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face. Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. So: a big corner on the right-hand side of the wall is this route. A ramp under the summit that leans left is not.

Confirm on the climb: seven pitches at III 5.10b, with chimney and offwidth pitches that readily snag ropes on the way down. Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes get you back down the route itself, trending generally climber's-right, starting from the summit block and then anchors near the top of pitch 5.

What going too far looks like on the approach: continuing south past Chianti along the glacier brings you under Pernod and toward the Pernod-Chablis notch, which serves different routes and involves loose fourth-class ground.

An ice axe is wanted for this traverse through midsummer; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning, and that is exactly when you will be crossing them.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself. The original party approached from a camp at the head of Silver Star Creek, climbed 500 ft of difficult rock to the notch between Chianti and Pernod, made a 250 ft rappel on the west face, and followed a loose gully to the Chianti-Burgundy notch, where the north face was found to hold the only route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 200-300 ft re-ascent to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
Loose main gully below the col, with rockfall from parties above
Sand-over-slab descent above the bench, unanimously described as the worst part of the day
A short loose scramble on scree and boulders for the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway
A route with a single detailed historical account and little modern traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the notch between Chianti and Burgundy spires, and the modern way in is to traverse to it from Burgundy Col rather than to rappel into it from the west as the first ascent did. From the notch, the north face is climbed directly to the summit.

So the test is that you are in a gap between two named spires with a wall rising north of you. Burgundy on one side, Chianti on the other, and the face you are about to climb between them.

The discriminator against the peak's other lines, and it is a side-of-the-spire test: the two East Face routes are reached by descending 200-300 ft south from Burgundy Col and traversing on snow beneath Burgundy's east face until Chianti's east face comes into view. This route stops short of that, at the notch. If you are standing on snow looking at a big east-facing wall with a dihedral on its right side, you have gone past the notch and are under Rebel Yell.

And the other notch on this spire is the one at the far end: the first ascent reached the Chianti-Pernod notch first, on the other side of the peak, and had to rappel 250 ft off the west face and follow a loose gully to get to this one. Two notches, one at each end of Chianti. This route uses the Burgundy end.

What coming back looks like, and it is the same sting the East Face routes carry: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block onto the north face, reverse the line to the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col. Firm morning snow makes that far easier than afternoon slush or bare sandy rock.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Trailhead elevations are given from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further. Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half. The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and parties consistently describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest between the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. The path starts at an obvious logjam that gives a creek crossing, only about twenty yards inside the forest. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on. One known wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues left through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth. The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. A rock buttress above the waterfalls is known as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and planning three days is a common recommendation for what many parties attempt in two.
approach_variants.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bivy the thing to identify is the U-Gap, the notch that almost every party climbing this peak passes through. Chimney Rock is the second peak to the right of the U-Gap. Fix that relationship from camp, in daylight, before you are on the glacier. Getting onto the upper glacier is a three-way choice and it is always the same three: a rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall (the usual, described as grungy and wet), a snow finger far to the left, or the icefall climbed directly if you have screws and the conditions for it. The moat is the arrival, and whether you can get from snow onto rock at all is the crux of the day rather than a formality. Parties describe reaching the bergschrund at the foot of the face and finding it large, then getting across only because fallen ice blocks had tumbled in and built a ramp and platform to step off. If there is no such ramp there may be no way onto the rock, and that is a condition of the season, not a route-finding failure. Above the U-Gap the traverse across the South Peak toward the Main Peak is a sequence of ledges that one party fairly called improbable — the first of them begins about fifteen vertical feet below the U-Gap on its east side, so a search at gap level finds nothing. Negative marker worth carrying: the blind chimney on the way to the broad ledge under the summit tower was found by one party to be a very loose, dangerous, grungy gully. They backed out of it and instead downclimbed about fifty feet from the Main Notch and picked up an obvious reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp leading to the small notch they wanted. If you are grovelling in rotten grunge you are probably in the feature they abandoned. A final sanity check on how rarely this is done: the summit register suggests roughly one party a year. Do not expect a boot track or fresh tat to confirm anything for you.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, the Aasgard trail, then left through the brush to the base gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead on FR 7601, take the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 toward Colchuck Lake — four miles and 2,280 ft, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at about 1.5 miles, left at the Lake Stuart junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet in about two and a half to three hours. Fill water here; it is the last source. Head round toward the lake's south and east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and gain talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake, thirty to forty minutes. Then leave it: break climber's left through a dense band of slide alder and heather, fifteen to twenty minutes of real bushwhacking, to the obvious gully leading up to Colchuck Balanced Rock. The final scramble to the wall is loose third and fourth class; rope up if in doubt. Reckon three and a half to four hours car to base.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse above the lake holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips
hazards: A wet-snow traverse above Colchuck Lake into July with a history of serious slips
Fifteen to twenty minutes of dense slide alder and heather to reach the gully
Loose third and fourth class scrambling in the base gully with parties above
No water above Colchuck Lake
Above the fourth-pitch anchor there is no rappel retreat — the route must be finished
A long walk-off round the peak after topping out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The marker is a bolt with a black hanger about eight feet up a left-facing corner, and it is the only unambiguous thing at the base of this wall. Get to it in three steps.

Step one — the sandy ledge. Scramble the base gully as for the wall's ordinary line until you reach the sandy ledge that every route here starts from. If you have not found a sandy ledge, you are still in the approach gully.

Step two — ten feet and step left. From the sandy ledge, climb about ten feet of easy ground and step left onto a small ledge. There is a tree on it. A small ledge with a tree, one short step left of the sandy ledge, is the belay.

Step three — look up. Above that ledge is a left-facing corner with a bolt roughly eight feet off the deck carrying a black hanger. That bolt is the confirmation, and it is why this route is worth a base finding while its neighbours are not: it is a fixed, findable object rather than a relative position.

Where this sits on the wall: to the left of both the ordinary west face line and the harder line beside it. So if you never stepped left off the sandy ledge, you are on one of those two instead.

Grade check on the first moves: getting off the ground is thoughtful 5.11 with a second punchy section midway. The wall's ordinary line starts far easier. If the first moves are casual, you are not on this route.

And a retreat fact worth knowing before you leave the ground: the anchor at the top of the fourth pitch is the last point from which a rope reaches back down — two 40 m rappels return you to the base gully from there, with an intermediate anchor if your rope is short. Above it you are committed to finishing over the top.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 to Colchuck Lake — roughly four to four and a half miles and 2,200 ft, commonly two and a half hours. Before the road opens, add about four miles of Eightmile Road each way on foot or ski, which is the single biggest variable in the day.

When the lake is frozen (typically until around mid-May) parties ski or walk straight across it. Otherwise take the boot path around to the far, south side; the large flat boulder there is the usual gear-up and pack-stash spot.

From the south side, climb up and gain the lateral moraine. In spring there is often a boot pack this far and nothing beyond it. Follow the moraine crest right (west, toward the glacier) and then drop into the couloir. From the flat boulder to the couloir entrance is about an hour when trail-breaking is easy.

Overnight parties camp at the south end of the lake.
approach_variants.season: Mar-Jun, as soon as road access allows and while the couloir is continuously filled; by late summer it bares out
hazards: Moat at the couloir entrance opens as the season progresses and can force a higher traverse in
Avalanche hazard on the moraine and in the couloir in spring
Four extra road miles each way before FR 7601 opens
Descent is over the back onto the Colchuck Glacier — soft afternoon snow there has been reported as slow and exhausting
Do not confuse with the Northeast Couloir, a separate route east of the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The North Buttress Couloir rises directly out of the edge of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine — that relationship is the identification. From the far side of the lake you gain the moraine, follow it right, and the couloir is the first major gully the moraine runs you into. You do not traverse across the face looking for it; the moraine delivers you to its foot.

The route that gets confused with it is the Northeast Couloir, which is the main north-side cleft and starts east of the summit. If you are working east along the base of the north side toward an obvious big cleft, you have walked past the NBC. The NBC is the one to the west, coming off the moraine.

The couloir runs about 2,000 ft from the base up to a notch. Once inside, you are in a defined gully with walls, not on an open snow slope — if the ground stays open and fanned out you are still on the moraine apron.

The moat at the entrance is the recurring problem and it changes the approach: when it has opened up, parties contour along the lateral moraine and traverse into the couloir higher rather than entering at its true base. If you cannot get from snow onto the couloir at the bottom, that traverse is the accepted workaround, not a sign you are in the wrong place.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction and fork left for Colchuck Lake — straight on goes to Stuart Lake and a different valley. Switchback up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles and 2,200 ft in, and fill water: it is the last easy source. Take the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end. Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Now the important part. Do not continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route. Traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face. If Eightmile Road is gated in early season, add roughly four miles of road each way.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb; by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock
hazards: Rockfall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face
An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer
Avalanche-prone slopes above Colchuck Lake in spring and early summer
Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit
Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The couloirs come in order, and counting them is the test. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier along its true-right margin you pass features in a fixed sequence, and this one is the second deep slot you meet, not the first.

Lowest on the glacier: the North Buttress Couloir. Above it, and starting with two rope-lengths of ice below a hidden couloir: the Holsten-Hilden. Higher up the glacier than either: the Northeast Couloir — the one you want. Above it: the rock of the Northeast Buttress.

So the paired check is slot-and-rib. You are correct when you are standing in an obvious narrow slot splitting the face, with the prominent rock buttress directly above you. If the buttress is not there, you are too low on the glacier. If you are scrambling onto the toe of that rock rather than into a slot, you are on the Northeast Buttress and on a fourteen-pitch rock route instead of a snow and ice one.

The moat is part of the arrival, not an obstacle before it: gaining the couloir means crossing the moat at the glacier's edge, and it runs from a step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by late summer. If you reach rock with no moat to cross at all, you have probably reached it somewhere it is filled and should confirm the slot above you before committing.

What it does above, as confirmation: the couloir winds up, steepens, and runs into a steep wall. The exit is along the base of that wall to the climber's left, finishing on 60-plus degree snow or ice to the summit ridge. A couloir that simply keeps going without hitting a wall is not this one.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 and the Coleman Glacier to the bench beneath the north faces
approach_variants.notes: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR-39) near 3,700 ft, follow Trail #677 about two miles through forest, over a plank bridge on Grouse Creek and across one avalanche path below Hogsback that can hold debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near the Coleman icefall viewpoint around 4,900-5,000 ft — the last reliable running water before the moraine. Gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track, staying on or near the moraine crest before dropping onto ice. Rope up here. Contour and ascend the Coleman climber's right — northeast — toward the bench beneath Colfax's north faces, staying low and left around the large crevasse that guards the direct line. Parties in good booting conditions commonly reach the bench in three to four and a half hours from the car. Four routes share this bench.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Oct-May. This is a cold-season route: it wants the north faces frozen, and it avalanches after new snow
hazards: An overhanging bergschrund that is the crux obstacle of the approach in lean years
Avalanche on this aspect after any new snow — do not climb it on a loaded slope
Crevasses on the Coleman, including one large one that guards the direct line to the bench
Sun-warming of the north faces later in the day, so the schrund must be crossed early
A glacier descent that multiple parties specifically warn against doing after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From left to right as you stand on the bench facing the face, the four lines are: Kimchi Suicide Volcano, Polish Route, Cosley-Houston, Ford's Theatre. Learn that order before you leave the car. It is the only thing that separates a WI4 from a WI6 in the dark, and all four start within a few hundred metres of each other above the same bergschrund.

Cosley-Houston is the second from the right and the easiest line on the face. Cross or tunnel the bergschrund and go up and right of the Polish Route. If you have gone left of the continuous ice line up the middle of the face, you are on the Polish Route and you are on a grade harder than you came for.

The positive test, and it is the strong one: above the schrund this route opens with a low-angle ice ramp leading up to the base of an obvious crux pillar. Low-angle first, pillar second. If your first ground above the schrund is steep — a continuous fat ice line that stands up immediately — you are on the Polish. If it is rock with face holds and mixed moves rather than ice, you are far left on Kimchi.

The bergschrund is the crux obstacle of the approach, not a formality. It is frequently overhanging and in lean years it has needed a mixed traverse in from the right. Cross it early, before the north-facing slopes see any sun.

What being too far right looks like: Ford's Theatre is hidden from the standard approach, tucked in a cleft around the right side of a buttress. If you have walked right until the face disappears behind a buttress, you have gone past Cosley-Houston entirely.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the schrund guarding the middle of the face
approach_variants.notes:
The trailhead and the lower approach are the same as Cosley-Houston: Heliotrope Ridge trailhead near 3,700 ft, Trail #677 for roughly two miles through forest, water at the moraine/treeline break, then the standard Coleman-Deming boot track onto the glacier and climber's right toward the bench under Colfax's north faces. Rope up for crevasse travel on the glacier.

Parties leaving the car around 3:30 am with a well-consolidated track have reported the bench in under three hours; that figure varies enormously with snowpack and traffic and should not be planned on.

Gear up on the bench. The bergschrund here guards the Polish Route directly, is frequently large and overhanging, and has required parties to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow and ice to gain the first ice pitch.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May
hazards: A large, frequently overhanging bergschrund that has needed tunnelling
WI6 ice on a face that catches afternoon sun despite its northwest aspect
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow — do not do the schrund on a loaded slope
A retreat from partway up by short V-thread rappels on threads you build yourself; the normal way down is a walk-off
Crevasses on the Coleman on the way out, with the glacier descent flagged as hazardous after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right on this face: Kimchi, Polish, Cosley-Houston, Ford's Theatre. The Polish Route is the second from the left and it takes the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of the face, just left of and parallel to the Cosley-Houston gully.

The test is the ice itself, and it works without seeing the whole face. This is a WI6 — the hardest line here by a wide margin — and above the schrund it stands up immediately. If the first ground above the schrund is a low-angle ramp you can walk up, you are on Cosley-Houston, which is the easiest line on the face and sits immediately to your right. That single difference, ramp versus steep ice off the deck, separates WI4 from WI6 at the moment of committing.

If the rock matters more than the ice, you are too far left. Kimchi Suicide Volcano takes an independent line to the left of this route and is described by its first-ascent party as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on well-featured rock with plenty of face holds. Continuous ice with no rock moves is the Polish; face holds and mixed ground is Kimchi.

Confirm with the schrund: the schrund that guards this route specifically is frequently large and overhanging, and the documented workaround is to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow. If you crossed a schrund comfortably on a snow bridge and walked straight onto easy ground, you have probably crossed at the Cosley-Houston line.

Why it matters to check the parallel gully: the two lines run parallel up the same face, so being one line out does not become obvious until you are committed on steep ice with the wrong rack.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes saddle and the west spur
approach_variants.notes: From the Twin Lakes saddle around 5,000 ft, leave the trail and go cross-country up the east side and east crest of East Twin Peak. Most parties never reach the lakes: a distinct path forges off to the left somewhere between about 5,200 and 5,400 ft, roughly a hundred feet below the junction where the way trail drops into the lake basin, and taking it saves several hundred feet of regain. Traverse talus and heather toward a dip in the ridge, follow the bootpath up through boulders, rock, scree and heather, then stay close to the ridge crest across a meadow and a gravelly slope, keeping high. On the connecting ridge stay LOW rather than crossing its crest — climbing over the top has been tried and reported as a poor idea.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock in the gully above the buttress — keep the party close together and wear helmets
Snow lingering on the upper ledges into early summer makes the route significantly more hazardous
Route-finding through the boulder fields in cloud
A tiny ledge with a big runout just below the final summit scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two different heights, and they are easily confused. The snow patch at about 6,300 to 6,400 ft is where walking ends and scrambling starts — a short class 3 step, avoidable on the left up very steep dirt, with a boulder field above it. The buttress that holds the route's one hard move is higher, at roughly 6,700 to 6,800 ft, and it arrives as an impasse. A use trail runs left around that buttress and it is the trap: taking it opens a view of the Columbia Glacier, so if the glacier comes into sight you have gone the wrong side. Instead climb straight up the buttress's left side for a five-foot fourth-class move, choosing either the chimney or the crack beside it; an alternative stays right and south on the boulder field and enters a roughly fifty-foot gully by an easier reach. Above that, cross the southwest face to the slabs, and where the headwall appears go all the way to it before traversing climber's right — stopping short and staying right makes the ground harder. A stone-staircase formation near the top confirms the line.

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach_variants.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: No drivable trailhead; ferry and shuttle logistics, closed by a recent flood and landslide
Creek crossings run high in early season; one depends on a footbridge that may be out
Standing dead timber and loose footing on the steep burned hillside above the tailings
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully to the notch and a short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge
Very remote, no cell service, multi-day self-rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding: The arrival test is a notch, and it is the best negative marker on this peak: several notches cut the spur ridge and most of them are class 5 from below. The one you want is the highest notch you can reach easily, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's right — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. How you know you are under it: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. The stream is the handrail from camp: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the outlet stream that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. What happens immediately after the notch, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn left and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. The last obstacle is one move, not a pitch. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A note on the route's name: the south-east in this route's aspect is the glacier remnant itself, which faces south-east from under the spur ridge on the peak's east side; the finish is on the upper north-east ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
approach_variants.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead, walk up through Spider Meadow and the Spider Glacier to Spider Gap, drop past the Lyman Glacier to Lyman Lake, then follow the Railroad Creek trail down the valley to Copper Creek. It avoids the boat and shuttle but is far longer, with a steep snow climb to the gap.
hazards: Far longer approach with a steep snow climb to Spider Gap
Descent past Lyman Glacier, then a long valley walk to Copper Creek
Burned hillside with standing dead timber and loose footing on the Copper Creek trail
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the glacier remnant, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully and a short exposed Class 4 step; very remote, no cell service

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then Lewis Lake and the Lewis Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: From the Rainy Pass trailhead (4,855 ft) on SR-20, 52 miles east of Marblemount where the PCT crosses the highway, take the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the one below Mount Shuksan. At roughly 1.25 miles stay right at the Lake Ann junction; the lake just below it is the last reliable on-trail water. Switchbacks through heather meadows lead to Heather Pass at about 6,080 ft, roughly 2 miles in, where the maintained trail ends and the off-trail travel to Lewis Lake and the glacier begins.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the off-trail travel beyond Heather Pass
Snow, bare ice and moats on the Lewis Glacier remnant; carry an axe and crampons early season
Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass well into July
Loose ground on the 400 ft downclimb into the west-face cirque; move one at a time
One distinctly steeper class 4 step on the descent, with no fixed anchor reported
Lake Ann is the last reliable on-trail water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route is a chain of notches, and the first one decides the day. From Heather Pass, head west across talus, passing south of Lewis Lake (about 5,700 ft), to the crest of the Lewis Glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Follow the moraine onto the glacier remnant and climb southeast, bearing left near the top, to a notch in the ridge at about 7,500 ft. Bearing right instead puts a party on narrow, sand-covered ledges and a steep, constricted snow gully — a much harder line.

From the first notch, follow the ridge west to a second notch, then downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the west face. The ground is loose; space the party out.

From the cirque, an easy gully leads to a large notch on the Southwest Ridge, and the ridge crest — exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves — goes to the 8,107 ft summit.

So the sequence of heights is 6,400, 7,500, the cirque below it, the ridge notch, 8,107: moraine, first notch, downclimb, ridge gained, summit.

The descent reverses the same line, including the climb back out of the cirque to the 7,500 ft notch. Fix the notches in your mind on the way up; they are easy to lose from above.

approach_variants.name: West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 to Fish Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the spur off East Buttermilk Creek Road, sign in at the wilderness register and follow Trail #411 up the West Fork valley through ponderosa and larch. The creek is crossed unbridged within the first half mile on unsecured, often wobbly downed logs, and several more crossings follow — all of them push hard with snowmelt through June. Maintenance is light and blowdown is common in the lower miles, so expect detours where the flagging and tread both thin out. The trail climbs steadily to Fish Creek Pass, where it tops out and meets the Fish Creek Trail; Star Lake sits just below the far side and is the last reliable water and the usual high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late June through early October; a popular early-October objective for larch colour along the crest. Snow lingers in the gullies off the crest into July.
hazards: Unbridged creek crossings on unsecured logs, worst during June snowmelt
Heavy blowdown in the lower miles where the tread and flagging both disappear
Lingering snow in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July
Loose class 2+ blocks in the last few hundred feet where the boot path breaks up
No water above Star Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: You arrive at Fish Creek Pass through larch and look down on Star Lake — and which way you turn is the whole test. Trail #411 tops out on an open saddle reached through a beautiful larch forest, and from the crest you look down on Star Lake with a second larch forest around it on the far side. Do not descend. Star Peak, the higher neighbour less than a mile southeast, is the one you reach by dropping past that lake and climbing again; this peak goes the other way, straight up the ridge from the pass with no loss of height at all. So the test is simple: if you are giving back elevation, you are heading for the wrong summit. Leave the tread at the pass and take the boot path up the open ridge on tundra and small talus — a genuine worn path rather than a line you invent. A few hundred feet below the top the path breaks up and the ground turns into large class 2 blocks; that boulder ground is the top of the route and not a sign you have lost it. There is no false summit on this ridge to catch you out.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch
approach_variants.notes:
The South Face is reached from the notch between Concord and Lexington, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord notch that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass) follow the maintained trail until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left marked by a large cairn.

Instead of trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers. Higher in that gully a reasonable climbers' path appears along its left side; take it rather than fighting up the gully bed. It leads to the Concord-Lexington notch.

This notch is the quieter of the two — it sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose ground in the Concord-Lexington gully
easy to end up in the Liberty Bell-Concord gully instead — check which two towers flank your notch
no reliable water above the stream near the climbers'-path junction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You want the Concord-Lexington notch, meaning the saddle with Concord Tower on one side and Lexington Tower on the other. From it, the South Face is on the Concord (north) side, and it begins gently: a class-2 walk across gravelly, slightly down-sloping ledges gets you to the first belay, so if your first move is a hard pull you are on the wrong line. Higher, a roped scramble along the crest brings you to a sandy stance under a thin blade of rock that climbers call the shark fin, and the last pitch goes over that fin onto the summit block, belaying from bolts. The shark fin is the confirming feature — it is unmistakable and there is nothing like it on the North Face side.

The common error is arriving at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch instead. That col has Liberty Bell on its far side, not Lexington, and from there the Concord wall in front of you is the North Face crack system, not walkable ledges.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then drop 50 feet down the north side
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs, talus and meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. That gully is often snow-filled and icy into late June and carries high rockfall risk after snowmelt.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: An approach gully that is often snow-filled and icy into late June
High rockfall risk in the gully after snowmelt
A 5.8 R grade, so a fall on the wrong ground is consequential
Two notches on one ridge reached by the same path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the notch, drop about 50 feet down the gully on the north side of Concord Tower to the start of the two diagonal cracks that mark the route. That is a measured descent and a countable feature: fifty feet down, then two cracks running diagonally.

So the test is that you go down, not up. Every other line off this notch starts at the notch or above it. If you have arrived at the notch and started climbing straight away, you are on the standard North Face or one of its variations, not on this route.

Which notch, because the peak has two and they are reached the same way: this is the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, and the test at the top of the gully is that A steep crack system rises in front of you. If instead the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges, you are at the Concord-Lexington notch, which serves the tower's south face, and you are on the wrong side of Concord.

Countable on the route: three pitches at 5.8 R. If you are more than three pitches up and still climbing, you have linked into something else.

Descent: the same as the standard North Face. Rappel chains at the summit allow a doubled-rope rappel toward the notch, or downclimb and scramble back to it.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
camps: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
hazards: Mandatory hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; river not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River trail, about two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
Loose Class 4-5 rock on the upper route; weathered fixed tat on the horn
Exposed 5.8+/A1 summit headwall; extreme remoteness, multi-day self-rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the foot of a snow couloir on the northwest side, and the couloir is the only thing on the peak you can identify in cloud. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

Arrival at camp, which is the harder find: the camp is a lateral moraine, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

Confirm on the climb: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.water: glacier meltwater
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze

bivy.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

approach_variants.notes: Take the water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing and follow the Big Beaver trail up the valley toward Luna Camp. Leave the trail and climb Wiley Ridge off-trail to the basin on its south side, then continue to the Challenger Arm and cross to West Challenger Notch above the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Expect several days and serious bushwhacking.
hazards: Water taxi, then serious bushwhacking up Wiley Ridge off-trail over several days
Crossing the Challenger Arm to West Challenger Notch above the glacier
Crevasses and big moats on the Crooked Thumb Glacier late in the season; loose moraine camp
40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
Loose Class 4-5 rock on the upper route; weathered fixed tat
Exposed summit headwall; extreme remoteness, multi-day self-rescue

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 pullout, over the rib south of the South Buttress into the basin east of the peak
approach_variants.notes: From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its east end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Six pitches, Grade III, first climbed in 1976.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall that must be avoided rather than climbed
A descent by a different route than the one climbed, with no route-specific beta
A creek crossing and brushy climbers' path low down
No published marker at the base of the route itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: Traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak. That second basin is where the East Face routes begin. So the count is two basins, and the rib between them is the thing you cross: first the basin below the peak's south side, which is where the South Buttress and North Ridge parties go, then over a rib, then the east basin. If you have not crossed a rib, you are still in the south basin and you are under the wrong side of the mountain. The negative test against the North Ridge, which leaves the same boulder field: that route bears right and north into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch, and gains it by a loose runout 5.7 pitch. If you are roping up for a single hard pitch to reach a notch, you are on the North Ridge, not on the East Face. A hazard that is also a route-finding instruction, and it is stated in both routes on this side: avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in. If your line into the base is up a confined chimney full of scree, you have picked the wrong way through and should back out and go round. There is no named crack or flake at the start; the basin, the rib and the chimneys to avoid are the ground features to go by. Descent: parties commonly descend the South Buttress with multiple rappels, or the West Ridge on fixed-anchor rappels plus downclimbing, rather than reversing the technical face.

approach_variants.name: State Creek climbers' trail from the SR-20 pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the east end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: climbers' trail from the pullout is genuinely hard to find in the dark
State Creek crossing can be awkward in high spring flow
loose rock in the entry gully with parties above
the standard West Ridge descent is looser than the ascent line and has cairned traverses where the direct-looking line cliffs out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Standing in the boulder field, several large gullies come down out of the south buttress. Bear right and take the leftmost of those gullies — that specific choice is the crux of the navigation and it is where parties get it wrong, because from below the gullies look interchangeable.

Climb the gully as scrambling terrain. The place to rope up is not the bottom: continue up until you are about 100 feet from its top, where the gully forks and visibly steepens. That fork is the marker. Pitch one goes up the left side of the gully from there to gain the ridge crest. If you rope up down at the base you burn time on ground everybody scrambles; if you find yourself topping out of a gully with no fork and no steepening, you are in the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Roadside pullout west of the Blue Lake Trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
There is a broad shoulder with room to park on SR-20 roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake Trailhead, with a view through the trees to the peak. Parties commonly meet at the Blue Lake lot and then drive the short distance west to this pullout.

From there head up into the basin below the peak. Reported round-trip times are on the order of six hours up and four hours down for the whole climb, so this is a long day even though the walk-in is short.

On the way out, the descent line drops skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully further skier's right for the lower part — going straight down instead puts you into loose ground.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock throughout the ridge and on the descent gullies
long day relative to the short approach
route-finding on the descent — the direct-looking line down cliffs out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up into the basin, stay somewhat left to arrive at the notch at the base of the west ridge — that notch, not the ridge crest above it, is the reference point. From the notch, traverse along ledges for about 100 feet to reach the foot of a shallow gully that runs up and left to gain the ridge crest, and that gully is where the climbing begins. Three rope lengths or so above it you arrive at a sandy area at the top of the southwest gully, which is the natural regrouping spot and confirms you are on line. If you rope up at the notch itself without making the ledge traverse, you are starting one feature too early.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
This is not the approach to Cutthroat Peak, and the confusion is the commonest way people waste a morning here. The peak is approached from an unmarked highway pullout west of the pass with no maintained trail at all. This wall is reached from the signed Cutthroat Lake trailhead at about 4,500 ft, a mile up a spur road off the highway east of the pass, with a kiosk and a large gravel lot.

Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek trail. After a short distance — the first few minutes, still on the old roadbed running parallel to the main trail — leave it on the climbers' left and start uphill into the forest.

From there it is a climbers' path through light brush, trees and talus, trending climbers' right toward the buttress, until you reach a flat area beneath the cliff. Reckon on the better part of an hour to two depending on how well you read it.

A warning about the markers: there are cairns, and they are not all route markers. Trend right toward the wall and use the buttress itself rather than the rock piles.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September; the corners seep earliest in the season, and access is gone entirely while the highway is gated shut
hazards: Shares its name with a peak reached from a different trailhead with no trail at all
Two route starts about fifty feet apart on one slab platform
Cairns on the approach are not all route markers
The descent is the crux of the day; the obvious gully below the notch is the wrong one and is loose
Corners seep early in the season and stay wet after rain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark at the foot of the wall is a granite patio — a flat slab platform under the cliff where two routes begin about fifty feet apart. Everything here is decided by that patio.

This route is the left-hand of the pair. From the patio, head up and left into a corner. The route to the right of the patio, roughly fifty feet away, is a different line at 5.9 that wanders far more.

Confirmation is a striped corner, and it is the landmark to hold in your head for the whole climb rather than only at the base. There is a distinctly banded corner feature used as the on-route check throughout this line; it seeps water early in the season, which is itself a useful sign that you are looking at the right thing. If you never pass it, you are not on this route.

The hardest and best pitch is high: a hundred-foot right-facing corner that varies from hands to fingers, secure but sustained. Reaching a long right-facing corner near the top is the strongest confirmation the route offers.

Negative markers, both of them real. If you have walked uphill from the patio and are standing at a small outcrop of trees with an open book just left of it, you are at the third route on this wall, a hundred and fifty feet climbers' left and above this one, and it is a full grade harder. And if you started to the right of the patio and your second pitch ends on a ledge with two big gnarled trees, you are on the 5.9.

The descent is where this wall actually hurts people, so study it before you leave the ground: from the topout, reach the notch between the westernmost and the higher central buttress, marked by a slung horn or tree, rappel one rope length over a chockstone tunnel to a dirty ramp with a small cave, then find the upward-trending gully or ledge system on skier's left. Do not descend the obvious loose gully directly below the notch.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek Trailhead and the forest traverse to the wall's right side
approach_variants.notes: Turn off the highway a little over four miles east of Washington Pass, following signs for the Cutthroat Creek trail, and drive about a mile to the trailhead lot, which has restrooms. Do not confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout well west of here and serves a different objective entirely. Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail, then leave it a short way along and walk up through the woods toward the wall — the ground gains elevation quickly at first, then the line traverses leftward through open forest and across slabby benches. There is no maintained tread on this section; parties report cairns and an intermittent climbers' path, but treat it as open-forest navigation rather than a trail. The traverse ends on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, which is where the climbing starts. Allow the better part of a couple of hours from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, matching the neighbouring crags on the same approach. Early-season parties should expect bushier, dirtier cracks, since this wall sees very little traffic and the cracks have not been cleaned by use.
hazards: vegetated and dirty cracks, especially on the less-travelled lower pitches
runout terrain on the middle pitches
loose rock, given how rarely the wall is climbed
open-forest and slab navigation with no maintained trail to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding: The shoulder at the right-hand end of the wall is the arrival point, and the route starts on low-angle ground, not steep ground. The traverse through the forest and across the slabby benches deposits you on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side; that shoulder, rather than any point along the middle of the cliff, is where you should be standing. From it, the start of this route is clean, low-angle crack systems running up a big ramp that trends left as it rises. Low angle and left-trending together are the test. This wall holds only two known lines and the other one is several grades harder and sustained, so if what is above you is steep, continuous crack climbing with no ramp under it, you have walked past the start and are beneath the hard line. Likewise, if you are still in trees and have not come out onto a distinct shoulder with the right edge of the wall above you, you have not finished the traverse. Expect the cracks on the lower pitches to be bushy and dirty rather than clean — that is normal here and is another sign you are on the right, less-travelled line. The upper pitches merge into the harder route's corner and finish on its final blocky pitch, and the descent rappels that line.

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
camps: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
approach_variants.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection to gain the North Ridge Notch from the basin
Loose rock and poor gear on the notch-gaining pitch; the first two pitches of the ridge carry the worst rock, with a shifting flake
Creek crossing and brushy climbers' path low on the approach
Route-finding in the boulder field: bear right into the basin under the notch, not left toward the other route's gully
Descent drops into the notch and down a different route's four-rappel line; a more direct West Ridge descent is rockier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and Porcupine Creek into the basin northwest of the peak

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

approach_variants.notes: From Rainy Pass, follow the PCT north for about twenty minutes and leave it before the Porcupine Creek bridge, climbing through timber into the basin northwest of the peak.
