Two or three short low-fifth pitches reach the North Ridge notch. Longer than the south-side basin, but on cleaner rock to the notch; parties camped near Rainy Pass or combining objectives use it.
hazards: Two or three short low-fifth-class pitches to gain the notch from the north, on terrain that has no stored protection details
Off-trail climb through timber into the basin northwest of the peak, leaving the PCT before the Porcupine Creek bridge
Loose rock on the lower pitches of the ridge, with the worst quality in the first two pitches above the notch
Descent still goes to the notch and down the south-side rappel line, a long way around to the Rainy Pass trailhead
Considerably longer approach than the south basin

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; light crampons and an axe are worth carrying earlier for the snow patch below the base and for the descent gully
hazards: Perennial snow patch below the base, size varies year to year
Loose gully and gravel ledges on the approach scramble
Serious rockfall exposure on the lower face; a rockfall accident has occurred here
Cliffing-out on the bushy ramps is normal but disorienting for a party expecting a clean line
The standard descent gully ices up late season, which changes it from a walk-off into a rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Backbone takes the rib immediately left of Serpentine Arete as you face the northwest wall, and the two starts are close enough that people confuse them — about 200 ft apart, with Backbone's start roughly 200 ft lower on the face.

Tell them apart by what is under your feet. Serpentine starts on bare orange rock that is 5th class off the ground. Backbone starts on low-angle, left-trending ramp systems full of bushes. If you are pushing through vegetation on ramps, you are on Backbone; if you are pulling on clean orange rock immediately, you are on Serpentine.

The sequence from there is counter-intuitive and worth committing to memory before you are standing in cloud: scramble up and left on the bushy ledges until you cliff out — being stopped is part of the route, not a mistake — then turn up and right and work back toward the ridge crest. Zigzagging left and right along ledges and ramps on 4th-class ground is normal here.

The end of the approach scrambling is marked unambiguously: a short 5.4 step finishing at a tree with slings on it, which lands you on a large flat terrace. That terrace is the belay for pitch 1 and is where the real climbing starts. If you have not reached a spacious platform with a slung tree just below it, you have not finished the approach.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, spring — lake frozen or partly frozen
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Creek Road is plowed only as far as Bridge Creek Campground, at the junction with FR 7601, which leaves about 3.7 miles of road to walk, snowshoe or ski to the Stuart Lake / Mountaineer Creek trailhead at 3,400 ft. Plan for that; it is a substantial part of the day and it is why so many parties do this route on skis.

The trail follows the creek about 1.5 miles, crosses to the west side, and continues another three-quarters of a mile to the fork. Take the left fork, cross back, and continue south — about four miles from the trailhead in total — to the north end of Colchuck Lake. Campsites are on the western banks.

When the lake is frozen, cross it directly. That is the fast option and it puts you under the north face in minutes rather than an hour of shore boulders. It is also a judgement call about ice, and it stops being available once break-up starts.

Once FR 7601 opens for the season the road walk disappears and the approach shortens dramatically — but by then the couloirs are usually past their best.
approach_variants.season: Feb-Apr; the lake ice typically breaks up around mid-May
hazards: 3.7 miles of unplowed road each way in winter
Avalanche hazard on the approach and in the couloirs — this route needs a stable snowpack, not just cold
Crossing a frozen Colchuck Lake is an ice judgement, not a shortcut to take on faith
Steep, exposed snow with possible ice right at the couloir entrance, before any belay
5-9 hours one way from the lake means a benighting is a real outcome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Triple Couloirs starts on the north face, which is not where Serpentine and Backbone start. Do not follow the moraine southwest toward the Colchuck-Dragontail col — that is the northwest face and a different set of routes.

From the lake, go counter-clockwise to the south end, then head uphill aiming just a little east (climber's east) of the lowest point of Dragontail's north face. The face has a clear low point where it meets the basin; the entrance to the first couloir — the Hidden Couloir — sits slightly east of it, around 6,400 ft.

The visible marker is a prominent snow finger running down out of the face at that point. In poor visibility, work the base of the wall until the rock stops going down and starts going up — that low point is your reference — then move a short distance east and look for the snow tongue leading up into a cleft. The entrance itself is steep, exposed snow and sometimes ice; it is narrow enough that you will know when you are in it.

The couloir is called Hidden because it does not read as a continuous line from the lake. Do not expect to see the full route from below and pick it out; find the low point of the face first, then the snow finger, then commit.

Once in, you get roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before the route makes any decisions — if you have climbed several hundred feet of moderate snow inside a defined cleft, you are on it.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village — used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach to the climbing is a creek, and it is the only way through an otherwise cliffy face. From camp in upper Phelps Basin, leave the last of the boot path and head east-north-east beside a tumbling side creek. That creek cuts the one weakness in the cliffs above the basin; the broad talus-and-scree gully on Dumbell's south side follows it. If you are working up an open face with no water beside you, you are not in the breach.

The first arrival is a notch on the south-east shoulder, around 7,900 ft, reached by climbing that gully out of the basin directly south of the summit. Grass and heather give way to talus and — through about mid-August — moderate snow.

Then comes the measurement that decides the day, and it is counted in yards rather than looked for: from the notch, go 100 to 200 yards left — west — and take the gully there. Not the gully at the notch. Aim for the right-hand side of the south face, where the easiest gully system starts. Several parallel gullies and ledge lines look alike here and they do not all go: the wrong one cliffs you out below the summit ridge.

What confirms you chose right: a little scrambling above that gully gains a system of ledges which then zig-zags up onto the West Ridge. Ledges that zig-zag rather than a continuous line, and a ridge crest at the top of them, is the confirmation. A gully that runs out against steeper rock with no ledge system is the wrong one — go back down and try further west.

The summit warning is real and it is about lookalikes: from the west ridge a few hundred feet of easy but exposed Class 3 leads to the top, and similar-looking notches and false summits near the top have sent parties astray. Keep track of which top you are on rather than assuming the first one is it.

One object to know about: a party has reported an unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully. Treat the direct line under it as loaded ground rather than a shortcut.

approach_variants.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
camps: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
approach_variants.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
hazards: Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the saddle, straight on goes somewhere else and the peak is left and straight up. Above the flower basin the tread goes intermittent through upper meadows and switchbacks to a broad, largely treeless saddle on the divide between the two drainages, around 6,200 ft, with scattered flat tent sites on it. The climbers' track up the peak is obvious underfoot but carries no marker of any kind — no cairn, no post, no blazed tree — so the test is the fork rather than a landmark: carrying straight on to the east takes you toward the far creek and away from the mountain, while the summit line turns left, to the north, and goes straight up the ridge. If you are still among flower meadow and old-growth stands you are in the basin below and have not reached the saddle at all. The upper ridge is roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting loose scree, sand and broken rock with the track fading in and out. Accounts disagree about whether there is one false top or several undulating bumps below the summit, so treat any high point with more ridge rising beyond it as another bump rather than the end.

approach_variants.name: Standup Creek trail

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
bivy.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
bivy.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is prohibited anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

approach_variants.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.
hazards: Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge
Boot path on the upper southwest ridge; descent on loose sandy scree is more error-prone

approach_variants.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the Tepeh Towers saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a small col at the toe of the ridge, at the top of the McALLISTER glacier's 30-degree apron, and the thing directly above it is a line of gendarmes on the crest. Gendarmes on the skyline above a small col at the top of the apron is the confirmation.

Cross the moat at the col, not at the snow gully. There is an alternative snow gully nearby that parties sometimes use to gain the ridge, and it is guarded by a large moat that usually still needs a short rappel to bypass. The route's own start is easy fifth-class rock straight off the small col at the toe. If you are eyeing a snow gully with a big gap at its head, you are looking at the alternative, not the route.

The length test is decisive on this peak because the four routes are wildly different lengths: this one is three pitches, each well under 25 m. If you are running full rope lengths, or if you are still climbing after three, you are on the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from the other side) or the East Ridge (a long day off a different col).

A fixed-gear confirmation, and a warning with it: the crest carries a lot of old fixed slings on rock horns left by earlier parties, and higher up a piton marks a slabby section leading to a V-slot gully. Plenty of tat on horns is a sign you are on the trade line — but it is aging tat, an anchor block has failed here before, and it should be backed up rather than trusted.

And know which side of the needle you are on: this route is reached by climbing the McAllister's apron northwest. The Southwest Buttress lines are reached by continuing to the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass and dropping about 700 vertical ft to a snow gully below it. The East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle. Three different cols; check which one you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
approach_variants.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the toe of the buttress at the foot of a prominent, often year-round snow gully, and the gully is located by descending — it starts about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

At the top of that gully there is a fork, and it is the one thing on this peak most worth getting right. This route goes around to the right. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes straight up from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

The strongest negative test is published as a warning and it is worth carrying verbatim: do not climb directly below the ridge crest at the start. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 overhanging terrain on loose rock. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

Confirm on pitch one: it is a full rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly right, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

And confirm by which col you crossed: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish). Walk the pleasant, level main Barclay Creek trail for about 20 minutes and roughly a mile to a bridge crossing a large creek — often dry by mid-to-late summer.

Do not cross the bridge. Just before it, break right into the forest around a large boulder. Bushwhack through relatively open forest, or walk the creek bed, until you reach an open boulder field. Cross the boulder field to large trees and an open wash.

The wash leads to a steep, chossy, dirty waterfall; climb around its right side, staying out of the bushes — this stretch is exposed. Above that a ramp with hand lines, then a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, including a low-fifth step in a gully protected by a fixed line, and a small rock face with a bolt. Then roughly 800 ft of mostly roped slab in 35-50 m pitches on bolts and natural gear. Competent parties with good beta take two and a half to four hours; the approach is technical and hard to get right even with information.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Exposed scrambling around the right side of the chossy waterfall
Fixed lines of unknown age and condition
60-70 degree forested rib — a fall here is not survivable ground
Loose rock and brush throughout
Route-finding: the correct line is not obvious even with beta
approach_variants.baseFinding: The end of the fixed and roped section is where you unrope and scramble up and left to the base of the tower. The test the first-ascent party wrote down is a negative one and it is the most useful thing on this approach: if what you are doing feels sketchy, you are off the line. The approach is unpleasant but it is protected the whole way — fixed lines, hand lines, bolts — so unprotected, committing ground means you have lost the route, not that the route has got harder. The base of the tower is the foot of a nearly 1,500 ft overhanging prow; there is no mistaking it once you are under it.

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Eye Col
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror around 6,050 ft, head west and drop about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek. Traverse north through Crescent Creek Basin, keeping the party together through the scree to limit rockfall and hugging the cliffs, then make a rising traverse beneath the Eye Col gully that carries you past an adjacent buttress rather than straight up at it. The notch at about 7,400 ft is reached by continuing past a gully that would otherwise force a rappel — that decoy gully is the thing to walk by. The last stretch to the col is scree you walk up rather than rock you climb.
approach_variants.season: Mid Jul-early Sep
hazards: Constantly falling rock in the Eye Col gully
Steep, loose gully climbing with genuine route-finding uncertainty on this south side
Disorienting in cloud or low light — the south side carries comparatively sparse route information
A multi-day committing approach over The Barrier before any of this begins
approach_variants.baseFinding: Chockstones are the gate, and the view through the col is the confirmation. Going up toward the Eye Col, the small chockstones low in the gully present no real problem and are scrambled past; higher, the larger chockstones put the ground into fifth class, and that size change is where the rope comes out. If you are still stepping over rubble you are low; if you are stemming past a jammed block you are at the transition. The Eye Col itself is the notch between East and West Twin Needle, gained on scree from the south, and it announces itself: from it you get your first sight through the gap to the Northern Pickets, and East Twin Needle stands directly above it. Know which line you intend before you leave the col — the Eye Col sits on the west side of East Twin Needle, while the peak's hard, tremendously exposed east arete is on the opposite flank and is reached along the ridge from the east, not from here.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a dug-in boot path; kicked rock runs onto parties below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies, correct one hidden until you round a buttress
Small summit area becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
South point is a steeply inclined slab; a slip runs down the East Face
Nearby sub-summits are convincing and have been tagged by mistake
No water beyond the meadow
Remote, minimal cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The small boggy meadow where the trail turns sharply left is the departure. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

approach_variants.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The trails in have been closed by the Little Giant Fire closure; check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for current closures before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

approach_variants.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan.
hazards: Approach trails affected by a wildfire closure; check status before going
Boat-dependent access from Lake Chelan
Rockfall and loose rock in the erosion-carved west gully
Exposure on the south summit slab toward the East Face
Basin tarns unreliable by mid-August; camp fully exposed to weather from the west
Remote, minimal cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
approach_variants.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
Scree gully descent off the col and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
Long open ridge fully exposed to afternoon weather
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: A larch forest and then Fifth of July Pass is the gateway to the south ridge. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
camps: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.
hazards: Burned and downed timber on the lower Entiat River and Cow Creek Meadows trails
Footbridge gone at the river crossing near the 4-mile mark
Open unmarked cross-country routefinding above Cow Creek Meadows
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Sun exposure and limited water on the steep final trail mile into the meadows
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
camps: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
approach_variants.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread through the woods; two ways to end up in the wrong basin
600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on return
Talus degrades from solid boulders to fist-size rock moving underfoot
Loose rubbly gneiss throughout
Access only by Stehekin ferry or floatplane and shuttle; long evacuation
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

approach_variants.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
approach_variants.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.
hazards: Long, involved route over Tenmile Pass and down into upper Riddle Creek before traversing to Castle Creek basin
Loose rubbly gneiss and shifting talus on the summit slopes
Remote wilderness; long evacuation if injured
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier, then north to the foot of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft on Cascade River Road, the old Diamond Mine roadbed runs about a mile to the mine site, then the climbers' path climbs hard through forest with four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at about 6,400 ft. From high camp, follow the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier up to about 7,500 ft and climb to Sharkfin Col at 7,720 ft — roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and 200 ft of a class 3 gully to gain it, on loose scree underfoot. The col is the commitment. From it you rappel roughly 100-150 ft, in one or two stages depending on snow, down a loose gully onto the Boston Glacier; retreat after that means re-climbing to the col. Traverse north through crevassed ground toward the north end of the glacier, then re-ascend to the ridge. Three Forbidden routes cross Sharkfin Col and use this rappel. Where you leave the Boston Glacier is what separates them.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, for dry rock and a glacier that is still bridged where it matters
hazards: A rappel of roughly 100-150 ft (depending on snow) down a loose gully off the col, with rope-snag on loose rock, and no easy retreat once you are down it
A heavily crevassed traverse of the Boston Glacier where a fall would be serious
A distinct moat where the glacier meets the North Ridge rock, sometimes needing technical work to exit, and worse late season
Steep snow gully sections on the ridge itself where a slip runs uncontrolled onto the Boston Glacier
A long, exposed crest with the descent on a completely different side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
First, identify Sharkfin Col correctly, because everything after it is committed. It is the low point on the ridge immediately left of Sharkfin Tower — a distinct rock tower stands beside it. A notch on that skyline with no tower beside it is not the col. You gain it by about 10 ft of 5.7 and a 200 ft class 3 gully; if you walked up to it, you are somewhere else.

Second, on the Boston Glacier, go north and keep going. The base of this route is at the far north end of the glacier, where the ice meets the foot of the ridge, and the crossing point is itself a notch rather than an arbitrary spot on the crest. You should pass a rock buttress on the way; if you have turned uphill without passing it, you have turned too early.

The positive test at the base is the first move, and it is unambiguous: the climbing starts with a short, steep left-facing corner at 5.6, straight off the col at the foot of the ridge. That corner is the route's crux and it is the first thing you climb. If the first ground above the glacier is 300 ft of low-angle rock leading toward an ice patch, you are on the northeast face and you turned west off the glacier far too soon.

And you should be at a col, not on a face. The base is the gap between Boston and Forbidden: ground falls away on both sides of you. If the mountain is above you and glacier below you and nothing behind, you are under a face, not at the col.

Confirm as you climb: above the corner the crest passes a wildly exposed bivy platform — two small snow-free spots just below the crest on the northeast side — and above roughly 8,400 ft the rock notably improves. Poor rock all the way to the top means you never got onto the upper ridge.

approach_variants.name: Sharkfin Col, the schrund rappel and an ice wall, then west across the Boston Glacier to the ice patch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft. Continue along the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col at about 7,720 ft, gained by roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and a class 3 gully.

The first-ascent party rappelled from the col into the bergschrund and climbed a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the Boston Glacier. Expect the schrund to be the awkward part of the day before the climbing starts.

From the glacier, traverse west — a short traverse, not the long northward one the North Ridge makes — to the base of the face.

This line is climbed rarely enough that no fixed gear should be assumed and modern first-hand descriptions are scarce; treat any description of it, including this one, as an outline.
approach_variants.season: Late spring to early summer, when the face still holds the best ice and snow
hazards: A rappel into a bergschrund and a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the glacier
A north-facing ice feature that has thinned over recent decades — verify there is ice deep enough to take a screw rather than assuming it
Everything on the face funnels through the ice patch, so it is the exposed spot for anything released from above
A remote position with a long, complex retreat and a descent by the West Ridge on the far side of the peak
So few ascents that conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ice patch is the landmark and your position relative to it is the whole test. From the Boston Glacier a large, conspicuous patch of ice sits on the lower face — about 300 ft tall. You start on rock below and to the left (west) of it, not on it and not to its right.

So the first-move test is: rock first, ice second. About 300 ft of rock, protected by a few pitons on the first ascent, comes before you reach the ice at all. If you are swinging tools within a rope-length of leaving the glacier, you have started too far right — you are on the patch itself rather than the rock beside it.

Count the three sections in order: 300 ft of rock, then 300 ft of ice at about 50 degrees, then about 600 ft of steep-looking but upward-dipping slabs to the top. A route that stays on one medium the whole way is not this one.

Tell it from the North Ridge by how far you walked. Both cross Sharkfin Col and use the same schrund rappel. The North Ridge then traverses a long way north to the far end of the Boston Glacier and starts at a col with ground falling away on both sides. This route turns west after a short traverse and starts under a face. If you walked past a rock buttress and kept going, you have gone to the North Ridge.

A genuine naming trap, worth knowing before you leave camp: Forbidden's 'northeast face route' is sometimes used loosely to mean a high traverse below the east ridge that skirts the gendarmes — an easier, quite different line, and the one some descent descriptions mean. This route is the technical ice-patch face above the Boston Glacier. If the description you are following has you traversing under a ridge crest rather than climbing a face, you are reading about the other thing.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail #1513 and the Pass No Pass way-trail
approach_variants.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead at 2,800 ft, follow Buck Creek Trail #1513 roughly nine to nine and a half miles, climbing through forest and an old avalanche debris field near 4,500 ft.

The turn is the thing to watch for and it is not marked: an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail bears right at about 5,800 ft. Follow the way-trail to Pass No Pass near 6,400 ft and the alpine camping benches beyond it, from which the face and the south ridge come into view.

Storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground around mile 16 (check its status before you go), adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way before you even reach the trailhead.

From a high camp in the Pass No Pass basin, parties report about three and a half to four hours up and two and a half to three back.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best Jul-Sep once the south-west face has melted out; an axe and sometimes crampons for early-season snow on the approach slopes below the pass
hazards: The direct south-west gully is the loosest ground on the mountain and is directly above anyone below
Steep snow on the approach slopes below Pass No Pass into early summer, needing self-arrest skills
An unmarked way-trail junction at about 5,800 ft that is easy to walk past on a nine-mile approach
Creek crossings and brushy, indistinct trail lower down
Roughly seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The pass is where the mountain becomes visible, and that is the arrival test: from Pass No Pass and the benches beyond it, Fortress's south-west face and south ridge come into view. Below the pass you cannot see the peak at all. If you are still walking with no mountain in front of you, you have not crossed it.

The climbing starts at a change of surface, not at a feature. From the basin below the pass, green slopes and scree steepen into Class 2-3 talus and slab. There is no step, no toe and no notch to arrive at — grass gives way to rock and that is the base.

The negative marker is the most useful sentence on this route: the direct gully up the face is the loosest ground on the mountain. If you are in a defined gully with rubble moving under every step, you are on the line to avoid, not the line to take. Angle right onto slabbier rock, or follow the south ridge crest instead. A party in 2015 found and cairned an alternate Class 3 line over more solid blocky terrain to skier's right of the gully, and later parties have followed it — so cairns on solid blocky ground here are a good sign, which is the reverse of the situation in the gully.

The discriminator against the other side of this peak: the East Ridge is reached from the Chiwawa-Fortress col at about 7,200 ft, approached cross-country off the Chiwawa River Trail, and it starts with a loose Class 3-4 gully onto a crest of notably better rock. Nothing on that route involves a way-trail or a named pass. If you walked over a pass to get here, you are on the south-west side.

The summit block is talus. There is no technical finish on this route; if you are looking at a fourth-class step you have wandered onto the east side's ground.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Road pulloff to the base of the west peak slab
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 east of North Bend, east on Edgewick Road, then right at the stop sign after 0.4 miles onto SE Middle Fork Road, which becomes FR 56. Drive about 12.3 miles to the Middle Fork / Taylor River junction just after the Taylor River bridge, keep right on the Middle Fork Road and go about a mile to a small gravel pulloff — five cars at most — near 47.54604, -121.52151 at about 1,174 ft. Washouts on the Middle Fork road have periodically added a mile or more of walking.

The path leaves the road a hundred to two hundred yards further along, on the left, marked by a cairn. From there it climbs steeply through forest switchbacks for roughly 30 to 45 minutes. The tread is not signed but it is genuinely worn: if you have been walking more than a few minutes on ground that does not look like a trail, you are off it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Rockfall down the lower slab pitches — bent hangers record it
Steep, loose, unsigned approach tread
Road washouts on the Middle Fork road adding approach distance
No water on the approach or the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
About 50 yards below the start of the climbing there is a large cairn built of flat white rocks — by a clear margin the biggest cairn on the approach trail, and the marker to look for. The base itself sits near 47.549, -121.5137 at about 1,700 ft.

From there the confirmation is bolts. This is a continuous bolted line up the slab, so a slab with no bolts on it is not the route. Two supporting details: the lower pitches are easy, low-angle and somewhat runout on solid, sometimes water-polished slab; and several hangers down there are visibly bent from rockfall coming down the route, which both identifies the ground and tells you why to keep moving through it. Parties simulclimbing the easy lower pitches have gone off-track precisely by not tracking the bolts.

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 near North Bend, then Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) past the Taylor River bridge junction to a pullout roughly 2.6 miles further on, beside a gravel wash. From the car the whole route is only about 1.5 miles horizontally but 4,400 vertical feet.

Start up the dry creek bed and leave it partway up into the woods, following a mix of pink flagging tape and faint tread up steep pine-needle slopes — 'scrumbling', pulling on whatever vegetation is at hand. Low down the path braids: take the higher up-and-down traverse rather than the flat early one that cuts to the slab too low. About an hour in, at roughly 2,200 ft, you reach the dirt gully.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, bone dry only
hazards: Loose 40-degree duff above the slab
No water above the trailhead creek
Slabs lethal when damp
Braided boot path low down
Exposed ledge traverse below the Y Notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The dirt gully at about 2,200 ft is the gate, and the first major slab at about 2,900 ft is the base. Clean rock after one to two hours of nothing but duff and scree is the confirmation. Reaching slab without having passed through the dirt gully means you took the low traverse and are too far along the base — go up and left.

Above the slab the pine-needle slopes run about 40 degrees on loose duff, and huckleberry stems make the best handholds. The sequence above is the tiny notch, the razorback, the glade saddle, the wooded ramp with a 20 ft step, the exposed ledge traverse, and then the Y Notch where the route joins the gully system. Reaching the Y is what confirms you are on the South Route rather than on one of the neighbouring gully lines.

approach_variants.name: Conrad Meadows and the Surprise Lake loop to the Meade Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin. Pass between a pair of big mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep snowfield below the summit requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
A receding glacier that can still hide crevasses and moats
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Basin navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Leaving the trail in the right place and finding the foot of the Meade is the whole route-finding problem, and everything before it is trail.

Take the right fork of the Surprise Lake loop and stay on it to its high point. From there climb west into a basin, pass between the pair of big mounds, and drop a short way to the foot of the glacier. If you are climbing onto a long ridge crest before you have reached any snow, you are on the ridge line to the south, not this route.

On the glacier, one rock band organises everything. It splits the lower glacier from the upper; go up near the center of the cirque and pass it on its right. Above it, stay right of the snow dome and the ridge comes easily.

The base of the scramble is a small saddle, and the summit is just west of it. From the ridge a rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to that saddle; the true summit is immediately to its west, a short, loose class 3 scramble. If the ground keeps rising well beyond a gap, you are at the wrong gap.

The negative that separates this from its sibling on the same peak: this line reaches the Meade from below, out of the basin. The other route from this trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit and drops onto the Meade from above. If you are on the Conrad Glacier, you are on that one instead.

Self-arrest is part of the base finding here, not an afterthought: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the foot of the glacier.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flats and the Goat Ledges traverse to the black prow
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat trailhead in the Chambers Lake area on the west side of the Goat Rocks, at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Hike Snowgrass Trail #96 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow; the flat itself is closed to camping, so camp at the established sites below it.

From camp, head cross-country and scramble east across the Goat Ledges and Goat Ribs — a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies — at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. This is often combined with Old Snowy and Ives in a single traverse day.

A lower variation holds a consistent traverse elevation of about 7,500 ft, which reduces exposure to rockfall knocked down by other parties.

The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous. Careful route-finding along the correct band and on goat paths is what makes it a reasonable class 4 passage rather than a bad one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the ledges are dry
hazards: Significant rockfall on the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse, worst with parties stacked at different elevations
Loose andesite, pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain
Steep, insecure sections approaching the summit block even in dry late-season conditions
Route-finding failure — the whole route depends on correctly identifying the white aggregate band
A class 4 downclimb through the notch on the way back, on the same loose ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The white band is the route. That is the entire finding and it is a colour test, which is why it survives bad light.

On the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft there is a band of solid, abrasive, white pyroclastic aggregate. It points at a notch behind a prominent dark rock tower — the black prow. So there are two objects to find and they are opposite colours: a white band and a dark tower, with the notch behind the tower.

The negative is tactile and it tells you immediately, without a view: the white band is solid and abrasive. The rock above it and below it is loose. If the holds are moving under your hands you are off the band — traverse back to the white rather than pressing on.

Hold your height at about 7,500 ft. Drifting high is worse than drifting low: it puts you above the band and above other parties, in the position that generates the rockfall this traverse is notorious for. The low variation is a deliberate choice, not a mistake.

The base of the climbing is the notch behind the black prow. Everything before it is traversing; the class 4 finish begins there. If you are scrambling steeply and you have not passed a dark tower, you have started up too early.

What going too far looks like: the traverse ends at the peak. If the ribs and gullies keep coming and you have not found a white band pointing anywhere, you are on the wrong tier of the mountain — go back to a rib you can identify and re-find the band, rather than gaining height to look.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and it is also reached from the Suiattle side. The walk in from there is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is normally reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly eighteen miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain, and a fire closure has also shut the upper Suiattle River Road, the Suiattle River Trail and the PCT from Mica Lake north; check with the Darrington Ranger District before planning this way in.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms and is closed to vehicles at that point under a closure order that runs into 2028 unless lifted sooner, with the campgrounds and trailheads up the road closed.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: Walk in may be far longer than the mileage because the road is closed at milepost 3.7
8,200 ft of gain from the trailhead
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the centre. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

What hugging the left wall costs: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
camps: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
approach_variants.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.
hazards: Long approach with real elevation loss on the way to the bench below the glacier
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation

approach_variants.name: Spur road end to Klinger Ridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail from the car. The line goes straight into thick huckleberry toward the talus above, but the mossy streambed running alongside that brush is far easier travel even though the rock underfoot is slick. Follow the drainage and its talus up into a rock basin around 4,300 ft, then make a rising traverse across talus into a gully and climb a heathered slope beneath a cliff band, which dodges a slide-alder tangle, onto the open meadow crest above 4,600 ft. Fog sits in the lower basin well past sunrise, and there are no markers to steer by.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: Slick moss in the lower streambed
Standing dead timber and heavy regrowth across the burned south side of Klinger Ridge
Morning valley fog on ground with no trail to follow
Loose, exposed granite at the summit notch
A short near-vertical downclimb with loose rock at the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at a notch just west of a prominent standing rock tower at about 5,300 ft, and the way to it is not the obvious one. Do not try to hold the literal east ridge crest — it cliffs out and does not go through as a route. From roughly 4,800 ft weave up through steep granite blocks and cross a final talus field to the notch, which is the gap immediately beside the one unmistakable tower on that stretch of crest. There is a decoy lower down: a single cairn near the meadow crest around 4,600 ft pulls parties off the direct line, and staying in the gully to about 4,800 ft is the straighter way. The move that confirms you are at the base is a DOWNclimb rather than a climb — a short, steep, near-vertical step drops off the south side of the notch, loose in places and the most exposed ground on the route, and only once you are through it does the gully below the summit block open up for the final class 3-4 scramble to the top.

approach_variants.name: Skyline Divide Trail #678 and the long open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Access first: from Glacier, WA drive SR-542 about a mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS-39), turn right, then immediately left onto Deadhorse Road (FS-37). FS-37 normally runs 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide trailhead. FS-37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle. Confirm before planning around it.

When open, Skyline Divide Trail #678 climbs through old-growth switchbacks into meadows and reaches the ridge crest at about 2 miles and its high point near 6,563 ft at about 4.5 miles. From there the route is cross-country along the open ridge — roughly three miles of it — to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley's summit block.

The trail's high point on the crest near 6,563 ft is the landmark parties use to re-find the maintained trail on the way back.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct — this trailhead may not currently be reachable at all
hazards: FS-37 closed at mile 0.03 during washout repair — the trailhead is not drivable until the work ends
Three miles of cross-country open ridge with no tread and no cairns
A short Class 3 step above loose scree and talus
Two unmarked divides converging on one summit, with very different roads at the bottom
No water once past the meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The 6,563 ft high point is the gate, in both directions. It is where maintained trail ends and where you rejoin it. In cloud it is the only reliable waypoint on this approach, because everything beyond it is three miles of undifferentiated open ridge. Note it on the way out — parties who do not, spend the return walking a crest that all looks the same.

The crest is the handrail. From the viewpoint the route runs south along the ridge and then southeast along Chowder Ridge, roughly three miles in all. Keep the crest under your feet with air on both sides; this ridge has heather benches falling away either side and it is easy to drift onto one and lose the line.

Arrival at the climbing: the summit block is a short class 3 step above loose scree and talus — the last stretch of the day and the only scrambling on it. Walking stops, one short step of rock, summit. That is the whole climb, and it is the test: if you are scrambling for a long time, you are on a false feature; if you have not left your feet, you are not there.

The discriminator against the other approach to this same block: Cougar Divide arrives on Chowder Ridge from the north, straight up its own ridge, and its trail high point is 5,920 ft. Skyline arrives from the west after roughly three miles of ridge from the 6,563 ft high point. If you are descending in poor visibility, going down the wrong divide puts you 11 miles of gravel road away from your car on a road that may itself be washed out.

approach_variants.name: Sahale ski track and the south-side talus fans
approach_variants.notes:
Park somewhere along Alpental Road. Parking on the road near the Sahale Ski Club is sometimes possible, but it often is not and you may have to leave the car further away and walk. Respect the posted no-parking on the private sections.

From there head up the Sahale ski track toward Guye for roughly three quarters of a mile to a mile. Where the track starts to peter out, climb through the boulder field and a short band of slide alder to reach the base of the cliff.

Then traverse east along the base of the wall. You will pass Blood Sport on the way. Keep going until you reach a taller talus fan, and go up that fan to the cliff.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct as rock; also done in winter
hazards: rockfall on the talus and in the gullies
slide alder between the boulder field and the base of the cliff
limited and partly private parking on Alpental Road
the ski track fades rather than ending at a definite point, so the turn-off uphill is judged not signed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The taller talus fan east of Blood Sport is the marker, and it is a comparative one rather than a described one: it reaches noticeably higher up the wall than any of the talus you passed getting there. When the ground under you starts climbing the face rather than just banking against it, that is the fan you want.

Blood Sport itself is the negative marker. It is a bolted line at the base of the south wall — arriving at it tells you that you are on the right side of the mountain but have not traversed far enough east. Do not start up there.

If you are still on the ski track with the wall above and to your left, you have not yet reached the point where the track fades and you are below the traverse entirely.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: An icy, choss-and-moat gully to the col in late season
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass
Two Barrier crossings, both loose and exposed, with rockfall onto any party below
No reliable water between the Goodell roadbed and treeline
No bolted or fixed rappel stations anywhere on the route; all anchors are built
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at a col you reach by a narrow gully, and the gully's character changes completely through the season. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto Col. In early season that is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top. By late season it turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left, climber's left.

So the marker is the boulder, and it is a countable one: there is one overhanging boulder near the top of the gully, and getting past it on its left is the last obstacle before the col. If you have bypassed several such blocks, you are in the wrong gully.

Arrival: you are at the col when the gully tops out into a gap with ground falling away on the far side. From there the standard route continues on easier ground, scrambling to low 5th class, onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.

Two crossings of the barrier exist and both are correct: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mount Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour. Both are loose enough that a party above another is the real danger.

What going too far looks like: descending north from the Himmel-Otto col rather than climbing from it. The north side is a different and harder proposition and leads onto the Mustard Glacier.

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the wilderness. The tread climbs gradually through mixed conifer and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks, and can be brushy and overgrown low down. A spring in the patchwork burn scar and then the ford of the North Fork of Libby Creek are the reliable water, with an established campsite on the far bank. At roughly four and a half miles a decaying old cabin stands in the middle of the trail, and that is where the climbing route leaves. Note that the standard line does not go to Libby Lake at all — the lake is the left-hand continuation and a fine camp, but the peak is reached from the cabin.
approach_variants.season: July into early October; especially popular in late September and early October when the basin and approach slopes fill with golden larch. Snow can hold in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June.
hazards: Brushy, lightly maintained tread and unbridged tributary crossings low down
The boot path fades in the clearing above the cabin and there are no cairns anywhere on the route
Choose-your-own-line boulder hopping to gain the ridge, with harder and easier ways and no defined route
Loose and unstable blocks on the summit ridge; test holds before weighting them
Lingering snow into June
Downloadable tracks for this peak are known to be wrong — do not follow one blindly
approach_variants.baseFinding: The decaying cabin in the middle of the trail is the junction, and you go right of it. About four and a half miles in, an old collapsing cabin stands right in the trail. Continuing left or straight past it takes you up the final hill to Libby Lake; the peak is the faint boot path leaving to the right of the cabin, into open forest. That building is the whole of the marker — there is no sign and there are no cairns anywhere on this route. Follow the boot path to a large clearing, where it gives out; that is expected, because from the clearing the forest is open enough to see the peak's west ridge rising to the north, and you simply pick a line for it. Below the ridge is a boulder field, and gaining the crest from it is choose-your-own-adventure with harder and easier ways and nothing defined. Once on the ridge it is straightforward boulder hopping, with one thing to know: traverse climber's right of the summit spire and hook around it rather than trying to climb it head on. If you have arrived at a lake shore, you have walked past the cabin.

approach_variants.name: The short loop trail at the ranger station, then the west flank to the heather knoll
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,600 ft and pick up the short interpretive loop that begins there. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on the mountain's western flank. There is no trail above the loop.

The forest goes reasonably on the way up and badly on the way down: parties consistently report dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as the time sink of the descent rather than of the ascent, so mark your line as you climb rather than trusting to memory.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the west flank is clear of snow
hazards: no trail above the interpretive loop, and a descent through jackstraw deadfall and brush that is far slower than the ascent
a creek crossing at Howlett Creek
route-finding on a uniform forested flank with no landmarks below the knoll
