steep snowfields low on the route in early season
loose class 3 and 4 rock on the ridge above
reaching the ranger station at all depends on a boat or on a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival is a change of vegetation, not a change of angle. Climb the west flank until the timber gives out onto a heathery knoll at about 5,900 ft. That knoll is where the north ridge is gained and where the route starts. If you are still in timber, or in jackstraw deadfall and brush, you are below it - the knoll is open ground and unmistakable when you reach it.

The ridge above the knoll is the route, and it should have air on both sides. If you are climbing a face with the crest still above you and to one side, you have gained the flank rather than the ridge and should traverse to the crest before continuing.

Check which summit you are under. This is the north peak, the higher and broader of the two main summits. The other summit should be to the south of you. If the higher ground lies north and you are looking up at a tower with a rotten connecting ridge running toward it, you are on the south peak's flank instead, and the ridge between them is not a way to correct that - it is a notoriously rotten traverse that parties deliberately avoid.

A cross-check on the descent: you must find the knoll again to get back into the correct drainage. From above, the flank is uniform timber in every direction, and the drainage you came up is only identifiable from the knoll's position. Fix it before you leave it.

approach_variants.name: PCT past the Kendall Katwalk to a point due east of the summit, then straight up
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft, hike the PCT northbound past Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then past Alaska Pass and around Alaska Mountain to Huckleberry Flats. The Commonwealth Basin shortcut rejoins the PCT and saves about a mile, and is the recommended line.

Walk on until you are essentially due east of Huckleberry's summit — roughly nine to ten miles in. That bearing is the trigger to leave the trail, not a named junction.

Many parties make this two or three days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake; a fit party has done it car to car in about eleven and a half hours.

About 17.4 km and 4,600 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: Stiff class 3 with class 4 moves on an exposed ridge — not a beginners' scramble
A loose block at the notch below the summit block
A crumbly class 2 ledge traverse above a big cliff
Rockfall in the alternative gully on the left, which has turned parties around
No simple walk-off: a 60 m rope is needed for the rappel off the summit block
A very long day, with parties commonly splitting it over two or three
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Leave the PCT when the summit is due west of you — a bearing, not a landmark, which is exactly what you want in cloud. From that point head cross-country west up steep heather or talus.

The base of the climb is where the mellow terrain ends and the ground turns rocky, at about 6,100 ft, marked by a rocky buttress. That change underfoot is the arrival, and it is felt rather than seen.

And then comes the one decision that decides which route you climb, which is the most valuable thing on this page. At the base of the rocks you have two options: left takes you into a steep loose gully leading to a notch and the summit block — that is the older gully line, and it has turned parties around with rockfall. Right takes you up the ridge on class 3+ terrain — that is the East Ridge, the historic first-ascent route, and it is what most parties now climb. If you are in a loose gully, you have gone left.

How to follow it once committed, because it does not look obvious from below: the route goes up the right side of the east ridge, essentially linking clumps of trees, tree patch to tree patch. Looking up at it, the line is genuinely hard to piece together by eye; once you start, the next move is usually clear. Staying towards the right is correct at the beginning.

Checkpoints higher up: about halfway, maybe a little further, leave the ridge proper by heading left on a short traverse to a blocky ramp, which you climb to a high point just before the summit block. Then descend about 20 ft to the notch at the foot of the block — either straight down, or skiers' right and a class 3 traverse to a ramp leading down to the notch.

The summit block itself: go up the middle to an obvious slabby ramp. From there either a short class 5 crack — one piece, a #1 Camalot at its start, protects it — or follow the ramp climbers' left to exposed class 3/4. Bring a 60 m rope: a 30 m is insufficient for the rappel off the block.

Scale of the thing, so nobody underestimates it: there is no walk-up on this mountain, the scrambling is stiff class 3 with class 4 moves, and one of the 1915 first-ascent party wrote his will on his shirt cuff over doubts he would survive the descent.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead to Lake Ingalls, then the north-east notch gully
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and walk exactly as for the South Ridge: Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of FR 9737, right at the low fork onto Ingalls Way #1390, left at the higher fork where Longs Pass branches off, over Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, and on to Lake Ingalls at roughly 6,400-6,480 ft, about 4 miles and the last water.

The two routes part company above the lake. Skirt the lake on its left (west and north) side and cross a band of slabs to reach a large talus gully. A boot path shows itself in patches through the talus. This gully runs more directly than the South Ridge slabs and is steeper and looser — expect Class 2-3 scree with real rockfall potential if anyone is above you.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the approach gully holds snow well into summer and is often climbed on snow
hazards: Steep loose talus in the approach gully, worse with parties above
Lingering snow in the gully into midsummer
No water above Lake Ingalls
A 60 m rope comes up short on the shared South Ridge rappel descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the east ridge of the north peak, and the notch it starts from is the one on the far side of the summit from the South Ridge — between the North peak's eastern terminus and the separate East peak. Two obvious gullies rise off the ground above Lake Ingalls to two different notches on the same mountain, and choosing between them is the whole navigational problem here. The South Ridge's gully leads to the notch between North and South; this one leads round to the north-east side.

Going up, the arrival test is a change in the rock rather than a change in angle. Climb the obvious gully — usually snow early in the season — until you reach an odd, anomalous rock layer that does not match what you have been walking over. From there move about fifteen feet left and you are at the base. An alternative published description of the same spot has you looking right for a smaller third-class gully and starting where it stiffens into easy fifth-class rock; either way the marker is the change in the rock underfoot, not the height on the ridge.

Confirmation once you are moving: there are slings with rap rings at the top of the first pitch, used as the belay for the second. If you climbed a rope length and found nothing fixed, doubt the start.

Touch test: the rock through here is serpentine — greenish, slick, and quite unlike granite friction. That slickness is normal for this peak and is not a sign you are on harder ground than intended.

Positive marker that reads like a mistake: a couple of pitches up, after passing a mid-sized gendarme on its right, you are forced to downclimb about twenty feet of fourth class into a notch in the ridge. That downclimb is correct here and is evidence you are on the East Ridge, not that you have gone wrong. The easy knife-edge traverse midway along is the same kind of confirmation.

The descent is the South Ridge rappels, ending at three bolts at the top of that route — so the 60 m rope warning from the South Ridge applies to this climb too even though you never touch its approach.

name: East Peak (Northeast Ridge to East Face)

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Trail, Lake Ingalls and the North–East col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Ingalls Way Trail #1390 north beside the creek on an old mining-road grade. At the signed fork bear right onto #1390 where the Esmeralda Basin trail stays low and left, and at the second junction stay left where the Longs Pass trail branches east. Steady switchbacks through open larch lead to Ingalls Pass; cross it, drop slightly and follow cairns and boot track around the basin rather than giving up height, then climb a large steep boulder field to Lake Ingalls. Filter there — nothing above the lake holds water. A climbers' path skirts the east shore and heads up-basin toward the notch between the main summit and the horn-shaped East Peak.
approach_variants.season: July through September once the pass switchbacks melt out; microspikes and an axe are worth carrying into July in a heavy snow year.
hazards: The chossy central gully below the col is the main rockfall hazard on the approach — favour the clean slabs on the left
Several sub-gullies lead toward the notch and the largest, most direct one is the loosest and most dangerous
A great deal of loose rock on the route, so protection can end up run out on easy ground
Snow and ice on the upper trail switchbacks into July
The descent uses three rappel stations down the face — count them on the way up
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The chockstone is the proof for this route — and it is the error signal for the one next door, so do not treat it as a generic marker. Follow the climbers' path along the lake's east shore and head up-basin toward the obvious notch between the main Ingalls summit and the horn-shaped East Peak, favouring the clean granite slabs on the left over the loose central gully. Climb the obvious snow gully; partway up a distinctly odd-looking band of rock crosses it, and fifteen feet left of that band is where the neighbouring East Ridge route starts. This route does not stop there — carry on to the notch itself, where a single chockstone is wedged in the gap, and the climbing begins about fifteen feet above it at a comfortable belay ledge. That jammed block is the confirmation. Several sub-gullies lead up here and the largest, most direct one is the loosest and the one to avoid. From the ledge, the first pitch takes slabs trending slightly left into a gully to a belay on route, and the second trends right onto the crest over a great deal of loose rock; three rappel stations take you back down the face.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake, then the Home Creek basin to the boulder camp
approach_variants.notes:
From US 101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn onto Louella Road, go about a mile to Palo Alto Road and turn left for roughly 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes Forest Service Road 28. Turn right on FS 2880, pass Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead just across the Dungeness River bridge. Large parking area, vault toilet, no potable water, Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass required.

Hike Upper Dungeness Trail #833 up the river — easy, shaded, river-grade — to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. Continue on the Constance Pass trail as it climbs out of the timber into rocky flowery terrain beneath Warrior Peak and Inner Constance, crossing into Olympic National Park, and climb to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles and roughly 5,308-5,330 ft, some 500 ft below Constance Pass.

From the lake, work up the Home Creek basin toward the peak. Camp at the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. That boulder camp is the documented basecamp for this route and it is where the first-ascent party camped.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Rock quality described by climbers who have scouted it as among the worst in the Olympic Mountains, and as bad as anything in the range near the summit ridge
No fixed gear anywhere on the route — every rappel station on descent has to be built and left
Sparse protection with long runouts
The published description for this line is thin and climbers who know it advise ground-truthing it in person
A 9+ mile approach, and the same distance back out
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route starts at the top of a scree field where an obvious ramp begins, and the thing that identifies the ramp is the biggest corner on the face. From the boulder camp, climb the scree field to the base of the wall and pick up the obvious ramp. Follow it round climber's right of the prominent dihedral — the one large, unmistakable corner in that section of face — to a steep Class 3/4 gully. If the ramp you are on is taking you left of the big corner, you are on the wrong side of it. The second test is at the top of pitch one and it is a colour you can read at arm's length: after the first pitch this route turns climber's left onto an obvious ledge running along a green-lichen-covered face. Green lichen on rock is visible in cloud in a way a skyline feature is not. If your first pitch does not end at a ledge beneath a lichen-green face, you are not on the Northwest Buttress — and specifically, if you have carried straight on up a crack system instead of stepping left, you are on Sean's Route / Second Wind, which shares this start and diverges exactly here. What the route's own text already tells you, and it is the honest limit: the face is in full view from the boulder camp and from below, and that is described as the only reliable chance you get to pick out the ramp and the green-lichen ledge. Look at it, photograph it and fix the line in your head from camp. This is a route to identify in the evening and climb in the morning; there is no marker sequence that will find it for you if you walk up into the wall in cloud having never seen it.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone-arrow boot path to Terror Basin, then the crevassed Terror Glacier to the bergschrund below the west end of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first roughly 4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed at easy grades from about 500 to 1,600 ft, crossing the creek and passing the last reliable flowing water around 1,600 ft. Fill up there; the trail is dry above.

A cairned stone-arrow junction, sometimes marked and sometimes not, sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades. Parties widely describe this as the crux of the whole approach.

The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft into meadows, slabs and often snow, and a rising traverse north-northeast leads to a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically just below it in Terror Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing below the peak's south side; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
A bergschrund and a moat at the base that open through the season
Compact rock with scarce placements on the lower pitches
Loose blocks on the lower ledges
No water for the last 3,500 ft of the climb to camp
A rappel descent of 12-14 stations, with traversing raps that are rockfall-prone and stations that are hard to spot
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at a bergschrund and climbs 300 ft of gully to the toe of the ridge, and that is an exact instruction. From camp, cross heather and snow slopes trending north-northwest, losing a little elevation to cross the outlet drainage from a small tarn just southeast of the McMillan Spires, then regain ground on slabs and snow up to the edge of the Terror Glacier. Leave the glacier at the bergschrund below the west end of the peak and climb roughly 300 ft of gully to reach the toe of the west ridge, where the roped climbing begins.

So the schrund is the marker and the 300 ft is the measure. The schrund and the moat where snow meets rock are the variable part; they open through the season and the crossing is easiest with continuous snow early. A party that has climbed a short gully and reached the toe of a ridge is at the base; a party still on ice has not started.

The discriminator against the south face, which starts off the same glacier and is the commonest confusion here: the south face starts at the lower-left corner of the south face where a small rock buttress meets the glacier. This route starts at the west end of the peak, at a schrund, and goes up a gully first. If you are roping up at a buttress toe that touches the ice directly, with no gully above you, you are on the South Face.

Confirm on the climb: the first pitches work through corner systems and lichen-covered ledges on compact rock where placements are scarce. Above them the line gains the crest itself and the rock quality improves steadily, described as extremely good on the crest. Total climbing above the schrund is about 1,300 ft in 14 pitches. If the rock is good from the first pitch, you are not on the lower corners of this route.

A housekeeping rule from the route's own practice: loose blocks sit on the lower ledges and the standard practice is to clear them deliberately once the second is out of the fall line rather than leave them for a following party.

approach_variants.name: Iron Peak Trail #1399 to Eldorado Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead on the forest road just past the campground, Trail #1399 pitches up the moment it leaves the lot — there is no flat warm-up — with a creek audible through the trees on the left for the first few hundred yards. Cross that creek early and carry what water you need, because the trail then rides a rib between two drainages and the water goes out of reach and stays there. Switchbacks climb a south-facing forested slope, tightening and turning rocky as the trees thin, and bump over a minor ridge where the Eldorado Creek drainage becomes audible below to the east. The tread then works up the ridge above that drainage at a steady moderate grade to a broad open saddle where the maintained trail fades out.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October. Snow lies across the upper slopes into late June and can bury the tread on the last open stretch below the saddle.
hazards: The maintained trail carries on over the saddle and descends the far side — following tread instead of leaving it puts you in the wrong drainage
The only water is the creek in the first eighth of a mile; the rest is dry and the south-facing slope bakes in the afternoon
Lingering snow on the open crest into early summer, which hides the boot path
Loose rock and mild exposure on the west side of the upper crest
The scree slopes falling away west are steeper and looser than they appear from above
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the saddle the peak is to the south, and the higher summit to the north is the neighbour. This is the one thing to get right here, because the ridge you walk is called the north ridge and the direction you walk it is south — the two are easy to conflate. Eldorado Pass is the broad open saddle where the maintained trail stops being useful; from it, this peak lies roughly half a mile south-southeast, and the noticeably higher summit a short distance north-northwest is Teanaway Peak. The terrain settles it even if the compass does not: the way to this summit is a simple open ridge walk on a climbers' trail, on low brush and rock with the whole line visible ahead. The neighbour's route immediately traverses around the east side and climbs gullies, so if you are sidehilling east into broken ground within a few minutes of leaving the saddle, you have turned the wrong way. The other failure is not turning at all — the maintained trail continues over the saddle and descends the far side toward the creek trail below, so a party following tread ends up in the valley rather than on either peak.

approach_variants.name: Jerry Lakes and the bench below the east glacier
approach_variants.notes: The East Ridge is most often met as a descent, because parties who climb the North Ridge come over the summit and go down this way, but it is the better of the two to climb and it is reached from the opposite side of the mountain. Access is from the south: the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR 20 at about 1,900 ft, a ford of Canyon Creek, then the McMillan Park and Jackita Ridge trail gaining some 3,400 ft in four miles to the Crater Mountain trail, up past Crater Lake, and off-trail somewhere between 6,400 and 6,700 ft to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, drop across the Jerry Glacier and down into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps. Reckon on three days minimum, and note that the summit day begins by losing several hundred feet into the next basin north before any climbing starts. The ridge itself runs about 1,400 to 1,600 ft from its base up to roughly 8,600 ft, where it dies into the Southeast Ridge and a single common crest carries on to the top. Parties disagree sharply about the rock: the lower third is good blocky class three and four, the upper third is fractured and loose, and the published class four understates the ground — a recent party found three short pitches of fifth class, including a wildly exposed 5.0 step in the middle of the crest, and made one rappel lower down off existing tat. There is no other fixed gear, so carry slings and cord.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to mid-September
hazards: Fractured, loose rock on the upper third with almost nothing dependable to protect it
Sustained exposure along the whole crest, with a thousand feet of air below the middle section
The line strays off the crest to the north in the middle third, which is where parties lose it in descent
Only one existing anchor on the route, so every other rappel is one you build and leave
Collapsing snow fingers where the snowfield meets the toe of the east glacier
Long cross-country approach with no trail for the final miles, and 800 ft to regain on the way home
Very remote, with a difficult retreat from anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Jack's east and southeast ridges hold a small pocket glacier between them like a bay, and finding this route is entirely a matter of working out which side of that bay you are on. The Southeast Ridge is the bay's right-hand edge, the East Ridge its left, and the two merge at about 8,600 ft. From the Jerry Lakes camp the day starts by dropping several hundred feet into the basin to the north, then climbing the southeast arm to a level bench at roughly 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That bench is where the mountain's two commonly climbed routes part company, and the decision there is a single either-or. Traverse left and west on scree under the south face and you are on the standard South Face route, whose landmarks are unmistakable once you start seeing them: a small snowfield, then a larger one likened to a fish or a lobster claw, a refrigerator-sized boulder with rope slung round its middle, a stream that only runs in the afternoon, and a short class four step into a hidden chimney. If you are hunting for a slung boulder, you are on the wrong route. Traverse right and north instead, onto the snowfield beneath the pocket glacier, and a few hundred feet of scrambling gains the crest proper. The confirmation is the view over the back. There is a notch at about 7,000 ft on this ridge, and from it the ground falls away onto a big broken glacier dropping north toward Devils Creek; if you can see that, you are on the East Ridge and not the Southeast. The second check is the rock, which low down is good blocky class three and four, where the South Face is loose almost from the start. One trap worth knowing: there are two cols at about 7,200 ft on this trip, the Crater Mountain saddle on the approach and this bench, and they lie four miles apart, so an altimeter alone will not tell you which one you are standing on.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to mid-September
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout with little that holds protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a low fifth-class pitch where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late season
Very remote, several days from a road with no realistic quick rescue; the usual East Ridge descent is sustained loose class 4
approach_variants.baseFinding: Nobody climbs this ridge from its toe; you meet it partway up off the Nohokomeen Glacier, and exactly where to leave the ice is unsettled, so treat the aiming points below as the frame and read the ground. Climb the glacier up its centre, passing just to the right of the large rock that stands out on the ice, and head for the crest to the left of the summit tower rather than for the tower itself. The glacier runs out against rock at about 8,000 ft. The one unmistakable feature on the route is there: a hole clean through the rock, a keyhole big enough to squirm through, and that hole is how the crest is gained. Parties travelling in both directions have used it as their marker. Taken from the very top of the glacier the exit costs a pitch of wet, junky low fifth class and a scramble over greasy slabs, and the party who did it that way came away convinced an easier line onto the crest exists a little lower down, short of the glacier's top edge, so it is worth traversing under the rock and looking rather than forcing the highest weakness. Above the keyhole the confirmation is instant and unlike anything below it: a knife-edged crest of genuinely solid rock, which is rare on this mountain. If what is under your hands is fractured and rotten, you are not on the crest yet. One decoy matters. The north side's other line, the headwall, rises off the same glacier and tops out within minutes of the summit, so if the snow you are on runs straight to the top with no ridge left to travel, you are on the headwall and not this route. The North Ridge leaves the ice well below the summit and still has a long way to go: knife edge, then an exposed snow traverse south across and below the summit tower with occasional protection along the upper moat, and a final pitch of low fifth class up the East Ridge to the top at 9,066 ft.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek

bivy.name: May Creek Camp, Ross Lake
bivy.notes: Designated camp on the East Bank Trail about 8 miles from the East Bank trailhead, where climbers leave the trail for the north side of Jack Mountain. It can also be reached by water taxi. Used as a first night or as the camp on the way out.
bivy.water: Ross Lake and May Creek; treat
bivy.permit: Ross Lake NRA backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Designated lakeshore camp with several tent sites

approach_variants.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open.
objHaz: steep timber and cliff bands on the approach
hazards: Several flat miles of lake trail each way before the climb begins: a long, committing trip with no quick way out
Steep forest with cliff bands above May Creek, hard to navigate in the dark and far worse to descend
Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe; crevasses low on the glacier
Loose, fractured rock on the ridge with little that holds protection
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Very remote with no realistic quick rescue

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead, Crater Lake, and the pass between Crater Mountain's summits
approach_variants.notes: Ford Canyon Creek at the trailhead and climb Trail #738's switchbacks to the Crater Lake junction, carrying water from the creek. Follow the Crater Mountain trail to about 6,700 ft, then traverse up to the pass near 7,000 ft between Crater Mountain's main and east summits. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier toward Jerry Lakes, then work around to a camp near 6,000 ft on the east side of Jack. Summit day starts by crossing the rock col east of the Southeast Ridge and downclimbing onto the glacier.
hazards: the Canyon Creek ford at the trailhead, high and hazardous into midsummer
crevasses and steep snow on the Jerry Glacier, crossed both ways
icefall and crevasses on the narrow, broken Northeast Glacier
loose rock on the ridge above the glacier
a long committing position several days from the road

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to the Glee Peak saddle camp, then through the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the lower-left corner of the face
approach_variants.notes: Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground at about 600 ft and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the Highway 20 corridor. The first 3.75-4 miles follow an old, gently graded forest roadbed along Goodell Creek, brushy with some downed logs in the first mile, and crossing two boulder-strewn washout sections where the tread disappears into the creek's flood debris and you pick a line across large boulders. That is the trickiest route-finding of the lower approach. About 200 yards past the second washout, at an obvious campsite with a fire ring, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed, historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. That is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach. From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest, hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches, and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline a rising traverse across meadow, slab and early-season snow reaches a saddle or notch at about 6,200 ft near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the early-season water source; by late summer parties melt snow.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the first ascent was made in mid-June in a low-snow year
hazards: Two boulder-strewn washouts where the tread vanishes, the lower approach's route-finding crux
A broken Terror Glacier icefall with open crevasses that worsens through the season
A camp water source that dries out by late summer
A sustained multi-rappel descent down the West Ridge and then the South Face, with no bolts anywhere on the peak and fixed pin stations of variable quality
Loose rock in the descent gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on traversing rappels
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the lower-left corner of the South Face where a small rock buttress meets the glacier. That buttress is the start of the route. It is a place where rock touches ice directly, with no intervening gully, and that is what tells it apart from the peak's other lines.

The discriminator against the West Ridge, which leaves the same glacier: the West Ridge leaves at a bergschrund below the west end of the peak and then climbs about 300 ft of gully before any ridge. If there is a gully above you, you have gone past this route's corner and are set up for the West Ridge.

Getting there is the icefall problem, not a navigation one: from camp, rope up and cross the Terror Glacier. The icefall in its middle is broken and often has open crevasses; parties commonly work a left-trending snow ramp or ice bridge above a large crevasse to get through it onto gentler slopes beyond. That crossing gets more serious as the season progresses.

So the handrail through the icefall is the large crevasse itself: the way through is above it, trending left. If you are dropping below the big crevasse looking for a bridge, you are on the wrong side of the feature parties use.

A countable approach marker lower down that saves the whole day: two washouts, then 200 yards, then a fire ring. That is how you find the turn in poor light. A stone arrow may or may not still be there; the second washout and the fire ring are ground features that do not move.

approach_variants.name: Tatoosh Creek, the timber band and the Lane-Denman saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road, open roughly late May through mid-October, or from Narada Falls when the road is gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber gains the road.

Walk the road roughly half a mile to where it bends sharply and begins heading east. Leave the pavement there and drop south through sparse open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft, losing a couple of hundred feet. Cross the creek — a rock-hop most of the season, more involved at peak snowmelt — and angle up a broad talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.

At the top of the talus, continue up through trees staying right of a short cliff band. Roughly 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft, you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue to the broad Lane-Denman saddle at about 5,440 ft.

From the saddle, turn right and climb moderate open ground to the gully weakness in the southeast face. Follow it up, trending left near the top for a final short scramble to the summit. Round trip is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain, and no water past Tatoosh Creek.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Cliffing out in the brushy timber band if the line drifts left of the cliff band
Loose rock and rockfall in the narrow summit gully, especially with parties above
Exposed fourth-class moves just below the true summit
Tatoosh Creek can be difficult during high spring runoff
Afternoon thunderstorms are common over this range in summer
Inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully once it melts out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route is on the other side of the mountain from the three couloirs, and the mistake it invites is walking into the north-face basin with the ice climbers. The single clearest separator is Tatoosh Creek: the couloir routes stay low in the basin. This route crosses the creek and climbs the other side.

The sequence, each item a check, in order:
1. Off the road at the 90-degree bend, south, down to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Cross it.
2. Up a talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.
3. Into trees, staying right of a short cliff band. This is the one place on the route where an error commits you to bad ground — the timber is brushy and drifting left cliffs you out. If you find yourself under rock in the trees, traverse back right before gaining more height.
4. Break out of the trees about 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft.
5. Arrive at the broad Lane-Denman Saddle at about 5,440 ft.

The saddle test is a count of peaks: you should have high ground on both sides of you — Lane on one hand, Denman on the other. A col with only one peak above it is not this saddle.

From the saddle, turn right — west. Denman is the other way, and it is an easy mistake in cloud because both directions climb.

The base of the climbing is the obvious gully weakness in the southeast face, and it is the feature the route is named for. The confirmation inside it is an object: a sturdy tree roughly 200 ft up the climbing, which is the main anchor and the rappel point. Reaching a good tree in the gully means you are in the right gully.

Last: trend left near the top for the final short scramble. Plentiful holds, minimal exposure — if it feels serious, you have drifted out of the gully onto the face.

approach_variants.name: Silver Star Creek to the east prow of Juno Tower
approach_variants.notes: Clean Break faces east, and the direct line to it is the Silver Star Creek drainage rather than the Burgundy Creek path used for the Wine Spires. Park at the small pullout on SR-20 roughly eight and a half miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses the creek and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward the foot of Juno Tower. At about 5,000 ft, make a rising traverse leftward across the slope; taken at the right height this threads most of the slide alder and lands you under the tower's east prow. Parties reverse this on descent, or cross west and drop back to the highway on the standard Burgundy Col trail.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slide alder on the rising traverse below the wall
Rockfall onto the lower pitches from parties above
Fifteen pitches with the crux in the first hundred feet — a committing day once started
Afternoon storms on an exposed east prow
approach_variants.baseFinding: The fixed pin beside a deep narrow gully is what settles it. The rising traverse from about 5,000 ft ends on a ledge under the east prow of Juno Tower. Find the deep, narrow gully that splits the wall: the route starts on the ledge immediately to its left, at a low anchor pin driven into the rock. Above that ledge is the feature the climb is named for — a single dead-vertical, clean-cut thin-hands splitter in white granite, roughly a hundred feet of it, with no alcove, chimney or vegetation anywhere in it. If the crack above you widens into a chimney, or you are standing in the gully bed rather than beside it, you are right of the start. If the rock above you is grey and broken rather than white and clean, you have wandered onto the flank of the prow instead of its nose.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass trailhead to the couloir apron
approach_variants.notes:
Effectively no approach at all. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft, walk back down the road — accounts range from a quarter mile to just under a mile depending on where you drop in — then descend a dirt and brush embankment into the valley and cross the Cascade River. In spring the river is often still snow-covered where you cross.

Over the terminal moraine and a snowfield, and within about twenty minutes of dropping off the road you are putting crampons on at the apron at roughly 3,300 ft. From there it is about 3,000 ft of continuous booting to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

In a big snow year Cascade River Road may be gated well below the trailhead — one ski party found it gated at mile 18 but snow-free to the last hairpin, and used bikes for the road section. Budget for that possibility rather than assuming you can drive to the end.

Season is the whole decision on this route. Early season is when the snow is continuous. As the Sill Glacier breaks up, the snow in the couloir goes discontinuous where it narrows near the hanging glacier and the breaks turn into a series of separate problems; by mid to late summer it is broken and considerably more hazardous.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun, while the Sill Glacier snow is still continuous
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier over the whole couloir
Discontinuous snow where the couloir narrows, worsening through the season
Cascade River crossing — snow-bridged in spring, a ford later
Spring wet-slide activity in a 3,000 ft snow chute
Road may be gated miles below the trailhead in a heavy snow year
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is easy to find and the hard part is judging it, which is unusual on this list. The couloir is the obvious deep gash in the skyline directly between Cascade Peak on the left and Johannesburg on the right, and it is in full view from the trailhead parking lot and the last road switchbacks. Identify it from the car, in daylight, before you drop into the valley — this is the one approach here where you get a complete view of your line before committing to it, and you should use that. On the ground, you are at the base when the moraine and brush end and you step onto a continuous snow apron at around 3,300 ft. From the apron, looking up the couloir, the line is unambiguous — there are no alternative gullies to confuse it with. What you cannot see from the apron is the part that matters. The couloir narrows higher up near the obvious hanging glacier, and that is where the snow goes discontinuous as the season progresses. A base that looks perfect in July tells you nothing about the middle. Judge continuity from the road, where the whole 3,000 ft is in view, and be willing to turn around at the car. The honest caveat carried by every source that describes this line: it is the most direct route on Johannesburg and also the most dangerous, guarded by overhead rock and ice fall that is hard to justify once the snow is not continuous.

approach_variants.name: Down into the avalanche moat before the couloir narrows, then the left-hand rib
approach_variants.notes:
A quick approach directly from the car, which is the only quick thing about this route. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, descend to and cross the Cascade River, cross the terminal moraine, and gain the couloir apron.

The start is unusual and it is the route's signature: you downclimb into an avalanche moat to gain the rock, around 4,400 ft, on sketchy lichen-covered dirty slabs.

What follows is honest about itself — initial fourth class into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby horizontal gully traverse of about 60 ft at 5.5 with minimal protection, steep heather taken by finger-pressing rather than by holds, and then roughly 700 ft of genuinely good 5.6 rock leading toward a bivy site near the glacier, two pitches below the summit.

Two starts exist: the original 1951 line, faster but with a scary 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds about 500 ft on more logical terrain to avoid it.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, July and August, once the rib is snow-free enough to climb but before it goes fully dry and looser
hazards: Extensive loose rock and lichen-slick slabs from the very first moves
Vegetation-dependent, largely unprotectable terrain — the climbing is real but the protection often is not
Icefall and rockfall from the hanging glaciers 5,000 ft above the route
Rockfall on the shared East Ridge and Sill Glacier descent
A descent whose steep heather section is repeatedly named as the most dangerous part of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You go down to get on. That is the base finding and it is unlike anything else on this side of the mountain: from the moraine you downclimb into an avalanche moat to reach the rock, at roughly 4,400 ft. If you are stepping up onto rock rather than down into a gap, you have not found the start.

The counting test is the couloir's shape, and it separates this route from the variation that shares its name: leave the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir before it narrows. The 1957 variation gains rock higher, close to where the couloir visibly pinches down. If you have climbed the couloir until it constricts, you have passed this route's start.

Then count the ribs, because there are two and they almost touch down low: two parallel ribs jut off the same buttress. The 1951 route takes the left rib. The 1957 route takes the more prominent right one. They nearly intersect at the bottom and only diverge as you gain height, which is exactly why the choice has to be made deliberately rather than by following the ground.

The first-move test is vegetation, and here it is the positive sign rather than the warning: fourth-class ground leads straight into dense vertical tree-root climbing. If you are on clean rock from the start you are not on this rib — the 1963 Northeast Ridge, one line over, is explicitly the route with no bush climbing on it.

And if you are still in snow at the top, you climbed the couloir itself — the 1938 original — which finishes at the Cascade-Johannesburg col and never touches either rib.

approach_variants.name: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,150 ft, then the standard Eldorado climbers' path: forest, boulder field, treeline, and camps in Eldorado Basin / Roush Creek around 6,000-6,300 ft. Climb the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge near 7,500 ft, then traverse roughly a mile and a half north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft.

Klawatti Col is not the start of this route. Continue past it, along a lobe of the McAllister Glacier under Klawatti Peak's west face, about 0.4 mile to the next break in the ridge — the Klawatti-Austera Col at about 7,900 ft. The scramble takes about an hour from that col, up to two hours if you count from Klawatti Col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, when the crest and the connecting cols are snow-free enough to scramble
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration and the upper McAllister lobe
A moat at the Klawatti-Austera col that ranges from class 4 to class 5 depending on where you cross it
Exposure on narrow sections of the crest, where route-finding is what keeps the grade at third class
Loose rock on the ledge traverses around The Smokestack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Count the cols: you want the second one. Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft is where the peak's other two routes start; this route starts at the Klawatti-Austera col at about 7,900 ft, a further 0.4 mile north along the foot of Klawatti's west face and a hundred feet higher.

The second col identifies itself by being a problem, and it offers a choice of two crossings — which is itself the confirmation. Receding snow leaves a moat here. The lowest notch is class 5 downclimbing; a crossing to the right (southeast) of the lowest notch is class 4. Parties have also found an old rappel anchor at this col and used it. A col you walked over without choosing between two ways down is Klawatti Col, one short.

Gain the lower ridge on its east side — the crest itself is harder than it needs to be low down, and the east flank is the easy way onto it.

The Smokestack is the confirming landmark and it is unmistakable. Class 3 scrambling up the crest brings you to a rock tower around 8,400 ft that the route is named around. You do not climb it: go round it on its west side by a short gully and regain the crest above. A party that has climbed a tower on the ridge rather than walked around it has gone off route. A party that reached the summit without ever passing a tower was never on the North Ridge.

Negative test for the other direction: if the ground in front of you is a snow face rather than a ridge crest, you are below the south-facing snow line and one col too far south.

What is thin here, said plainly: this ridge is barely written up. The col elevations, the Smokestack and the east-side start come from the route's own record; the detail about the two crossings at the moat and the old anchor comes from accounts that could not be retrieved in full, so treat the crossing description as a warning to expect a choice rather than as a promise about which side is easier this year.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
camps: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier are unreadable under early-season cover
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last stretch off maintained trail: navigation errors cost hours
Road washouts and closures on FR 49 and the Mountain Loop Highway can block this approach
Whiteout and weather exposure on the open glacier plateau; loose talus on the summit scramble
Remote: no cell coverage, self-rescue only
approach_variants.baseFinding: This route has two arrivals and they are different kinds of thing. The first is where glacier travel starts, and the second is where the scrambling starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place. Glacier starts at foam pass. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. Scrambling starts at the top of the snow. From Glacier Gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, up the snow headwall to the summit ridge; above the snow it is an easy talus-and-ledge scramble. Of the twin tops on the summit ridge the eastern one is the true high point by only 10-15 ft, so bag both. One thing to expect on the ice rather than look for: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.

approach_variants.name: White River trail from the east
approach_variants.notes: From the White River trailhead beyond Lake Wenatchee, walk the White River trail about 10 miles up the valley to the Lightning Creek crossing, then go cross-country up into the high basin east of the peaks. About as far on foot as the Sauk side, with less trail and more off-trail travel.
hazards: Roughly ten miles up the White River valley, the lower sections effectively unmaintained with dense brush
Lightning Creek crossing runs high and fast during snowmelt
Cross-country travel in the Lightning Creek drainage with serious route-finding, little trail
Open crevasses and blue ice on the White River Glacier, more exposed late in the season
Whiteout and weather exposure on the open glacier plateau; loose talus near the summit
Remote: many hours from help, no reliable cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Quartz Creek Trail over Curry Gap and the Pride Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is a different trailhead from the peak's scramble route — do not stop at the Blanca Lake trailhead. Drive on to the end of FR 63, begin at the North Fork Skykomish trailhead, and follow the Quartz Creek trail about four miles to Curry Gap, at the junction with the Bald Eagle Mountain trail. From the gap, head west and southwest along an up-and-down ridge toward the peak, leaving the ridge where the ground allows to cross the glacier west-northwest toward the cliffs below the neighbouring summit. The route-finding hazard on this leg is the cliff bands in the basin, not the glacier.
approach_variants.season: June to September; spring ski ascents and descents of this side are also recorded.
hazards: Crevasse-fall hazard on the glacier crossing
Cliff-band route-finding in the basin between the gap and the glacier
Rockfall on the third-class band above the glacier
The up-and-down ridge between the gap and the glacier is longer in practice than it looks on a map
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climbing is where the glacier meets rock on the peak's northeast side, at about six thousand feet, and the physical test is which hand the ice is on. The line climbs third-class rock along the climber's-left edge of the glacier, so once you are on rock the ice should stay on your right the whole way up to the summit's southeast corner. If the ice is on your left, you have crossed to the wrong edge. The second confirmation is what you passed: the cliffs below the neighbouring summit are an aiming mark on the crossing, not the objective — you traverse beneath them and then turn up onto rock. Negative markers: if you are still on low-angle ice with cliffs directly overhead and the summit well off to one side, you are under the neighbouring peak rather than this one; if you have come up a faint climbers' path from a small lake with a subsidiary point beside you, you are on the south-ridge scramble from the other side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. A longer alternative from the Slate Pass road end reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids that ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.
approach_variants.season: July to early October
hazards: Unbridged ford of Eureka Creek: thigh to waist deep in snowmelt (June to early July)
Abandoned, unmaintained tread on Pistol Ridge with heavy deadfall and brush, faint and followed by cairns
No reliable water between the Eureka Creek ford and the Lake of the Woods basin
Loose talus near the summit and on the ridge crest
Short exposed class 3 blocky granite on the east ridge; steep north wall and northeast face off the standard line
Late snow on the last few hundred feet
No cell service, bear habitat, multi-day self-rescue distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp near Lake of the Woods, head uphill out of the lake basin toward the peak, which rises directly above camp. The base is where the open slope steepens toward the summit, and the mountain tells you where that is by refusing the obvious line. A subsidiary rock knob blocks a direct ascent from the south, and a cliff band bars a straight finish near 8,000 ft, so if you are looking up at a clean unbroken slope from the south side you are not below the standard start and pushing on will cliff you out. Bend instead onto the mountain's lower east ridge. That ridge is identifiable at its foot by larch: the lower slopes are studded with scattered larch groves, and the climbing proper begins where the larches thin out around 7,800 ft and the ground turns to boulder-hopping and coarse scree. Several gullies of much the same difficulty run up from there and any of them will go; take the one where hands come out only occasionally and the footing stays blocky rather than sliding. Early sections often feel like a staircase of granite blocks, which is a good sign you are on the ridge rather than in a scree runnel beside it. Two warnings on where not to be. The north wall and the northeast face are appreciably steeper and are not part of this route, so if the ground ahead drops away rather than rising, move back south. And the last few hundred feet hold snow late; footprints in it are a reasonable line but not proof of a good one.

approach_variants.name: Slate Pass and the Pasayten side
approach_variants.notes: Start high at Slate Pass on the Harts Pass road and drop toward the Middle Fork Pasayten, then work east by Eureka Creek and around into the basin below the peak. Longer and more cross-country than Pistol Pass, but it starts thousands of feet higher.
hazards: Long trail approach from Slate Pass to Robinson Creek, then an unmaintained, hard-to-follow Ferguson Lake trail
High-water fords of the Middle Fork Pasayten River during snowmelt, dangerous in June
Open avalanche chute on the Ferguson Lake trail
Loose talus near the summit and on the ridge crest
Short exposed class 3 blocky granite on the east ridge; steep north wall and northeast face off the standard line
No cell service, bear habitat, multi-day self-rescue distance

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls, Tatoosh Creek and the debris apron under the north face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it is open, or at Narada Falls in winter and spring when the road is snow-gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber regains the road.

Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face.

From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche and rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloirs. From the top of that debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft of couloir to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel point.

Roughly 2 to 2.5 miles one-way with about 2,000 ft of gain to the notch, and no water past Tatoosh Creek. The basin and lower couloir cross avalanche terrain, so this is a start-early, read-the-forecast approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun; most ascents are in winter and spring
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the basin and lower couloir, with both loose-dry and wet-loose problems documented on this aspect
Overhead hazard from other parties — this face is busy on good winter weekends and all three couloirs get climbed at once
Variable ice and mixed conditions in the steps season to season
A rappel that is longer than a single 60 m rope doubled, and rope-snag potential on rock features
Short winter days leaving little margin for retreat
Rockfall and spindrift funnelling into the couloir from above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right on this face the three couloirs are: Lover's Lane, the Zipper, the Fly. Learn that order before you leave the car. All three drop onto the same debris apron and on a busy weekend all three have parties on them at once, which means overhead hazard from other people as well as from the mountain.

The Zipper is the middle one, and it is the one that leans left and splits the centre of the face. From the top of the debris cone, angle climber's left. If you are working right, you are heading for the Fly.

The strongest test is width, and it is a thing you feel rather than see: the Zipper narrows. About 40 ft wide at the base, closing to about 20 ft near the top. The Fly is broad — 40 to 50 ft — and it stays broad. If the walls are not closing in on you as you gain height, you are in the Fly, one couloir to your right, on easier ground than you came for.

The second test is countable and it is the one that settles it: the Zipper has up to three short steps — about 15 ft, then about 8 ft, then a 25 ft crux near the top. The Fly has none worth the name. If you have climbed a thousand feet of continuous 45-degree snow and met no step at all, you are not in the Zipper.

The top-out is an object, which is the best kind of confirmation: a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge. That tree carries the fixed rappel slings. If you have topped out onto open ridge with no tree, you are on something else — Lover's Lane finishes on the ridge above this notch, and the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch.

What the angle should do: build from about 40 degrees to about 45 near the top. It does not exceed that. Ground steeper than 45 sustained means Lover's Lane, which reaches about 60.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then break off the gully about 200 ft below the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The Temple is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, the same parking used for the neighbouring Hairpin Crags and Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus, faint and intermittently cairned, up to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour.

From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Expect about 11 hours car to car.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A 200 ft window in which to leave the gully, above and below which you are on a different route
Loose talus and a boulder-choked gully
Rope-stuck issues on the descent, which is why some parties break it into three shorter rappels
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully
No reliable water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The northwest face breaks off onto a climber's trail about 200 ft below the notch, instead of continuing into the boulder-choked gully. That is the whole find and it is a measured one: two hundred feet short of the top of the gully, an obvious bench and trail splits off right.

So the negative test is: if you have reached the notch, you have gone roughly 200 ft too far and you are at the start of the north face. And if you are fighting up a boulder-choked gully bed rather than walking a bench, you have missed the split.

Getting to the gully in the first place: from Kangaroo Pass, traverse left to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger, then ascend toward the notch. Do not drop straight down the far side of the pass; contour south below the slabs descending from Wallaby Peak, losing about 20 ft below the pass, on a good well-cairned trail beneath the slab bands.

What the other two routes do from the same place, so the three are separable: the north face goes all the way up the gully to the high notch. This route takes the bench 200 ft below it. The south face crosses the same pass but then drops below it and traverses across to the far side of the formation, and its face is not even visible from the highway.

Descent: from the summit, downclimb or scramble to the fixed rappel anchors on the north side of the formation. Accounts differ slightly, with some parties making two full-length rappels of about 30 m and others three shorter single-rope rappels, roughly 150-160-plus ft in total, to avoid rope-stuck issues, landing at or near the North Ridge notch. From the notch, the standard descent gully leads back down to Kangaroo Pass.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the Freedom or Death ramp
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

This route was equipped largely rope-solo and first freed in August 2016 and originally documented under an earlier name. It climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, then steps right onto Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before eight new pitches of its own.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No independent start; a party that mislocates Freedom or Death mislocates this route
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed for the descent
Loose talus in the upper approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does not have a start of its own. It starts on Freedom or Death, and that is the fact to carry up the talus. So the base finding is Freedom or Death's base finding: A small leftward-trending ramp just to the right of Liberty Crack, with bolts visible on the face above it.

Why that is actually useful rather than a dodge: it means you are not hunting for a fifth start among the East Face cluster. There are three pitches of shared, well-bolted climbing before this route becomes its own thing, and the decision point is up on the wall where you can see it, not down in the talus where you cannot.

The negative test: Liberty Crack is 40 ft left along third and fourth class ledges from the base of the talus. If you are scrambling left on ledges you are heading for Liberty Crack. If you have walked well right past a series of starts you are among the Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice and Independence lines.

Countable on the climb: three pitches of 5.10, 5.11 and 5.11, then a step right. If you are still going straight up after three pitches you have missed the junction with Thin Red Line.

And the descent follows Thin Red Line's, not Freedom or Death's: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge from a fixed pin and wire, then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base. Five rappels, all on bolted stations after the first.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, then contour off the East Face path onto the northeast aspect
approach_variants.notes:
The shortest approach of the major Liberty Bell technical lines. The first-ascent party describe the wall as about 20 minutes from the road. Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, the same general area as the East Face approach, and follow the cairned path from the pond toward the East Face.

Ten pitches, 1,100 ft, bolted ground-up by rappel over two seasons and completed in August 2019. Expect scrambling and scree underfoot near the base; carry a helmet through the loose sections.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Scree and scrambling near the base, with rockfall potential
A 5.13-plus grade over ten pitches with no easier escape
An 80 m rope needed to rappel the route as designed
A short approach that makes it tempting to start without a full weather margin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is a time and a turn: about twenty minutes from the road, and you leave the East Face path before it reaches the main East Face talus. Contour toward the northeast aspect of the wall rather than continuing all the way in. If you have walked a full hour and are standing in the big talus field under the East Face, you have gone past this route and are under Liberty Crack's wall instead.

So the negative test is the strongest one here, because the positive one is short: the East Face approach takes about an hour. This one takes about twenty minutes. A threefold difference in walking time is measurable in any visibility.

Arrival at the climbing: the wall is 1,100 ft on the northeast face, and it is the ground beyond the right-hand, north end of the East Face. The Independence Route marks that end, at the profusely overhanging northeast corner with a red roof, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m up. Dark Side is round the corner from it.

Confirm by the hardware, which is distinctive on this peak: the route was bolted with anchors at roughly 40 M intervals along good stances, all fixed and bolted, so no natural gear is needed to descend it. Most parties rappel the route itself on a single 80 m rope, working out at eight or nine rappels of up to 40 m. A fully bolted rap line at even 40 m spacing is not what any other line on this mountain offers.

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls to the debris apron, then the rightmost couloir
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the Zipper: from Reflection Lakes when the road is open, or from Narada Falls when it is gated, walk the road briefly and drop south into the basin toward Tatoosh Creek, then climb the debris triangle to the base of the couloir system. Roughly 2 miles with about 2,000 ft of gain; the approach usually takes 45 to 75 minutes from the road to the couloir base.

The Fly is a broad couloir about 40 to 50 ft wide, predominantly snow at around 45 degrees, and is the easiest objective on the north face with fewer technical sections than the Zipper. The most efficient line follows the obvious broad gully, trending slightly right as you gain height.

The runout zone at the base is avalanche-prone, so stable snow is essential.

From the top at the west-ridge notch, most parties continue round onto the South Face and descend the standard third and fourth class gully rather than reversing the couloir.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun
hazards: An avalanche-prone runout zone at the base of the couloir
Overhead hazard from parties on the neighbouring couloirs and from rockfall out of the walls once the sun hits
Variable snow and ice conditions season to season
Short winter days
Wet-loose avalanche activity documented on the slopes below the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right: Lover's Lane, the Zipper, the Fly. The Fly is the rightmost, and it is the broadest.

Breadth is the test and it is the only one you need at the bottom: 40 to 50 ft wide, and it stays that wide. If the couloir narrows toward about 20 ft and starts putting short ice steps in front of you, you are in the Zipper, one to your left, on harder ground than you came for.

The second test is what your hands are doing. This is the easiest line on the face — predominantly snow at about 45 degrees with no crux step. If you are swinging two tools into ice, you are not on the Fly.

Trend slightly right as you gain height. That is the route's own shape, and drifting left at the base is exactly how parties end up in the Zipper.

The top-out names the couloir retrospectively, which is worth knowing if you had any doubt on the way up: the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch. The Zipper finishes at a notch in the east ridge, at a dead tree carrying rappel slings. If you topped out at a tree, you climbed the Zipper.

A negative that is about people rather than ground, and it is specific to this face: on a good winter weekend all three couloirs carry parties at the same time, and a documented near-miss involved thirteen climbers and skiers spread across the three. Being able to see other parties is not confirmation you are in the right gully — it is a reason to watch what comes down.

What the angle should do: about 40 to 45 degrees for the main gully, easing to 30-35 in the last few hundred feet to the ridge. It does not steepen near the top.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, the steep forest path, and the treed ledge below the east face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20 about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass, a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond. The climbers' path starts just left, west, of the highway's east-side guardrail and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest.

It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes, some parties closer to an hour, of steep hiking and scrambling from the pullout to the base, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
A 5.8 pitch as one of the two ways to gain the base
Snow lingering in the talus into early-mid summer
No water on the approach
A descent that finishes at the Blue Lake Trail, not at the pond pullout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a treed ledge, and there are two ways onto it and snow decides which. From the talus, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow lingering in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer affects whether you gain the ledge from the left or the right.

So the arrival test is a ledge with trees on it, part way up the wall, not ground level. Trees underfoot on a bench beneath a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation, and it works without seeing the tower above.

The discriminator against the other route from the same ledge, and it is a left-right test: Tooth and Claw begins near the left side of the treed ledge and angles rightward across slabs to its first bolt. If you are traversing right across slabs looking for a bolt, you are on Tooth and Claw, a 5.12a, not on the East Face.

Helmet up before the gullies, not after: both gullies flanking the ledge see fairly frequent rockfall.

Where the day ends, which is on the other side of the ridge: the standard descent is a walk-off from the notch below the true summit, not from the summit itself. Head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left, about twenty feet of third class; old rap slings are present but most parties downclimb. From the base of that gully, traverse right, north, until you intersect the well-worn climbers' and cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road walking.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as the other Liberty Crack-area routes: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

Five pitches, about 200 m of climbing, established rope-solo in 2014. It shares some climbing with the old aid route Liberty Loop.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A ten-metre offset from a neighbouring route as the only positional marker
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach
Two ropes needed to rappel the route from its top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line, and ten metres is the entire margin for error on this wall. That is a measured offset from a known line, which is the best that exists here, and it means you must locate Thin Red Line first.

How to bound it without seeing the whole face, using the order along the base: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, then Liberty Crack, then Freedom or Death on a small leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, then Thin Red Line, then this route 10 m right of it, then Live Free or Die, then the Independence Route at the far right or north edge under a red roof.

The strongest confirmation is the hardware, and it is countable: every station on this line is a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners. If you top out a pitch and find no bolts and no biners, you are not on it. From the top of pitch 3 you can skip the pitch-2 anchor and rappel directly to the pitch-1 anchor, so two rappels get you back to the ground from P3.

What going too far looks like: keep walking right and the next thing you meet is the ground Live Free or Die and the Independence Route use, at the far right end of the face. The Independence Route's own marker is unmistakable when visible: a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m above its start.

And where it goes: at five pitches the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, from which you either continue climbing or rappel this route's own anchors with two ropes back to the base.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then the leftward-trending ramp just right of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. Roughly an hour, steep near the top, no water.

Four pitches, all belays bolted. The route can be rappelled with a 60 m rope from the top of pitch 3, or continued into the shared terrain of Liberty Crack toward the summit.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start only a few paces from Liberty Crack's, on a wall where several routes begin within a short distance
Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
Rappelling from the top of pitch 3 needs a 60 m rope
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is a small leftward-trending ramp, and bolts should be visible above it. That is the whole test, it is visual, and it works at arm's length in cloud where nothing else on this wall does: a ramp leaning left, low down, with bolts on the face above it.

Position: just to the right of Liberty Crack. Not fifty yards right, just right. If you had to walk more than a few paces from the base of Liberty Crack, you have gone past it toward the Thin Red Line starts.
