The negative test: Liberty Crack is reached by traversing 40 ft left on 3RD and 4TH class ledges from the base of the talus. If you are scrambling left on ledges, you have overshot past this route in the wrong direction.

A second confirmation if the ramp is ambiguous: this is a four-pitch route with every belay bolted. There is no gear anchor to hunt for at the top of pitch 1. If you finish a rope length and find no bolts, you are not on it.

And the route that shares this start, which is why getting it right matters twice: a Servant to Liberty climbs the first three pitches of this route before stepping right into Thin Red Line. Two parties standing at the same ramp may be going to two different places.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then left along the base to the loose corner system
approach_variants.notes:
Standard East Face approach: park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile to the East Face talus.

Fourteen pitches. Although it is technically the easiest all-free route up the East Face, the route takes about one and a half times as much effort as Liberty Crack, on often poor rock and gear, and apart from where it intersects Liberty Crack there are no bolted belay stances.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Poor rock and poor gear over fourteen pitches
No bolted belays except where the line crosses Liberty Crack
Roughly one and a half times the effort of Liberty Crack for an easier grade
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the only route on the east face that starts to the left of Liberty Crack, and that makes it the easiest start on the wall to confirm by elimination. It begins at a loose corner system about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack.

So the test is directional and countable: from Liberty Crack, walk left roughly 100 ft to a corner system. Every other line here is to the right of Liberty Crack. If you are walking right along the base, you are walking away from this route, and everything you meet in that direction belongs to something else: Freedom or Death, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All, Live Free or Die and the Independence Route in that order.

And Liberty Crack itself is found by traversing 40 ft left on third and fourth class ledges from the base of the talus, so this route is roughly 140 ft of leftward travel from where the path meets the rock.

A hardware test that cuts the other way from the rest of this face: there are no bolted belay stances on this route except where it crosses Liberty Crack. Several of its neighbours are fully bolted. If you reach a bolted anchor early, you are probably not on Freedom Rider.

What to expect so you do not second-guess the find: the corner system is described as loose, and the rock and gear on the route generally as often poor. Poor rock at the start is consistent with this line, not evidence you are off it.

Descent: the shared East Face rappel line into Beckey Gully, or downclimbing the sheltered Beckey Route slab in good conditions. Both put you on the west side of the mountain, away from the East Face pullout.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then all the way right to the north edge of the face
approach_variants.notes: Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. Twelve pitches, first climbed wall-style in 1966 with 180 pitons and five bolts over four days, and later freed. The line takes the profusely overhanging northeast corner of the East Face and joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A profusely overhanging corner, first climbed over four days with 180 pitons
A cairned forest path that is hard to follow before dawn
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Start on the far right, the north edge, of the east face, and confirm it by locating the red-coloured roof and alcove of the Baer Ceiling about 85 M above. That is the marker, it is coloured, it is high enough to be visible when the base is in cloud, and no other route on this wall has one.

So the test is a colour and a height: a red roof roughly 85 metres up, at the right-hand end of the face. If there is no red roof above you, keep walking right.

The order along the base, which bounds it on the other side: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, Liberty Crack, Freedom or Death on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All 10 m right of that, Live Free or Die, and this route last. You cannot go further right and still be on the East Face; the ground beyond turns the corner onto the northeast aspect, where Dark Side of Liberty lives.

A second confirmation from the shape of the rock: this is the profusely overhanging northeast corner. If the wall above your start leans back rather than out, you have not reached the corner.

Where it goes, which also settles the descent argument: the route joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge, and fixed anchors let parties rappel from the top of pitch 8 back down the East Face to their packs on a single 70 m rope, rather than continuing to the true summit and finishing on the far side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, the fixed-rope climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Drive east over Washington Pass and park in the turnout about two miles beyond it, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. This is a highway pullout, not a trailhead — nothing is signed.

The climbers' path leaves the west or south-west end of the turnout and drops steeply through loose dirt and rock into the trees. It is well worn but unmarked apart from intermittent cairns. It crosses Early Winters Creek on logs and resumes on the far side, then climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation.

Higher up the old line uses two or three fixed lines on an avalanche path before topping out on a flat area. A newer variation bears right just before the fixed lines are reached and needs only a small amount of scrambling; most parties now prefer it. Reckon roughly an hour and a half.

Do not treat the fixed ropes as maintained equipment. They are informal, weathered, and nobody replaces them on a schedule.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and the approach snowfield have melted out
hazards: Weathered informal fixed ropes on the old approach line; the newer right-bearing variation avoids them
Early Winters Creek is crossed on logs and is worse in high water
Long unroped scrambling between pitches on a route people rack up for as a 5.7
Rappelling the line is slow and ropes snag on flakes, sometimes needing re-ascent to free them
The alternative descent gully is loose and sits above the approach path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The marker at the base is dead trees. As the ground steepens toward the formation and before the gully, look on your left for tree snags — standing dead timber against the rock. The first pitch climbs cracks up from a snag. That is the start, and it is the only start on this formation with a landmark you can walk up and touch.

If you have entered the gully itself, you have gone too far right. The gully parallels this route and is used both as a descent and as a fast way to reach the bolted line beside it — it is not this climb.

Confirm on pitch two, which is the strongest check the route gives you: it traverses under a roof. If your second pitch runs sideways beneath an overhang rather than straight up, you are on line. Above that expect steepening ground with cracks and a good layback, then a wide ten-inch crack with finger and hand sections, then a corner crack to lieback, and a headwall finish.

Expect long scrambling sections between the pitches. That is this route's defining character and the main complaint about it — it is the reason a 5.7 with seven pitches takes a full day. Continuous roped climbing with no walking between would mean you are somewhere else.

Negative markers for the two neighbours. If you have traversed a long way rightward from the base on third and fourth-class ledges toward the middle of the face before starting, you are heading for the hard line that finishes on this route's last pitches. And if your first pitch is protected by bolts, you are on the partly bolted line — this route takes natural gear throughout.

Descent is most often a rappel of the line itself, and parties report it is slow and that ropes snag on flakes. The alternative is the third-class gully to climbers' right, faster but loose; stay high and skier's-right to limit what is above you.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path toward Concord, then the ten-foot step onto the northwest plateau
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail about 1.7 miles through forest to a small meadow below Liberty Bell. This is the opposite trailhead from the hairpin pond pullout used by the east face routes.

Leave the Blue Lake Trail on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits left just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Roughly 2,000-plus ft of gain over 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts, so helmet up through the talus and gully.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A rockfall-prone approach gully that holds snow into early summer
A ten-foot step that is easy to overshoot, leading parties onto harder ground
Queues at the popular Beckey rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep
One pitch of the descent can run slightly over 60 m, so a single-rope party may have to downclimb a short section
A loose gully downclimb from the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The entire find is a ten-foot step, and the route's own description makes it a negative test: if you are climbing more than about ten feet of easy fourth or low-fifth class to gain the plateau, you have missed the spot.

How you get to it: rather than dropping into the main Beckey and Liberty Bell-Concord gully, stay on the climbers' trail as it climbs toward Concord for as long as it reasonably can, then break left onto that short, well-trodden step. The step gains the little-visited northwest plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of larch groves below the northwest face proper.

So there are two confirmations and both work without seeing the summit: the step is ten feet and well-trodden, and above it you are standing on a bench with larch trees on it. Larches on a bench, on the northwest side, below a wall, is the plateau.

The negative test against the other routes off this path, which is where parties actually go wrong: if you have dropped into the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord and are climbing scree toward a notch, you are on the Beckey Route and Overexposure approach, not this one. This route never enters that gully.

Where the day ends up, which is not where it started: from the west summit you downclimb and scramble to the top of the Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the northwest face. Rappel about 20 ft down the upper Beckey pitch to a ledge, traverse left, east, to a tree hung with rap slings, one single-rope 60 m rappel to a flatter stance, then a double-rope rappel from a bolted anchor to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft, and downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers' path.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then right of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes: From the Highway 20 hairpin curve on the east side of Washington Pass, locate the small pond on the south side of the road; the pullout is on the north side of the highway. Follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond into forest and up to the East Face talus.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start that has to be sighted from a distance rather than found along the base
Snow travel at the base into early summer
Several route starts within a short distance of each other on the same wall
A summit descent that strands you on the opposite side of the mountain from your car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and the published method for finding it is to work downward from the features above rather than along the base. Look climber's right of Liberty Crack and connect the line down from the features higher on the wall. Some mellow snow travel is usually necessary to reach the base.

So this is the one east face route whose start is honestly described as a sighting problem, and that is worth knowing before the cloud comes down. Fix the line from the talus while you can see the wall. If you cannot see the wall, you cannot locate this start by walking the base, and no description will change that.

What you can do without a view is bound it, because the order along the base is known. Left to right: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, Liberty Crack, Freedom or Death just right of it on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All about 10 m right of Thin Red Line, Live Free or Die, and the Independence Route at the far right or north edge of the face beneath a red roof and alcove called the Baer Ceiling about 85 m up.

So: if you are standing at a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above it, you are one route left, on Freedom or Death. If you can see a red roof about 85 M above you, you have walked all the way right to the Independence Route.

The descent decides which car you end at, and this route has both options: from the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face, returning to your pack and the East Face approach. If you instead continue to the true summit and take the standard Liberty Bell notch descent, you finish on the west side of the mountain and need a shuttle or a road walk back.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then 40 ft left along the base
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve. This is a different trailhead from the Blue Lake Trailhead used by the southwest and northwest face routes, and confusing the two costs an hour and a mountain.

Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway. A cairned climbers' path leaves the pond's east end and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. The approach is short, about an hour, but steep in its upper section with loose talus underfoot near the top. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
A start that is only forty feet from a different route's start
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face trailhead
Snow lingering in the base talus into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the base of the talus, traverse 40 ft left on third and fourth class ledges. That is the instruction and it is a measured one: forty feet, climber's left, on ledges you scramble rather than climb, and then the crack system starts.

Liberty Crack is the reference line for the whole face, which means every other route here is described as so-many-feet left or right of it. Get this one right and the rest of the wall becomes navigable. Left to right along the base the order is: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, then Liberty Crack, then Freedom or Death just right of it, then Thin Red Line, then Liberty and Injustice for All about 10 m right of that, then Live Free or Die, then the Independence Route at the far right or north edge.

So the positive test is: you are on the crack system that runs continuously up the centre of the wall, reached by scrambling left rather than right from where the path meets the talus.

The negative test, and it is the one that matters in poor light: if you are looking at a small leftward-trending ramp with bolts visible above it, you are on Freedom or Death, one line to the right. And if you scrambled right from the talus instead of left, you are among the Thin Red Line and Independence starts, which are further right again.

Where the route ends and how you get down, because it decides which car you walk back to: this line tops out at the same alcove and bolted anchor the original aid route uses. From there, ledges lead to a double-bolt rap anchor and two rappels drop into the Beckey Gully, the same rap line the standard Liberty Crack and Beckey Route descents use, landing near a tree anchor. That gully runs down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch on the west side of the mountain, which is the opposite side from the East Face pullout you parked at.

name: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)

approach_variants.name: Smith Brook road trailhead via Union Gap
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead on Smith Brook road, climb to Union Gap on the crest trail and follow it toward Lake Valhalla and Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail for the base of the west face.
hazards: Loose, lightly-traveled alpine rock: test holds before weighting them
Off-trail route-finding to Lichtenberg Pass from the crest trail, with no path anywhere on the mountain
Almost no modern trip-report or grade documentation: unknown rock quality and committing route-finding
Steep heather and slide-prone slopes, brush, and exposure on the west rib
Descent by the northeast slope is easy to lose; cliff bands above Lake Valhalla in poor visibility
Sandy chutes on the rib are unpleasant to downclimb

approach_variants.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. Campfires are prohibited at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Stevens Pass North Lot (crest trail northbound)

approach_variants.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and follow the crest trail north to Lake Valhalla, arriving from the west below the face. It is a few miles longer than the Smith Brook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.
hazards: Long start from Stevens Pass along the crest trail, a few miles longer than the Smith Brook start
Off-trail route-finding below the west face on arrival at Lake Valhalla, with no path on the mountain
Loose, lightly-traveled alpine rock: test holds before weighting them
Almost no modern documentation: unknown rock quality and committing route-finding
Steep heather, slide-prone slopes, brush and exposure on the west rib
Easy to end up above cliff bands over Lake Valhalla in poor visibility on the way down

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier straight to the foot of the wall, without going to the col
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Green Creek one: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing — the unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the marked ford is what most parties use — then off-trail to Green Creek, cross it, and ascend a rock buttress near 3,800 ft onto the Green Creek Glacier.

Where the Southeast Ridge continues to the Cinderella-Little Sister col at the glacier's head, this route stops at the face itself. It is graded around 5.4 and is the hardest of the peak's documented lines.

Descent is either rappelling the climber's-right side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier, or downclimbing the easier Southeast Ridge to the col and returning to the glacier from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: No published line along the base of the face — the party chooses its own start
Scattered fixed pins and tat of unknown age as the rappel descent option
A north-facing wall that holds snow and ice at its base
A moat where the glacier meets the wall
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here
approach_variants.baseFinding: The glacier runs into a wall, and the wall is the route. That is the arrival and it is the whole test: walk up the Green Creek Glacier until the ice ends against rock that goes up rather than along. There is no col, no notch and no ledge system to identify. The col is the overshoot marker and it is the most useful thing to know here. If you keep going and arrive at a low point on the ridge with Cinderella on the far side of it, you have walked past the north face and are at the base of the southeast ridge — a different route, two grades easier, on a different aspect. Reaching a col means turn round. The aspect is the confirmation. This face is north. It is in shade, it holds snow and ice at its base later than anything else on the peak, and the rock is cold. If you are standing in sun at the foot of your intended line, you are somewhere else on the mountain. Be honest about what is published here: no source consulted gives a per-pitch start point along the base of this face. What is documented is the aspect, the grade, the approach glacier and the fact that the face is roughly a thousand feet high. A party arriving at the wall still has to choose its own line along the base, and should expect to. Descent decides the day and must be decided on top: the two options are rappelling the climber's-right side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors — old gear, unknown age, treat it as found rather than as fixed — or downclimbing the Southeast Ridge to the col and back to the glacier that way. The second is more walking and less trusting.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier on its looker's-left side to the Cinderella-Little Sister col
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Green Creek one shared by every route on this peak: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on whatever log is currently in place, then Elbow Lake Trail #697 and the blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaving it near a switchback around 2,600 ft.

Up the Green Creek drainage past the Wiseman Lake outlet, through brush, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier.

This route then differs from its neighbours in one instruction: travel the glacier staying on the looker's-left — south — side, up to the Cinderella-Little Sister col, which is where the ridge starts.

The route is graded around 5.3 and runs about three pitches.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A moat at the glacier margin that grows through the season
A dangerously loose connecting ridge toward Cinderella that must not be used as a traverse
Fixed pins and tat of unknown age on the north-face descent option
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to gain the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a col, and that is what separates this route from every other line on the peak. The southeast ridge starts at the Cinderella-Little Sister Col, at the head of the Green Creek Glacier. You have arrived when you are standing in a low point on a ridge with a peak at each end of it — Cinderella one way, Little Sister the other — and glacier behind you.

The glacier instruction is the one thing to get right and it is a side: stay looker's-left, the south side, on the way up. The other routes on this peak do not go to the col at all, so drifting right across the glacier puts you under the north face instead.

So the discriminator is simply whether you reached a col. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a wall, you are at the north face and you are on a different, harder route. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a notch you can walk through, you are at the start of this one.

The moat at the glacier margin is the last obstacle, and it is a season problem rather than a route problem: trivial in a heavy snow year, a real step late in the season, and the same in reverse coming down.

What not to do from the col: do not continue along the connecting ridge toward Cinderella. At least one party describes that ridgeline as dangerously loose and recommends dropping back to the glacier instead. The col is a start point for two peaks and a through-route for neither.

Descent note that double-checks the start: most parties downclimb this same ridge back to the col. The alternative is to drop onto the north face side and rappel scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier — which is a different aspect and needs deciding on top, not in the moat.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie, then cross-country into Summit Chief Valley
approach_variants.notes: Do not walk the trail to Dutch Miller Gap. From the gate at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, head up the valley on the closed road and then the trail until you reach a small steel bridge, well short of the gap — that bridge is the turnoff. Leave the trail there and travel cross-country in a southerly direction into the mouth of Summit Chief Valley, then up the valley to a camp at around the level where the timber thins. From camp the peak is on the east side of the valley: look across and up, not back at the trail.
approach_variants.season: August to September for the documented ascents; snow can linger in the approach gully system earlier in the summer.
hazards: Loose rock on the approach talus and on the lower pitches
Exposed, unprotected final ridge pitch to the summit
Residual snow and ice on the pocket glacier and the polished slabs used on the descent, into midsummer
The turnoff is a small bridge on a long valley trail with no sign — miss it and you commit to a very long day getting back
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the valley camp, the base is at the top of a talus field roughly nine hundred feet above you, and the marker at its top is a prominent left-trending gully. That gully is the start: the first several rope lengths climb it at fourth and low-fifth class and can be moved together. The physical test is the direction of the gully — it leans left as it rises, and it is the dominant weakness on this side of the peak; a gully that runs straight up or leans right is not it. Above the gully system the climbing becomes continuous crack and groove work on sound rock, so if you are still on broken talus-strewn ground after nine hundred feet of gully you have not reached the route proper. Negative markers: if you have tread underfoot and are standing in a saddle with a trail crossing it, you walked past the steel bridge and are at Dutch Miller Gap on the other route; if you are climbing heather and rock steps directly out of a saddle toward an open bench and a snowfield, that is the gap route too.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the roadside pullout near milepost 166 and start straight uphill to the west, away from the creek — there is no trail and no sign. Head for the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Two ledge systems break the wall. The lower one comes first; keep going past it to the upper ledge, where the long routes start. The wall faces due south and there is no shade below the cave, so on a hot day the approach is the hottest part of the route.
approach_variants.season: Late June to September, once the gully has melted out and the lower pitches have dried; the highway over the pass is gated shut all winter, so there is no cold-season access at all.
hazards: Loose talus and creek-bed footing in the approach gully, with rockfall from anyone above you in it
Full south-facing sun on the whole approach with no shade until the cave
Water and seepage on the lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years
The highway is gated closed through winter and well into spring, so the approach can be unreachable by car
approach_variants.baseFinding: Get onto the upper of the wall's two ledge systems — not the first ledge you meet coming up the gully. Then walk right. This is the right-hand line on the wall and the huge cave that gives the wall its name is directly above you, not off to one side. The check on the ground is the first pitch itself: a left-facing corner about forty metres long that runs to a stance directly beneath a pair of twin cracks slanting left. Count the corner's length and look for the twin cracks above the first stance — that pair is unique on this section of wall. Negative markers: if the corner above you is short, slabby and only about twenty-five metres to its anchor, you have drifted left into the middle of the wall and are under the eleven-pitch line; if you are standing on a treed ledge that two separate lines leave from, you are further left again. And if the cave is high above you but you are on a narrow ledge with one lone bolt at ground level, you never left the lower ledge and are on the three-pitch apron route.

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
Bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
Creek crossing on a footlog that needs care in high runoff
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft is the arrival, and you know it by what becomes visible rather than by the altimeter: it is the first place the Whitman Glacier comes into view. Until you can see a second glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

The base of the climbing proper is higher still, and it is a change of surface: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a short step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

The route-finding trap is low, not high, and it is the one thing on this climb that regularly commits parties to bad ground: between Summerland and Meany Crest, if you find yourself contouring climber's right into a bowl under rock bands, you are cliffed out and off the line. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

The summit-crest test is a negative and it is unambiguous: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

Timing as a finding: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

approach_variants.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

approach_variants.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.
hazards: Trailhead and spur closed for the bridge replacement into 2029; limited parking at White River Campground
Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
Cliff-out potential above Summerland if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest

approach_variants.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
approach_variants.season: Nov-May, while the White River road to Summerland is shut
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
Cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, so elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
Long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
Missing the 8,600 ft departure point and continuing onto the busy Camp Muir track
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision is at 8,600 ft and it is a leaving, not an arriving. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft below Camp Muir. If you reach Camp Muir you have gone too far — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

Count what you cross: three glaciers and one rock cleaver, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a notch in Cathedral Rocks, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are below the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

The base is a ramp, and it is the only ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

The negative that separates this from the peak's other route: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the Fryingpan side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from Paradise, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest.

Why this route exists and when it stops working: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Basin high camp and the sheepherder's trail through four cirques
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft, White River Trail #1507 and then Boulder Creek Trail #1562 lead to a ford and camp around 3,700 ft, and on up into Boulder Basin. High camp is a grassy knoll overlooking the basin at about 5,800 ft. From camp the route traverses a saddle into the White River drainage and then follows the old sheepherder's path across a chain of cirques. The path is fairly well defined but the first cirque is where parties lose it and regain it repeatedly; the second, Clark Basin, is less brushy, more open and park-like with clear tread; the third, Luahna Basin, has good tread and is where parties describe camping as heaven on earth. There is a great deal of up-and-down and side-hilling on this traverse — the recorded elevation figure is far larger than for the peak's other route, which is what all that sidehill costs. This line is deliberately glacier-free, which is its whole reason to exist beside the other route on the peak.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep. A September ascent works but expect cold and the possibility of early snow on the traverse and the summit ledges
hazards: An exposed Class 3+ traverse on the north side just beneath the summit, crossed with nothing to protect it
A long sidehilling traverse across four cirques with heavy elevation loss and regain, and a path that vanishes in the first one
Loose scree and rotten rock below the summit block
Lingering snow on the traverse and ledges early in the season
Remoteness measured in a day's walk from any road, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You find the base of this route by counting basins, and the answer is four. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: boulder, then Clark, then Luahna, and the peak's base sits above the fourth — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

The intermediate marker is a number on the ridge: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft ridge point, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus above the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

The positive test at the base is the grade, and it is easier than you expect: the scramble begins on easy class 2 ledges on the south face, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

The confirmation comes high and it is on the wrong side of the mountain: just beneath the summit the route crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the north beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

The negative marker against the peak's other route: the east slopes line crosses the upper Richardson Glacier from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A note on what is published versus what parties find: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
approach_variants.notes:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Sustained bushwhacking, blowdown and route-finding in the Access Creek drainage, the approach crux
A ford of Big Beaver Creek that can run high with snowmelt
A narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest between the false and true summits, with cliffs on both sides
Loose talus and scree on the upper ridge with rockfall risk onto parties below
No reliable water above the Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt
Losing the boot path in poor light on the way down, which several trip reports record
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route contours where the south ridge climbs, and the difference starts above camp rather than at the col. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above. Once on the ridge, traverse south of point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600 ft level to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

So the fog test is an altimeter test: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

Arrival: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

Confirm on the climb, and the count is short: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit, then one short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

The one technical spot, and its tell: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

No water above the access creek basin. The summit push is done on what you carry.

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier, then west across the glacier head to the face
approach_variants.notes:
This route and the Northeast Couloir come at the mountain from the other side to everything else on it. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then cross the pass and descend east toward the Stehekin side. Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the yawning glacier, which runs roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft. Rope up. Follow the glacier southwest to the Magic-Pelton Col at 6,480 ft, between Magic Mountain and Pelton Peak.

From the col this route does not go straight up. It bears back and crosses the head of the glacier westward to reach the north face, where about 600 ft of steep class 4 rock leads to a notch immediately northwest of the summit.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug; glacier cover and couloir conditions vary more year to year here than on the peak's south side
hazards: Crevasses on the Yawning Glacier — rope up rather than treating it as a snowfield
A steep couloir below the Magic-Pelton col that is exposed to rockfall
A schrund at the base of the rock that opens through the season and can be the crux by August
Broken, north-facing gneiss that is often wet or verglassed, with slung blocks for anchors and no fixed gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two routes leave the Magic-Pelton Col and the test is whether you walk or traverse. At the col at 6,480 ft, the northeast couloir goes straight up from where you stand. This route first bears back and crosses the head of the glacier to the west. If you started climbing at the col, you are in the couloir.

The second test is what is under your hands, and it settles the same pair from the other end: this route is rock — about 600 ft of steep class 4 above a schrund. The Northeast Couloir is snow, 40 to 50 degrees for 2,000 ft. If you are placing pickets you are in the couloir; if you are slinging blocks you are on the face.

The schrund at the base of the rock is the base itself, and it is the thing that changes most between June and August — by late summer it can be the hardest move of the day.

The finish is a notch immediately northwest of the summit, and that notch is shared with the northwest ridge, which reaches it from the peak's southwest side by easy walking slopes and a chimney. So arriving at the notch does not confirm which route you climbed — but it does confirm you are 600 ft above the glacier on the correct face, and the summit is a short scramble from there.

And you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely if you came over cache col: that is the Kool-Aid Lake approach, which serves the South Ridge, the West Ridge, the Northwest Ridge and the Southwest Cirque. This route and the Northeast Couloir come from Pelton Basin.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead off I-90 exit 52, about 3,000-3,040 ft. Follow the PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles through second-growth, climbing gently, to the signed junction with the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033).

Follow #1033 into Commonwealth Basin. Not far past the junction it crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last reliable water on the approach, and a tricky ford in early season at high snowmelt.

Immediately beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread. There is no trail from here. Climb cross-country to the northwest, first through open timber and then boulder and talus, into the open cirque at the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek beneath Lundin's south face.

An equivalent description used by many parties: stay on the Commonwealth Creek trail until soon after the stream crossing, where it starts moving up onto the flank of Red Mountain, then leave it and head northwest into the basin. Many climbers deliberately come early in the season, when snow covers the brush and boulders and the cross-country leg is quick.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; early season on snow is preferred
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail from the creek crossing onward - open timber then boulder and talus
lingering snow patches in the upper basin into early summer
route-finding across talus to locate the true toe of the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The south face rises straight out of the head of the basin, and the route begins at the low point of the face, directly beneath the summit.

The way to get this right is to line yourself up by eye before you walk in: pick out the summit from the basin floor, drop that line to where it meets the bottom of the face, and walk to that point. Parties who instead head for the first inviting rock they reach end up starting left or right of the low point, and the climbing above does not match — the route runs several low-fifth pitches to a slab, with the final pitch steeper.

If the ground at the foot of your line rises noticeably before it meets rock, you are off to one side; the true start is where the face is lowest.

In poor visibility this is a hard place to be sure of yourself, because the basin is featureless talus and the face is continuous. The summit-to-toe line is the only test that works, so take the bearing while you can still see the top.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, go directly uphill through talus and forest toward the gully below the wall, taking the forced dogleg out left and back in. Pass the lower ledge and keep going to the upper ledge. There is an exposed easy-fifth step in the gully on the way, so this is not a walk with your hands in your pockets. Rockfall in the gully is worse when another party is above you and worse again after rain.
approach_variants.season: July to September; the highway over the pass is gated shut through winter and into spring, so the wall is car-inaccessible for roughly half the year.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, particularly with parties above or after rain
South-facing aspect gives full-day sun and real heat in summer
Two routes leave the same treed ledge — confirm which anchor you are heading for before you commit to a rope length
approach_variants.baseFinding: On the upper ledge, work to the centre of the wall — this line is neither the right-hand cave line nor the apron below. The start is a treed ledge, and it is shared: two routes leave from the same spot, so identify it by the ledge and the trees, then identify the route by where you stop. The first pitch here is short — a slabby left-facing corner, about twenty-five metres, ending at a belay well below the first roof. Negative markers: if you run the same corner out to more than sixty metres and finish at a pin-and-gear anchor tucked under a roof, you are on the free variation of the old aid line, which shares this ground; if the corner you started up is forty metres long and leads to a stance under twin left-slanting cracks, you are on the right-hand cave line; and if you are on a narrow ledge below the whole wall with a single bolt beside you, you stopped one ledge too low.

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip to the true summit. Drive US-2 to milepost 42 in Baring — the turnoff is directly across from the store — and turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (FR 6024). Cross the railroad tracks immediately and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Roughly 4.3 to 4.5 miles of gravel reach the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft: parking for around 20 cars, a vault toilet, picnic tables, and no potable water.

Do not start on Barclay Creek Trail 1055. The climbers' path begins behind the outhouse, on the overgrown abandoned logging road that continues uphill from the parking area. Follow that road two or three tenths of a mile to the first creek. Look right for a cairn where a steep, heavily eroded path turns straight uphill toward the ridge. Orange, green or pink tape has been reported and may or may not be present.

You cross the creek twice — that double crossing is a useful confirmation you are on the correct path. From there the path climbs relentlessly and directly up the forested north/west side, with a short badly eroded class 3 step where hand lines have been reported, and several places where the tread braids. Trekking poles help on the loose lower section. There is no reliable water above the creek.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct; the notch gully holds snow into mid-summer
hazards: Very steep, loose, heavily eroded lower path — braided tread easy to lose
Cliffing out by staying high on the west ridge crest
Loose ash and obscured tread through the 2022 burn scar
Snow in the notch gully into mid-summer; the step at the notch varies year to year with snowpack
Loose rock in the summit basin — helmet
Creek crossings have been a ford when the log is out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The transition from approach to route is a change in the ground, not a landmark: the path tops out on the west ridge crest at about 4,000-4,100 ft, where the angle suddenly eases and the tread visibly improves. If you are still fighting steep eroded dirt, you have not reached it.

Follow the crest east for roughly a mile. Where the cliff bands appear you must drop below them — this is where parties go wrong. Staying high on the crest feels natural and cliffs you out, forcing steep and dangerous downclimbing to recover; hold a lower trajectory, cross the wooded gully, pick up the faint path on the far side and traverse into the talus basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin the main gully to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit is obvious and navigation is straightforward. A 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope has left loose ash and dirt that can obscure the tread along the crest.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
approach_variants.notes:
Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near Baring; Northwest Forest Pass at the self-issue kiosk.

Leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse, not on the main trail. Follow the old abandoned logging road about a third of a mile to a cairn at roughly 2,450 ft where a rough unmaintained path splits off toward the base of the mountain. That split is easy to miss and carries no trail sign.

From the cairn the boot path climbs steep loose dirt and crosses the creek draining the face several times. Stay close to the water: the tread is faint and repeatedly lost in the brush, and the creek is the handrail. In total the lower approach fights through roughly 2,300 vertical feet of dense slide alder, vine maple and devil's club before any technical rock. Allow around seven hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear boots or sturdy approach shoes rather than carrying them.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; snow lingers in the couloir into August
hazards: Missing the unsigned cairn split at ~2,450 ft
About 2,300 ft of slide alder, vine maple and devil's club
Faint tread constantly lost in brush — losing the creek loses the line
Steep loose dirt slopes
Snow in the couloir between the ribs into August
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Couloir camp at about 4,300 ft — around 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — is the landmark that tells you which approach you are on. It is a used bivy shelf directly beneath the wall, historically the base camp for the first-ascent siege, and it remains a reasonable first night for parties splitting the approach. Above it, the ground to follow runs between two precipitous brush-and-cliff-covered rock ribs that flank a large couloir; snow often lingers there into August, so an axe is worth having early season. Follow that ground to the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead.

Negative marker: if you have gained a ridge crest and the walking has suddenly got easier, you are on the northwest-ridge scramble line on the west side of the mountain, not on the face — the face approach never eases.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
camps: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
approach_variants.notes: From the Suiattle River Road, follow the Downey Creek trail up the valley, then turn up Bachelor Creek on a faint, brushy path toward Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. From the ridge, cross the glaciers east toward the Gunsight Range. Plan on a long two-day approach.
hazards: Long multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and brushy bushwhacking
Crevasse fields on the Chickamin Glacier approach and descent
Bergschrund or moat at the route base may need boulder-hopping or a bypass
Exposed alpine climbing on the east face with significant fall consequence
Afternoon rockfall on the south-facing rappel descent
Rapid weather changes in exposed positions
Remote, self-rescue-only terrain

approach_variants.name: From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks
approach_variants.notes: From High Bridge on the Stehekin Valley Road, follow the Pacific Crest Trail south up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence, crossing both creeks on logs. Then go cross-country, through dense brush, up toward the Icy-Spruce col for a high camp facing the Gunsights. Reaching Stehekin takes a boat or floatplane, so this is a multi-day trip.
hazards: Roughly ten miles up Agnes Creek with two log creek crossings
Dense brush on the cross-country climb toward the Icy-Spruce col
Reaching Stehekin needs a boat or floatplane, so the trip is multi-day and committing
Bergschrund or moat at the route base may need boulder-hopping or a bypass
Exposed alpine climbing on the east face with significant fall consequence
Afternoon rockfall on the south-facing rappel descent
Remote, self-rescue-only terrain

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Trail to the Ellation crag
approach_variants.notes: Drive SR-542 east about 46 miles from the interstate, then turn onto Forest Road 32 and follow it to the road end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Mamie Peak is the large, complex mass of granite standing directly above the trailhead, and its tiered walls come into view from the trail within a few minutes of setting off. Walk the trail roughly four minutes to a clearing where a large white boulder is visible perched several hundred feet overhead, and leave the trail there. Reckon on about an hour and 1,200 ft of gain to the base. The descent is by rappelling the route, which goes with single-rope raps on a 70 m cord.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct
hazards: The approach is faint and easy to lose — parties have gone astray at the gully
Mossy slabs are slick when wet
Sustained 5.10 face and friction climbing; partially bolted, so a medium rack is still needed
Loose rock in the approach gully if another party is above you
approach_variants.baseFinding: A bolt low enough to clip from the ground is the confirmation. From the white-boulder clearing, work up to a mossy slab and, standing literally at its base, cut left and up a slight hill on a reasonably well-defined trail running along the foot of the slab. About five minutes of that reaches a dry streambed under a gully. Scramble the gully thirty feet or so, then cut hard left through brush into open forest and a dry creekbed, and follow the creekbed up to a large white boulder. Switchback up the woods above it and cut out to the right once you are 50 to 100 ft from the base of the wall. Ellation starts up a series of shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, and the proof is that bolt near the ground with a couple more on the first pitch. If you are standing at the foot of a single-pitch crag, the route is above and left of you; if you cannot see a bolt near the ground, you are not at the start.

approach_variants.name: The pocket glacier under the west face, and the schrund that guards it
approach_variants.notes:
Approach by the general Cascade Pass and Ptarmigan Traverse access: Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, the trail to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then the climbers' path across Mixup Peak's flanks, over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col near 6,900 ft, and down toward the Kool-Aid Lake basin.

From the basin, easy slopes on the west-southwest side lead to the small pocket glacier under Magic Mountain's west face. That pocket glacier is the base area, and the bergschrund at its head is where the route begins.

About four pitches: shelves to a blocky open book, the 5.6 open book, the slab taken on its easier left side, and an easy chimney on the left to gain the crest between the false and main summits.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with the bergschrund crossing and the pocket-glacier conditions varying by snow year
hazards: A bergschrund below the west face whose difficulty varies by year and which can be the crux of the route by late summer
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees and bare ice late season
Broken gneiss with slung blocks for belays and no fixed gear
A thin slab pitch where protection is limited
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The bergschrund is the route's identity and it is the one-look test against both its neighbours on this side of the mountain. This is the only Magic Mountain route from the Kool-Aid Lake side that crosses a schrund. The Northwest Ridge walks up easy slopes to rock and a chimney; the Southwest Cirque goes up heather gullies. If you have not crossed a gap between glacier and rock, you are not on the west ridge.

The positive landmark above the schrund is a named shape: shelves lead up to a blocky open book — a dihedral corner. That open book is the 5.6 crux and the best-protected pitch on the route. If you cross the schrund and find no open-book corner above you, you have crossed it in the wrong place.

Count the four features in order, because they are all different shapes: schrund, shelves, open book, slab. The slab is taken on its easier left side, not up the middle.

The finish tells you which summit you are under: from below the ridge between the false and main summits, an easy chimney on the left gains the crest. So the route deliberately arrives on the ridge between the two tops — if the chimney you climbed put you straight onto a summit, you are on the false one and the ridge continues.

And if you have to retreat below the summit, the schrund has to work in both directions: a retreat reverses the chimney and slab, downclimbs the open book and re-crosses the schrund. Look at it on the way up with that in mind, because there is no walk-off from this side of the mountain; the walk-off starts at the summit and goes down the South Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the Chiwawa valley, fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit and follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 upstream through forest, watching the west side of the tread for the marker described below. Ford the river at that point — it can run thigh-deep and swift with early-season snowmelt, so cross in the morning when flows are lowest — and pick up the old sheep-drive path, which climbs steeply on a mix of axe and burn blazes and intermittent boot track to Massie Lake. There is essentially no reliable water between the ford and the lake. From the lake the faint sheep and game tread of the high route contours northwest toward the pass ahead; leave it and turn uphill onto the peak's broad west ridge.
approach_variants.season: The high country here is typically not fully snow-free until mid to late July; shaded sections of the high route and ridge hold snow and ice well into summer.
hazards: A false set of markers has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction and cost a party hours of bushwhacking
Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, thigh-deep and swift during snowmelt, with driftwood piles the only aid
Route-finding is the main hazard: the sheepherder path disappears in places and the whole line beyond the river trail is unsigned
Snow and ice on shaded sections of the high route and ridge into midsummer
No reliable water between the river and the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two things facing each other across the trail mark it: a large boulder jutting in from the east, and an 'M' with an arrow carved into a tree on the west. The boulder is what you actually see first. There is no sign and no trail number, and the path it marks is an old sheep-drive route that is easy to walk straight past. The river is forded immediately below the junction, with piled driftwood the only help across, so the ford and the carved letter go together. The serious trap here is a decoy: a false set of markers — a boulder in the bank and logs and arrows suggesting the lake — has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction, and a party that took it spent hours bushwhacking up the wrong hillside and came out on the ridge high above the lake. So do not settle for arrows alone; you want the boulder and the carved 'M' opposite one another, and cairns have since been built on both sides of the trail at the true crossing. Above the ford a steep, poorly-marked boot track climbs to the lake on axe and burn blazes that thin out with height. From the lake the faint high route contours away; leave it and turn uphill onto the broad west ridge, the only named feature near that decision being a shoulder around 6,420 ft.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, then the sidehill traverse to Mesahchie Col
approach_variants.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. Leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down into Fisher Creek, and sidehill cross-country west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall almost directly below the peak on an easy bench; the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, the usual high camp, which has water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the approach gullies, on the traverse and in the basin into July.
hazards: genuinely rotten rock in the summit gullies — every hold needs testing and anything knocked loose funnels down the gully onto the party
the cliffy gully-and-rib maze on the summit pyramid, where parties repeatedly get cliffed out without a track or route photos
steep, loose Class 3/4 rock at the base of the west gully
the waterfall crossing below the peak, which goes easily only on the bench near 6,500 ft
a long, exposed ridge with few bail options and real exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at Mesahchie Col, the col at the foot of Mesahchie's west ridge. From the basin, the shoulder crest leads up to cairned ground; follow the cairns to the base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, and traverse slightly exposed slabs down to the col, which holds a well-built bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the first obvious gully leading up the west ridge. The right gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, then enters a broader, gentler gully past a string of cairns and tops out on the ridge crest; the crest is then followed east, exposed but moderate, to the summit. Negative marker: if you reached the peak along the crest from the east and are starting from a flat spot at the foot of the summit pyramid, you are on the East Ridge, not this route.

approach_variants.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
approach_variants.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block, Class 3 or harder
Snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this rain-shadow climate
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is marked by water, which is convenient because you should be stopping there anyway. From high camp, traverse northwest to the saddle below Lake Mountain around 7,400 ft, then drop into Lower Monument Basin at roughly 6,100 ft. The outlet creek running from the lake in that basin is the last dependable water on the peak and it sits directly beneath the route; late in the season it can shrink to a trickle but the drainage is still obvious. Fill bottles, then look up and to the left for a ramp system that angles left across the face above you.
