That ramp is the start of the climbing and it is the feature to identify: it is a continuous weakness slanting up and left, not a gully, and it delivers you onto the south ridge crest at about 6,900 ft. Once you are on the crest the ground flattens into a broad talus highway that runs for well over a mile toward the summit, and that flatness is itself the confirmation that you gained the ridge in the right place rather than on a side rib. Two things mislead near the top. A false summit around 8,000 ft takes a short scramble and looks convincing; the true top is a distinctive leaning horn of granite, so if what you are standing on is not leaning you are not finished. And a steep snowfield sits just below the true summit well into midsummer, which can be crossed with an axe or turned on rock to its left, but should not be glissaded on the way down because it stays firm.

approach_variants.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. No parking pass or fee is needed at this trailhead. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

approach_variants.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain.
hazards: Long approach via Slate Pass, the Robinson Creek trail and the Ferguson Lake trail to Eureka Creek, remote with no cell service
Eureka Creek crossing near the peak, cold and high in early-season melt
Loose blocky talus on the upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
Snowfield below the summit into midsummer
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this climate

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Killen Creek trailhead (~4,600 ft) is reached by Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from either the Randle or the Trout Lake side. FR 2329 is gravel, runs north from Takhlakh Lake along the northwest edge of the wilderness, and is commonly still under snow into early summer — parties have had to park low and walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road to reach the trailhead. Call the Mount Adams Ranger District rather than assuming.

Killen Creek Trail #113 runs about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest and wildflower meadow to the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,100 ft, in the area known as Adams Creek Meadows. Cross straight over the PCT onto High Camp Trail #10 and continue about 1.0 mile to its end at roughly 6,900 ft at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Small cairns mark the upper section when it is under snow.

Camping: High Camp at about 7,000 ft has established flat dry sites; there are more between 7,000 and 7,600 ft; a glacial lake camp at about 7,650 ft gives the easiest glacier access; and some parties push to sheltered bivouacs around 7,100 ft in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine.

Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water — above camp, melt snow. The tread thins to a moraine and gully scramble above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or under snow, so record landmarks or a track on the way up.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.
approach_variants.season: June into early July, while the icefall is still filled in
hazards: Serac collapse in the icefall between roughly 9,200 and 11,800 ft
Large crevasse near 10,800 ft that can force a long traverse to find a crossing
Losing the thin moraine tread above treeline in dark or whiteout
FR 2329 snow-blocked into early summer, adding road walking to the approach
No running water above Killen Creek
Very loose volcanic rock on the North Ridge descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the rare approach where the objective is in full view the whole way, and that is the strongest tool you have: as you walk up the High Camp Trail the Adams Glacier is directly in front of you, tumbling from the summit icecap, with the enormous crevasses of the main icefall facing you. If you cannot see a broken icefall ahead, you are not on the right side of the mountain.

The base is the toe of the glacier at roughly 7,000–7,300 ft, above camp. The test is underfoot: while you are still on rubble, moraine crest and scree you have not reached it. The toe is where continuous snow and ice begins and the scrambling stops — that is where you rope up.

Starting position matters. Begin on the right (climber's right, west) side of the glacier at its base and stay in the right third for most of the climb; the standard line then works left higher up to avoid crevasses.

The route above has its own confirmations. The angle steepens noticeably at about 8,500 ft. Around 9,500 ft you traverse toward a ramp beneath seracs. The real icefall — the crux, roughly 4,000 ft of tortured ice between about 9,200 and 11,800 ft — is where the maze of seracs begins and where screws and belays get used. Near 10,800 ft a large crevasse commonly forces an eastward traverse before a crossing appears. Above roughly 11,400 ft the ground relents to easy névé and you are on the summit plateau.

Negative marker for the descent: the North Ridge is the usual way down and it is very loose volcanic rock. If you are descending on ice with crevasses you are still on the Adams Glacier, not on the ridge.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass, the PCT north and the ridge above Porcupine Creek
approach_variants.notes: Follow the PCT north from Rainy Pass about a mile and a half, to just before the Porcupine Creek bridge, then climb the ridge northeast for about two miles to the base. The shorter way, with the cleaner gully to the base.
hazards: Approach gullies hold most of the loose material; rockfall from loose blocks and flakes
Loose rock is the biggest climbing problem on all terrain, with quality varying across the steep jointed granite
Off-trail climb up the ridge northeast from the PCT beyond the Porcupine Creek crossing
Descent uses three rappels on the north ridge or an 80 ft rappel southwest; anchors must be tested and loose blocks watched for

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin below Cutthroat Peak. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. On this approach the lake is on the way: the trail continues past it and climbs to Cutthroat Pass, from where the crest leads south about a mile to the base of the North Ridge. From the Rainy Pass side it is off the route entirely.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

approach_variants.notes: The eastern way: on trail most of the way, to Cutthroat Lake and up to Cutthroat Pass, then south along the crest for about a mile.
hazards: Rotten rock on the final ridge-crest approach from Cutthroat Pass
Loose rock is the biggest climbing problem on all terrain, with quality varying across the steep jointed granite
Rockfall from loose blocks and flakes in the gullies on the descent back toward the pass
Long approach with about 2,300 ft of gain via Cutthroat Lake and the pass
Descent uses three rappels on the north ridge or an 80 ft rappel southwest; test every anchor

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then east past Lava Ridge to the Lyman at 8,000 ft
approach_variants.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; climbed in late spring and early summer as moderate to steep snow and sometimes alpine ice
hazards: Crevasse and serac navigation on the Lyman, particularly on the south lobe's upper half
A short steep crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies from 45 to 65 degrees year to year
Long sustained high-altitude climbing with a late-season low-snow route-finding problem on the traverse
A descent down the North Ridge on loose rotten volcanic scree, with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Count the ridges, and for this route you must get past two.

East of High Camp the order is: Adams Glacier, North Ridge, Lava Glacier, Lava Ridge, Lyman Glacier. You cross the Lava Glacier and then go around or over the toe of Lava Ridge. Lava Ridge is the second ridge and it is the gate. If you have crossed only one ridge and stopped at a glacier, you are at the Lava Glacier Headwall — a different climb with a triangular face — not at the Lyman.

The positive test is a fork, and it is unmistakable once you are on it: the Lyman splits around a narrow rock outcrop into two lobes. The north lobe is the original line; the south lobe runs 40-degree unbroken neve on its lower half and is broken by crevasses and serac walls on its upper half. A glacier that forks around an island of rock is the confirmation you are where you meant to be.

The crux confirms it a second time, higher: both lobes lead to a chute near 10,000 ft that runs anywhere from 45 to 65 degrees over about 50 ft depending on the year. One short steep chute, then easier snow to the summit plateau. If you meet no constriction at all, you are on a neighbouring glacier.

The base elevation is the third check: about 8,000 ft. Arriving on ice much higher than that means you gained the glacier well above its toe and may have come onto it over the ridge rather than around it, which is fine but changes where the lobes sit relative to you.

What the descent means for the approach, and it is worth deciding at the car: you do not come back this way. The walk-off is the North Ridge, back toward High Camp. So the ridge you counted past on the way in is not the ridge you come down.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
The same walk in as the Adams Glacier and the Northwest Ridge, and High Camp is the shared base for all three. Killen Creek Trail #113 from the trailhead (~4,600 ft) runs about 3.1 miles to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft; cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to its end at about 6,900 ft on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine. Camping is spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft, including a glacial lake camp near 7,650 ft.

Access is by FR 23, 21 and 2329; FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. East Fork Adams Creek, crossed about 2.5 miles up the trail, is the last dependable water.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.

This is a longer and more committing day than the South Climb from a much quieter side of the mountain, and crevassed glacier lies on both flanks of the ridge and on the summit ice cap, so glacier skills are expected, unlike the South Spur.
approach_variants.season: June through September; a snow route early, a loose rock route once it melts out
hazards: Very loose volcanic rock the length of the ridge — helmets, and spacing between climbers
Crevassed glacier on both flanks if you leave the crest
Exposed snow travel between rock sections
Thin moraine tread above treeline, easy to lose in dark or whiteout
No running water above East Fork Adams Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From High Camp the line is southeast, toward the foot of the ridge, and in clear weather you can see the whole thing from the approach — parties describe it as impossible to miss.

The recognition problem is entirely a poor-visibility one, and the test is what is under your boots. The North Ridge is the rubble-and-cinder rib that separates the Adams Glacier on its west from the Lava Glacier ground on its east. You should be on loose volcanic rock and scree, on a defined crest, with glacier falling away on both sides. If you are on ice with crevasses, you have slid off the rib onto one glacier or the other, and which one tells you which way to correct.

A smooth, clean, snow-only ascent is the wrong sign on this route: it is a choss pile, and the loose rock is the confirmation rather than the complaint. Expect short easy scrambling steps low down.

The angle eases noticeably around 11,000 ft, which is the sign the ridge proper is behind you and the summit plateau ground is ahead.

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs trailhead and the Lunch Counter
approach_variants.notes:
From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Road to the Forest Road 23 junction, bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 turn for South Climb, then FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, and FR 8040 for 8.1 miles — steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks, no RVs or trailers — to the South Climb / Cold Springs trailhead at 5,600 ft.

Permits: a Cascade Volcano Pass is required to travel above 7,000 ft in the Mount Adams Wilderness during the summer season (May 1 to September 30), and a free wilderness permit is needed for the trailhead. The wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead; the climbing pass is a single-trip pass sold only online, so buy and print it before driving up.

The trail begins on an old roadbed through burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadow, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge toward the snowfields. In early season there is often no trail at all — just a snow slope leading out of the parking lot. Above the Crescent Glacier the way is meandering snowfields to the Lunch Counter.

The Lunch Counter (roughly 9,250–9,400 ft) is the standard camp: a broad rocky bench with hand-built rock windbreaks. Water is snowmelt. This is a route where the crowd itself is a factor — it is the most-climbed line on the mountain and the bench fills on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Late May through September; earlier in the season the whole route is a snow climb from the parking lot
hazards: Rockfall and soft-snow postholing on the Crescent Glacier slopes in warm afternoons
Whiteout on the featureless snowfields between Crescent Glacier and the Lunch Counter
Turning around at Piker's Peak believing it is the summit
Uncontrolled glissading — the standard descent line has caused injuries
No water above the Lunch Counter; snowmelt only
Sharp switchbacks and rough surface on FR 8040, and snow blocking it early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no bergschrund and no ice step on this route, so the question 'where does the climbing start' has two answers, and the second one is the one that turns people around short of the top.

The first: the Lunch Counter is the transition. You are there when the meandering snowfields end at a broad, flat, rocky bench with rock walls built on it and the South Spur rising directly above as one continuous slope. Above the bench there is no more wandering — it is 2,400 ft of steepening snow on a bearing of roughly north-northeast.

The second, and the important one: what you top out on is NOT the summit. The rounded high point at 11,644 ft is Piker's Peak, the false summit. The test is unmistakable if you know to look for it — the ground ahead of you flattens into a broad saddle and plateau, and a separate dome rises about 600 ft beyond it to the north. If the slope has stopped and the true top is still visibly above and away from you, you are on Piker's. Parties turn around here every season believing they have finished.

Negative marker on the way up: if you are scrambling on a rocky crest rather than kicking steps on snow, you have drifted onto Suksdorf Ridge. That is a legitimate alternative when the snow is soft, but when the snow is firm it is the slower choice, and in a whiteout it is the wrong handrail.

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.

Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, crossing the Klickitat Glacier and Big Muddy Creek on the way. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for the headwall itself; the surrounding east-side walls are rockfall-prone once warm
hazards: Persistent rockfall from the east-side cliff bands, directly over the contouring approach
A steep ice and snow headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Wilson
A long, mostly off-trail traverse with creek crossings and route-finding, and a full day just to reach camp
Rarely climbed, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic and rescue would be slow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision happens about a mile from the car and it is a turning, not an arrival. At the junction of the South Climb Trail with the Round the Mountain Trail, the standard South Spur route goes north toward the Lunch Counter; this route goes east. If you are climbing toward the Lunch Counter, you are on the standard South Climb and this route is already behind you.

That is the one error worth guarding, because it is recoverable only by walking back down. Everything after it is a long contour.

The positive test at the base is a glacier split by a rock rib. The Wilson runs from about 10,600 ft down to about 7,400 ft and a rock rib divides it. A headwall above a glacier that is bisected by a rib is the confirmation. An unbroken glacier with no rib in it is not the Wilson.

The second positive is aspect and it is the coarsest but most reliable: you must be on the east side of the mountain. Going around the eastern flank is the whole approach. If the sun is rising behind the mountain rather than in front of you, you have not come far enough round.

The negative that matters for safety rather than navigation: the contour runs directly beneath cliff bands that shed rock. It is a place to keep moving. Persistent rockfall on these east-side headwalls is among the reasons most of them remain unrepeated, so a rope-length of comfortable ground is not evidence the ground above you is quiet.

What being on a neighbouring basin looks like: coming round from the south you meet the Klickitat first, the biggest glacier on this side, then the Rusk; the Wilson lies north of the Rusk, above Avalanche Valley. A big glacier met soon after leaving the Bird Creek side is the Klickitat, not the Wilson.

approach_variants.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
approach_variants.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow choking the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a fall of well over a hundred feet
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbers' path leaves the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail at an unsigned fork roughly 2.3 miles out: bear left and uphill to the north, where the maintained tread carries on right along the ridge toward Victor Pass and Lake Angeles. From the fork the primitive path climbs rocky meadow on the peak's west side and does about eight hundred of the day's feet in a little over half a mile, topping out near 6,000 ft in a scree bowl beneath the summit block. The identification that matters here is which notch, and it catches people every season: do not scramble the first notch you reach. The boot path keeps traversing higher and the gully that goes is further along, directly beneath the true summit. Stay on the worn tread climber's-left of the open scree fan rather than going straight up the fan itself, which is the rockfall funnel. You are at the base when the meadow ends and you are standing on dirty, fractured ledges with a roughly forty-foot exposed step above you. If the ground has levelled off or you are back on maintained tread heading toward Lake Angeles, you have overshot.

approach_variants.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains about 700 ft in six-tenths of a mile to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge, then about half a mile west along that trail and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
bivy.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

approach_variants.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.
hazards: Steep, short trail from the road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow in the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a long fall
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge

approach_variants.name: Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains about 700 ft in six-tenths of a mile to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge, then about half a mile west along that trail and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.

bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Heather Park Trailhead (Heart O' the Hills)

approach_variants.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.
hazards: Long approach on the Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills, around the west side of the peak
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow in the summit notch and shaded gullies into July
Exposed Class 3 moves with a long fall
Fast-building afternoon storms on exposed terrain

name: Standard Scramble (Appleton Pass / Boulder Lake approach)

approach_variants.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
camps: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
approach_variants.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully where several holds are vegetation
Narrow goat ramp on the final approach to the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes
Snow near the pass and in the basin below the summit into July
Braided, unmarked climbers' path that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote backcountry with unreliable cell coverage, long carry-out
Black bear activity in the drainages; scented items need an approved canister
approach_variants.baseFinding: Appleton Pass is a true gap with scattered tent pads just below it and maintained trail running on north toward Boulder Lake and east toward Oyster Lake. Leave the tread at the gap and take the climbers' path north along the ridge crest. The base of the real scrambling is a rock step at about 5,800 ft, and the way you know it is a distinct rock horn standing on its south, or left, side — that horn is the marker, and there is nothing else like it on the crest. Below the step you have been on easy heather with a talus basin crossed on the north flank near 5,400 ft; above it you are on exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully and ledge system. Minor outcrops lower on the crest can be turned on either side and are not the step, so do not stop at the first thing that makes you use hands. The narrow goat ramp people talk about comes after the horn, not before it. If you are still traversing level ground with the basin below and no horn in view, you are too low; the notch below the true summit sits near 6,000 ft between the peak's two rocky humps.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek from the Elwha

bivy.name: Appleton Pass
bivy.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
bivy.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

approachLogistics.trailhead: Boulder Creek Trailhead (Olympic Hot Springs Road)

approach_variants.notes: From the Elwha side, follow the Boulder Creek trail past the old hot springs and climb to Appleton Pass, where it meets the Sol Duc line. It is the longer way, since the road below the trailhead may have to be walked or biked. Boulder Lake makes a good side camp.
hazards: Longer approach since the road below the Boulder Creek trailhead may have to be walked or biked
Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully above Appleton Pass with vegetation holds
Narrow goat ramp near the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge
Lingering snow near the pass and in the basin into July
Braided climbers' path above the pass that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote with unreliable cell coverage; black bear activity in the drainages

approach_variants.name: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to the moraine, then the lower Boulder Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Boulder Ridge Trailhead at the end of FR-1131 off Baker Lake Road (about 2,700 ft — the lowest trailhead of any Baker route, which is where the 8,000+ ft of gain comes from), follow Boulder Ridge Trail #605. The first two miles are nearly flat through old clear-cut and timber and end at a boggy clearing at the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary; the maintained tread effectively stops there. Beyond it the route is a steep, unmaintained boot path up heather. Around 4,700 ft it crosses a Class 3 rock band, which parties have sometimes found protected by a fixed line left by an earlier team — treat any fixed line as unknown gear, not as trail furniture. Above the rock band the path gains the crest of a lateral moraine and follows it. Between the meadow and the basalt cliff, stay on or near the moraine crest north of Boulder Creek: the game trails here drop toward the creek and lead nowhere useful. Camp is on the ridge, roughly 5,500-5,900 ft; the snowline moves through the season, so plan to camp where the ridge runs out into snow rather than at a number.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul. This is a short-season route: the Boulder shrinks and breaks up early, and by August the crevasse field that is walkable in June is a maze
hazards: A Class 3 rock band around 4,700 ft on an unmaintained boot path, sometimes with an unknown fixed line on it
Losing the moraine crest onto game trails that drop to Boulder Creek
A crevasse field that opens fast — this route has one of the shortest usable seasons on the mountain
Rockfall from the buttress near 9,300 ft on the upper mountain, on the way down as well as up
8,000 ft of gain from the lowest trailhead on the peak, so a late turnaround is a long descent in the dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The moraine crest is the handrail, and the route starts where it dies. Everything from the rock band upward is a walk along a single narrow spine of moraine with the drop into Boulder Creek on one side. In cloud you do not need to see anything: keep the crest under your feet and keep the creek noise on the same side of you the whole way. If the ground under you goes flat and broad, or you are suddenly walking with the creek on the other side, you have come off the moraine and are on the game trails below it.

Arrival: the ridge runs out into snow and ice, and that transition — trail-and-heather to glacier — is the base of the route. There is nothing subtle about it; the ground stops being walkable in boots.

The discriminator against the other route from this camp, and it matters because both start from the same spot: this route stays on the glacier. The Boulder-Park Cleaver route crosses the lower glacier northwest to the toe of a rock cleaver and gets onto rock. If you find yourself walking toward a rock rib and looking for a place to step off the ice, you are on the cleaver route, not this one. This route goes up the ice.

What going too far looks like: contouring so far northwest that the Park Glacier headwall comes into view above you. That is the neighbouring aspect and its own set of routes.

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead at about 3,400 ft, at the end of the Sulphur Creek road. Cross Sulphur Creek near the start — bridged or on logs, but a genuine ford during peak snowmelt — then climb through the meadow and forest switchbacks.

At about two and a quarter miles a signed junction sends you right onto the Railroad Grade Trail 603.2. Stone steps take you up onto the crest of the lateral moraine. There are three established camp areas along the way; Sandy Camp at about 5,900 ft is the usual one for climbing, roughly four miles in with 2,600 ft of gain.

Above Morovitz Meadows there is no reliable water other than melted snow.
approach_variants.season: May-Sep
hazards: Sulphur Creek crossing during peak melt
exposed, loose moraine crest in wind
crevasses on the broad Easton, worse late season
volcanic gas and unstable ground at Sherman Crater
no water above Morovitz Meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the start when the moraine crest simply runs out. The Railroad Grade tapers off just before 6,000 ft into the sandy flats and rock-walled tent platforms of Sandy Camp; that is where the trail stops being a trail and where parties rope up for the glacier.

The simplest confirmation on the way up is which side the ice is on: walking the moraine crest toward the mountain, the Easton Glacier drops away on your right the entire way. If the glacier is on your left, or if there is no glacier beside you at all, you never took the signed junction and are still on the Park Butte trail heading for the lookout.

Higher, the feature that tells you the glacier is done is Sherman Crater — steaming, sulphurous ground at the head of the ice. The Roman Wall is the steep snow rising beyond it, and the true summit is a short traverse past the top of the wall. Smelling sulphur means you are at the top of the glacier and should be turning up onto the wall, not continuing toward the crater.

approach_variants.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
camps: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
approach_variants.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Days of off-trail travel along the Bailey crest with no quick bail-out and no cell coverage
Firm snow on the small glacier below Bear Pass: axe and traction needed
Few reliable water sources beyond Heart Lake on the long crest traverse
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Steep scree and lingering snow patches on the contour to the summit scree slope
Deep interior isolation; a high self-rescue burden with helicopter evacuations recorded
approach_variants.baseFinding: Bear Pass is a broad saddle marking the southeastern end of the Bailey Range proper, and from it the ground drops into a flat meadow before the mountain itself. Cross the meadow and contour southeast over scree and lingering snow patches until you are southwest of the summit. That position is the base, and you will know it from the change underfoot: the sidehill traversing stops and the slope above turns into a straight fall-line of moderate, evenly sized scree with a boot track curling left, to the north, onto it. Aside from one brief patch of brush the terrain here is open and the top is in view, so the navigation problem is behind you once you are on that track. Decoys: the ridge running east off Bear Pass is not the summit ridge, and the first obvious scree fan you meet while still traversing leads onto broken ground short of the peak. If the boot track has stopped curling north and you are dropping toward the Queets side, you have gone past the turn.

approach_variants.name: Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, Mount Barnes, Mount Noyes and Mount Queets are all short days, Mount Meany is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts Mount Ferry and Mount Pulitzer within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and cross-country zones cannot be booked online — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

approach_variants.notes: The eastern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the full length of the valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp to Elwha Basin, then climb onto the peak from the basin. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.
hazards: 'The maze': dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha River and Elwha Basin that can take hours
The Elwha Snowfinger has largely melted out; expect steep scree, crumbly slabs and an icy snow hump instead of a ramp
Hazardous fords on the upper Elwha in high water
Closed road adds a 6-7 mile walk or bike ride each way before the trail even starts
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Committing multi-day access in deep interior with a high self-rescue burden

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin to the Northeast Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness / Royal Basin Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail and then the Royal Basin Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about another mile into Upper Royal Basin at roughly 5,600 ft — a meadow and tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba and Hal Foss.

A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead, and Royal Lake is an Olympic National Park quota area, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the upper basin, leave the trail and cross the moraine southwest to the snow slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, where the climb begins. Allow about three hours from the upper basin to the top of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Apr-Jun, while the gully still holds snow
hazards: loose rotten rock throughout the upper mountain
snow in the gully in early season, and the left-branching variation melts out by late season
scree and talus in the basin
steep and exposed ground on a peak generally described as serious
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the upper basin tarn, cross the moraine southwest to the large snow slope (mud and scree once it melts out) on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, and climb it toward the low point of the Deception-Martin ridge.

Do not go all the way to that low point: the ridge crest there is the standard route, which drops onto the small glacier beyond and circles Gilhooley Tower. Arriving on the crest at the low point means you have passed the branch.

The Honeymoon variation proper takes a left-branching snow gully off the main line — climb nearly to the low point and then branch left. By late season that branch is largely melted out and the feature disappears. It is graded class 3 but is reported to feel harder than that.

approach_variants.name: Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road
camps: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
approach_variants.notes: Up Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road off the Cascade River Road, then south through the Buckindy high country to below the north side. A longer two-to-three-day approach.
hazards: Notoriously thick slide alder, devil's club and old-growth deadfall in the Kindy Creek drainage
Small glaciers (Kindy and Goat Creek) on the massif carry open crevasses; rope up with crevasse-rescue kit
Loose, rotten breccia rock on the summit block
Two-to-three-day approach with a rough spur road to the pullout
Very remote: no cell coverage and long carry-out times if a rescue is needed

approach_variants.name: Green Mountain trail and the Horse Lake saddle

bivy.name: Horse Lake saddle camp
bivy.notes: First-night camp on the Green Mountain approach, past the south shoulder of Green Mountain. Beyond it the traverse toward Misch and Buckindy is slow sidehill travel.
bivy.water: Horse Lake and snowmelt nearby; treat it
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites just above the saddle

approachLogistics.trailhead: Green Mountain Trailhead (FR-2680 off Suiattle River Road)

approach_variants.notes: The usual way: up the Green Mountain trail off the Suiattle River Road, then cross-country east and southeast along the ridges past Misch to Buckindy's north side. Check the Suiattle River Road before you go; it has been closed to vehicles for long stretches.
hazards: Green Mountain Road and Suiattle River Road closed to vehicles by flood damage, adding roughly twenty miles of closed road
Slow sidehill cross-country travel along the ridge system past Misch and the Horse Lake saddle
Small glaciers (Kindy and Goat Creek) on the massif carry open crevasses; rope up with crevasse-rescue kit
Loose, rotten breccia rock on the summit block
Very remote: no cell coverage and long carry-out times if a rescue is needed

approach_variants.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
camps: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
approach_variants.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.
objHaz: cliff bands within the ascent gully
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Avalanche debris choking the lower gully (snapped timber, rubble)
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Short rock steps and cliff bands within the gully
Steep cliffed north face immediately off the summit crest; stay on the south side
Difficult creek crossings during snowmelt (June-early July)
Limited water on the high traverses between the peaks
Afternoon thunderstorms common on exposed ridges in July-August
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a gully, and it identifies itself by being a mess. A scree-and-talus gully drops south off the Carru-Lago col and runs down to meet the trail; where it meets the trail it is typically choked with avalanche debris, meaning snapped timber, jammed branches and rubble piled in the bed. That debris is both the marker and the reason not to start there. Instead, climb the open forest on the right-hand, western side of the gully and step into the bed higher up, at about 6,600 ft, above the worst of the wreckage. Once in the gully the route is contained and hard to lose: scramble up it, weaving round a couple of short rock steps and small cliff bands, until the walls fall back and the ground opens out near the col. That opening-out is the second checkpoint. At that point turn left, to the west, onto the broad southeast ridge and follow the parallel scree ribs to the summit; the ribs run in the direction of travel and any of them will do. The single thing to watch on the upper mountain is which side of the crest you are on. Carru's north side is a steep, cliffed face and is not part of any route here, so if the ground in front of you falls away as a wall rather than a slope you have crossed the crest and should step back south.

approach_variants.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

approach_variants.notes: The shorter and more common start. From Slate Pass the trail drops north to the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it up-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb toward Fred's Lake and Shellrock Basin below Carru. Most parties combine Carru with Osceola and Lago over two or three days.
objHaz: possible lingering snow/ice in the gully early season
hazards: Blowdown and faint tread on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail; off-trail navigation required
Difficult crossings of the Middle Fork Pasayten and Eureka Creek during snowmelt
Long remote approach, about 15 miles one-way with no mobile service
Limited water on the high bench and ridge traverses; seasonal tarns and snowmelt only
Snow holds on north sides of passes into late July
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Steep cliffed north face off the summit crest; avoid

approach_variants.name: Illabot Creek Road, Arrow Creek switchback and the west slopes
approach_variants.notes: The trailhead is not a formal one — it is the point where the Illabot Creek Road reaches the Arrow Creek switchback, and you park on the road. A boot and fisherman's path leaves the road about twenty yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it is reasonably distinct with occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence is an easy boulder hop by late summer, a genuine wet ford in early season, so check the flow before committing. Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder, which is the worst brush of the day, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000 to 4,300 ft. That band is the route-finding crux of the walk-in: intermittent cairns and flagging at best, and it is easy to end up in the wrong gully. Last dependable water is around 4,000 ft. Above, the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes and traverses and climbs east toward the summit block.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The road and the approach gullies typically do not clear of snow until July, and the peak sees almost no traffic outside that narrow window.
hazards: a pathless, committing approach through steep brushy old growth with stream crossings and sustained sidehilling
the cliff-and-gully band at 4,000 to 4,300 ft, where it is easy to commit to the wrong gully in either direction
snow-filled entrance gullies below the west face that can sluff or slide in warm or unstable conditions
exposed, moss- and heather-covered steps on the summit block ramp, worse descending than ascending
weak and unreliable water above 4,000 ft
frequent afternoon thunderstorms in the approach basins
approach_variants.baseFinding: You must cross to the north side of the ridge before the ramp exists. From the open west slopes, climb northeast across the basin and up a steep gully to a pass in the ridge at about 5,920 ft, then cross over to the north side of that ridge and traverse east until the west face of the summit block is in front of you. The line up that face is one large, obvious ramp, and its direction is the test: it climbs the face diagonally from left to right to reach the summit ridge, where you turn left and scramble to the top. If the ramp you are looking at runs right to left, or if you are still on the south side of the ridge, you have not reached the correct face. If you can see no single dominant ramp at all — just broken ground and heather steps — you are still short of the summit block and should keep traversing east. The rock on the ramp carries heather and moss rather than clean stone, so treat it as insecure, and note that the same ground is considerably harder facing outward on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and Surprise Basin to the Clark–Johnson col
approach_variants.notes: Seven miles or so to Royal Lake, a mile more into Upper Royal Basin for camp, then off-trail over heather and talus to the moraine rim and down onto the Surprise Basin snowfields. Bear canisters are required through the basin and there are no fires. The corkscrew above the col is the standard line and the route-finding on it, not the climbing, is the difficulty.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Sustained loose rock in the corkscrew's gullies
An exposed Class 3 to 4 crack that reads as a cliff-out from above
Snowfields in Surprise Basin, icy early and slushy by afternoon
Complex route-finding around the summit block that is easy to lose
A long carry-out with no cell service if anything goes wrong
approach_variants.baseFinding: From Upper Royal Basin climb the moraine rim, drop into Surprise Basin, and aim for the low saddle between Clark and Johnson at roughly 6,900 ft — only about six hundred feet below the top. Standing in it, Johnson is on your left and Clark's summit tower on your right. The corkscrew starts here. Walk up talus to the base of the cliffs and skirt right onto a wide, low-angle southwest-facing ledge that looks exposed from below and is easy walking. Follow it until the cliffs above split into a clear Y-shaped gully — that Y is the confirmation you are on route. Go straight up it to a boulder, then right to a notch on the southeast ridge. The one feature worth memorising for the way back is the cairn at the top of the diagonal crack down on the east ledge: from above, that ledge appears to cliff out at a corner and the cairn is the only thing that says otherwise. If you are walking a broad easy ledge with no Y-gully forming above you, you have skirted too far right and should come back.

approach_variants.name: Flapjack Lakes and the Needle Pass couloir
approach_variants.notes: Old roadbed grade up the valley to the Flapjack Lakes Trail, a steep climb with one slide bypass to pick through, and camp at the lakes. From camp, up-basin toward Gladys Divide, then a steep snow and scree couloir of several hundred feet — often 35 to 40 degrees and firm — to Needle Pass. Access on this side has been closed by fire damage; confirm the trail itself is open, not only the road.
approach_variants.season: Late June to September
hazards: Firm, icy snow in the Needle Pass couloir — often the real crux of the day
Late-season moat opening between snow and rock in that couloir
Loose rock in the Class 4 approach gully and around the chockstone
Old rusted quarter-inch bolts and pitons beside the newer station
Sparse, run-out protection on the face pitch and marine fog on the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: From Needle Pass turn east and scramble the exposed crest to Beta Peak, drop through its right-most summit notch on one Class 4 move and a short gully, traverse high toward Cruiser, then take the longer connecting gully down to Cruiser's south side. The base of the roped climbing is the mouth of a Class 4 gully and you identify it by the large chockstone wedged in it above you — pass that block on its left and squeeze through the short tunnel behind it. That tunnel is the Cannon Hole, and coming out of it puts you on the broad, airy platform where the rope comes out; from the far end of the platform the low-fifth face pitch runs to a belay on the summit crest. Two decoys: the couloir up from Gladys Divide has more than one apparent exit and the correct one is Needle Pass itself, not the first gap in the rock, and Beta Peak's other notches cliff out below. Above the platform, look hard at the anchor before you weight it — the good two-bolt station sits near older rusted hardware that should not be trusted.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek log crossing, Stump Hollow to the Chopping Block camp, then the upper Barrier crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead at the Goodell Creek Group Camp, about 500-600 ft, off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before narrowing to a boot-beaten track.

Roughly 4 miles in, near Terror Creek, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off, historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post and a large cairn. Route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devil's club lower down.

Cross Terror Creek at about 2,000 ft. The customary crossing is a large log roughly 500 ft upstream of where the path hits the creek, but in high water that log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternates. From the creek the path grinds directly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4,000 ft in under two miles through forest and then open heather. It eventually merges into Stump Hollow and follows the narrow crest north to the basecamp area near Chopping Block Camp at about 6,000-6,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: An unmarked junction at Roost Creek that is a genuine route-finding crux
A Terror Creek log crossing that can be submerged in high water
Close to 4,000 ft of gain in under two miles on steep, loose ground; a torn calf muscle is on record here
The Barrier: loose, exposed, and consistently described as feeling far harder than its class-3 rating
The chossiest rock in the Southern Pickets, with running meltwater over slabby sections as a slip hazard
Old, weathered tat on the one summit-tower rappel anchor
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is the notch immediately south of the summit, and that notch is also the upper barrier crossing. Those are the same feature, which is what makes it findable: it is a place hundreds of parties pass through for a different reason. From camp, traverse Stump Hollow to the roughly 6,400 ft saddle near the Chopping Block, descend about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, then cross a snowfield and small glacier below Degenhardt's south side and claw up dirt and broken rock to the notch immediately south of the peak, which is the top of the upper Barrier crossing.

Two barrier crossings exist and this route wants the higher one: a lower crossing over loose ledges at the base of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moats and steep choss near the top of the glacier just below Degenhardt. The higher one is the preferred option precisely when Degenhardt, Pyramid or Terror is the objective, because it puts you at the notch. If you took the low ledges you will have to climb back up.

How you know the notch when you are in it, in cloud: it is the top of the worst rock on the route, and the route's own description says this ground marks the end of any good climbing in the area. Dirt and broken rock underfoot steepening into a gap in a rib, with the Terror Glacier behind you and the ridge running north above you, is the place.

From there the count is short and the error is always the same one: follow the ridge north over exposed but moderate ground. Parties report traversing much too low and having to regain height. Stay near the crest. A small tower guards the final notch and is turned rather than climbed direct, and the last moves onto the summit are short 4th class on poor rock.

Degenhardt is widely regarded as the chossiest peak in the Southern Pickets. Helmets and careful rope management matter more than the grade suggests.

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / O'Neil Pass approach)

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: Route-finding is the crux: Fernow is not visible from Leroy Basin and cairns are sparse
About a thousand feet of descent from the col into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Open crevasses and icy slopes at the Gloomy Glacier remnant; rope up or give it a wide berth
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing earlier in the season
Roughly two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
Exposed gravel-covered sloped slab traverse (about 30 m drop) and narrow exposed ledges off the col; avoidable
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Fernow is not visible from Leroy basin, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go up the waterfall, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

First: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the right side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

Second, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, do not go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at nine thousand on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat.
hazards: Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
Boat-dependent access via Lake Chelan to Holden

approach_variants.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure.
hazards: Longest way in, with a long Entiat valley walk before the glacier
Entiat Glacier crossing; crevasses and glacier recession can change conditions (unconfirmed for this variant)
Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, the traverse corridor to the Red Ledge, and the Formidable Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A deep objective reached along the same corridor as its neighbours, and the walk-in is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain rather than a hike. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, take the maintained trail to the pass, then leave it and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow bands, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake, climb out of the basin toward the cliff band running west off the knoll above; the Red Ledge cuts through it, usually entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and a few feet of easy rock, and it is broad and walkable unless it is holding snow or verglas. Roughly a quarter mile past the ledge, descend several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between the two large icefall sections, cross that bench, and continue to the foot of the Formidable Glacier. Note that this is a different objective from the peak's ordinary walk-up on the south side, which is the descent line rather than the approach.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer suits it best: early enough that the couloir still holds firm snow or ice rather than bare, rockfall-prone rock, but late enough that the moat at the top of the glacier has opened enough to allow access to the face.
hazards: large blocks have come down on this route
the approach crosses above a heavily crevassed glacier
the standard descent on the south side has difficult route-finding, constant exposure and loose rock, and has been the scene of a fatality
a snow couloir that steepens past sixty-five degrees with overhanging chockstones at its top
sparse protection on the crux, with one long pitch reported as protected by a single piece
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go right on the glacier, and the moat is the gate. Ascend the Formidable Glacier by traversing right, to its northern end, and climbing the easier, safer section there — the direct line up the middle weaves through many large cracks and is not the way. At the top of the glacier, stop and hunt along the margin for a place to cross the large moat, because that crossing, not the climbing, decides whether the route goes at all on a given day. Above the moat, the route begins in a rubble-covered fourth-class gully, and the rubble is the identifier: this is broken, dirty ground rather than clean rock, and it feeds directly into a snow couloir hidden from below.
