If what rises above your moat crossing is clean, steep rock with no rubble gully and no couloir behind it, you are too far along the face and should traverse back toward the glacier's northern end. Once in the couloir it steepens past sixty-five degrees in a couple of spots, with good cracks for rock protection on its right side and overhanging chockstones to pull through at the top, landing on a large ledge. The crux above that is two pitches around a loose thirty-foot granite tower split by a three-foot crack — if you have not passed a tower like that, the crux is still ahead of you.

approach_variants.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,400 ft), just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The entry is marked: a narrow ledge with a cairn on it leads into the southwest gully. After skirting snow you scramble talus and loose scree to that ledge. A cairn on a narrow ledge is the confirmation; an unmarked scramble straight into a gully is not this route.

Inside the gully the test is colour, and it is both a route-finding and a safety instruction: hug the left side, where the dark rock is solid. Parties call that band the black stairs and it offers cleaner scrambling than the middle of the gully. If you are on pale, rubbly rock, you are in the gut of the couloir and on the loose line.

Expect one short low-fifth pitch low down, then class 3 and 4 in the main gully, steepening near the notch between the summit and the West Tower.

Black Tooth Notch is the upper landmark and it is shared, so it identifies the mountain rather than the route: a foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse, with a fixed sling marking the crux step, and loose rock throughout. The Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge both descend through it; this is the only one of the three that climbs up through it.

And the most useful negative fact is about going down, because that is when it bites: the couloir's mouth opens onto cliffs above a waterfall. Exit left onto easier heather benches rather than continuing straight down. A party that is still descending the fall line when it hears water below has gone too far.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek to Access Col, then the sidehill traverse around Luna Peak to the Fury-Luna connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at milepost 134, this is a multi-day approach and not a day hike. The standard option follows the Big Beaver Trail: hike, or take the seasonal water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, roughly 6 miles up the west shore of Ross Lake to the Big Beaver Creek trailhead, then the maintained trail up-valley through old-growth cedar past the Big Beaver and Luna camps to a point about 1.5 miles north of Luna Camp, roughly 10-11 trail miles in.

Leave the trail there, ford Big Beaver Creek and climb steep pathless forest and heather along the north side of Access Creek to break out into the open, meadow-floored Access Creek basin below Luna Peak, which is relatively brush-free compared with neighbouring drainages. Continue up-basin past a camping area near the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to a notch around 6,100 ft, Access Col, which gives the first view north into Luna Cirque and the Southern Pickets skyline.

From the col a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass and Luna Cirque, then gains the Fury-Luna connecting ridge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug
hazards: Picking the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail in poor visibility, a documented error here
Cliff-band route-finding on broken ledges where a wrong tier cliffs you out
Poor, vegetated rock that takes gear badly, and shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif
Gullies dropping into Access Creek involve cliffy downclimbing and occasionally short rappels
Water is abundant along Big Beaver and Access Creeks but scarce above Access Col
One of the most remote summits in the range, with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route is entered from a small glacier, not from a ridge, and that is the discriminator. The northwest side of West Fury is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel on it is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions. If you are scrambling rock to reach the start of this route you are in the wrong place; the start is where you step off snow onto dirty, ledge-broken ground on the northwest flank.

The route-finding warning is the base finding, because the mistake happens here: leaving the glacier, you work up broken ledge bands to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated with few obvious anchors, and A wrong tier will cliff you out. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty, not the climbing. Pick the tier that keeps going; if you have to make a hard move to stay on a ledge, you are on the wrong one.

Confirm higher: from the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly east of the summit. Topping out east of the top and having to walk back west is correct on this line, not an error.

What does not belong here: this line is documented mainly as a descent by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent. Expect to be route-finding from first principles and treat any confident-sounding description of the ledges, including this one, as less precise than it sounds.

A named navigation hazard lower down, which is where the day is actually lost: poor visibility has caused parties to pick the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail. Some parties cairn the correct creek crossing on the way in. Access Creek's basin is the open, meadow-floored, relatively brush-free one; if you are fighting continuous brush you are in a neighbouring drainage.

approach_variants.name: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead off SR-20 near Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound about ten miles, losing steadily along Bridge Creek, to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp. Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail and head upstream; it gets brushier and less maintained the further you go, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek.

Around mile 13-14 the maintained tread effectively ends. Ford the North Fork — cold and sometimes knee deep, and easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn — then work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall draining toward the Goode Glacier, which is the way to avoid the worst brush. Look for the alder tunnel: a boot-path corridor through the slide alder that saves a great deal of thrashing.

Camp around the glacier toe at roughly 5,400-6,800 ft depending on how far you push. Plan on three to four days round trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late July through September. The moat crossing is easiest once the glacier has receded, around the third week of July, and gets harder again as the season goes on
hazards: A moat and bergschrund at the toe of the buttress with a steep step of about 50 degrees where the route steps off the Goode Glacier onto rock — worse as the season goes on, and reported by some parties as impassable late
Open crevasses and overhead serac hazard on the Goode Glacier
Loose and wet rock on the approach slabs beside the waterfall
Cornices on the approach in early season
A route that is difficult to retreat from once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window
A descent by the Southwest Couloir that several parties report taking 8-10 hours from summit to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark is a colour: the red ledges at the toe of the buttress. Three independent accounts name them, and one quotes a published description doing so. You are looking for a band of red rock where the Goode Glacier meets the foot of the buttress. If the rock in front of you is grey, keep looking along the toe.

The base is the moat at those ledges, and how you cross it is the measure of the season: a collapsed or intact snow bridge, a jump, a downclimb, or a short rappel followed by re-climbing on the far side. Published elevations for this point range from about 6,400 to 7,800 ft across different years and different parties, which is a real disagreement rather than a single number — the glacier has retreated and the crossing point moves. Navigate to the red ledges, not to an altitude.

Above the moat, expect one or two pitches of low fifth on precarious blocks, trending climber's right to gain the buttress crest proper. If your first ground above the glacier is clean and solid, you are not on the toe.

Tell it from the peak's other long route by whether you ever touched the glacier: Megalodon Ridge is gained from the east without crossing the Goode Glacier at all. If you crossed a moat off glacier ice, you are on the Northeast Buttress. If you never left brush and rock, you are on Megalodon.

Confirm as you climb: over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class on the crest, often soloed or simul-climbed, then around 8,000 ft a short unprotectable 5.7 slab on the crest that most parties deviate right to avoid, then roughly five pitches of 5.4-5.5 easing toward the summit. A route that is hard from the bottom is not this one.

approach_variants.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

approach_variants.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Long Duckabush valley approach, largely off-trail and unbridged on the Marmot Lake alternate
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed corridor
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer; ice axe advisable
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully system
Very long, remote walk-out far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

approach_variants.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
camps: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
approach_variants.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.
hazards: North Fork Skokomish Trail closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Rockfall, treefall and landslide hazard in the burn scar along the Staircase corridor
Deep, swift ford of the river at Nine Stream Camp in high snowmelt or heavy rain
Brushy, steep trail between Two Bear Camp and First Divide; abandoned Hopper Way tread lost under brush
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow on the approach and in the summit gully into early summer
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Very long, remote wilderness approach far from help

approach_variants.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
camps: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
approach_variants.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties stacked below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Difficult crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow in couloirs
Grizzly and black bear country; food storage required
approach_variants.baseFinding: Everything about this climb is on the south side, and the base can be picked up from either of two places. Coming across from the Carru col at about 7,600 ft, the start is where the col's flattish talus stops being flat and tips up into the peak's southwest face, a mixed slope of scree, talus and occasional patches of solid rock with no path, no cairns and no single obvious line, which is itself the signature of this face. Coming up from Shellrock Basin, the start is the toe of the broad south slope above the last stunted trees, at the point where heather gives out and continuous rock begins. In both cases the confirming feature is what is not there: this side carries no cliff band across it. If you are looking up at a wall rather than a long, tedious, uniform slope, you have drifted round onto the wrong aspect and should traverse back south. The mountain's real hazard sits on the far side of the crest, so the top is where care is needed rather than the base. The north side of the summit ridge is an enormous cliff, and the moment you can see straight down you have gone too far north. Which of the crest's several rises is the true high point is not obvious from the face below, so gain the ridge first and judge from up there; a faint boot-worn line runs along the crest and following it is more reliable than picking a top from the slope.

approach_variants.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

road.name: Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) and Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600)
road.status: Narrow, steep gravel with few turnouts above the end of the pavement; no trailers. The 2026 Ptarmigan Fire burned into the Middle Fork Pasayten, and its closure shut the Buckskin Ridge and Eureka Creek trails this approach uses; check the Methow Valley Ranger District's alerts before you go, and expect burned forest and blowdown in the valley.
road.driveNote: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement and continue on the gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and drive about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area.
road.seasonalGate: Usually snow-free and open July to September

trip.approach: From the Slate Pass Trailhead (about 6,900 ft), take Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 a short way north to the Whistler Cutoff and drop to the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail #478 on the valley floor, about 3.1 miles and 5,280 ft. Follow it north about 4.8 miles to the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp. From the lake, cross the crest east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained trail, where the creek can be hard to cross in snowmelt, and continue up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.
trip.itinerary: A common 3-day plan: Day 1 - hike in from the Robinson Creek or Slate Pass trailhead to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin. Day 2 - climb Mount Lago (often combined with Mount Carru via the connecting saddle) from a Shellrock Basin camp, roughly a half-day round trip. Day 3 - hike out. Many parties extend to 4-5 days to add Osceola Peak, Mount Rolo, or a full Pasayten ridge traverse (e.g. via Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain).

waypoints.name: Slate Pass Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement, then the narrow gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass; trailers are not allowed. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and climb about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area, about 6,900 ft. Fill out the free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten Trail junction
waypoints.directions: Head north on Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 and take the Whistler Cutoff where it splits off, dropping steeply off the ridge to the Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail #478 on the valley floor. The slope just below the pass holds snow into summer, and the river here is crossed without a bridge.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.directions: Turn north and follow the Middle Fork trail down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction. About 4.8 miles from the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin camp area
waypoints.directions: From Fred's Lake, climb to the pass on the crest above the lake and drop east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail; the crossing of upper Eureka Creek can be difficult in snowmelt. Continue east and up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount Lago Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb north up Lago's broad south slope, leaving the heather for continuous scree, talus and loose rock ribs; there is no path and no single line. Gain the summit ridge and follow the faint boot path along the crest to the true high point, staying back from the north side, which drops off in a huge cliff.

approach_variants.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt on the way to camp
Long walk down the Middle Fork Pasayten then back up to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms; grizzly and black bear country
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
camps: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in
approach_variants.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
approach_variants.season: July and August
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season as the snow finger melts, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft can hold snow or ice
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Hazardous footlog crossings over Thunder Creek at night or high water; no fixed anchors for rappels
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the northeast; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

approach_variants.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead.
hazards: Footlog crossing on Park Creek, hazardous at night or in high water
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft above Park Creek Pass can hold snow or ice
Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp; no fixed anchors for rappels

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
approach_variants.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
hazards: Gated trailhead tied to SR-20 seasonal closure limits when this way in is open
Crossing of a 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin before dropping to the lake camp
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow; snow bridge collapse risk on the Banded Glacier
Crevasses on the Banded Glacier; talus over hard glacier ice is treacherous in a whiteout
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy summit ridge and rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail route-finding; heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and Fisher Creek

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
bivy.notes: Reached via the Fisher Creek Trail fork off the Thunder Creek Trail (~9 miles in); the standard overnight camp below the Banded Glacier.
bivy.water: Lake at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — reserve via Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20) to Colonial Creek Campground
road.driveNote: Colonial Creek Campground is on Diablo Lake near milepost 130; the Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground.
road.seasonalGate: West of SR 20's winter closure gates (milepost 134 to 171), so this trailhead can be reached all year.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable permit fee, mid-May through early October; free the rest of the year; free for youth 15 and under.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: NPS wilderness/backcountry permit required for all overnight stays; reserve on recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA (SR 20 milepost 105.3).
access.closures: Easy Pass Trailhead (primary approach, SR 20 MP151) sits inside SR 20's winter closure zone (gates at MP134-171) and is unreachable roughly December through mid-spring; exact open/close dates vary year to year (2026 reopened unusually late, June 14, due to storm-repair work) — check WSDOT before a trip. The alternate Thunder Creek/Colonial Creek Campground trailhead (~SR 20 MP130) sits outside the closure gates and is open year-round, but is a longer approach (~13 mi one-way vs. Easy Pass's ~10 mi one-way to the lake camp). Thunder Creek Fire: North Cascades National Park's fire-closure list (updated September 14, 2026; no end date given) closes the Thunder Creek Trail from the Fisher Creek Trail junction to Park Creek Pass, and Junction Camp (hiker and stock sites) at that junction. The Thunder Creek approach turns onto the Fisher Creek Trail at the junction, which the list does not close, but Junction Camp cannot be used while this stands. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (NPS) — Ross Lake National Recreation Area / North Cascades National Park
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota reservation or walk-up
overnight_permit.where: Reserve a night-by-night itinerary online via Recreation.gov during the early-access lottery, or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites) at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount up to 24 hours ahead.

trip.approach: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground (SR 20, milepost 130) about 9 miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about 3 miles to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier, and follow it up to the lake.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead (Colonial Creek Campground, Hwy 20)
waypoints.note: Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit, reserved on Recreation.gov or picked up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to Colonial Creek Campground near milepost 130 on Diablo Lake. The Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Lake camp below the Banded Glacier
waypoints.note: Unnamed lake near 5,160 ft on Logan's north side; the usual high camp for the Banded Glacier. Mosquitoes are heavy in June and July, and getting around the lake can be awkward.
waypoints.directions: Take the Thunder Creek Trail about 10 miles to the Fisher Creek Trail, then the Fisher Creek Trail about 3 miles to just past a handrailed log bridge over the stream that drains the lake. Leave the trail and follow that drainage up to the lake at about 5,160 ft.

waypoints.name: Mount Logan summit
waypoints.note: Gain the northeast ridge on solid rock near 8,800 ft rather than climbing straight off the glacier at the summit block. Reverse the route to descend; the scree below the glacier is much harder going down than up.
waypoints.directions: From the lake, climb south-southeast up talus and snowfields to Christmas Tree Col, an orange-brown notch that is hard to spot from the lake. Drop onto the Banded Glacier and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col, then gain the northeast ridge on rock near 8,800 ft and scramble the Class 3-4 summit block.

approachLogistics.trailheadDirection: From the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (~1,200 ft)

camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The longer way in, and the one that stays open all year: the Colonial Creek trailhead is west of SR 20's winter closure gates. Take the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft about nine miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about three miles, past the handrailed log bridge, to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft. Roughly thirteen miles one way, with Neve Camp under two miles in for a late start.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

Talus lying on bullet-hard glacier ice is treacherous, especially in a whiteout descent

Sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding on the upper two-thirds; scree much harder to descend
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July

approach_variants.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Reached by climbing East Fury first: crevasses, a moat/bergschrund fall site at the glacier margin, loose Class 4-5 rock
Dense brush and devil's club on the Access Creek approach
Chossy, unconsolidated granite on the towers, prone to failure
Poor-quality anchors for rappels on chossy rock; each rappel makes retreat harder
Exposure on tower sections with 100+ ft drops and scarce reliable protection
Loose Class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
Extreme isolation: a committing ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of this route is a summit, which is the one thing on a mountain you cannot walk past. You are at the start when you are standing on the top of East Fury with the ridge running west toward the West Peak. There is no gully to find, no bench to identify and no chance of starting the wrong line: if you are not on East Fury's summit, you have not started.

What that means in practice, and it is a decision rather than a landmark: the commitment happens at the first rappel, not at the summit. Getting off each tower on the traverse means rappelling off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, and each rappel down makes retreat progressively harder. The place to decide whether the weather and the hour justify the traverse is on East Fury's summit, before the first pull.

What going too far looks like, on the other end: once off the traverse, the way home is back over East Fury and down its east side to the saddle on loose class 2-3 talus, then down the Southeast Glacier to Luna Col. Descending anywhere off the north side of the connecting ridge drops you into Luna Cirque, 2,400 ft below the col you camped at.

approach_variants.name: Low Divide and Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany col
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
approach_variants.notes: Low Divide is reached up the North Fork Quinault, or from the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Almost nobody comes for this peak alone — it is normally tagged while linking Christie, Meany and Seattle from one camp near the divide or in Seattle Basin.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Steep snow fingers in the approach cols into early summer, reported up to about 60 degrees
Loose rock on cliff bands below the summit cirque
Eroded, compacted sidehill gullies on the traverse beneath the peak; easy to start up the wrong chute
Unbridged creek fords on the approach (Wild Rose, Elip, Sixteenmile)
Off-trail travel over talus and heather toward the Noyes-Meany col; black bears in the corridor
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, any rescue is multi-day
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of this climb is a col rather than a face, and it is the same gateway parties heading for Meany use. From camp near Low Divide or in Seattle Basin, cross the head of Seattle Creek and work up talus and heather to the saddle between Noyes and Meany, gained by a loose rock couloir that tops out on a patch of snow. Standing in it, Meany's summit block is the abrupt tower on the north side and Noyes is the broader, lower ground opposite; the standard slopes leave the col directly and there is no gully mouth or rock step to identify, so the col itself is the landmark. The long sidehill traverse across eroded gullies that gets you there is the approach, not the climb, and the several similar-looking chutes cut into it do not go — resist the temptation to start up the first one that points at the summit. Above the col the ground is Class 2 to 3 along the summit ridge. If you find yourself over the far side and dropping toward the Elwha headwaters, you have crossed the divide instead of turning up it.

approach_variants.name: Elwha River to Low Divide

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

approach_variants.notes: The Elwha trail about 28 miles to Low Divide, plus the closed road walk at each end. Much longer, and used for traverses from the north.
hazards: Elwha River ford near Chicago Camp, hazardous at high water or snowmelt
Off-trail travel above Chicago Camp / Low Divide is unmaintained and choked with alder in places
About 28 miles one way plus a road walk or ride at each end because the access road is closed
Wasps in the lower forest sections in late summer; stings have put people out of action for days
Steep snow fingers in the approach cols into early summer; loose rock on cliff bands below the summit cirque
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, any rescue is multi-day

approach_variants.name: FR-62 road end to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes: From US-2 near Index take FR-62, bear left at the first junction around 1,600 ft, left again at the second near 2,380 ft, and drive the last increasingly rough mile to a small pullout at the road end around 2,800 ft. The road crosses private industrial timberland and its gate at the highway is locked at the owner's discretion with no warning, so be prepared to walk or ride an extra five miles and 2,500 ft of road. Above the pullout it is more boot path than trail — it vanishes intermittently in brush and is steep enough in places that you pull on trees.
approach_variants.season: June to October, or on winter snow
hazards: Dense brush and undergrowth that hide the boot path in several sections
Loose talus along the ridge traverse near Point 5017
A locked private-timberland gate that can add miles of road on short notice
Lingering snow and ice on the upper ridge and around the summit ponds into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no sign, no cairn and no marked trailhead: the start is an unmarked, steep, well-trodden gully directly opposite the road-end pullout. Stand at the small parking area at the very end of the road and look across it — the line is the obvious trodden gully cutting straight up the hillside on the far side, not any of the spurs running off into the clearcut. It is steep from the first steps and stays that way; the first mile carries almost all of the day's 2,650-odd feet of gain, through young forest and clearcut into older cedar and Douglas fir. You know that section is behind you when the path levels out onto the ridge crest and begins crossing talus fields. From there the ridge runs east past Point 5017, dips about a hundred feet, and climbs past two small ponds to the true summit — so if you top out at a viewpoint and the ground drops away ahead of you, keep going.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: The unmaintained Depot Creek trail crosses the border to Ouzel Lake, then the bench leads east to the south side. The easiest and most used way, but it means crossing the border on foot away from a port of entry, so confirm the entry rules first, and the road needs high clearance.
hazards: Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; it must be downclimbed
Steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season
Border crossing on foot away from a port of entry; high-clearance road to the trailhead
Ouzel Lake camp reached by an unmaintained trail; Custer-Spickard saddle and terrace traverse are cross-country

approach_variants.name: Silver Creek from Ross Lake
approach_variants.notes: The all-US way: a water taxi up Ross Lake to the mouth of Silver Creek, then a long bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake and north to the upper terrace. Harder and much brushier.
hazards: Long, brushy bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake; harder than the other way in
Water taxi up Ross Lake needed to reach the mouth of Silver Creek
Climbing above lakeside cliffs or talus and slabs to reach the upper terrace
Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season

approach_variants.name: White River, Glacier Basin, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From White River Campground, hike the Glacier Basin Trail about 3.5 miles and 1,700 ft to Glacier Basin near 5,900 ft — a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camp. Continue on climbers' path up to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, another 1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree and snow.

At the pass, rope up. Drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west and southwest between roughly 7,200 and 7,400 ft, threading crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east side.

This is the same corridor Liberty Ridge parties use, so in season there is often a boot track and other parties on it. Above St Elmo Pass there is no water at all.

Rockfall on the traverse concentrates in three places: immediately after you drop onto the glacier, roughly halfway across, and at the far end. Move through those, do not rest in them.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, in cold stable conditions when the rock is frozen in place
hazards: Serac-threatened sections below the Willis Wall icecap
Loose rock and mixed ground with complex route-finding
Rockfall concentrated at three points on the Winthrop traverse
Longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats running along the line of travel
Remote position with a long exit and no water above St Elmo Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach is shared with Liberty Ridge, so the only question that matters is where you stop. Curtis Ridge is the first ridge you meet after crossing the Winthrop. Liberty Ridge is beyond it, past the Carbon.

Count the glaciers. Between St Elmo Pass and this base you cross one — the Winthrop. If you have dropped onto a second glacier you are on the Carbon and you have walked past Curtis Ridge onto the Liberty Ridge approach.

The positive test is the view, and it is unmistakable once you have it: at about 7,200 ft the ridge gives you snow-free rock ground with the Carbon Glacier and the Willis Wall opening up on the far side. Standing on Curtis Ridge you are looking across at Willis Wall, not up at it. If the great capped wall is not in front of you, you are not on the ridge yet.

What being short looks like, and it happens in the dark: if you walked into Glacier Basin and kept going up the valley, you missed the turn for St Elmo Pass. The pass is gained by leaving the basin, not by continuing through it.

What being low looks like: the traverse holds 7,200 to 7,400 ft deliberately. Losing height on the Winthrop puts you into longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats that run the same way you are walking, which is the worst orientation to fall into one.

One more thing worth knowing before you commit: this ridge is more confusing and more committing than either of its famous neighbours, with 4th-class scrambling through rock bands and at least one rappel on the way up. If the ground is going smoothly you may be on the wrong feature.

approach_variants.name: White River Campground, Glacier Basin, Inter Glacier and Camp Schurman
approach_variants.notes:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,700 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.
approach_variants.season: Late spring through August, once the White River road and campground are open and before summer melt opens the upper crevasse fields
hazards: Crevasses on the Inter Glacier, which open through the season despite its mild reputation
Loose, brittle volcanic rock on the direct scramble down the Prow into Camp Schurman
Rockfall onto the moraine path above Glacier Basin
Crevasse maze above 12,000 ft where the Corridor ends
Bergschrund near 13,000 ft, which can be impassable direct in late season
Creek crossings and old slide paths on the Glacier Basin trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Three recognition points, in order.

At 0.9 mile from the trailhead there is a signed junction where the Emmons Moraine Trail branches left and crosses the Inter Fork on a seasonal footbridge. If you cross a bridge over the river this early, you have left the climbers' route. The way to Glacier Basin stays right, on the old mining road grade, and does not cross the river there.

The start of glacier travel is the toe of the Inter Glacier, roughly a mile past Glacier Basin and about 7,000 ft. You get there by following the moraine crest; the test is that the ground turns from rubble and moraine to continuous snow, and there is no more path. Rope up when it does.

Camp Schurman is the third. It sits at the foot of Steamboat Prow, on the saddle where the Emmons and Winthrop split, with a hut on it. If you have topped out on the Prow's rocky summit you are above camp — there is a short, steep, very loose scramble down the front of the Prow to the huts, and the more usual line drops from Camp Curtis onto the lower Emmons and comes at the camp along the Prow's southern side instead. Coming back down in cloud, the Prow is the handrail: keep it on your side and you will find the camp.

Above camp the climbing starts as soon as you step off the platform — the first thing under your boots is the Emmons. The feature to find is the Corridor: a smooth, wide ramp of about 30 degrees trending slightly east, running from camp up to roughly 12,000 ft. The test is smoothness. If the slope you are on is broken by parallel crevasse trains and you are already end-running, you have drifted out of the Corridor into the icefall on either side of it. Above 12,000 ft the smooth ground ends and the glacier does become a maze — that is expected, not a sign you are lost. The bergschrund is crossed near 13,000 ft, and late in the season it can force a long traverse onto the upper Winthrop toward Liberty Saddle.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, Glacier Vista and the Nisqually crossing to a Wilson Glacier camp
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,400 ft) take the paved Skyline Trail about a mile to the Glacier Vista overlook (~6,300 ft). This is where the route leaves the tourist ground: a climbers' path drops several hundred feet west off the moraine onto the Nisqually Glacier, crossing at roughly 6,200 ft. Most parties rope up before stepping onto the ice — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under an icefall and is genuinely committing in poor visibility.

On the far side, a boulder-filled gully angles up and right onto the left-hand side of the Wilson Glacier. About 700 ft up that gully there is a sheltered rest point with bivy sites. The more usual choice is to continue onto the Wapowety Cleaver and follow its crest to a high camp at roughly 9,000–9,200 ft at the edge of the Wilson Glacier, where there are rock windbreaks and a large rock buttress for shelter.

Use the daylight from camp. The traverse of the Wilson Glacier under the Wilson Headwall to the foot of the couloir has real route-finding, and you will be doing it in the dark. Scope the line the evening before.

The route is climbed early in the day for one reason: the ground above the couloir catches sun very early, and the couloir is the drain for everything it loosens.
approach_variants.season: Spring, while the couloir is snow-filled and the rock above is still frozen
hazards: Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing at about 6,200 ft
Route-finding on the Wilson Glacier traverse, normally done in the dark
Rockfall funnelled down the couloir once the sun reaches the ground above it
Avalanche hazard in the couloir
Large crevasses on the upper slopes that can force long end-runs late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the mouth of the Fuhrer Finger, on the eastern side of the Wilson Headwall at around 9,500–10,000 ft, and the identification problem is that there is more than one gully there.

The Finger is the wide one, with an hourglass constriction partway up. The Fuhrer Thumb is the narrower gully immediately west of it — steeper, more constricted, and it can cliff out. If the gully you have entered pinches down immediately, walls closing on both sides, with no wide apron below the constriction, you are in the Thumb, not the Finger.

Positive test: from the base, you should be looking up roughly 2,000–3,000 ft of continuous snow at about 40 degrees, wide at the bottom, narrowing to an hourglass, and widening again. That is the Finger. It runs out onto the west side of the upper Nisqually Glacier and eventually joins the upper Kautz Glacier ground near 13,000 ft.

Negative marker on the approach itself: if you have crossed the Wilson and are directly beneath a broad steep ice face rather than beneath a gully system, you have gone too far and are under the Wilson Headwall proper.

The other test is time of day. If the sun is on the rock above the couloir and you are still in the lower half of it, you are in the fall line of the day's rockfall and the correct decision is to be out of it, not to keep climbing.

approach_variants.name: Paradise to Camp Muir, then straight up the Ingraham
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical to the Disappointment Cleaver: Paradise (5,420 ft), Skyline Trail past Panorama Point and Pebble Creek, then the Muir Snowfield above McClure Rock to Camp Muir (10,080 ft). Pebble Creek is the last water. The snowfield is unmarked and unmaintained and is bounded by crevassed glaciers and by the corniced cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock; the Park Service's published bearing from Pebble Creek toward Moon Rocks is 355 degrees true.

What is different is the season. This is the winter and spring line, so the snowfield is more often a navigation problem than a walk, the camp is colder and quieter, and self-registration for the climbing permit is done at the Paradise old station kiosk in the winter season rather than at a staffed wilderness desk.

Above Camp Muir the route crosses the upper Cowlitz eastward, passes through Cathedral Gap and reaches Ingraham Flats (~11,200 ft). From there it stays on the glacier the whole way instead of stepping onto rock. Between roughly 11,800 and 12,300 ft it weaves back and forth, end-running large crevasses. Large seracs overhang the western side of the glacier near 12,500 ft. The route rejoins the standard line at the top of the Cleaver (~12,300 ft), or in some conditions trends toward the top of Gibraltar Rock at about 12,600 ft on slopes up to 50 degrees.

A hard overnight freeze is what makes this route reasonable; without one the bridges are unreliable and the seracs are active. Parties leave camp in the small hours for that reason, not for the view.
approach_variants.season: Roughly January through the end of May, while the Ingraham is filled in and before the Cleaver route opens
hazards: Whiteout navigation on the Muir Snowfield, with crevassed glaciers on both flanks
Winter cornices and hidden cliffs between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock
Overhanging seracs on the western Ingraham near 12,500 ft
Crevasse bridges dependent on a hard overnight freeze
Avalanche hazard on the glacier slopes in winter and spring conditions
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision point — and the thing to recognise — is at Ingraham Flats, because up to there this route and the Disappointment Cleaver are the same walk.

Stand on the bench. The rock rib rising on your north and west is Disappointment Cleaver. The Direct does not touch it. Your line goes up and right of that rib, staying on snow and ice, aiming into the broken ground below the Ingraham icefall.

The test that you are on the Direct and not the Cleaver: after leaving the Flats you should never put a crampon on rock. If you find yourself scrambling a rock rib, you have joined the Cleaver.

The test that you are too far west: seracs. The western portion of the Ingraham near 12,500 ft has large overhanging ice above it. If ice blocks and debris are lying on the snow around you, you are under the icefall's fall line and need to be moving, not navigating.

The end of the crevasse maze is legible: at about 12,300 ft the ground you are on merges with the top of the Cleaver and the weaving stops. If you are still end-running individual crevasses well above that, you have drifted west toward Gibraltar Rock — a legitimate finish on steeper ground, but a different one.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the glacier. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
hazards: Roped travel and crevasse rescue readiness needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually; complex crevassed Kautz glacier travel
Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and Kautz Icefall in the approach zone, plus The Fan gully
Two steep ice steps (about 35-40 and 45-50 degrees) beneath serac and rockfall
Brittle or hard ice on the upper step with screws the only protection; dinner-plate ice onto belayers
Short rappel or fixed-line downclimb off the Camp Hazard bivy rock to reach the base
Descent rappels on self-built ice anchors; old threads not to be reused; altitude and fatigue near 12,000 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The headwall and the standard Kautz Chute are two different lines off the same camp, and the test is how many steep steps you meet.

Count two. This route presents as two ice steps separated by a band of lower-angle snow: the lower step around 35-40 degrees, the upper around 45-50. Step, bench, step. If you climb one sustained runnel and the angle then eases the whole way to the summit plateau, you were in the standard Kautz ice chute, not on the headwall.

The upper step is the one that settles it — noticeably steeper and more sustained than the lower, needing two tools and screws in ice that is often harder or more brittle. The lower step is broad and stepped out and rarely steeper than about 35-40 degrees, and most parties get up it with a single tool and a couple of screws. If the harder ground came first, you are not on this.

Where you rope up is part of the finding: on the Turtle or Wilson Glacier below the headwall, often after a short rappel or a fixed-line downclimb off the bivy rock at Camp Hazard. Descending off camp before you climb is correct and is a good sign you are on the right line rather than walking out along the chute.

The approach has two starts and they land in the same place, so do not let the difference unsettle you: Paradise via Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, or the Comet Falls and Van Trump Park trail from a lower trailhead. Both cross the Nisqually onto the Wilson and climb the Turtle. If you find yourself on maintained trail beside a waterfall you are on the second of those, not lost.

What being too late looks like: seracs and rockfall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall hang over the steep ground. The upper step must be climbed efficiently and early. The honest reading of arriving at it warm and in the sun is to go down.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park

bivy.name: Castle camps on Wapowety Cleaver
bivy.notes: Two camp areas on the ridge below Wapowety Cleaver at the edge of the Wilson Glacier. Lower Castle, about 9,250 ft, has a few closely spaced rock rings for small parties; Upper Castle, 9,400 to 9,500 ft, has large rock rings and is where most parties camp. Wind-exposed.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites behind old rock windbreaks

bivy.name: Camp Hazard
bivy.notes: On the climber's left of the Turtle Snowfield at about 10,800 ft: three large rock rings below the Kautz Ice Cliff, and the highest regular camp on the route. It shortens summit day. The original Camp Hazard, nearer 11,000 ft, sits in the fall line of ice from the cliff and is not used.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent sites on rock and snow

approach_variants.notes: Climbs from the Comet Falls trailhead past Van Trump Park and up the moraine beside the remnant Van Trump Glacier, joining the Paradise line around the Castle and the base of the Turtle. Preferred late in the season: it never crosses the Nisqually and has running water low down, but it starts about 1,700 ft lower and the descent is easy to lose in the trees.
hazards: Starts about 1,700 ft lower than Paradise and the descent is easy to lose in the trees
Never crosses the Nisqually; moraine beside the remnant Van Trump Glacier joins the Castle approach
Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and Kautz Icefall in the approach zone
Two steep ice steps beneath serac and rockfall; brittle ice on the upper step, screws only
Crevassed glacier travel on the Kautz approach; dinner-plate ice fracturing onto belayers
Descent rappels on self-built ice anchors; altitude and fatigue near 12,000 ft

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass, Curtis Ridge and the Carbon Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Glacier Basin trailhead in White River Campground and follow the Glacier Basin trail. At about 6,700 ft leave the trail to the right and climb snow slopes to St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft). There are bivouac sites in this area.

From the pass, descend onto the lower Winthrop Glacier and traverse west across it, holding elevation, to the broad slopes of Curtis Ridge. Cross Curtis Ridge and aim for the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier at roughly 7,300 ft. Then ascend the Carbon southward toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, negotiating the crevasse fields on the way.

Access onto the ridge is somewhere between about 8,600 and 8,800 ft, and either flank can be used depending on conditions.
