Above that it is 30–40 degree snow with scree and rock traverses up to Thumb Rock at about 10,500 ft — the standard bivouac, with additional sites just above in the saddle. There are also bivouacs around 11,000 ft.

Most parties do not reverse this. The usual plan is a carry-over: finish at Liberty Cap and descend the Emmons–Winthrop to Camp Schurman and out to White River, which is why this route is often permitted as a multi-camp itinerary rather than an out-and-back.

Rainier permits apply: per-person climbing permit and a wilderness permit for each night.
approach_variants.season: May and June — after the winter storm cycle and before the ridge melts out to loose rock
hazards: Serac and icefall discharge from Willis Wall onto the traverse below it
Crevasse fields on the Carbon Glacier below the toe
Rockfall from the bands above Thumb Rock, worse as the season melts the ridge out
Committing terrain — retreat down the ridge is difficult, most parties carry over and descend the Emmons
Bergschrund and short vertical ice gaining the Liberty Cap Glacier near 13,500 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the toe of the ridge on the Carbon Glacier, and the whole approach is a sequence of things you must leave rather than things you arrive at — so the negative markers do the work.

Leave the Glacier Basin trail at about 6,700 ft. If you reach Glacier Basin Campground you have walked past the turn; the branch is a climbers' line up snow to the right, aiming at the notch of St Elmo Pass at 7,400 ft.

After St Elmo Pass you should be losing height onto the Winthrop Glacier and then traversing, not climbing. If you are gaining, you are heading up the Winthrop toward the Emmons ground and Camp Schurman — the wrong side of the mountain for this route.

The crossing under Willis Wall is the marker that you are close and the marker that you are exposed. Between Curtis Ridge and Liberty Ridge you pass beneath a huge dark face capped with ice cliffs. That is Willis Wall, it is not your route, and its summit seracs discharge onto the ground you are crossing. If you are still under that face, you have not reached the toe yet — and this is ground to cross without stopping, not ground to navigate on.

The positive test: Liberty Ridge is the rib that divides the Carbon Glacier from Willis Wall. When Willis Wall is behind and to your east and there is a defined rock-and-snow rib rising in front of you out of the Carbon, you are at the toe. Start looking for access between roughly 8,600 and 8,800 ft; take whichever flank is in condition rather than insisting on the crest.

Thumb Rock at 10,500 ft is the confirmation you got it right — the first real flat ground on the crest, with established bivouac platforms and a saddle just above.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and Ptarmigan Ridge, then up the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and seasonal. In a normal year it opens well after the roads on the east and south sides of the park — commonly not until July — and closes with the first significant snow. Since April 2025, though, the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge that carried the only public road to it has been closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers, so Mowich Lake itself is now a long wilderness walk from another park entrance.

From Mowich Lake, follow the Wonderland Trail about 0.3 mile to the Spray Park Trail, then take that trail roughly 3-4 miles up through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Spray Park Trail tops out and begins to descend toward Seattle Park and the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge.

Near 8,300 ft you leave the ridge and drop about 1,000 ft of loose rock and snow to the North Mowich Glacier. Rope up there and climb the glacier, watching for fresh rockfall debris on the ice, to camps at roughly 9,600-10,200 ft below the face.

There is no water above Spray Park and no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds of this approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for ice; the face bares out and starts shedding rock as it warms
hazards: Sustained steep ice and snow with multiple line options and no obvious separation between them
Serac and rockfall hazard on the face; the North Mowich crossing collects the debris
A bergschrund that is frequently impassable direct and must be turned
Roped glacier travel with crevasses under thin snow bridges on both the drop from camp and the return
No walk-off: topping out commits the party to a carryover and a car shuttle
Road access on this side has been closed since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two named rocks are the only hard markers on the whole cross-country section, and they work in cloud because they are big and they are a pair. You leave the Wonderland Trail and go between Echo Rock and Observation Rock. Not past one of them — between the two. If you can only see one rock, you do not yet know which one it is.

The second thing is counter-intuitive and it is where parties go wrong: at about 8,300 ft you leave the ridge and go down. The face is across the North Mowich Glacier from Ptarmigan Ridge. If you keep climbing the ridge past that point, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge, which is a different route to a different top-out. Losing height off the ridge is correct and is the single clearest signal that you are on this climb and not its neighbour.

The bergschrund is the arrival and it is frequently not passable direct. It has to be turned, so budget time for looking rather than treating the schrund as a formality. Reaching a schrund you cannot cross straight over means you are probably in the right place.

This is the umbrella face, not a single line, and that is the most important thing to carry in. Four separate climbs share this wall and this camp — the North Mowich Headwall, the Central Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge above and to the side of them. They are told apart by which glacier you cross from camp and by what the first ground above the schrund is, not by the walk in, which is identical for all of them. Decide which one you are doing before you leave camp in the dark; there is roughly 4,000 ft of 40 to 55 degree ice and mixed ground above, and being one line out is not a thing you discover early.

What retreat looks like, because it is not the way you came: there is no walk-off from the top of this face. Topping out commits you to a carryover down the far side of the mountain to Paradise or White River and a shuttle back. Backing off means reversing the North Mowich Glacier, climbing about 1,000 ft of scree and talus near Observation Rock, and walking out through Spray Park.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Skyline Trail and the Nisqually Glacier to the lower bergschrund
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at about 5,400 ft, follow the Skyline Trail up past Glacier Vista and Pan Point, then leave it and drop west onto the Nisqually Glacier. This is the same access point the Wapowety Cleaver lines use. Rope up before you step onto ice; there is no maintained trail from here on and no reliable water once you leave Paradise, so plan on melting snow.

Ascend the Nisqually alongside the Wapowety Cleaver, gaining steadily to about 9,900 ft where the lower bergschrund marks the start of the technical ground — typically 40 to 50 ft of steep ice or snow to gain the icefall itself.

Above that the route threads broken, crevassed terrain in the upper Nisqually basin toward the top of the Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft. That basin is the most time-consuming and the most dangerous section of the whole climb: it sits directly under active icefall and rockfall, and the correct tactic is to move through it without stopping to regroup. The seracs rearrange themselves every season, so expect to find your own way rather than follow anyone's line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is an early-season line: the icefall wants to be frozen, and hazard rises steeply through the summer as the glacier warms
hazards: Active icefall with collapsing seracs directly above the upper basin
Complex crevasse and serac navigation that changes every season
Hazard rises rapidly with warming through the day, so the upper basin must be crossed early
Documented history of large slide activity in the icefall
No reliable water above Paradise
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the lower bergschrund at about 9,900 ft. Everything below that is glacier walking, and the whole recognition problem is not confusing that walking with progress.

First test, and it is the one that decides the day: which way you go at Glacier Vista. This route drops west off the Skyline Trail onto the Nisqually. If you are still walking uphill on maintained trail toward Pebble Creek and the Muir Snowfield, you are on the Camp Muir approach and the icefall is behind your left shoulder. Parties have made that mistake in the dark because the first mile is identical.

Second test, and it works in cloud because it is a side, not a landmark: the Wapowety Cleaver — the rock cleaver dividing the Nisqually from the Kautz — must stay on your left the whole way up. If it has ended up on your right you have crossed onto the Kautz side of it and you are on the Kautz Glacier route.

Third test, positive: the schrund is the first steep ground on the route. If you have walked moderate glacier for hours and met nothing steeper than a crevasse crossing, you have not arrived — keep going, do not start climbing something because it is steep.

The negative test is the most useful one here, and it inverts the usual instinct: a boot track is evidence you are wrong. This route is circuitous enough and dangerous enough that it is rarely climbed in any given season. A trench underfoot on the Nisqually almost certainly belongs to parties walking to Camp Muir, not to anyone on this line.

What being too high looks like: if you are in the upper basin with seracs above you and have not crossed a bergschrund, you have wandered into the icefall from the side rather than climbing into it, which is exactly the ground you least want to be standing still in.

approach_variants.name: Westside Road, Round Pass, St Andrews Park and the Puyallup Cleaver
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate at Dry Creek near 2,900 ft, about 3 miles up Westside Road, which leaves the main road a mile past the Nisqually entrance. The road is gravel and open to vehicles only for the first few miles; beyond that it is foot or bike travel, and has been that way for years because of flood damage in the Tahoma Creek drainage. Treat the walk as part of the route rather than as an inconvenience that might be lifted.

Walk the road about 3.8 miles to Round Pass, then take the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to St Andrews Park. Leave the trail there and climb north through alpine meadows onto the Puyallup Cleaver, passing Tokaloo Spire.

Leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft and traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater. Camps are used on Colonnade Ridge, on the Puyallup Cleaver near 9,000 ft, in the open near 9,600 ft, and at the bergschrund in the amphitheater itself.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, best frozen; typically out of condition by July
hazards: Serac and icefall hazard above the Sunset Amphitheater
Rockfall in the amphitheater headwall
A long crevassed traverse of the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers just to reach the base
Rotten volcanic rock on the knife-edge ridge between the gendarmes
Remote west-side position with a road walk at both ends of a very long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision is a leaving, not an arriving, and it happens at about 8,500 ft on the Puyallup Cleaver. Up to there you are simply walking a ridge. At 8,500 ft you step off it onto glacier and traverse. If you keep climbing the cleaver you will end up over on the Tahoma Glacier side and this route is gone.

Passing Tokaloo Spire is the confirmation that you are on the right cleaver. It is the named rock feature on the way up from St Andrews Park. No spire, no cleaver — you left the trail in the wrong place.

The positive test at the base is that the ground closes around you. The Sunset Amphitheater is a bowl shut off by a headwall, with the serac band above it. If you are traversing open glacier that does not close into a bowl, you are still contouring and have not arrived — or you have dropped too low and are heading out across the South Mowich toward the Mowich Face, which is a different climb reached from a different trailhead on the far side of the mountain.

The climb's own signature is two gendarmes, and it confirms the route rather than the base. Above the steep ground the ridge runs as a knife edge between two prominent gendarmes on notably loose, rotten volcanic rock. If the ridge above you has no pair of towers on it, you are on a neighbouring feature.

What the crux looks like, so you know you are on it: roughly 1,000–1,300 ft of 55- to 60-degree neve or ice, and it is the only sustained steep ground on the route. Anything shorter and you have not started; anything that keeps going far past that and you are on the amphitheater headwall rather than the ridge.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop-to-Carbon traverse under Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
The traditional approach was the Carbon River road to Ipsut Creek and up the Carbon Glacier. Carbon River access ended in April 2025, when the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge, the only public road in, was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; the Carbon side is now a very long wilderness walk rather than a drive-in.

The approach most parties now use starts at White River Campground: Glacier Basin Trail to Glacier Basin, climbers' path to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, then rope up, drop onto the Winthrop and traverse west and around beneath Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft.

From the Carbon, walk up under the wall. Bivy sites exist in the Curtis Ridge access gully and on Curtis Ridge itself.

This is one of the most objectively dangerous pieces of ground in the range. The whole wall is capped by the summit icecap and swept by what comes off it. Nothing in the rack protects you from that; being there in the cold hours does.
approach_variants.season: Cold, hard-frozen conditions only — a narrow and unpredictable late-spring window, and the route is more often not in condition than in it
hazards: Extreme objective hazard from the hanging summit icecap seracs, along the entire wall
Continuous rockfall down the face
No easy retreat once committed; a long, serious approach on both sides
Crevassed glacier travel on the Winthrop and Carbon, and again on the summit icecap above
Carbon River road access has been closed since April 2025, which makes that side a multi-day walk
approach_variants.baseFinding: The test is what is above you, not what is in front of you. Willis Wall is capped along its entire top by the hanging summit ice cliff, and all three of its ribs rise from the base of the wall directly above the Carbon Glacier, underneath that cliff. If you are standing beneath a face that is not capped by a continuous ice cliff, you are not under Willis Wall. The two ways to be wrong are on opposite sides, and the ridges name them. Willis Wall is bounded by Curtis Ridge on one side and Liberty Ridge on the other. Facing the wall from the Carbon Glacier, Curtis Ridge is the rib you came around to get here and Liberty Ridge is the rib beyond the far edge of the wall. If you have walked past Liberty Ridge you are under Liberty Wall, which is a different wall with a different reputation. Count the glaciers: two. Winthrop, then Carbon. One means you stopped at Curtis Ridge. The route does not name a rib, and that is the fact to carry in. This wall carries three distinct ribs, climbed in different years by different parties and of materially different character. Which one you are under is a decision to be made at the base, from photographs taken before you left, and not something the approach settles for you. Do not treat 'the base of Willis Wall' as though it were one start. What being too late looks like: nothing visual. The wall does not change. Time of day is the variable that kills here, so the honest base finding is that arriving under it after the sun has been on the icecap means turning round, not looking harder for the rib.

approach_variants.name: Indian Creek Trail and the Airplane Creek bushwhack to Airplane Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead above Lake Wenatchee, the Indian Creek Trail crosses the White River on a footbridge — which has washed out in past years, forcing a ford — and runs up the valley through old growth and sections of burned, dead forest. Somewhere near Airplane Creek you leave the maintained tread; nothing marks the departure and it is easy to lose in brush or fog. The bushwhack from there to the lake is the hard part of the day: roughly two thousand feet of gain through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, made worse by the standing dead timber. Favouring the drainage about a quarter mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush. Snow cover typically begins around 4,000 ft and becomes continuous near 4,700 ft in early season, so step-kicking on firm snow is normal here into July. Airplane Lake is the last reliable water and the only sensible flat camp. Time the White River and Indian Creek crossings for the morning, when the water is lower.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. In July expect snow from around 4,000 ft and continuous cover above 4,700 ft, which makes the upper slopes a snow climb and calls for an axe.
hazards: off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, worsened by burned standing timber
White River and Indian Creek crossings that get harder through the afternoon as snowmelt rises
hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that can cliff out a party working toward the northeast ridge
lingering snow on the upper east slopes into July
loose rock and steep talus on some summit variations
a sheer northwest face that is not a descent or a bail option
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go east-facing and clean, not north and broken. From Airplane Lake three distinct lines go to the summit and you have to pick one; the two face lines start at the foot of the upper east face at roughly 6,200 ft, while the northeast ridge is gained north of the lake. The one to aim for is the direct ascent of the clean upper east-face slabs — recognisable because the rock is continuous and relatively clean rather than piled and broken, and because it faces the morning sun squarely. The other two are a steep, looser talus variation and the northeast ridge. The northeast ridge is the one to be careful of, and it carries its own negative marker: gaining it means working around a cliff band north of the lake that is not visible until you are on it and that has cliffed parties out. So if you find yourself traversing north of the lake into broken ground and then meeting a wall you did not expect, you are on the northeast-ridge variation, not the direct line. Snow coverage should decide the choice; on a snowy year the direct slabs may be a snow climb wanting an axe. The summit itself is broad with jagged rocks at the top, and the register sits west of the highest point among rocks about fifteen feet below it — worth knowing, because the true high point is not where the register is.

approach_variants.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
approach_variants.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Unbridged river and creek fords on the North Fork Quinault approach that become dangerous after rain or in snowmelt
Multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp; emergency help far away and frequently impossible to contact
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below
Northeast aspect drops thousands of feet — stay off that side
Lingering snow into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

approach_variants.name: Up the Elwha to Low Divide

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

approach_variants.notes: The long northern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the whole valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp, then climb to Low Divide. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.
hazards: Elwha River trail is several days long; a road walk or bike ride is needed to reach the trailhead
Unbridged river and creek fords on the Elwha approach, dangerous after rain or in snowmelt
Wasps in the lower forest sections in late summer
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below; northeast aspect drops thousands of feet
Extreme remoteness; emergency help frequently impossible to contact

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek crossing near milepost 3, then the Wall Street couloir to the Northwest Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to the pullout near milepost 3, just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir, at about 2,950 ft. This is NOT the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of the road.

Cross Ruth Creek. There is no bridge; parties cross on whatever logs are in place, and a three-log cluster has been used. Then about 45 minutes of thrashing through slide alder and devil's club to the avalanche debris at the foot of the snow gully.

The couloir runs roughly 1,500 vertical feet and opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft; from there the route crosses the glacier to a saddle near 6,500 ft and scrambles the southeast ridge to the summit.

Timing is the whole trade: earlier means more snow and more avalanche risk, later means thicker brush and discontinuous snow.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep for the scramble; the couloir has also been climbed and skied in winter, when it is an avalanche path rather than a walk
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Ruth Creek on logs that change year to year
45 minutes of slide alder and devil's club with no tread
A 1,500 ft avalanche path — the debris at its foot is the evidence
Crossing the Northwest Glacier above the couloir
Shattered summit rock on the southeast ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Wall Street is a corridor with walls on both sides, and that is the test. Once you are in it, the gully holds a remarkably uniform gradient of 30-35 degrees and a uniform width of about 50 feet, with very steep rock walls on both sides, for roughly 1,500 vertical feet. Nothing else on this side of the valley does that. In cloud you do not need to see the top: if you can touch rock on your left and rock on your right and the angle is not changing, you are in Wall Street. If your gully fans out, or has a wall on only one side, it is not.

Getting to it: the marker at the bottom is avalanche debris. After the creek crossing and roughly 45 minutes of alder and devil's club, the brush ends at the debris pile at the foot of the snow gully. Debris is what tells you the gully above you actually runs — and it is also the reason to be there early and cold.

The arrival at the top of the couloir is the glacier. The corridor opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft. Walls end, glacier starts.

The discriminator against the peak's other two routes, and it is decided in the car park rather than on the mountain. Three routes on Sefrit start from three different places: this one from the Ruth Creek pullout near milepost 3 on Ruth Creek Road; the Bloody Head Couloir from the Ruth Creek trail higher up the valley near 3,450 ft; and the Southwest Ridge from the Nooksack Cirque trailhead at the end of FR-34, a different road entirely. If you drove to the end of FR-34 you cannot reach this route today.

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead at the end of FR-34, then an ascending traverse through the cliff band
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34), and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. This is a different trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32, and from the milepost-3 pullout the Wall Street route uses.

Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge.

Follow the old roadbed and Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west and southwest ridge, passing through or around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system.

A separate, lower-angle line on the north side — Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier, finishing on the southeast ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed Class 3 traverse and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak. The two are easily confused in planning and impossible to confuse on the ground, because they start on different roads.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Early summer high water can make the Ruth Creek ford at the trailhead difficult or unsafe
hazards: An unbridged ford of Ruth Creek at the trailhead, difficult or unsafe at early-summer high water
A cliff band to be negotiated on an unmarked ascending traverse
Several similar-looking forks in the summit gully, only one of which is the easy line
Loose rock near the summit ridge
Fixed slings of unknown age at the crux step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The cliff band is the gate, and the gully you want is above it. Fifty minutes up Trail #750 you leave the trail and traverse upward, passing through or around a cliff band. Everything below the band is approach; the summit gully system starts above it. If you are still under continuous rock, you have not got through the band yet.

The gully splits, and the answer is leftmost. Above the cliff band the summit gully divides into several forks. Take the leftmost fork — or, put the other way round, the one immediately west of a snow couloir lying to its right. Those two descriptions are the same instruction from two sides and together they are checkable in poor visibility: find the snow couloir, then take the rock fork on its left.

The rock itself is a confirmation. On this line the rock is generally solid low down and gets looser near the summit ridge. If your fork is loose from the first moves, you are probably in one of the other forks.

Which side of the mountain am I on? This is the coarse test and it is settled by the drive: this route starts on FR-34 at the Nooksack Cirque trailhead and works up the peak's west and southwest side. Sefrit's other two routes are both reached from Ruth Creek on the north side and neither of them can be reached from here without going back to the car.

Descent note that cross-checks the start: parties reverse this line, and some rappel the short crux step off pre-existing slings rather than downclimb it. Slings on a short step above a cliff band is the same feature seen from above.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then take the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge.

The wall these routes are on sits in the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, rising about 1,000 ft out of the snow. It is known as the West Face Wall — worth saying plainly, because it faces west and some descriptions of the mountain's south side sweep it in with the south face, which sends parties looking on the wrong aspect.

Bivy sites are at Stuart Pass and at Goat Pass. Most parties camp at one of them and walk in to the wall in the morning.

The descent goes over the top: continue up the West Ridge to the summit, or take the main West Ridge gully down with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right onto a large bench where a single-rope rappel gets you back toward the Stuart Pass bivies.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-early Sep, once the snow below the wall has gone down enough to reach the start by a short scramble and before autumn storms
hazards: Snow at the foot of the wall early in the season, making the short scramble to the start awkward
Long runouts between placements and hidden loose chockstones
A west-facing wall that gets full afternoon sun and afternoon weather
Topping out high on the West Ridge with a long descent still to do
An unplanned bivy is a real outcome; parties carry for it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Walk the foot of the wall until you find a splitter you can put both hands in. The start is an obvious hand-and-finger splitter crack, and it does not begin at ground level — it starts on a small ledge about 15 to 25 feet above the snow or talus, reached by a short scramble. That gap between the ground and the first moves is the single best confirmation you are in the right place: a crack running all the way to the snow is not this one.

Where on the wall: you are in the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, roughly halfway between them, under about 1,000 ft of rock. If you are still on either pass you have not arrived; if the wall has ended and you are back on open talus you have walked past it.

Shared start, and say it out loud before you rack up: this route and the other two lines on this wall begin at the same crack and share the first four pitches. The differences are higher up, at the major ledge system splitting the wall — this route goes left there where the original line continues right. So finding the base correctly does not settle which route you are on, and the choice has to be made deliberately at that ledge rather than followed.

What to expect above, as confirmation you started right: two pitches of corners and arêtes to a bolted anchor, then a long horizontal traverse rightwards on the third pitch. If nothing on your third pitch traverses, you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the West Face Wall — same base as the other two lines on the wall
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the approach for the other West Face Wall routes. From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below the West Ridge and on to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camp at either pass.

This line is a direct start and direct finish grafted onto the existing routes: it climbs the first four pitches of the original line, steps left onto the middle pitches of the direct, and then breaks out onto its own two-pitch finish up an overhanging headwall splitter.

Because of that, none of the decisions on this climb are made at the bottom. The base is shared; what makes it this route is a pair of choices at the ledge system and again below the headwall.
approach_variants.season: Late summer into early September, before autumn storms; the headwall is the point of the route and it wants dry rock
hazards: Significant runouts between protection placements
Loose rock with hidden chockstones
Thirty-plus metres of overhanging exposure on the headwall pitch, with retreat from it awkward
Alpine weather on a west-facing wall late in the season
An unplanned bivy is a documented outcome on this route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the same splitter the other two routes use — a hand-and-finger crack starting on a small ledge 15 to 25 feet off the snow or talus, gained by a short scramble. There is no separate King Kong start to look for, and hunting for one is how parties waste an hour at first light.

So the real arrival test is the wall, not the route: you want the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, with about 1,000 ft of rock rising straight out of the snow above you. Anywhere still on a pass, or anywhere the wall has petered out into talus, is wrong. And the aspect is west — this wall takes the afternoon sun, so if you are standing under a face that has been in shade all afternoon you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

Where this route actually becomes itself, which is what you have to know at the base because you cannot see it from there: four pitches up the original line, then left onto the direct for two pitches, then the two-pitch finish. The connector out to the finish is a roof bulge and a stem-box on overhanging jugs; the headwall pitch above it is a splitter on a steeply overhanging wall with more than thirty metres of air under it and two fixed nuts at its top.

If you reach a ledge system and simply continue right, you are on the original line and will finish on it. Nothing will stop you or tell you. The decision is yours and it is made in the middle of the wall.

name: Lena Lake to Mt Stone traverse

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake, Upper Lena Lake and the way-trails to St. Peter's Gate
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at about 750 ft, the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail #810 runs about 3 miles through second- and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Beyond the lake the trail narrows to steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage, roughly 3.5 more miles and 2,700 ft to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft — 6.5 miles and about 4,000 ft from the road, the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp.

From Upper Lena Lake the traverse goes cross-country: the Scout Lake way-trail west across meadows and huckleberry-heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake, contour high round it into Scout Basin, then up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft overlooking Ullin's Bathtubs. From Ullin's Pass a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp angling across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending at a loose grungy moraine, then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft — roughly 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake.

No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Scout Pass and Ullin's Pass are largely clear; many parties still carry an axe
hazards: Extensive off-trail and way-trail route-finding over multiple ridges and passes
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate
A very long outing, up to about 16 miles and 9,000 ft of gain, with limited bail options partway through
Fog and whiteout navigation on Mount Stone's upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route
Exposed headwall sections with several-hundred-foot drops on the Putvin Trail below Lake of the Angels, some using a fixed handline or tree roots
Unbridged stream crossings requiring downclimbing to the bed and back out
The exit is at a different trailhead and needs a shuttle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the summit climb is 300 ft below St. Peter's Gate, and the first move is downhill — which is the whole test. Reach the Gate (the traverse's high point at about 5,950 ft, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge). Then descend about 300 ft to the base of a basalt cliff and cache your overnight packs there. The climber's path up the south-face gully starts at the foot of that cliff. A route that goes up from the Gate is not this one.

That is a good fog test precisely because it is counter-intuitive: standing in a notch with the summit above you, the instruction is to lose height first and pick the line up from underneath the cliff band.

Second test, in the gully: it is a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mount Stone's south face, and it leads into a rock bowl below the summit block. The bowl is the confirmation — an enclosed basin of rock, not a ridge and not open slope. From it the line joins the standard west-ridge route for a final 100 ft or so of Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the true south summit. That last detail is worth trusting: the rock at the top of this peak is noticeably better than anything below it, so if the last hundred feet is still rubble you have not reached the summit ridge.

What goes wrong here, and it is recorded rather than hypothetical: fog is common on Mount Stone's upper mountain and multiple parties have lost the route and ended up in unplanned harder terrain, and in cloud the true south summit is confused with the Middle and North summits. Count your summits and do not accept the first one.

Exit note that is part of the plan, not an afterthought: the standard finish continues southwest half a mile to the Lake of the Angels basin and out the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake. Arrange a shuttle or stash a bike before you start.

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 from SR 542
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Lake Ann trailhead on the east side of the Mount Baker Highway, roughly a mile below Artist Point. The trail goes down first — several hundred feet over its first mile and a half — before climbing back to the broad saddle above Lake Ann at roughly four miles.

Just past the saddle there is an unsigned fork. The right branch drops to the lake, the campsites and the outlet, which is the last easy water. The left branch is the climbers' boot path, and it is distinct and well trodden — a very obvious break heading east toward the mountain.

That path sidehills north beneath Shuksan's lower moraines, switchbacking and crossing two gullies over talus and lingering snow tongues, and becomes vague right where you need it most: just short of the first chimney. Parties typically reckon around six hours from the car to the high camp on or above the chimneys, and expect the snow tongues to be firm enough for microspikes and an axe in the early morning well into July.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: rockfall inside the chimneys, especially with parties above
firm or icy snow tongues on the talus traverse before the sun hits
the route-finding itself — the boot path deliberately goes obscure right at the chimney entrance
several dead-end side paths ending at cliff edges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the crux of the whole approach and it is regularly got wrong. Where the boot path fades, stop and look east at the cliff band. You want a small snowfield pushed up against the base of the cliff, with a right-slanting ramp of slope at its foot and, almost straight across from you, a deep green gully. Drop about fifty feet and cross straight over the talus and snow — usually there is an obvious boot pack — until you are at the cliffs.

The test that settles it: the correct gully has a beaten dirt trail running up it and rock scoured clean by thousands of boots, and at its foot there is a rappel station slung around a tangle of dead tree roots. Look for the trail, not for a plausible line of weakness.

The negative markers are unambiguous. If you are looking up a gully whose rock is furred with moss or lichen, it is the wrong one. If you are climbing on heather with no path underfoot at any point on this route, you are off it. And there are tempting side paths that lead out to cliff-edge viewpoints and stop — if the ground ahead simply ends at a drop, reverse and find the trail again rather than pressing on. The chimneys are a braided ledge-and-step system, so it is also easy to overshoot the entrance entirely and end up traversing along the base of the cliff band past it; if the cliff on your right has become continuous with no green break in it, you have gone too far.

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trail #750 via Hannegan Pass Road
approach_variants.notes:
Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) off the Mount Baker Highway, then Nooksack Cirque Road (FS-34) to its end. There is no bridge over Ruth Creek at the trailhead — the crossing is on a large logjam a little downstream, and in high water or after rain it has turned parties around before they started.

Beyond the crossing the old roadbed runs about two miles through old growth to the original trailhead, then it is river-bottom travel along the North Fork Nooksack: gravel bars when the water is low, riparian brush when it is not. You pass the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary at roughly three miles and the national park boundary at about four.

Rather than continuing into the cirque, leave the tread and watch across the valley for the steep drainage of Price Creek. Cross the Nooksack on a log and climb the forested hillside toward Price Lake — steep, open forest with old flagging, about an hour and a half from the river to the lake basin at roughly 4,700 ft. Budget the better part of a day for the approach; most parties treat the whole climb as two to three days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun; a heavy snowpack is preferred
hazards: unbridged Ruth Creek log crossing, sometimes impassable
brush and vague route-finding along the river flats
steep, loose, unofficial climbers' path to Price Lake
rockfall and icefall down the gully between Nooksack Tower and the glacier's main lobe — large blocks reported
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two candidate stopping points and they are not the same place. From the moraine below Price Lake, work up through the cliff bands onto the heathery ridge on the lake's south side, then ascend the rock slabs up and to the right. The first bivy sites are flat granite just below the ridge crest at the glacier's margin, around 6,000-6,500 ft — that is a camp, not the start of the route.

The start of the climbing is the exposed snow saddle beneath Nooksack Tower, roughly an hour further along the glacier. You get there by gaining the glacier at the ridge crest and traversing climber's right. You will know you are there because Nooksack Tower's mass is directly above you and the gully between the tower and the main lobe of the Price is the thing you are trying to get past — it is the rockfall funnel, and it has delivered blocks the size of a television down onto the traverse.

If you are still on heather and slabs above Price Lake with no glacier underfoot, you are below the start. If you are on flat granite with a view down to the lake, you are at the bivy, not the saddle.

approach_variants.name: Shannon Ridge Trail #742 (standard)
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road (FR 11) north from SR 20 near milepost 82, then FR 1152, then the 1152-014 spur to its end. The spur is rough and rutted; high clearance is the sensible minimum. An overnight in the park needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, obtained in person at Marblemount or arranged in advance with the wilderness office.

The trail opens as an old roadbed running northeast. It stays easy for roughly the first two miles, then a long-standing blowdown belt makes for tedious weaving before the tread turns into a real trail and angles left through brush onto the open crest of Shannon Ridge.

Above treeline the ridge rolls along through meadow and scattered timber to a pass at about 5,400 ft, where a major north-south ridge is joined and the Sulphide Glacier with the summit pyramid behind it comes into view for the first time. One party logged roughly four and a half hours and about 2,800 ft of gain to this point. Camps are established on the glacier's lower flats at about 6,200 ft and higher at about 6,500 ft; both have had composting toilets, but the upper one has been closed when full, so carry blue bags. There is no reliable running water above timberline late in the season.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: loose rock funnelled down the summit-pyramid gully, worst late season when the snow has melted out of it
moat between glacier and pyramid, which widens through the season
crevasses on the Sulphide as snow bridges thin after midsummer
blowdown belt on the lower trail is easy to lose in the dark
no reliable water above timberline
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts where the glacier ends against the summit pyramid, and the whole navigational problem is picking the right groove out of several parallel ones. Walk the glacier to its high point directly beneath the centre of the rock pyramid — not around either shoulder. The correct line is the central gully: it is the one carrying fixed rappel anchors and old slings, because every party that summits rappels back down it, and its rock is scoured and boot-polished rather than mossy. If you are looking up a steep parallel groove with no anchors visible and clean-cut, untravelled rock, you are one gully off; traverse back toward the middle of the face.

The last few metres before rock are the giveaway that you have arrived: a short steep snow patch and then a moat where the glacier has pulled back from the pyramid. Early in the season a snow bridge spans it; by August it is an open gap you step or scramble across, and that step is the true start of the climbing. If you are still walking on flat glacier with rock only in the distance, you are short of it.

A second, separate option exists — a gully on the southwest side, reached by continuing around the western edge of the glacier until the pyramid stands squarely in front of you. It is a distinct line, not a variation of the central gully, and parties who take it still descend the central one.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass to upper Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail (it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail at about 0.3 mile) and, at the junction about 1.7 miles from the car, near 5,440 ft, turn right for Longs Pass rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin. Switchback up open slopes to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

Descend the steep dusty north side of the pass, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, and cross Ingalls Creek in the timber below. In normal summer flow this is a rock-hop; it is also the last reliable water before the ridge, so fill up.

Pick up the climbers' path heading west up the valley toward Stuart Pass. You leave it well short of Stuart Pass, in the upper meadows at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft, and traverse climber's-left (north) across talus and heather benches to the foot of the ridge. There is no tread on this traverse and it is the part of the day people get wrong.

Some parties break the approach by camping near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for dry rock; snow lingers on the Longs Pass north side into early summer
hazards: No maintained tread on the talus/heather traverse from the Stuart Pass trail to the ridge — several minor gullies look alike
Steep loose descent off the north side of Longs Pass; icy at dawn in early summer
Loose talus below the ridge with rockfall exposure from parties above
No water past the Ingalls Creek crossing
Descent is the Cascadian Couloir, and 'not staying right' near the top of it is a documented route-finding error
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is identified by counting gullies, not by elevation. Three roughly parallel gullies come down the lower west ridge; the route takes the middle one, and it is deeper than its neighbours. The confirming feature is at its foot: a single enormous block, described by everyone who has been there as the size of a house, sitting at the base of that gully. If there is no house-sized boulder, you are one gully over.

From the boulder you push up through scrub into the gully and climb up and rightward inside it. The gully ends at a notch — scramble through the notch and Long John Tower is directly in front of you, a distinct pinnacle on the crest. That sighting is the second confirmation that you took the right gully; if you top out of a gully and there is no tower, you are not on the West Ridge.

The climbing past Long John Tower goes up a chimney on the tower's left — about three quarters of a pitch, with a chockstone near the bottom. (An alternative works a short dihedral with a fixed piton, or a layback further along the ledge, before regaining the crest.) Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse beyond it are the two places parties most often stall for route-finding.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek south fork to the basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the Lake Stuart / Colchuck Lake trail past the fork and leave the maintained tread near the meadow at about 4,500 ft, heading southwest and following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream.

After a couple of miles a steep talus and boulder slope leads into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak. This is the standard camp for the whole north side, and the flat ground itself is the arrival cue.

The glacier has three parts and it is worth knowing them before you set off in the dark: a lower snowfield, the glacier proper, and a steeper couloir in its northwest corner. Parties rope for the short glacier section and take the rope off above it.

This is a compact two-day outing, and it is the line most parties descend after climbing the Ice Cliff Glacier — so if you meet people coming down it at midday they are probably finishing a different climb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul while the glacier still carries continuous snow; it is also the standard early-season descent off the north side, which is when most parties are on it
hazards: Crevasses in the middle section of the glacier and an icefall at its toe
Wet-snow avalanche and rockfall onto the glacier as the day warms
Straying right into the Ice Cliff Glacier's serac fall zone in poor visibility
A steep, unmaintained talus climb into the hanging valley with no trail
Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that move with the snowpack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Sherpa is the one with no ice above it, and that is the whole test. Standing in the basin facing the mountain, the three features run in this order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the huge rock rib of the North Ridge.

So the Sherpa is the leftmost — the easternmost — of the two glaciers, and it is the one with nothing hanging over it. The Ice Cliff, immediately to its right, carries an obvious hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. If there is a serac above you, you are one glacier too far right.

Touch test, and it is the one that works when you cannot see: the ground under the Ice Cliff is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of ice. The Sherpa's toe is ordinary snow over ordinary moraine. Standing on rubble made of ice is direct evidence you have drifted right.

Where it takes you, as a confirmation rather than a route description: the Sherpa's couloir tops out on the crest of Mount Stuart's east ridge at roughly 8,500 ft, followed by a Class 3 scramble west along the ridge over the head of the Cascadian Couloir. It does not lead to the West Ridge — that is the Stuart Glacier Couloir, on the other side of the rock rib.

And the steep part is in the glacier's northwest corner, not up its middle. If the steepest ground you can see is straight above the centre of the snowfield, look again at which feature you are under.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better
hazards: Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties
Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail
A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions
An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt
Early-season snow and ice in the cirque
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The cirque is the arrival, and it is unmistakable even in cloud because it closes around you. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

Which clearing, which is the actual problem: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is east of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

Confirmation at the base: the technical pitches start up the centre of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

Preview it from Longs Pass. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the south-face basin, then the heather-and-talus slope to the ESE notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at I-90 exit 52, about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through Commonwealth Basin and up the Kendall Ridge switchbacks. At roughly 5.5 to 5.7 miles you cross the Kendall Katwalk, the exposed cut in the cliff band most parties use as a progress checkpoint.

Continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, the last reliable water before the high basin, and on to the foot of Bumblebee Pass. A short, steep, unmaintained climbers' path with loose tread climbs to the 5,400 ft pass, then drops down the north side into the open basin directly below Mount Thomson's south face — the same basin West Ridge parties camp in.

Roughly eight miles one way with about 3,600 ft of cumulative gain, since the up-and-over at Bumblebee adds height beyond the net summit gain. Three to five hours car to basin, nine to eleven hours round trip is typical.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk when icy or windy
Loose tread on the unmaintained Bumblebee Pass path, awkward with a pack
Loose talus and minor route-finding on the slope to the notch
A short but exposed class 4 step at the summit, downclimbed or rappelled on the way back
A long day with an up-and-over on the return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the basin, look for the steep heather-and-talus slope that leads to an obvious notch at about 5,600 ft on the east-southeast ridge. Heather and talus rather than clean rock is the signal you are on the correct slope; the West Ridge side is scree and gendarmes.

The altitude is the discriminator between the peak's two routes, and it is worth setting your altimeter for: this notch is at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side. The West Ridge notch is at about 5,960 ft on the other end of the mountain. Roughly 360 ft and a full traverse of the peak separate them.

What follows confirms it: from the notch, scramble up and traverse left along the ridge crest on mostly class 2-3 ground to the base of the final summit block. Easy scrambling with a leftward traverse is right for this route. Chimneys and fifth-class corners are the West Ridge.

And the route ends at one specific obstacle, which is the best confirmation of all: a short, exposed 20 ft class 4 step guarding the true summit. Most parties protect it with a rope or a handline. If you reached a summit without meeting that step, you are on a false one.

Useful context: this is the easiest way up the peak and it is also the standard descent for West Ridge parties, so a party coming down at you is normal rather than a sign of a mistake.

approach_variants.name: Standard trail to the falls junction, then the unofficial boot track
approach_variants.notes: Start from the same paved trailhead as the standard route — the Teneriffe lot, 2.9 miles up the road and past both the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, not either of those. Take the graded trail up the access path and onto the old logging-road grade to the signed falls junction at about 0.9 mile, then turn right on the falls trail and switchback up to the falls viewpoint at about 2.8 miles. From just below the viewpoint the unofficial track leaves and climbs the forested southwest flank directly, and it is steep, rocky and eroded rather than graded.
approach_variants.season: May to October. Snow lingers near the ridge crest into early summer, and the track is markedly more slip-prone when wet.
hazards: The unofficial track is steep, root- and rock-covered and prone to erosion, and is worse on descent than on ascent
Wet or mossy rock on the ridge raises slip risk sharply compared with the standard trail
Route-finding on the boot track is less obvious than on the signed trail, especially in poor visibility
Loose rock and minor exposure on the ridge crest, with lingering snow near the crest into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the falls viewpoint, where the maintained falls trail ends, leave the maintained trail. The boot track bypasses the falls on climber's right — that is the physical test, because the falls themselves are the landmark and the track goes round them on one specific side. Above the bypass the tread changes character completely: it stops switchbacking and climbs the fall line on roots and rock, gaining a saddle on the southwest ridge. From the saddle the route is a direct, largely switchback-free push up the open ridge crest through meadow and a rock band, with a short scramble move at the true summit. Negative markers: if the trail underfoot is still graded, signed and switchbacking with the falls spur behind you, you missed the turnoff and are on the maintained trail; and if you are dipping to a saddle after a viewpoint over the valley, having never left graded tread, that is the standard trail's saddle, not this ridge.

approach_variants.name: Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead
approach_variants.notes: From the freeway exit into North Bend, continue through town and turn north onto the road running below the peaks. Carry on 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, to the paved seventy-car lot — this is the Teneriffe trailhead, not the Si one, and the two are easy to confuse. A short access path switchbacks up to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for a mile and a half through young forest and meadow. The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk; vehicles left past closing risk being locked in.
approach_variants.season: March to November, best from June to October. Snow lingers on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June and makes an otherwise easy trail steep and icy.
hazards: Seasonal snow on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June, creating steep icy sections on otherwise easy trail
No reliable water beyond the falls — carry what you need for the round trip
The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk
approach_variants.baseFinding: The checkpoint is the signed spur to the falls at about 0.9 mile, on the old road grade. Stay on the road grade there rather than branching right to the falls; beyond the road grade the trail narrows into switchbacks. Continue through the switchbacks, past a viewpoint over the valley to the north, and on to a saddle at around forty-two hundred feet where the trail dips before the final stretch. The base of the only hands-on ground on this route is above that saddle: a short rocky step at the true summit, about a mile further on, needing sure footing but nothing more. Negative marker: if you have left the graded tread at the falls onto a steep boot track of roots and rock climbing the fall line beside the falls, you are on the unofficial ridge line and are committed to a much steeper day.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Terror Creek crossing and the flagged climber's track into Crescent Creek Basin, then the west gully to the chockstone notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track marked with pink flagging past moss-covered cliffs to reach Crescent Creek Basin. Total approach gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

This is the standard descent route for every north-side line on the peak, so it sees traffic in both directions and its features are described mostly from above.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully with little shelter
An undercut, melted-out snow moat in the gully by mid to late season
A loose and marginal final 100 ft of the gully
Stuck ropes in the confined terrain
Dropping into Crescent Creek Basin from the wrong notch north of the Chopping Block
Early-season snow and ice in the choss gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The top of this route's gully is marked by a large chockstone, and that chockstone is the single best feature on the peak for orienting in cloud. From Crescent Creek Basin, the west gully system climbs to the low notch between Terror and The Rake, and a large wedged chockstone sits near the head of it. Everything on this side is described relative to that block.

So the confirmation is countable from below: climb a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully out of Crescent Creek Basin and keep going until a chockstone blocks it near the crest. That is the notch. Above it the route is a short summit tower.

On the approach, the drop into Crescent Creek Basin is the thing parties get wrong: do not use the low notch north of the sub-peak known as the Chopping Block. The correct line from the Chopping Block ridge down into Crescent Creek Basin is about 100 yards north of that notch, at a flat, bivy-site shelf on the ridge. A flat shelf big enough to sleep on, 100 yards north of the obvious low notch, is the marker.

What the gully is like, so you know you are in the right one: narrow, with little shelter from rockfall, frequently holding an undercut melted-out snow moat by mid to late season, and with a loose and marginal final stretch. Two or three rappels in the gully, plus one or two above the notch, get parties down, on a mix of pre-existing slings and natural chockstone and horn anchors.

At the top: the summit tower is downclimbed or a short section rappelled back to the notch off existing sling anchors.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the PCT North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft: cross under I-90, take the first right, lot on the right. Follow the PCT northbound through timber on long switchbacks for roughly 5.5 to 6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk at about 5,400 ft, a narrow ledge blasted into a granite cliff on the ridge north of Kendall Peak — solid underfoot, very exposed, and worth care if icy or windy.

Continue north about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake at about 5,260 ft, the last reliable water and a common camp; roughly two to two and a half hours and about seven miles from the car.

About 0.4 to 0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT. It climbs a steep 200 ft to Bumblebee Pass at about 5,400 ft, above Alaska Lake. Drop off the far side into Bumblebee Basin, then contour and climb northwest across talus and scree toward the ridge.

About 8 to 8.5 miles and 2,900 to 3,000 ft to the base, typically four to five hours for a fit party.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk, exposed and dangerous when icy or windy
Loose and eroded tread on both sides of the Bumblebee Pass boot path
Talus and scree in the basin below the ridge
A descent by the East Ridge, meaning a route-finding descent on unfamiliar ground at the end of a long day
A long day: many parties climb it car to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the lowest point in the ridge, and know in advance that it is further left than it looks. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is not where you want to be. The notch you want is left of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

The notch is small, and its size is the confirmation: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

Expect short fourth-class scrambling around gendarmes to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

The first move settles it absolutely: pitch one begins with a step left into a well-featured chimney. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

And the other route on this peak is on the opposite side: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River and the Blue Glacier via Snow Dome
approach_variants.notes: The long rainforest walk to Elk Lake and then a steep last couple of miles to Glacier Meadows, including a washout crossed on a fixed ladder — one person on it at a time. From camp, the moraine trail, then roped travel across the Blue Glacier and up Snow Dome. A Bailey Range crest line reaches the same col from the north.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Genuine crevasse hazard on the White and Hubert glaciers, not just covered talus
A steep, loose descent off the Olympus massif that has turned parties round
Rotten shale, sandstone and pillow basalt prone to rockfall
Route-finding across the massif in poor visibility with no landmarks
No cell coverage and a long, complex evacuation from anywhere up here
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow Dome is the broad snow basin above the Blue Glacier and it is the fork in the day: the Olympus lines carry on east and up, while the Mount Tom line leaves it westward. Traverse horizontally along the snowy upper massif, staying below the main Olympus summits, until you can drop onto the White Glacier on Tom's northeast flank or the Hubert on its south side — either way the aim is the col between Tom and the Olympus massif. The base of the scrambling is where that glacier ends against rock at the col, and the give-away is the terrain immediately before it: a steep, loose descent off the Olympus massif, which is the crux of the day rather than a link between two easier halves, and the point where otherwise strong parties have turned back. Above the col a Class 3 to 4 scramble on loose rock gains the summit block. The obvious continuation off Snow Dome leads to Olympus and not to Tom, and the White Glacier is genuinely crevassed rather than a snowfield, so stay roped until you are standing on rock.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp and the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The traverse starts by climbing Torment's South Ridge, so the approach is the South Ridge approach. From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount), take the old mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four creek crossings, treeline at about 5,300 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft — call it 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft from the car.

From high camp traverse the upper basin northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, beneath Forbidden's south spur, crossing a rock rib and a couple of snowmelt channels, heading for the toe of the Taboo Glacier and the lower South Ridge.

Because the traverse is long and committing, many parties instead carry over and camp at about 7,100 ft on the Taboo directly under Torment's southeast face at the foot of the east couloir, which turns a very long day into a reasonable one. Others bivy on the ridge partway across.

Overnight permits for Boston Basin are picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Moat and bergschrund at the foot of the east couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 gully with parties above
Whiteout navigation across the basin-to-glacier traverse
Early-season avalanche exposure and buried creek crossings
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The traverse's start is the same notch that starts the South Ridge, and finding it is a glacier problem, not a rock problem.

Rope up at the toe of the Taboo and follow the glacier up on its climber's-left side, watching for crevasses. You are looking for the one deep gully that breaks the rock band on the left — the east couloir. A bergschrund and a moat sit at its base; the moat where the glacier pulls away from rock can require a short awkward move onto rock, and this crossing is where a picket, axe and crampons for the leader earn their weight.

Above the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 to the notch. Standing in the notch you are on the crest with Torment Basin dropping away to the west and the Taboo below to the east — that two-sided view is the confirmation that you are at the base of the climbing and not partway up a blind break in the rock band.

Later in the season, when the moat is bad, parties cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain it from the Torment Basin side instead. Adjacent scrambling lines that avoid the snow couloir and rejoin the same notch are also described.

The whole basin-to-glacier traverse is genuinely easy to lose in a whiteout — it is uniform open ground with no trail — so if you cannot see the Taboo, do not start the traverse on dead reckoning alone.

approach_variants.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
