approach_variants.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October
hazards: Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Loose pea gravel over hardpack on the lowest switchback set
Steep open slope below the summit ridge holds consolidated snow
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
No dependable creek on the trail; hot, exposed switchbacks
Small upper lot fills early on summer weekends
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no scramble on this route, so the questions that matter are which fork and which top. Above Camp Windy, at about 5,500 ft and roughly three miles in, the trail meets the Silver Lakes Trail: stay right and uphill. The left fork drops toward Silver Lakes on loose, unmaintained ground and is not the route. You have taken the right branch when the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the grade eases markedly for the final stretch, with the last quarter mile crossing open, low-angle grassy and rocky tundra rather than anything steep. The high ground is a broad, flat ridge with more than one apparent top. The south summit is the true high point; the popular viewpoint where most people stop and turn round sits a short, easy walk below the actual crown, and the north summit further along the crest is lower still. Rock outcrops on the south top give the only wind shelter up there. Early season, snow on the upper meadow and on the steep open slope gaining the ridge is where the tread is easiest to lose in flat light.

approach_variants.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
approach_variants.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.
hazards: Open, exposed, dry ridge for the last mile, with no water
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek washout, Nooksack Cirque, Price Lake moraine and the ridge to the 5,900 ft slab bivy
approach_variants.notes: From the Mount Baker Highway, turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) immediately before the Nooksack River bridge, about 13 miles past Glacier. Stay left at 0.5 miles, then bear right onto Nooksack Cirque Road (FS-34) at about 1.4 miles, and park at the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway, by Ruth Creek at about 2,156 ft. Walk the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 ft. Ford the Nooksack. There is a recorded log crossing near N48.87097 W121.61267 — new logs get swept away every year, so treat the coordinate as where to start looking rather than as a bridge. Go up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting on the west bank of Price Creek until a good log turns up. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake at 3,911 ft, then follow the ridgeline between the Price and East Nooksack Glaciers up to a rock slab bivouac around 5,900 ft. From the bivy, get onto the glacier, traverse climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. This route belongs to Nooksack Tower and not to Mount Shuksan — it was merged from a duplicate Shuksan entry, and the Price Glacier route on Shuksan is a different climb sharing much of the same ground.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier the river is high and the couloir is safer; later the river drops but the couloir bakes and sheds rock
hazards: Fording the Nooksack on logs that are swept away and replaced yearly
Rockfall down the couloir, recorded on the first ascent and in every account since
A hollow bergschrund that has forced parties to swing wide left
A descent of roughly ten 60 m rappels off gear you build yourself — fixed anchors here should not be trusted
Parties routinely still on the couloir or the lower approach after dark; one team took 21 hours from camp back to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The bergschrund at roughly 6,500 ft is the base, and the couloir above it is the only one. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

The ridge between the two glaciers is the handrail. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

The saddle is the hinge, and it is counterintuitive. From the bivy the traverse is climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you drop down onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

Confirm at the schrund: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung wide left to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on Shuksan, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.

approach_variants.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
camps: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing from Goat Pass
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully to the notch, with parties above
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
Awkward retreat from the Gendarme's offwidth; navigation above the notch is on you
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The notch is a place you can sit down, and that is the test. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class gully off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

Orientation at the notch, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

What you have deliberately given up: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.
hazards: Stuart Glacier climbed to reach the notch; crevasse hazard on the glacier
Snow-filled gully to the ridge, usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge
Off-trail climbers' path from Mountaineer Creek into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
No water on the ridge; bivy ledges are few and exposed

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and a large cairn, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces.

The objective from here is the huge cleft that splits the two Early Winters Spires, seen from the west side. Head for its foot. Note this is the west-side gully — the couloir that splits the same two spires on the east side, reached from the highway hairpin, is a different feature and a different route.

Be ready to swap between rock shoes and boots if snow is still lying in the gully.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: snow lingering in the gully early season — axe and crampons
loose rock funnelled down the gully, including from parties above
wind in the gully; it channels weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is at the very foot of the enormous chasm dividing North from South Early Winters Spire — it is the biggest single feature on this side of the group and it is unambiguous even in poor visibility, because nothing else on the west faces is a full-height cleft between two summits. The route opens with a short step of low-fifth-class slab and layback moves, and then it is walking up the gully bed; if you are pulling on anything hard in the first rope length you are on one of the face routes to either side, not in the gully. Pitch one takes cracks and ramps along the left edge of the gully rather than the middle. The house-sized chockstone that names the route sits much higher up the same gully, so do not expect to see it from the base as your confirmation.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the north side of North Peak
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 35.2 turn south on Mount Index Road and drive 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs roughly 3.6 to 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft to the lake at around 2,500 ft, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur near mile 1.6. The maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

From there, traverse talus and very large boulders along the west and south side of the lake, near an old rockslide, toward the base of North Peak's wall. In early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and snow and ice piled at the water's edge.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep, after several consecutive dry days
hazards: Wet moss on downsloping slabs — low-angle ground that is genuinely serious
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early season
Vertical brush steps with no protection
Loose, vegetated rock throughout; slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing does not start on the clean wall you first walk under. The original line begins on the broken, bushy spur on the northeast, which rises out of the wooded ridge above the lake — you start on third and fourth class slabs and grass, not on clean rock. The confirmation is uncomfortable but reliable: the first few hundred feet are downsloping holds on generally solid slab, often sopping wet with moss, and that is what being on route feels like here. Dry, clean, positive rock at the start means you have wandered onto one of the harder faces.

The first fixed reference above the slabs is a vertical wall with a two-piton anchor — that is the normal point to rope up. Above it a ramp system passes as the 'hidden ledge', then a steep brush tunnel with vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps pulled on vegetation. Between roughly 3,000 and 3,600 ft the brush is at its worst. This face does not dry out at the rate other alpine rock does; several dry days beforehand are part of the route conditions, not a nicety.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse left (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch
approach_variants.baseFinding: Keep traversing north along the base. The Northwest Corner begins at a distinct corner-and-crack system whose first pitch — around 45 metres of 5.8, including a short chimney section with sparse gear — runs up to a broad ledge covered in trees. That treed ledge is the landmark: it is visible from below and from across the basin, it is the top of pitch one, and the route continues up and left off its left-hand edge. If you are under blank slab with no corner leading to a treed ledge, you have not gone far enough north yet. The corner start is shared with the West Face route, so being at the right corner puts you at the right place for either — the two diverge above the ledge, not below it.

approach_variants.name: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
approach_variants.notes: Access is the hard part and it has changed. The classic way in is by passenger ferry up Lake Chelan and a village shuttle to the Railroad Creek trail, then a long valley walk to the Lyman Lakes basin — but that corridor has been shut by flood and landslide damage with no near-term reopening, so plan instead on the longer route in from the Phelps Creek side over Spider Gap, which is eleven or twelve miles one way and involves glacier travel with an axe. Either way this is a camp-in-the-basin objective, not a day out. Maintained tread effectively ends at the lakes; everything above is picked by eye with no path and no cairns. It is commonly paired with the lower summit less than a mile to its south from the same camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September; axe early
hazards: Unconsolidated talus and scree with no path, releasing rock onto anyone below
Snowfield at the foot of the south flank persists through late summer and may need an axe early in the season
The lower southwest ridge is cliffed and drops off; it is not an ascent line
Wet, lichen-covered rock near the summit
Extremely remote; the corridor to Railroad Creek has been closed since the 2025 storm damage, so access is uncertain
Afternoon thunderstorms and long emergency response times
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the Lyman Lakes basin the mountain shows as a broad talus flank above open meadow, and the base is a specific, findable thing rather than a general slope: a snowfield lying at roughly 7,000 ft at the foot of that flank, which survives into late summer most years and is visible as a white patch from the camps when you look up from the lake. Cross the meadow, round onto the south and southeast side, and climb to it. Above the snow a broad ledge leads rightward into the main gully, and the gully takes you to a notch on the crest from which the ridge runs to the top. Do not try to gain the crest lower down on the southwest side — that ridge is cliffed below the notch and the drop-offs are the reason parties are warned off it. The other thing to keep straight is which summit you are under: a lower, closer peak sits under a mile to the south, and if the ground ahead is easing toward a rounded top rather than steepening into a gully, you are on that one.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

approach_variants.notes: The Phelps Creek trail to Spider Meadow, over Spider Gap and down to Lyman Lakes, then the same basin to the south flank. No boat needed.
hazards: Glacier travel with moats and crevasses crossing Spider Gap and the Lyman Glacier; ice axe and traction needed even in August
Permanent snowfield below the gap must be crossed
Unconsolidated talus and scree on the south flank, releasing rock onto anyone below
Wet, lichen-covered rock near the summit
Long approach of roughly 11-12 miles one way, in an area affected by fire and road closures
Remote terrain with long emergency response times; afternoon thunderstorms

approach_variants.name: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Tiffany Springs Campground sits at about 6,760 ft and is reached by long gravel drives from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, from the Methow Valley, or over Baldy Pass on the South Fork. The Conconully line is the roughest of the three. Expect an hour or more on gravel whichever you choose.

Trail #373 leaves the campground east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, about forty-five minutes of easy walking. From the pass, traverse south on the grassy east slope below the crest into the small cirque at the base of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft, then climb the boulder field to the foot of the climbing at about 7,600 ft.

Compared with anything else in this corner of the state the approach is short and easy, which is most of this face's appeal. Roads are snowbound for much of the year and generally open around late June.
approach_variants.season: June through early September, once snow has cleared the lower rock
hazards: Shares its entire lower half with the easier arete beside it; the split is at the tower, not at the base
The flaring chimney and offwidth crux takes awkward and sparse gear
Loose rock and teetering blocks on the ridge and near the tower
The old descent trail above the lower lake is faint and easily lost
Long gravel access from every direction with no quick exit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the cirque, read the face as two halves: snow gullies on the left, and a distinct rock tower with a ridge running up to it on the right. Both rock routes are on the right half. If you are looking up a continuous snow chute, you are on the wrong side of the face.

Both rock routes gain the same ridge and finish over the same tower, so the base is genuinely shared and the split happens on the climb. Start up the lower rock on the right side of the face, two pitches of fourth-class ground, and follow the ridge scramble to the foot of the tower. Everything to that point is common.

Here is the test, and it is a physical one. At the tower this route goes straight up it. The pitch is about seventy-five feet of good climbing that turns into a wide flaring chimney with an offwidth section, and the gear placements in it are awkward. That chimney is the crux of the route and it is the single thing that identifies this line rather than its neighbour.

So: if you are standing under a steep tower wall looking at a flaring chimney and reaching for your widest pieces, you are on this route. If instead your line traverses left to avoid a vertical step and stays at fourth class, you have taken the easier arete beside it — same tower, same summit, no technical crux, and you should know that is what happened rather than believing you climbed this.

Above the chimney it is fourth class to the top of the tower and then third-class walking along the crest to Tiffany's main summit slope.

Negative marker on the descent: it is not a reversal. Take the north-west ridge down to about eight thousand feet, contour north-east toward the smaller lake, and pick up the faint old ridge trail that returns to Honeymoon Pass.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the traverse corridor to the LeConte Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is a side trip off a multi-day high traverse, not a day climb. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass, where the tread ends. Leave the trail there and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands, then onto the Cache Glacier and up it to Cache Col; the step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer. Descend the steep snowfield on the far side to the bench holding Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. From there the Red Ledge bypasses the cliff band west of the knoll above, entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin. Past the ledge, the corridor crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which a ledge system leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. Camp near the col between LeConte and Sentinel, or at White Rock Lakes, and climb the peak from there.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August is most reliable, since the route depends on the whole corridor being passable rather than on local conditions. Early trips face larger cornices at Cache Col and a more consequential Red Ledge; a low-snow autumn exposes more bare glacier ice.
hazards: roped glacier travel with crevasses on the LeConte Glacier, and a bergschrund or moat at the foot of the snow ramp late season
loose rock on the upper scramble
remoteness with no easy bail once past Cache Col
steep early-season snow on the col approaches and on the ramp itself
the ramp softens to punchy postholing by afternoon, with the runout back onto the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: One snow ramp rises off the glacier to the summit ridge, and the moat at its foot is the gate. From the LeConte Glacier the peak shows a single moderate, gradually-angled snow finger running up to the summit rocks; that ramp is the route, and getting onto it — finding the spot where the moat or bergschrund at its base allows a step across — is usually the awkward move of the day. It is a few hundred feet of steep snow, best taken early while it is firm, because by afternoon it turns to punchy postholing and the runout is straight back onto the glacier. Above it, the finish is a short scramble of a few hundred feet on blocky, high-friction gabbro that takes hands and stays straightforward. Two negative markers. Sentinel Peak is the adjacent summit immediately west of this one and is a few feet lower than this one — if the peak you are under is the western of the pair, you are below Sentinel. And if the rock above the top of your snow ramp turns into two pitches of mid-fifth-class climbing rather than a hands-on scramble, you are on this peak's east ridge, which is a real route but not this one. Stash the axe and crampons somewhere you will find them; the descent reverses the same ramp.

approach_variants.name: Slate Pass, the Middle Fork Pasayten, and Fred's Lake to Lake Doris
approach_variants.notes: Drive FR 5400 from Mazama to Harts Pass, at roughly 6,181 to 6,204 ft. Trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed, so judge it on the day. From Harts Pass turn right at the guard station onto FR 5400-600. The Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and Slate Pass at the second, at about 6,900 ft. Early in the season you walk the last half mile or so. From Slate Pass take the Buckskin Ridge trail #498, and at about half a mile a cut-off drops to the Robinson Creek / Middle Fork trail #478. Follow the Middle Fork of the Pasayten — an unbridged crossing, reported anywhere from ankle deep to needing boots and trousers off — for roughly nine miles to the Fred's Lake turn-off. The tread through here is in good condition with essentially no brush. Then over the pass to Lake Doris at about 6,975 ft, reported at just under six hours from the car. A naming caution before you cross-reference maps: this water is usually called Lake Doris and sometimes Lake Dorothy. Do not assume they are separate. Despite the route name, the ordinary way up this peak works the south or south-west slope, not a west one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the pass above Fred's Lake holds snow on its north side and softens through the day
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork Pasayten crossing of very variable depth
Blowdown that worsens beyond Fred's Lake, in places hundreds of logs through burn zones
Lingering snow on the north side of the pass above Fred's Lake, soft late in the day
Wet lichen making the talus slippery
Fourteen hundred feet of loose scree with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Leave the trail at the stream crossing just before the lake, not at the lake. Two independent accounts do exactly that: cross the stream, head north-east up into open forest, and break out of the trees onto talus.

The arrival test is the ground itself. The talus is continuous and endless — no benches, no trees, no interruption — running roughly fourteen hundred feet straight to the top. There is no elegant line on it; you put your head down and climb. If you are still weaving between trees and heather benches you have not reached the slope proper.

Negative marker for leaving too early: one climber went up toward what he took to be the south-west ridge, found it was not, and had to work up and down to reach the real one, where bits of use trail run through the least-bad talus. Use-trail fragments are a sign you are on the right slope.

Summit test: the top is ringed by cliffs on every side except the scree slope you came up. If you are on a summit with more than one walkable side, it is not this one.

How to know it is Osceola and not Carru: Mount Carru is about a mile east and it is higher — 8,595 ft against Osceola's 8,587. From the top of Osceola you look east across a deep notch at a higher peak. The ground between the two is described by one climber as somewhere between awful and impassable, so that notch is a wall, not a link. Osceola, Carru and Lago all keep their steep and cliffy ground on the north, which gives a broader check: a peak in this group whose easy ground is on the north side is none of the three.

Nothing published reports a false summit on Osceola.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit with parking but no trailhead sign, follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber; the tread then levels around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile.

Around mile 3.5, at about 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream, the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up the Barrier. Fill bottles there.

From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees, to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Heather benches and slabs then lead to the crest of the Barrier, a roughly 6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and a common bivy. From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then contour on a long rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin holding roughly the 5,800 ft level to a camp near Mount Terror and Himmelhorn.

A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees on the Barrier climb
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose exposed bypass
A moat at the col that can become an overhanging pit by August
A fresh rockfall scar reported about 30 ft below the summit ridge
The north side of the col takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors; do not descend it by mistake
Steep grassy ledges on the Barrier that are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route begins at the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and you crampon the last of the way there. From camp, continue the rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin toward the col, and crampon up the final snow and scree pitch to the col itself. Once melted out late season that last pitch turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling, with an overhanging boulder near the top sometimes forcing a chossy class 3 or 4 bypass on the left.

So the overhanging boulder is the arrival marker: one block near the top of the gully, passed on its left, and then the col. The route text stops at the col because the col is the start.

The negative test, and it is the most important line here: from the col, this route goes up the east ridge and its walk-off returns down the south side, back into Crescent Creek Basin. The north side of the col is a different and harder proposition. Parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn and the Mustard Glacier descend that side by a single-rope rappel from an established station about 150 ft below the col, or a steep snow couloir when well filled in. If you are looking down at a glacier and rigging a rappel, you are on the wrong side of the col for this route.

Confirm on the climb, and the measurements are small: from the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling, class 3, and parties have done it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. It is one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. If you are on sustained fifth class you are not on the standard line.

One conditions-dependent complication, recorded because it changed a party's day: at least one party found the easy line broke into a fresh rockfall scar about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope for about two pitches of juggy 5.7. Do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

The moat at the col is the thing to scout on the way up: where the snow meets the rock it is a non-event when snow-filled early season and can be an overhanging pit by August. Note where you crossed it; you will want that on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the basin, past South Early Winters Spire, then left along the base
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 west of Washington Pass, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, pass South Early Winters Spire, and traverse left along the base to the shared start with the Northwest Corner. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base.

Six pitches, 5.11-, first climbed in 1965 and freed in 1985.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Two spires in a row on the same approach, with the near one carrying its own routes
A free-hanging rappel over a chockstone on the original descent line
Sustained 5.11- climbing over six pitches
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The two spires are passed in order and this route is on the second one, which is the whole navigation problem on this side. Coming up the climbers' path into the basin, south Early Winters Spire comes first. You must walk past it. North Early Winters Spire is beyond, and this route is on its west face, reached by traversing left along the base.

So the negative test is: if you have stopped at the first wall you reached, you are under South Early Winters Spire, which carries its own cluster of west-side routes and is a different peak.

The feature that separates the two spires, and it is the best landmark in this basin: a massive chasm, a chockstone-filled chimney, splits North and South Early Winters Spires. It is the Chockstone Route's line. You must have that chasm behind you or beside you before you are under North Early Winters Spire's west face.

Arrival: this route shares its start with the Northwest Corner, reached by traversing left along the base after passing the chasm. It also sits immediately right of Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and this one. So the order across this wall, from the chasm outward, is: Chockstone Route in the chasm, Labor Pains on the clean face beyond it, then the west face.

Descent, which gives you a third confirmation if you top out unsure: two options exist. The original drops down the left side through a notch with three single-rope rappels, including one free-hanging rappel over a chockstone, and finishes with scrambling back to the base. The bolted alternative is six bolted rap stations starting about 15 feet right of where the finishing cracks top out, and is generally faster and less committing.

approach_variants.name: Hairpin pullout to the Poster Peak drainage
approach_variants.notes: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass — not the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the far side of the Liberty Bell group and puts you on the wrong mountain. Take the climbers' path south up the valley toward Kangaroo Pass. About half a mile along, before the path rears up for the pass, a drainage comes down off Poster Peak on the right; leave the path there and follow it up over talus and slab benches toward the two northeast-facing buttresses on the skyline. Reckon on a little over an hour from the car to the rock. Coming out, walk southeast off the summit to the col on the southeast ridge near 7,130 ft, drop the loose gully back to the foot of the buttresses, and pick the cairns back up to the hairpin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Considerable loose rock on the buttress crest — the ridge sheds onto anyone below
Talus and slab benches in the approach drainage are slick when wet
Lingering snow in the drainage and in the descent gully into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: The roof is the proof. Poster Peak throws two buttresses down to the northeast and from underneath they look alike; the one you want is the southerly, left-hand one as you look up from the highway, and the feature that separates it is a large, obvious roof low on the buttress at its base. Walk up the drainage until that roof is directly overhead, then traverse around its left-hand (southeast) side to a system of easy ledges that lets you step onto the crest — the climbing starts just uphill from the roof, on ledgy ground rather than on a clean wall. If you are standing under a buttress with no roof over you, you are beneath House Buttress, the northern of the pair, and need to walk back south. If you are on steep clean granite from the very first move, you have started above and right of the ledges.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then up and right past two minor buttresses into the talus gully under the tallest wall
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff heading west from Winthrop and roughly 4 miles east of Washington Pass. A climbers' boot path drops steeply off the highway shoulder through loose talus and duff and reaches Early Winters Creek at about 4,080 ft, where log crossings get you across; use caution in early-season high water.

From the creek the trail firms up for roughly a quarter mile through forest before angling steeply uphill between two feeder gullies, gaining close to 2,400 ft to a flat bench at about 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard bivy and staging camp for the Wine Spires. Water there is unreliable late season; some parties find a small seasonal trickle in a dry sandy side-gully near the bench, but do not count on it.

Roughly 3,000-3,500 ft of gain over about 2-2.5 miles one-way from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place
Old aid bolts on the route, one reported missing a hanger and another loose in its hole
Ball-bearing scree over slab in the last few hundred feet of the approach gully
A descent onto the opposite side of the spire followed by a substantial re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Unreliable water at the bench camp late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Pernod's West Face is the tallest wall in the Wine Spires, and that is the test. From the bench camp, continue up and right, east, passing A couple of minor buttresses, to gain a broad talus and scree gully that runs directly to the base of that wall.

So the count is: two minor buttresses passed, then one broad gully, then the biggest wall in the group. If the wall above you is not obviously the largest thing here, you have stopped at one of the buttresses you were supposed to pass.

The critical difference from every other route in this basin, and it is the thing that makes this approach distinct: this route does not go to Burgundy Col. It leaves the main Burgundy Col trail at the bench. If you are grinding up loose scree toward a notch between two spires, you are on the Burgundy Col trail and have missed the turn at the bench.

The last few hundred feet of the gully are loose ball-bearing scree over slab, with cairns marking the better line. Helmets should go on well before entering the gully because of rockfall from any party above.

Eight pitches at 5.10-plus R. Descent is not back down this face: rappel east down the gully to the Pernod-Chablis Notch, then a couple more rappels down steep slabs to the neve below, three rappels total, on two 60 m ropes. From the neve, trend north around the base of Chianti Spire and climb back up to Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' path to the bench and the boot path to the highway.

So you come down the other side and walk out past a col you never visited on the way in. Budget real time: the three rappels only reach the neve, after which there is a substantial re-ascent to the col before the walk-off begins.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue about half a mile farther.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the footbridge that once crossed near McAllister Camp is gone — check current park conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Leave the maintained trail there, cross Thunder Creek, and climb the climbers' path up Lucky Ridge, the ridge between McAllister and Thunder creeks: roughly 4,000 ft of gain over a couple of miles through brush and devil's club, with two short cliff-band scrambles. Camp near the northeast corner of the proglacial lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier around 6,000 ft, with the icefall in view above.

Rope up around 7,000 ft on the flat snow shelf and climb the glacier's eastern margin — the central icefall splits the lower and upper tiers and has caught parties who drifted climber's-left.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, while enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses; by late September the glacier is largely bare and the pass can be bullet ice and loose rock
hazards: A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises
The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin
Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season
Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely
A long, remote approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is Lucky Pass at about 7,200 ft, and the pass identifies itself by what it divides: it is the notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier between Primus and Tricouni Peak, and the route to Tricouni splits off east from the same spot. If the ground only falls away on one side of you, you are not at the pass.

From the pass the east slope rises directly west — a bouldery class 3 slope, not a ridge crest and not a face. Parties describe the climbing above the pass as nothing more than a walk, which is the honest summary: the difficulty of this route is the creek, the brushy ridge and the glacier, all of which are behind you by the time you are at the pass.

The counting test is the false summit, and it is the one thing above the pass that can go wrong. A false summit stands at about 8,270 ft. You traverse climber's-left around it — you do not go over it — and the true summit at 8,508 ft is beyond. If you reached a high point without having traversed around anything, you are 240 ft short.

Negative test against the peak's other routes, and it works before you ever leave the car: this route is the only one reached from the Thunder Creek side. The South Ridge is reached from the Eldorado ice cap across five glaciers, and the North Ridge from an unnamed glacier north of the peak. If you walked up a creek trail from a campground on Highway 20, you are on this one.

approach_variants.name: Round to the unnamed glacier north of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
This is a genuinely obscure line and every recorded approach to it is a variation on getting round to the mountain's north side, which no other Primus route visits.

The first recorded ascent reached it from the Klawatti side: descend a couloir where the North Klawatti Glacier meets Primus's west ridge, then traverse an unnamed glacier north of Primus to the foot of the crest. The first-ascent account says in as many words that it was unlikely this approach had been used before.

Other parties have come from the Thunder Creek side instead — the same trailhead, creek crossing at McAllister Camp and climbers' trail up the ridge as the East Slope, to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the toe of the Borealis Glacier — and then reached the ridge by circling the glacial lake at the glacier's terminus and crossing a short section of glacier to the base, rather than climbing the glacier toward Lucky Pass. One party took that line specifically because conditions at the standard Primus-Tricouni saddle were hazardous that day.

The ridge itself is about 1,000 ft and took the first-ascent party roughly an hour.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August; a documented late-September attempt found the crux notch glazed with bullet ice and the loose rock unbonded, which made the route markedly harder and more dangerous
hazards: Very loose, serrated rock along the entire crest — blocks and towers described as good but somewhat loose
A 5.6 crux notch with no fixed protection: natural gear and slung blocks only
Verglas glazing the notch in cool or wet weather, which is what defeated a late-September attempt
Committing retreat once above the crux — the recommended descent is the East Ridge to Lucky Pass, not this ridge
Glacier travel on an unnamed, rarely visited glacier with no established line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is which side of the mountain you are on, and it is decided by whether you had to go down to get there. Every approach to this ridge involves losing height onto a glacier north of Primus — down a couloir from the North Klawatti Glacier where it meets Primus's west ridge, or down and around the glacial lake at the Borealis Glacier's terminus. If your day has been a continuous climb, you have not reached this route.

The negative test is unambiguous and it is the one to carry: Lucky Pass is not this route. If you are standing at a col at about 7,200 ft at the head of the Borealis Glacier, with Tricouni Peak's route splitting off east, you are at the start of the East Slope — a class 3 walk. The North Ridge is reached by turning away from that pass, not through it.

What the base itself looks like: the foot of a 1,000 ft crest of blocks and towers, met from a glacier rather than from a notch. There is no published cairn, marker or fixed anchor at the start; the ridge is very rarely repeated and nothing on it should be assumed to be in place.

Confirm on the ground you climb, not on the approach: the lower ridge is 3rd and 4th class blocks and towers; the upper ridge is banded rock at low fifth, and that banding is what the first-ascent party singled out. A ridge that stays third class to the summit is not this one — and a ridge that never carried you above a glacier on the peak's north side never was.

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
approach_variants.notes: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays lower, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The river ford is the timing constraint — thigh deep in the morning has been recorded as waist deep on the same day by evening
hazards: A real ford of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, thigh to waist deep and colder in the afternoon than the morning
Dense slide alder on both banks, worse to the north-east of the standard crossing
Moats around the margin of the Overcoat Glacier
Crevasses part way up the snow finger
Poor protection and loose rock on the summit pyramid
A long decommissioned road walk or ride at both ends of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

The dark towers are the transition. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner east and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its east or north-east side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
approach_variants.notes: A long, largely off-trail approach through burned country for a summit that is barely a scramble. From the North Fork Entiat road end the tread runs up-valley past the Fern Lake spur to the Pyramid Mountain junction, which is the usual last camp with water; fill there, because the drainages between it and the pass are seasonal and often dry. Gain Saska Pass by climbing the drainage directly rather than following the sidehill traverse, which is slower and more tiring across scree. From the pass you lose about 1,500 ft into the Snow Brushy burn, where the tread is gone entirely and ash-covered slopes and fallen snags erase any line, then regain nineteen hundred feet or so out of the creek — that descent and reclimb are what make the day long, not the peak. A separate approach exists up the Entiat River trail and the sheep driveway from the south, also through heavy fire blowdown.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe early
hazards: Loose scree on the headwall below Saska Pass, dangerous for anyone beneath you
Burn-zone deadfall and standing snags with no surviving tread in the Snow Brushy burn
Scarce water above the last creek crossings; the drainages near the pass are seasonal
Steep, loose couloir on the final approach to the crest saddle
Loose talus and scree on the class 2-3 summit slopes
Long, remote, mostly off-trail approach with little cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the saddle on the Chelan Mountains crest immediately south of the peak, reached by a steep couloir of loose rock, and the thing to know before you get there is that the true summit is hidden from it. Standing on the saddle you see a rocky bump close by to the south — a point just over 7,760 ft — and a broad, easy-angled slope running north. The bump is not the mountain and is only a short side trip for the view; the slope is your line. Turn north and climb the south-facing talus, keeping to the west side of the crest where the scrambling stays easiest, and the top only reveals itself in the last few hundred feet. The rock underfoot changes noticeably as you go: poor scree low down where the burn ends, then firmer blocks on the crest that make a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk. If the ground ahead drops away toward the Emerald Peak basin instead of rising, you have crossed the crest too far east.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River trail and Snow Brushy Creek to Borealis Pass

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

approach_variants.notes: From the Entiat River trailhead just past Cottonwood Campground, walk the Entiat River trail about six and a half miles to the Snow Brushy Creek trail, then follow it up-valley about five miles; the creek crossing there is a reliable place for water. A faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail branches north and climbs to Borealis Pass in about a mile, below the easy south slopes of the peak. Much of the valley is burned, so expect downed timber.
hazards: Burned valley with downed timber and a faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail to Borealis Pass
Wildfire burn-zone deadfall and obscured tread on the lower approach
Fire closure and landslide near the river trailhead can block the drive; confirm access
Scarce water above the last creek crossings
Loose talus and scree on the class 2-3 summit slopes
Long, remote approach with little cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle and the south gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Pinnacle Peak trailhead — a signed unnumbered trail directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the Reflection Lakes pullouts at about 4,860 ft — the maintained trail climbs at a steady, fairly steep grade through sparse subalpine forest. Around half a mile you get the first partial view of Rainier through the trees, then the trail switchbacks up through meadow. At about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 1,000-1,050 ft you top out at Pinnacle Saddle near 5,900-5,920 ft, where the maintained trail ends and the view opens south. Carry water from the car; there is no reliable source on the trail or in the gully except lingering snowmelt early in the season. Past the saddle the route becomes an unmaintained climbers' path. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in places and rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks with parties above or below. This is a fully exposed ridge with quick-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer; plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July in a cold year
hazards: Loose, unstable rock through the south-facing summit gully
Steep dropoffs and exposure on sections of the maintained trail itself, not only above the saddle
Snow lingering in the summit gully into early or mid summer after the trail has melted out
Rockfall onto parties below on a heavily travelled line
Sudden afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed south Cascades ridge
No water anywhere on the trail or the scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Pinnacle Saddle, the peak is east. Pinnacle is the peak east of the saddle and Plummer is the peak west of it, and the boot paths fork there. Going west from the saddle puts you on Plummer — a different summit, and a party can climb it believing it is this one.

So: contour or scramble east into the gully system on the south and southeast face.

The sequence inside the gully is what tells you it is the right one, and one item in it is unexpected enough to be a real test: it starts as class 2 scree and blocky steps, steepens into sustained class 3 with real exposure over its upper third, then works through a band of trees, then a final short scramble to the summit block. Trees high in the gully are the confirmation. A gully with no tree band in it is not this one.

Multiple gully lines exist here, and the correct one is the most travelled. The negative is tactile: if you are dislodging blocks with every step, you are off the beaten line. Loose rock is worst away from it.

The early-season negative is a turn-around, not a route-finding problem, and it is worth stating plainly: snow or verglas in this gully turns easy scrambling into a slip you cannot stop, on ground with no protection. That is the condition to go home on rather than to push through with an axe you are not going to be able to use in a chimney.

One more thing at the saddle that is not a navigation marker but will be the first thing you meet: mountain goats here are habituated and come for the salt. They are not a sign you are on route.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest for about four miles to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Descend the climbers' path east toward the Chilliwack River and Boundary Camp area, the last reliable water for a while, then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old lookout foundation and antenna remains on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often holds snow into summer and usually needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, and it is the cross-country crux of the approach and a common turnaround point in poor conditions. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; fog here is a real hazard and parties have mistakenly set off toward the wrong wall. On the second day, rope up at the Challenger Arm and cross roughly three miles of upper glacier into the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits, detouring high above the first crevasse band in low-snow years when the icefall blocks the direct line.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier crevasses are more consolidated and the pass approach is snow-free enough to travel. Earlier attempts find more snow on the glacier, on the route and on the connecting ridge.
hazards: sparse protection on the crux pitch, with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable dike climbing off the bergschrund
crevasses on several miles of glacier approach each way
extreme remoteness with no quick outside help
the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge, wet and slippery above a deep gorge
a descent that is not back down the face — it continues over the connecting ridge and off the neighbouring summit's glacier, so glacier gear has to be carried over the top
approach_variants.baseFinding: A huge shield streaked with dikes like bolts of lightning is the proof, and you can see it from out on the glacier. This is the southernmost of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its outline: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before committing to a line across the ice. Leave the glacier at the tower's foot. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the base is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should keep going south along the base. Once established, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face and takes essentially no gear for that whole stretch; cracks appear higher and the pitch runs the better part of a full rope length.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col, then the loose fourth-class traverse round the east side below Chianti to the Pernod-Chablis notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately at around 4,080 ft via logs, and climbs steeply, gaining nearly 2,400 ft, to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to Burgundy Col at 7,770 ft.

Two pitches at 5.9 A0, Grade II. Carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose fourth-class traverse around the east side of the ridge below Chianti
A two-piton summit anchor equalized with cord, and a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger on the short summit aid block
A single 60 m rope can leave a party several metres short of the notch on the descent
Rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station; build that anchor as high as practical
Loose rock underfoot for the whole approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the notch between Pernod and Chablis, and there are two ways to it that arrive from opposite directions. Both are worth knowing before you leave camp, because the choice is made at the col and not at the base.

Option one, from Burgundy Col: rather than dropping straight to Pernod's south side, most parties continue traversing and scrambling around the east, Silver Star Creek, side of the ridge below Chianti, aiming for the Pernod-Chablis notch. Expect loose fourth-class terrain on this stretch, which is itself the confirmation: if the ground you are on is walkable, you have not started the traverse.

Option two, and it is the common one because the route is short: climb Chablis Spire's east face first, then downclimb or make a short rappel across loose rock to reach the base of Pernod's south face. That approach arrives from above rather than along.

So the negative test is about which spire is above you: this route sits tucked between Pernod's bigger west face and Chablis. If the wall above you is the tallest in the group, you are under Pernod's west face and on the Direct West Face ground, not here. That route is reached from the bench, not from the col.

And the notch is a named gap between two named spires, which is the most reliable kind of feature in this basin: Pernod on one side, Chablis on the other.

Descent is by rappel and it links back onto Chablis: rappel the south face to the notch on two 60 m ropes. A single 70 m can just barely work, but a single 60 m can leave you several metres short of the notch. From the notch a short fourth-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis, and two double-rope rappels down it reach the base rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col.

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain above rather than for the spires, and nothing marks the climbers' path.

The path drops down the talus and into the forest, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log, and then climbs steeply up the timbered rib on the left — the north side — of the creek that drains the col above. Two hours or so of steep walking puts you on the basin bench at about 6,500 ft. There is a spring near the bench camp and it is the last reliable water.

From the bench the trail continues another three-quarters of an hour to the col at about 7,720 ft, which is the hub for the whole cluster. This route does not need to go that far.

The pullout doubles as the overnight for most parties. Nothing there is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access disappears when the highway closes
hazards: Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path with no trail signs anywhere
The start is a single jammed block; the lower ridge offers several plausible wrong starts
The final pitch is runout exposed face climbing with marginal protection
Rope drag on the long crest pitch if slings are not managed
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route starts lower than everything else in the cluster, and that is the fact to hold onto. The spires above the col get climbed from the col; this one does not.

Leave the col trail at the bench, around 6,600 ft, and contour right — south — around the bench toward the pinnacle's lower section. You are aiming for the toe of the ridge rather than for anything above you. There is a dry sandy gully on this contour with a spring in it, which is a useful confirmation that you are on the right ground and the last water before the climb.

The start itself is marked by a chockstone — a jammed block at the foot of the ridge. That chockstone is the identification, and it is the reason accounts of this route keep saying to pay attention to the topo: without it, the lower ridge offers several plausible ways on and parties have burned an hour sorting it out.

If you come at it from the col instead, drop about two hundred feet of mostly fourth-class rock to sandy ledges just left of the pinnacle's top and work down and along; that reaches the same ground from above.

Confirm on the climb. Seven or eight pitches of sustained mid-fifth-class hand and finger cracks along the ridge crest, with big comfortable belay ledges. The technical crux is about halfway up, on the fourth pitch, on a short section of steep twin finger cracks. The last pitch is exposed, runout face climbing that most parties call the real crux for reasons that have nothing to do with the grade.

Negative marker: if you walked all the way to the col, then dropped a few hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank onto a third-class ledge system and walked it rightward to a steep clean corner, you are at the other route on this pinnacle, several number grades harder. A ledge system leading to a corner is not this climb; a chockstone at the toe of a ridge is.

Second negative marker: the neighbouring spire's north face is the usual link-up partner and its routes start from the col itself. Being at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are at this route.

Descent is a few hundred feet of downclimbing, then two rappels of about thirty and twenty metres into the gully beneath the col, downclimbing between the anchors, then the trail back past the bench.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
Long, exposed, somewhat dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side; check slings and tat
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass
Avalanche-prone approach in shoulder season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Pace it off from the left-flank classic: this route starts about 100 feet to the right of it, on the west side of the south face.
