That is a measurable distance rather than a description, and it is what makes the start findable — everything else on this end of the face is identified relative to the same outside corner.

So the procedure in poor visibility is two steps. First find the outside corner where the south face turns onto the west side. The classic left-flank line starts just right of that corner. Then walk right roughly a hundred feet along the base. That is where you are.

What tells you you have overshot: keep walking right along the base and the ground under the middle of the face is where the summit route starts, and beyond that the two large V-features of the next line along. Reaching either means you have gone several hundred feet too far.

What tells you you are short: a large roof at the base means you have crossed the corner onto the west face entirely and are two routes left.

First-pitch confirmation: a short crack and slab leading to a corner. It is not a long lead and it is not hard. The long, exposed, somewhat dirty face crack is the second pitch. If your first pitch is long and dirty you have started one pitch too high or on the wrong line.

And the top-out check: this route finishes on the West Ridge, not the summit — the same as its two neighbours on this flank. That shared finish is why they share one rappel descent on the north side.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
The roof at ground level is the marker, and it is the only one you need. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

It is on the left side of the south face, just left of Solid Gold. If you have turned the corner onto the west side of the peak, you have gone too far left.

Mid-route confirmation: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

And the top: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.

approach_variants.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
approach_variants.notes:
This is the way to Primus's south side, and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the Thunder Creek approach. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the North Fork Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse below the south side of Austera's east ridge, rounding its end near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
hazards: A heavily crevassed North Klawatti and McAllister glacier system, especially late season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August and September — probe before committing weight
Complex glacier route-finding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility
A short technical step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch that has to be reversed at the end of the day
Extreme remoteness: a multi-day approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The one findable feature on this route is the notch at the McALLISTER-Klawatti Col, and it is findable because it is the only place all day you need a rope for rock. It is a step of roughly 50 ft: downclimbed, hand-lined, or rappelled off a sling on a horn or block — there is no fixed hardware. If you have crossed a col without a technical step, you are not through it yet. After the notch, the test is what you are standing on rather than what you can see. You drop onto the Klawatti Glacier, traverse below Austera's east ridge and round its end onto the North Klawatti Glacier. The climbing begins where you take the rope off: snow-covered talus, class 2-3, straight to the 8,508 ft summit. There is no notch, no rib and no marked start above the glacier — the honest answer is that this route has no rock landmark at its base, and the col behind you is what tells you where you are. The negative test is the strong one and it settles the whole peak: the other standard line on Primus is reached from Thunder Creek, and it starts at Lucky Pass — a notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier where the route to Tricouni Peak splits off east. If you are at a pass with a second peak's route leaving it, you are on the east slope and you came up the wrong valley for this route. The two lines are on opposite sides of the mountain and share no ground below the summit. And watch the false summit whatever side you came from: a false top stands around 8,270 ft and is passed on climber's-left. A high point reached without traversing round anything is not the summit.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The other way onto Primus comes from the north, and it finishes on a different line: the east ridge, not this route's south side. From Colonial Creek Campground on the North Cascades Highway, walk the Thunder Creek Trail about six miles to McAllister Camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek there has washed out, so expect to ford cold, fast water or hunt for a log crossing.

Across the creek, a faint, steep boot path climbs the long, brushy lower north ridge of Tricouni Peak to the toe of the Borealis Glacier near 6,000 ft, where there is good camping. From camp, climb the glacier along its eastern edge, keeping clear of the icefall in its middle, to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni near 7,200 ft, and follow the east ridge to the summit on class 3 ground.

The brush on the ridge above Thunder Creek is slow going in either direction, and worse carrying skis or a long pack.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
Fifty feet left of the standard South Face route. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

The first pitch is the check, and it is a brutal one. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

What the first pitch looks like from the ground, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing left-slanting crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

Belay confirmation: pitch one ends at a two-bolt anchor after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

And the named pitch higher up: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

Descent note that affects the approach decision: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, left and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
Go to the outside corner and start just right of it. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the right of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

That corner is the anchor for the whole left end of the face, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

The honest warning about where this route ends, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the west ridge, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

Sequence check: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow

approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

approach_variants.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach: about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain on the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Faint, easily lost path over granite up to Gnome Tarn and the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line

approach_variants.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
camps: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
approach_variants.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Brush-choked valley approaches and heavy blowdown, thousands of downed logs on the Middle Fork valley
Faint or obscured tread near the Eureka Creek turn
Creek fords that can run high in early season
Short exposed scrambling on the connecting ridge to the south; loose rock on the ridge crest
Sheer north face immediately off the summit; stay on the south side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the Hidden Lakes

approachLogistics.trailhead: Billy Goat Trailhead (end of Eightmile Creek Road)

approach_variants.notes: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.
hazards: Rough, brushy cross-country of two to three miles beyond Ptarmigan Creek to reach the base
Long trail approach from below 3,500 ft with little maintenance
Loose talus and scree underfoot on the summit slopes
Sheer north face; stay on the south and southeast side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek to Remmel Lake
approach_variants.notes: The shortest line to the peak. Walk the Andrews Creek trail up the valley past the Meadow Lake and Peepsight junctions, then continue to Remmel Lake at the foot of the northwest ridge. The lower valley is burned and can hold a lot of blowdown.
hazards: Burned lower Andrews Creek valley can hold a lot of blowdown
Off-trail bushwhack from Remmel Lake through boggy, mosquito-heavy forest to the treeline camp
Remote, seldom-visited technical terrain far from help, with no cell coverage
Exposed rappels on the west side of the gendarmes
Loose, exposed granite on the upper ridge and exposed gendarme scrambling
Lightning exposure on the summit area
Steep scree and loose boulders on the west-slope descent

approach_variants.name: Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. It is also the piece of this zone most likely to be open. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

approach_variants.notes: A longer but gentler and generally better-kept trail. From the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road, follow the Chewuch River trail north toward Four Point Lake and on to Remmel Lake. Most parties break the walk with a night along the river.
hazards: Long walk-in along the Chewuch River trail; most parties spend a night on the way
Off-trail bushwhack from Remmel Lake through boggy, mosquito-heavy forest to the treeline camp
Remote, seldom-visited technical terrain far from help, with no cell coverage
Exposed rappels on the west side of the gendarmes
Loose, exposed granite on the upper ridge and exposed gendarme scrambling
Lightning exposure on the summit area
Steep scree and loose boulders on the west-slope descent

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead, about 2,790-2,800 ft. Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth along the creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in at a large brushy washout below the basin.

Scrambling the washout is the route-finding crux of the approach. Look for a cairn marking the exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves left around 3,500 ft near 48.0560, -121.3631 and is often flagged with pink tape — and follow it in steep forest switchbacks to about 4,900 ft.

Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench between 4,900 and 5,300 ft, passing a stagnant tarn at the Bedal-Sloan saddle. Last reliable water is there or at the cascading streams just below. The ground beyond turns rocky and exposed toward the glacier toe at about 5,800 ft.

A fit party familiar with the line reaches the base in around three hours. The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk trailhead on FR 49 converges with this line between 5,000 and 5,500 ft but adds a ford of the North Fork Sauk.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the approach snow has cleared
hazards: Boulder- and blowdown-choked washout at the end of the maintained tread
Steep, exposed scrambling above the meadow bench
Firm snow near the glacier toe early in the season
Ford of the North Fork Sauk if using the FR 49 alternative
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Southwest Face and the standard Corkscrew part company at the saddle, and the discriminator is a low connecting ridge rather than a signpost. From the 5,300 ft saddle, cross the low ridge that divides the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin and drop into the meadows on its far side. The Southwest Face wall rises straight out of meadow — you should reach its foot without touching snow or ice. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel, you have followed the Corkscrew line and the face you want is behind and to your right.

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that matters here is the southern one, and it is not the Spires Trail. The climbers' path from the unsigned pullout further west serves the spires and the col on the other side of the crest. It does not put you under this face.

For the south face, walk the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. After roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn, where a rough path follows the right-hand side of the creek that drains the south side of the formation.

There are good meadows for camping at about 6,200 ft. This is a rarely visited corner and there is no established climbers' camp, no fixed gear on the approach and very little traffic — expect to see nobody.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead. This is national forest, so there is no permit system and no quota, and the general dispersed-camping rules apply.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are the driest and most reliable
hazards: The Wine Spires pullout and its climbers' trail lead to the far side of the crest, not to this face
Rarely climbed, so there is no traffic, no chalk and essentially no current conditions information
Rappel anchors on the descent are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Two long routes share this face and its summit
Remote enough that a retreat from high on the face is slow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is clean white granite, which is the first confirmation and a good one — it is visibly paler than the rock either side and it is why the formation gets climbed at all. Follow the creek up to the meadows and then to the foot of that white wall. Two long routes share it and they share a summit, so the identification has to be done at the ground and re-checked on the climb.

The start is a flake, and it is a big one. This route begins with a layback off a large clean flake that leads into a long left-facing corner system carrying finger cracks. Large detached flake at the bottom, left-facing corner above it: that pairing is the whole identification and there is nothing else on this face like it.

Confirm with the roofs, in order. Above the corner system the route crosses right beneath a roof into a splitter crack that reaches a ledge partway up the face. Higher, a second roof leads to a hand crack and then stemming corners with a hard exit. Two roofs, the first crossed rightward and the second climbed through, is the sequence.

The summit pitch is the cleanest test of all, and it is worth knowing before you leave the ledge: this route tops out through a deep summit chimney. You finish inside the chimney. The other long route on this face finishes on blocky ground just right of that chimney and never enters it. If you are stemming a deep slot to the top, you are on this route; if you are scrambling blocks beside one, you are on the neighbour.

Negative marker at the start to match it: if you began on the right-hand side of the face on flakes, corners and splitters and arrived at a broad ledge running most of the way across the face at about half height, you are on the neighbouring line. This route has no such crossing ledge low down; its mid-height ledge is reached from a splitter after a rightward move under a roof.

Protection throughout is cams and nuts to about three inches. Descent is a series of rappels down the south-east side; a seventy-metre rope is the standard, fixed anchors are sparse, and you should expect to build some — carry extra webbing.

approach_variants.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
approach_variants.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

approach_variants.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and Ruth Mountain first, then down to the Ruth-Icy saddle and across to the Icy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the Ruth Glacier route: Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead up Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond, around the cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft.

The traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another 800 ft or so — about 1,600 ft in total off Ruth's summit — to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft.

From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and follow talus and boot path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper.

The re-ascent of Ruth on the way home is the sting in the tail and cannot be avoided on the standard car-to-car version.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep loose 'death gully' that is the natural fall line off Ruth and the wrong line
A long horizontal crevasse near the top of the Icy Glacier below the towers
A bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock funnelled through a single summit gully with the whole party in it
Roughly 1,600-2,000 ft of re-ascent over Ruth on the way home, at the end of a twelve-hour day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision that matters is which line you take off Ruth, and it is not the obvious one. There are two ways down the 1,600 ft to the Ruth-Icy saddle: a steeper, more direct gully that parties call the death gully, and cairned heather slopes and game trails to climber's left holding second and third class ground. Take the heather, on the left. The direct gully is the one you will drift into if you simply point downhill, which is what makes this worth stating rather than assuming.

Arrival at the saddle: it is the low point between the two peaks, around 5,700-5,800 ft, and there are trees in it. Trees are the confirmation — you have dropped below the alpine on both sides. If you are still on open snow or talus with nothing growing, you have not reached the saddle.

The notch west of the northwest spire is the base of the climbing, at about 6,500 ft. From the saddle, cross the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier and aim for a notch or saddle just west of Icy's Northwest Spire. Watch for a long horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier below the Icy towers, and for a bergschrund near the notch in some seasons.

The summit gully is the final test and it is unambiguous. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class up an obvious left-hand, light-coloured gully system reaches the base of the summit block. The climbing is a single 100 ft fourth-class gully with solid jugs and ledges, real exposure, and rappel slings around a horn at its top. Take the first prominent gully. Sling anchors at the top of a 100 ft gully are the arrival marker; if there is nothing at the top and the gully keeps going, you are in the wrong one.

And the one that catches people at the very end: the true high point is the southeast point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top. The register is on the northwest summit. Decide before you leave the notch which one you are going to.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 and the climbers' path past the pond to the toe of the Ruth Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Read the name carefully. This route is filed under a name that encodes the direction you walk, not the side you climb: the line goes over Hannegan Pass and up the north-side Ruth Glacier. Its aspect is N. A party expecting south-facing slopes will be looking for the wrong mountain-side all day.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FR-32, about 5.3 miles off SR-542, follow Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley. The first 2-2.5 miles climb gently through old growth with Ruth Creek alongside and views north to Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge. Around mile 3, Hannegan Camp is a designated backcountry camp and the last reliably running water on the standard line; above it the trail switchbacks through meadows to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, about mile 4 and roughly 2,000 ft of gain.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail for a climbers' path heading east then south. Most parties camp on the far side of the notch northwest of Ruth's summit, on snow, to keep impact down.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A faint climbers' path at Hannegan Pass that parties routinely lose in flat light
A glacier that looks like a snow walk and has produced a crevasse fall
No reliable running water above Hannegan Camp in a typical snow year
Route-finding around a cliff band on a shoulder with no cairns
A long valley walk out after a summit day, commonly finished tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The pond is the single hardest thing to find and the route turns on it. At Hannegan Pass you leave maintained tread for a faint climbers' path that goes east then south, staying on the south side of a small pond. The tread here is faint and partly hidden in trees, and this is the easiest place on the entire route to lose the line — flat light and early morning are when it happens. Find the pond, put it on your left, keep going south.

Second marker, and it is tactile: after the pond the path goes up and left around the base of a cliff band onto a shoulder. A cliff band you have to walk around is a physical thing you cannot miss in cloud. If you are climbing straight up into rock, you have not gone far enough left.

Arrival: from the shoulder, traverse south across heather and talus to gain the broad ridge feeding the toe of the Ruth Glacier's north slope at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. That is where you rope up, and it is the base of the climb. The transition is obvious underfoot — heather and talus give way to permanent snow.

Treat it as a glacier from the first step, and that is the most important thing on this route. The lower Ruth is a moderate, welcoming-looking snow slope and it looks like a walk. It has produced at least one documented crevasse fall in years with thin or soft cover. The pleasant appearance is exactly the hazard.

What too far looks like: continuing up and climber's-left brings you to the broad notch just northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft. That is the camp and the start of the traverse toward Icy Peak, not the base of this route.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to camp, 3-4 more to the col
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Missing the sharp right turn off the mine roadbed onto the climbers' trail
Bergschrund at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, open both sides late season
Rockfall from the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower during the rising traverse
Exposed rock-and-snow ridge above the col, corniced into early summer
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The rock climbing begins at the Boston-Sahale col, and everything below it is glacier work.

The navigational problem on the way up is the bergschrund, at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides late season. Late in the year the standard solution is to traverse climber's right to end-run the schrund, then cut back up and left above it to the col — a party that pushes straight up the fall line into the schrund is not off route so much as too early in the season for that line.

You know you are at the col because the glacier ends against a defined saddle in the rock ridge and the ground on the far side drops away toward Boston Peak. This is where parties unrope and coil.

From the col the route is a short, exposed ridge of rock and snow: a little rock, then an exposed snow traverse south on crampons and axe, well back from the cornice, to the base of the summit block. The block is then finished as on the Sahale Glacier route, by a short chimney-like exit on its south side to the slung rappel block on top.

In poor visibility the col itself is the reliable target: it is the only low saddle at the top of the glacier, and the ridge beyond it cannot be confused with glacier travel.

approach_variants.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
camps: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
approach_variants.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
hazards: Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed; rope up and carry a rescue kit
Red Ledge is serious when banked with snow, common into early July
Cornices near Cache Col and approach ridgelines, worst in early season
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Le Conte-Sentinel col is the reference: a flat notch at the top of the glacier carrying dry gravel bivy platforms, the only level dry ground for a long way in any direction. From the notch the peak's west side presents one continuous basin of snow running up to a rock face, and that snow is the route. Its top is the only place on the face where a broad, walkable ledge cuts leftward, to the north, beneath a short cliff band. Those two features together are the proof: continuous snow steepening as it rises, and an obvious ledge running left off the top of it. If the snow you have chosen tops out against blank rock with no ledge leading off it, you are too far south in the basin. If you are on bare rock with no snow beneath you at all, you have wandered onto the east side, which degrades into rotten rock and steep snow — that is the side parties get wrong on the descent, and it is not the route.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The camp at the south end of the high traverse, under the Dana and Chickamin glaciers. Sentinel and Old Guard are climbed from here or from the col above.
bivy.water: The lakes and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
bivy.capacity: Several sites on slabs and heather near the lakes

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: Say it plainly: these are not sites, they are wherever a party gets to. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Downey Creek Trailhead (Trail #768, Suiattle River Road)

approach_variants.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, walk the Downey Creek trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge, then cross the Dana Glacier country to White Rock Lakes. From the lakes, work back up onto the South Cascade Glacier to reach the peak. Plan on several days of off-trail and glacier travel.
hazards: Several days of off-trail and glacier travel from Downey Creek via the brushy Bachelor Creek path, Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge
Crevasses on the Dana and South Cascade Glaciers
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The approach shares everything with the West Ridge as far as the basin: Longs Pass Trail from the Esmeralda trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft, down to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft, ford, east on the Ingalls Creek Trail to the Beverly-Turnpike junction, then off-trail up the rib and into the basin beneath Sherpa.

From the basin the two routes diverge. Instead of heading for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's left — east — traversing a grassy slope and then climbing a talus and scree gully toward the notch east of the summit.

This is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge line, and picking the right gully is the main problem. There is another level of basin higher and southwest of the summit; ending up in it means you have gone the wrong way. Carry a 50m rope from the notch, since the route above uses fixed slings at several obstacles.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the north-facing approach gully holds snow into early July
hazards: Loose talus and scree in the approach gully
Route-finding: the higher basin southwest of the summit is the overshoot trap
Snow lingering in the north-facing gully into early July
Ingalls Creek ford and the long brushy off-trail section, same as the West Ridge
Fixed slings on the route and on the descent are weathered — carry replacement cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is a notch at roughly 8,000 ft, east of the true summit and about 600 vertical feet below it. Gaining the ridge crest itself happens about 100 ft above (east of) that notch, on class 2 ground — so the notch is a waypoint, and the crest is gained just past it, not in it.

From the basin the gully leading to it is the obvious one heading up toward that saddle east of the summit, and trip reports confirm that the gully that looks right from below is the right one. The failure mode is overshooting rather than picking the wrong-looking line: parties climb too far and end up in the higher basin to the southwest of the summit.

The orientation check: at the notch the summit should be up and to your west, roughly 600 ft above you. If the summit is above and east, or if you are level with the summit, you are in the wrong saddle.

Sherpa's Balanced Rock sits on the summit ridge and is visible from below — it is the West Ridge's landmark, not this route's start, but it tells you where the summit ridge runs and therefore which way to count from.

Most parties do not reverse this ridge. The accepted descent finishes near the summit, traverses to the top of the West Ridge, and uses that route's rappel line — so plan to end the day on the other side of the peak from where you started climbing.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and up from Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Esmeralda Basin / Longs Pass Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FS-9737), about 4,300 ft. Longs Pass Trail (#1229) for roughly 2.3 miles and 2,300 ft to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft.

Drop the north side, losing 1,300-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft — early season there are snow fingers here that glissade well. Ford or rock-hop the creek, join the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it right (east) about a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at about 4,700 ft.

Leave the maintained trail there. Ascend rightward across the meadow to where the slope steepens at about 5,000 ft, cross the stream, and climb the rib staying left of its crest. At around 5,800 ft traverse right, cross over the rib, and contour into the basin below Sherpa.

There is a flat table-rock shelf at about 7,400 ft that parties use as a bivy or gear-up spot. Around 6,000 ft the climbers' path enters a spot where the gully narrows; from there some parties gain a few hundred feet east to the divide separating that gully from the one leading more directly toward Sherpa, then drop grudgingly into the correct gully and take class 2 slopes up to the table rock.

Six to seven hours one way is typical. Water at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; snow lingers on the approach benches and north-facing ground into early July
hazards: Steep loose drop off the north side of Longs Pass
Ingalls Creek ford runs high in early-season melt
Brushy bushwhack between the Ingalls Creek Trail and the open basin
Long boulder and talus field beneath Sherpa — a stamina and route-finding crux both
Picking the correct gully out of the basin: the obvious narrowing at ~6,000 ft is a decision point, not the line
Descent is rappels off mixed fixed slings, some reported as poor — carry cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark that settles this route is Sherpa's balanced rock — a distinctive perched block on the summit ridge, and it is visible from the basin below. Use it.

From the basin, climb class 2 snow and talus past the table rock to the Stuart-Sherpa col at about 8,100 ft, aiming for the notch closest to Sherpa. That is the start: the ridge rises east from the col to the summit, and the balanced rock stands beyond the summit on the crest to the east.

So the check in cloud is: at the col, Mount Stuart's east ridge rises behind you to the west and Sherpa's summit is ahead to the east, with the balanced rock beyond it. If you reach the crest with the balanced rock to your west, you have come up the East Ridge side of the peak.

The flat table-rock at about 7,400 ft is the intermediate confirmation on the way up — it is a distinct flat platform in otherwise broken ground and it sits on the correct line. Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

The descent uses a rappel line back to a notch west of the technical climbing, so know where the notch is before you go up.

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.notes:
The Spires Trail is the wrong approach for this face. The unsigned pullout further west and the col above it serve the spires on the other side of the crest, not the southern wall this route is on.

Take the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. At roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn; a rough path then follows the right-hand side of the creek draining the south side of the formation. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping.

This is a quiet corner by the standards of this highway. There is no established climbers' camp, no fixed approach gear and effectively no traffic.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead; there is no permit system and no quota on national forest ground here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are typically driest
hazards: The Wine Spires pullout and its climbers' trail lead to the far side of the crest, not to this face
No descent has been described for this line itself; plan on the neighbouring route's southeast-side rappels
Rappel anchors are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Rarely climbed, so there is no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
Two long routes on one face that share a mid-height ledge and a summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The wall is clean white granite and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

This route is the right-hand line. Start on the right side of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

The defining feature is a broad ledge at half height, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you walk leftward before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

Confirm on the upper face. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the left side of the most prominent arete or pillar in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends rightward to the summit.

The summit pitch separates the two routes absolutely. This one finishes on blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out through a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

Negative marker lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

No descent has been described for this line itself. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Go up prepared to make anchors.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to the northwest clearing, then the climber's path up into the basin.

Three pitches at 5.10b as counted here, but understand what the route is: it is pitch 5 of a combined line, about 100 ft of sustained climbing under and through a pair of roofs.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No ground start: three pitches of the Southwest Rib must be climbed first
Loose rock on the first pitch and a loose block at the start of the roof pitch
Pendulum-fall hazard for the second climber if gear is pulled through the roof
Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward; bailing means natural-gear anchors
Rib below has runout slab sections and crowds on summer weekends, with rope-induced rockfall
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no ground start, and that is the most important fact about finding it. You reach it by climbing the first three pitches of the southwest rib, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and then going left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view.

So the base of the day is the base of the southwest rib, and that has a landmark you can stand under: the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the southwest rib, left of the southwest couloir. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

The in-route test is visual and binary: go left at the ledge where the two roofs come into view. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A hazard right at the start of the pitch, recorded because it is exactly where a party is committing: there is a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.

What nobody does here, which answers the obvious question: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the rabbit ears then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted stations climber's right of the gully, which land at the foot of the South Arete rather than back at the larch.

name: Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington go south on Madison Ave to a T, right onto Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and drive to the washout that gates it.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing and on toward the old trailhead. The South Face turn-off is a made object, not a natural feature: look for two cut logs, one on either side of the road, with old logging cable visible. At those logs turn right onto a well-beaten boot track.

The boot track drops to the creek for a ford, then climbs steeply through old-growth forest. The upper part is steep and dirty before it breaks out into open grassland. Around three hours from the trailhead to the main bivy.

This is a different turn-off from Waterfall Basin, which is further along at the wide white-boulder streambed. Two cut logs with cable = South Face; 50-foot streambed of white boulders = Waterfall Basin.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the boot track is steep and dirty and the saddle bivy is snow-free only in high summer
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek on the boot track
Steep, dirty ground in the upper forest
Long approach with no maintained trail above the cut logs
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The reference point for the whole South Face is the grassy saddle bivy, and Concerto is the route that starts at it — the saddle sits near this route's start, which is why every other line here is described relative to it. A second, smaller saddle lies about ten minutes west along the wall; if you are at a small saddle with no route starting off it you are at the wrong one.

Standing at the main saddle, the granite apron of the South Face runs out in front of you. Concerto starts off that apron at the saddle itself. If you are crossing the apron away from the saddle you are heading for Nature's Way; if you are ascending class 4 ramps to a dihedral you are on the Primal Scream / Miracle Ramps side.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the West Face meadows
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft; Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread gives out at a washout below the West Face basin, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in.

Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft and is usually flagged pink — then climb steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench, and reach the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Water here or at the streams just below.

From the saddle stay in the meadows below the broad West Face. Do not continue southeast toward the glacier toe.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Brushy, blowdown-choked washout where the maintained trail ends
Route-finding through the forest band above the washout
Loose rock in the meadow-to-face transition
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Northwest Buttress is reached on foot with no glacier travel at all, and that is the test: if you are putting crampons on, you have walked past it onto the standard Corkscrew line. From the meadows, the route starts at the lowest and left-most point of the face, on a corner of noticeably darker rock than the wall either side of it. Rock you can walk up to dry-shod, with grass and meadow underfoot rather than ice, is the correct base.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the northwest clearing, then the basin below the northwest face and the steep corner system
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles, roughly an hour, to the clearing and meadow on the spire's northwest side. Leave the trail on the well-worn climber's path and ascend talus and heather into the basin directly below the northwest face.

This is the same basin used to access the southwest rib, Mojo Rising and Free Mojo, so route-finding to the base is shared and only the last few dozen feet along the wall separate the lines.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Several closely spaced starts on one wall, separated by tens of feet
Committing 5.10 moves on the first pitch before any belay
No documented rappel-the-face option; bailing mid-route means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is identifiable by a steep corner system, and the first pitch traverses into it. That is the positive test: a steep corner, not a face and not a chimney, entered by traversing rather than climbing straight up. The first pitch makes committing moves at about 5.10 up to a prominent ledge, where some parties belay while others continue to a tree-anchored stance.

The landmark every line on this wall is measured from, and the one to find first: a large chockstone-filled chimney and notch between the two spire formations. Get to that and the wall becomes readable.

Relative to it, the order is countable and in feet: Mojo Rising starts on an obvious bolted face about 20 ft downhill of the chockstone chimney, just left of this route's first pitch. Free Mojo starts roughly 40 ft down and right of the same chimney, on a nondescript crack leading to a two-piece fixed anchor on a pedestal.

So the three-way discriminator is: bolted face 20 ft downhill of the chimney means Mojo Rising. Nondescript crack 40 ft down and right means Free Mojo. Steep corner entered by a traverse means this route. If you are clipping bolts off the ground you are not on the Boving-Pollock.

Six pitches, which makes it the shortest of the west-side lines on this spire, and parties typically continue to the true summit rather than rappel it, then take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete, third and fourth class with a short fifth-class step, to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a quarter until it opens into a clearing. Leave it at the small stream — often cairned — and follow climbers' tracks up through the slabs alongside the stream into the basin under the west side of the spires.

The meadows here are fragile and heavily used; stay on the established tracks and off the heather.

From the basin, work up the talus toward the west face of South Early Winters Spire, north of the Southwest Couloir.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: fragile alpine meadow crossed by braided tracks — erosion damage and easy to lose the line
loose talus in the basin
shared descent line with South Arete parties, so expect congestion at rappel stations
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the route is marked by a larch tree that forks into two trunks in a clear Y — it is the single agreed-upon landmark for this climb and people navigate to it by name. In front of the Y-larch an easy ledge runs up and away from the tree; scramble that ledge and belay off a solid tree, and the first proper pitch follows cracks straight up through an awkward bulge, well protected, to a ledge at the foot of the feature climbers call the Wavy Crack. If you start at a lower or higher point on the rib you skip that first 5.8+ pitch and arrive at the Wavy Crack having missed the best of the lower climbing — so hunt for the Y-larch rather than roping up at whatever looks like the toe. The rib you want is the buttress immediately north of (left of, looking in) the Southwest Couloir.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to the fir tree and double cracks
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the climber's trail reaches the South Arete base in about 2.5 miles and 2,000 ft of gain. Seven pitches at 5.11d, first climbed in October 1991.

The traverse to the start eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain, so expect to lose height rather than contour.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Two routes starting about 100 ft apart on the same traverse
Loss of height along the base to skirt steeper terrain, which has to be regained
5.11d over seven pitches with no route-specific rappel line
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the South Arete base, head down and right along the base of the wall for about ten minutes to a start at double cracks beside a fir tree. A tree at the foot of a pair of cracks is the marker, and a tree is something you can walk into in cloud.

So the two checks are a duration and a tree: ten minutes of scrambling and traversing from the South Arete, and a fir. Not thirty seconds and not half an hour.

The negative test against its neighbour, and it is short and countable: the Hitchhiker begins roughly 100 ft further along the same traverse, at a small left-facing dihedral with four bolts. If you are standing at a dihedral with four bolts in it, you have gone 100 ft too far.

And if you have not lost height, you have not arrived: the traverse eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain. Contouring level along the wall keeps you on South Arete ground.

Where it ends: the route is not commonly rappelled top to bottom. Parties top out and use the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete, third and fourth class with one short more exposed step, to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base, and out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the west basin (snow)
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the main trail roughly a mile and a half to the well-worn climbers' trail and take it up into the basin on the west side of the Liberty Bell group. Early in the season the trailhead lot itself may still be snowed in.

On a cold morning parties approach in boots and crampons without flotation; later in the day the same snow softens badly. Start early and plan to be off the couloir before the afternoon.

This is the quickest line to the summit of the south spire, and it exists only for a short window: it comes into condition once the highway opens and deteriorates as the snow goes. Late in the season the couloir empties out into loose rock and is not worth climbing.
approach_variants.season: A few weeks to a couple of months after SR-20 reopens — roughly May-Jun
hazards: avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a sun-affected slope, worsening through the day
snow and occasional ice to around 50 degrees in the upper narrows
late season the couloir fills with loose rock and becomes a rockfall trap — not recommended once melted out
route depends entirely on SR-20 reopening, typically mid-April to early May
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin, the couloir is the snow gully rising on the southwest side of South Early Winters Spire, immediately left of the South Arete rib as you look up. It broadens low down at a modest 25 to 30 degrees, and the identifying feature is the fork higher up where the gully splits — the right-hand branch is the route, and it steepens to 40 to 50 degrees and narrows above the split. If you are in a gully that never forks, you are in the wrong drainage. Because the whole thing is a snow feature there is no rock start to find; the transition is simply from basin snow into the gully bed, so the navigational work is choosing the correct gully from the basin, in daylight, before the ground steepens.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate, bike the Dailey Prairie roads, then Orsino Creek Basin to the 5,200 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River near 1,200 ft at the end of FR-38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate most parties mountain-bike the old quarry and logging road system for roughly 6-7 miles and well over 2,000 ft of gain, threading several forks near Dailey Prairie, until the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride — usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. GPS or a GPX track is genuinely recommended on this network.

Stash bikes and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot: brushy, wet, occasionally overgrown, but not hard to follow. It drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope which often holds snow well into summer.

From the talus, traverse rightward — south — up and across, over a timbered rib, past the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then up into Orsino Creek Basin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water before the climb.

About four miles of foot travel from the bike cache to the summit, four to five hours one way for most parties, with combined bike and foot gain around 6,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Oct, with snow-free scrambling typically Jul-Sep. Earlier or later trips want an ice axe for lingering snow near 6,500 ft
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network near Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
A red talus slope holding snow into summer, and lingering snow near 6,500 ft
A steep loose dirt gully to gain the notch
Low fifth-class steps on the upper crest that force an improvised rappel if the bypass is missed
Orsino Creek is the last water for the whole climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ruins of an old log cabin are the one man-made thing on this approach and they are the checkpoint. From the red talus slope where the climbers' path fades, traverse right — south — up and across, cross a timbered rib, and pass the cabin ruins. If you have not passed a collapsed cabin, you have not made the traverse and you are still below the basin.

Orsino Creek is the last water and the entry to the basin. Fill up. There is nothing above it.

The base is an obvious notch in the ridge crest at about 5,200 ft, and you get to it up a steep loose dirt gully. That combination — an unpleasant slog up steep dirt, scree and talus, then a defined notch in a crest — is the arrival, and it works in cloud because a notch is a thing you stand in with air on the far side. This is the standard start and it is where the West Ridge is gained down low.

The discriminator against the other route out of this basin, and it is a single number: the North Ridge route continues higher and further climber's left — north — up basin snow or talus to a saddle around 5,800 ft between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge. So 5,200 ft and the obvious notch is the West Ridge; 5,800 ft and a saddle between two peaks is the North Ridge. Six hundred feet and a bearing separate two routes that share every step of the approach up to the basin.

The rock confirms the range: dunite, olivine-rich, exceptionally grippy, like coarse sandpaper. It is why parties choose to gain the ridge low rather than high — to maximise time on it.

Higher up, the false-summit bypass is worth carrying before you need it: leave the crest to the right — south — traverse ledges, and regain the crest about 200 yards short of the false summit, roughly 500 ft above where you left it. Staying exactly on the crest through that step is what forces parties into an improvised rappel.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pullout and Spire Gully to the last large tree, then right across the talus toward the inter-spire notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same as the Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20 east of Washington Pass. This is the east-side trailhead, not the Blue Lake trailhead used by the spire's west-side routes.

Nine pitches. The route shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final five pitches.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Vague, unfixed belays on the upper headwall, so bailing means building natural anchors
A shared start with a much more travelled route, with the split made mid-height
Talus and snow on the traverse below the inter-spire notch
Two trailheads on opposite sides of the pass serving this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Hike spire gully, which is cairned, to the last large tree. That tree is the turn. From it, traverse right across talus and snow to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress.

So the sequence is three moves and a tree: up the cairned gully to the last large tree, right across talus, then left to the buttress base. The tree is the only thing in that sequence you can put a hand on, which is why it is the marker rather than the gully.

Why the notch matters even though you do not go to it: the gully you aim at is the one running to the gap between the two spires, the same continuous cleft that on the west side is the chockstone-filled chimney. It is the biggest feature on this side of the group. Aim at it, then step left before reaching it.

So the negative test is: if you have reached the notch itself you have gone up too far, and if you are on the far side of the cleft you are on North Early Winters Spire, where Flycatcher Buttress starts from a flat ledge.

What separates this route from the east buttress it shares a start with, and it is a decision made halfway up rather than at the base: Southern Man splits off around mid-height onto the south-facing headwall. Its own belays are described as vague and not yet fixed, which is itself a tell: do not expect a fully bolted rap line if you need to bail from the upper headwall. Natural anchors would be required there.

Descent: from the summit, the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed fifth-class section to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Skykomish riverside to the northwest saddle
approach_variants.notes: Everything above the valley is off-trail. Leave the riverside near the road and head directly up the steep, blowdown-choked slope — the first several hundred feet are the worst of it — onto a well-defined hogsback that runs from about 2,700 ft to roughly 3,300 ft. Above the hogsback the slope steepens toward cliff bands, and there is no tread anywhere on the mountain.
