Carry water from the river; there is none once you leave it, and there is no usable cell coverage anywhere on route.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Entirely off-trail with sustained blowdown and brush low down
Cliff bands on the north side between roughly 4,200 and 4,400 ft that need careful route-finding to turn
A moat or bergschrund forming at the saddle depending on snow cover
Permanent snow and ice on north and east aspects near the summit even in late summer
A short exposed class 5 step considerably harder than the route's overall grade suggests
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts at a saddle around 5,940 ft northwest of the summit, and you identify it by what you crossed to reach it. Large cliff bands block the north end of the peak between roughly 4,200 and 4,400 ft; the way past is a traverse southeast beneath them onto the mountain's west and northwest side, and that traverse ends by rising onto a distinct notch on the ridge rather than onto any summit. Depending on the season a moat or bergschrund forms right at the saddle and is the last obstacle before you get on rock. Spire has three summits and the crest above the saddle is airy: mostly class 3, but with a short exposed mantle step of roughly ten feet at about 6,100 ft where many parties put a rope on, harder than the peak's overall billing prepares you for. Do not stray north or east off the crest — that ground steepens quickly into permanent snow and cliffs — and note the traverse line carefully, because reversing it through the cliff bands with no tread to follow is slow work.

approach_variants.name: West Fork Buttermilk to Star Lake
approach_variants.notes: Seven and a half miles of trail from the West Fork Buttermilk road end to Star Lake, and the tread is inconsistently maintained through the middle of it — long stretches of blowdown with only brief clear sections, so navigate by map or track rather than by looking for tread. Several fords of the West Fork are the main early-season problem and can force a detour upstream to find a log. Two miles below the lake the trail enters the lowest larches, and half a mile before it the trail crests Fish Creek Pass, an open viewpoint with water nearby and the first clear look at the peak. The lake basin is the standard camp and also serves several neighbouring summits. A boat-in approach from Lake Chelan up Prince Creek reaches the same crest from the other side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Large, deeply unstable talus at the base of the summit block
Rockfall onto anyone below on the loose scree track, worst on descent
Off-trail route-finding above the lake, including a contour that is easy to lose in snow
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on a wholly open ridge
High fords early in the season
Long and remote with minimal cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From Star Lake the peak stands to the east, above the head of the basin, and the base of the scramble is a notch on the ridge just west of a rocky point about 600 ft above the lake. Pick up the climber's path leaving the basin south and southeast of the lake and follow it as it switchbacks up genuinely poor scree to that notch; the point immediately east of the notch is Point 7,912, and it is the landmark that tells you the notch is the right one. From the notch the route turns north onto the peak's west and southwest ridge, and the ground changes character at once: broken blocky rock and sandy patches instead of running scree. Stay on or near the established contour rather than dropping into the steeper loose gullies below it, which look like shortcuts and are not. Above this the ridge is talus-hopping with occasional hands-on moves. If snow is still lying in the bowl the path disappears entirely, and the notch beside the point is what you navigate to.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
camps: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and hard patches on the basin traverse into early August
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit with real fall consequences
Aging in-situ slings at the crux that need backing up before use
Easy to drift off-line in poor visibility; the route is indistinguishable from the neighbouring peak's below 7,400 ft
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation for a serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The most important thing to know about this approach is that below 7,400 ft it is indistinguishable from Goode Mountain's. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

The counting test is the notch, and the word is right-most. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the right-most one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

Cross to the north side of that notch and the ground changes character completely: a fun ledge traverse on the backside of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. If you have not crossed to the north side, you have not found the ledge traverse, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

Confirm on the ledge: it includes a squeeze under a slight overhang, and there are in-situ slings at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

The last move is a choice, not a crux: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its left side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

And know which top you want: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the easternmost is the true high point.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.
hazards: Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail approach
Lake crossing and shuttle schedule: a missed connection puts you a day behind
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn
Lingering snow on the basin traverse into early August
Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, rockfall onto parties below
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.
hazards: Long approach over Cascade Pass and down the upper Stehekin valley before the Park Creek trail
Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn
Lingering snow on the basin traverse into early August
Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, rockfall onto parties below
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin to the northeast gully
approach_variants.notes: Seven miles or so up the Royal Basin Trail to Royal Lake, then about a mile more and five hundred feet past Shelter Rock and through Arrowhead Meadow into Upper Royal Basin below the Needles. It has no designated sites (camping there is on bare ground or gravel only, by a permit arranged through the Wilderness Information Center), so most parties camp at the lake; the tarns are the last dependable water before the talus. Off-trail from the basin onward.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose, rotten basalt on the gully and ridge with rockfall onto parties below
Snow or sluffing in the northeast couloir well into July — axe and self-arrest
An exposed Class 3 ridge traverse to the true summit
A spot on the ledges that appears to cliff out and is passed by a cairned crack
Lightly visited terrain where a rescue takes considerably longer than usual
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the tarns of Upper Royal Basin, look up at the Needles wall and pick out the northeast-facing gully on the climber's-right side of the group. Early in the season it holds snow, which makes it the obvious white line on an otherwise dry face and is the easiest identification you will get. Cross the talus to its foot; the base is where the loose scree fan narrows and steepens into the gully proper. Climb it and watch for the dogleg — the gully bends left below a notch on the summit ridge, and that bend is the confirmation you are in the right one rather than a neighbour. From the notch a short, exposed Class 3 scramble runs south to the true summit. The Needles hold several similar gullies and Clark stands immediately northwest with Johnson west, so a peak that looks right from the basin may not be the one you want. Higher up, on the broken ledges, one spot appears to cliff out where a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner is the way through. Everything on this face is loose — keep out of each other's fall line.

approach_variants.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
approach_variants.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Long, mostly waterless final push above Cooney Lake
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Iced summit blocks in shoulder season
Mosquitoes in the lake basins through mid-July
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the lake the trail keeps climbing for roughly another mile, crossing a saddle at about 7,900 ft on the peak's southeast side, and then runs into the broad southeast ridge of the mountain. The point where the tread meets that crest is the base — everything to there is walking on a path, and everything above it is off it. The ridge itself is easy and broad, so the confirmation is the last few hundred feet rather than the first: the crest steepens into a field of large, mostly stable blocks that wants hands only occasionally, with a few more exposed steps possible right at the top. The neighbour to watch for is the similar summit under a mile north along the same crest, which is a comparable height, a comparable walk and shares a lake name with this one in places — parties do link the two, but if you have walked north along easy open ridge for the better part of a mile you are on the other peak.

approach_variants.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

approach_variants.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.
hazards: Creek ford on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lakes side
Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Dry ground above the lakes; no water on the pass or crest
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Snow lingers on the north side of Horsehead Pass later than the approach suggests
Trail shared with motorcycles and stock

approach_variants.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread below the lower basin. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The flat upper basin is near 5,200 ft; the granite slabs and two small tarns at the top of the basin, near 6,400-6,500 ft, are a higher camp closer to the col. A far longer alternative comes in from the west — North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path below the lower basin — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

name: Brothers Traverse (North Peak to South Peak)

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake Trail and the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp, then the North Peak side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FR-25 (Hamma Hamma Road) at roughly 685-750 ft, take Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Past the lake the trail runs up a remote forested canyon known as the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp roughly 6 miles from the trailhead. Most parties camp at Lena Lake or at the climbers' camp rather than trying it in a day.

From camp this route splits away from the ordinary South Couloir line: cross the creek westward, cross a slide meadow and old burn scar, and climb a wide gully north to about 5,500 ft to gain the North Peak side of the mountain. The traverse is recommended north to south, so the North Peak is the start and the South Brother is the finish.
approach_variants.season: June is the usual recommendation, with consolidated snow in the Great Basin; conditions vary a lot year to year
hazards: The 6,200 ft notch drops onto a 200 ft cliff — a documented dead end that costs time and exposes a party on retreat ledges
Steep snow descent into the Great Basin
Exposed fourth-class scrambling to the notch
A sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side of the ridge
Moat belays on the mixed sections, which move with the season
A long committing day with no easy bail once across the Great Basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival test is a step in the ridge crest at about 6,100 ft, and the way you know it is the right one is the thing that happens if you go 100 ft higher. Working up and rightward from camp on scree, heather and lumpy basalt, crossing many small ribs and gullies, you meet the crest. There are two places you can meet it. The higher one, at about 6,200 ft, is a small notch whose far side is a 200-foot cliff — a party that tops out there has to back off and traverse out on exposed ledges with Class 3-4 slots between them. The one you want is the small step in the crest at about 6,100 ft, from which the ground drops steeply but climbably into the snow-filled Great Basin.

So the fog test is: top out, then look down. If the far side goes, you are at the step and on route. If the far side is a cliff, you are a hundred feet too high — do not try to force it, come back down and traverse.

Second test, once in the Great Basin: from it you climb a moderately steep snow couloir angling toward the North Brother, narrowing to a snow finger that reaches the summit ridge. If your couloir is running away from the north summit rather than toward it, you crossed the basin in the wrong direction.

What the traverse itself feels like, so nobody mistakes the connecting ridge for a mistake: the crest between the two Brothers is giant boulders forming a jagged run of horns and pinnacles, and traversing it is slow. Slow is correct here. The route is roughly seven roped pitches — fourth class to the notch, steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed ground with moat belays, and a final steep couloir to the South Brother.

approach_variants.name: Standard Tooth approach, but break off north of the Pineapple Pass gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, follow the Snow Lake trail about a mile and a half, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and start up toward Pineapple Pass on the standard line. The difference is at the top. Do not finish the gully to the pass. Break off to the north of it and climb the open books on the face above instead. This is the route parties take when the South Face is backed up, and it is deliberately the path of least resistance between The Tooth Fairy and the South Face. About 4.8 km and 2,500 ft from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to September, once the approach snow has gone; heavy weekend traffic in that window
hazards: Loose blocks on the open-book corner pitches
The route sits directly above the busy South Face — rockfall onto parties below is the documented concern here, not just a generic one
Rockfall risk to and from routes sharing the approach gully and the summit area
Descent route-finding: the broken west and north side offers several plausible gullies, and the loose east-side gully should not be rappelled
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival test is a thing you do not do: do not go up to Pineapple Pass. Hike the stable talus toward the pass and then leave it, heading north of the gully that finishes at the pass. If you have stood in the notch at Pineapple Pass, you have overshot the start of this route and you are at the start of the South Face.

What you are looking for on the rock: open books. Pitches one and two climb open-book corners that begin north of the Pineapple Pass gully, and they lead to a left-facing slab. Corner, corner, then slab facing left. That sequence is the confirmation, and none of it requires seeing the summit.

And a third-pitch check if you are still unsure: pitch three finds three cracks running up to an overhang, and the route face-climbs to the left of those three cracks. Three cracks under a roof, and you go left of them. If you are climbing the cracks themselves you have drifted right.

How it differs from its two neighbours: The Tooth Fairy is further left again and goes at 5.9; the South Face starts from the notch at the top of the pass at 5.4. This route sits between them, both physically and in difficulty, at 5.5. If your first pitch feels like 5.9, you have gone too far left.

A warning that belongs with the finding: this face is loose, and it sits above the popular routes. Being on the correct start also means being above other people.

approach_variants.name: Colonial Glacier col to the Neve rim
approach_variants.notes: Take the maintained trail to Pyramid Lake, then the unmaintained climbers' path around the lake's east side up steep root-laced forest into heather and boulders, along a narrowing ridge and across a scree traverse to the toe of the Colonial Glacier. Camp on the flat bench below the glacier. From camp, rope up, climb south to the col at around 6,900 ft, drop a couple of hundred feet onto the Neve icecap and work west along its rim.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, while the snow arete is still continuous and the bergschrund can be turned
hazards: Open crevasses scattered across the east side of the Neve Glacier
The bergschrund at the foot of the snow arete has to be turned or bridged and moves through the season
Sustained class 3 with full exposure on the ridge, on loose rock
A knife-edge section immediately below the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: Work west along the rim of the icecap rather than out into its middle, passing Horseman's Pack and then The Horseman. Once The Horseman is behind you, turn north and keep following the ice edge until a snow arete runs up out of the glacier to a rock ridge. That arete is the base of the route and there is nothing else like it along this rim — everywhere else the ice edge simply meets broken ground. The bergschrund at its foot is the proof and also the thing to inspect on arrival, because it has to be turned or bridged to get onto the arete and how far along you must walk to do that changes through the season. Above it the ridge runs north and then west around a corner into sustained class 3. If you are still south of The Horseman, or you have drifted into the middle of the icecap toward the bigger peak, you have not reached the turn. If the ground above you rolls back at an easy angle instead of narrowing to a crest, you are on the glacier rim and not on the spire.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes and High Pass, then the col in Larrabee's south arm and the gully to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles to the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead are passenger-car friendly; beyond that the road narrows and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, and high-clearance is recommended for the final two miles to Twin Lakes. If the upper road is out, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and add roughly four miles round trip and 1,500 ft of gain.

From the isthmus between the Twin Lakes take the High Pass Trail — about two miles, losing roughly 300 ft as it skirts below Winchester Mountain before climbing to the pass.

From High Pass, ascend the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's South Arm; there is a trail here in summer. From the col descend slightly and traverse the basin.

The Pleiades are a series of jagged spires on Larrabee's east ridge, so this is not one summit but several.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose sandy rock where downclimbing is as hazardous as ascending
A rough final two miles of FS-3065 that may add four miles and 1,500 ft to the day
Three separate objectives leaving from High Pass, easy to confuse in the basin
The first (west) Pleiad is far more serious than the second and looks similar from the notch
No water past High Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climb starts at a gully leading to the notch between the first and second Pleiades, and finding it is a three-step sequence from High Pass. Up the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's south arm. Down slightly from the col. Across the basin. Then up the gully to the notch. The descent in the middle is the step people skip, and skipping it puts you on Larrabee's south ridge instead. The notch is between two spires and that is the confirmation. You are not aiming for a summit, you are aiming for the gap between the first and second towers of a jagged row. Arriving somewhere with rock on both sides of you and the basin below is the arrival. From the notch the two peaks are very different, and the choice matters. The second peak, to the east, is an easy scramble. The first peak, to the west, is third class in summer and has been reported as a snowy knife-edge with slabby, high-consequence exposure in winter conditions. Going the wrong way out of the notch is the difference between a walk and a serious ridge. What being on the wrong objective looks like: Larrabee's own South Ridge route leaves the same basin and its base is two parallel channels about 30 ft apart on a southwest spur at 6,900 ft — take the right-hand one for Larrabee. American Border Peak's route contours much further north around Larrabee's west flank to a col at 6,200-6,300 ft. All three leave High Pass. Only this one crosses the basin under Larrabee's east-side spires. The rock is loose and sandy throughout, which makes downclimbing as hazardous as the climb up. Keep the party close so nobody is under a falling stone.

approach_variants.name: Terror Basin, the upper Barrier crossing and the Degenhardt col
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead the climbers' path parallels the creek on easy old roadbed before a punishing push to treeline in Terror Basin — faint tread, dense brush, and class 3 root-pull sections through cliff bands. Most parties reach the basin in one long day. From the basin cross the Barrier at its upper notch, near 6,200 ft, by way of heather benches and loose rock and moats, into Crescent Creek Basin below the peaks. A direct line into Crescent Creek Basin exists but is buggier and less consistent.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the Crescent and Terror Creek approach is snow-free enough to be reliably passable
hazards: Broken, loose ground working across to the notch
Rock quality flips repeatedly between clean gneiss and dirt-covered choss
A few low fifth-class moves off the ridge crest with no easy retreat
The lower Stump Hollow Barrier crossing leads to a different objective and is the wrong one here
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col between this peak and Degenhardt is the base, and the climbing starts by dropping a few low fifth-class moves off the crest at the col onto the peak's western side — you do not start below the col and climb up to it. The proof once you are on that side is a gully or couloir system leading up and right toward the summit with a band of clearly overhanging rock capping it directly above. The line stays left inside the gully and avoids that overhang entirely; parties who take the roof head-on have found the hard and unnecessary way. Two negative markers. If you crossed the Barrier at the lower Stump Hollow notch rather than the upper one near 6,200 ft, you are set up under a different peak entirely. And a stretch of rubbish, dirt-covered rock is not on its own evidence you are off route here, because this peak's rock alternates between surprisingly solid gneiss and choss on the same face.

approach_variants.name: Standard Tooth approach, then left past the Southwest Face
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the South Face approach as far as Great Scott Bowl: Alpental upper lot, Snow Lake Trail about 1.5-1.6 miles to the Source Lake junction, bear left, cross the Source Lake basin near 4,000 ft, crest the lip into Great Scott Bowl around 4,400 ft, and climb the bowl toward Pineapple Pass beneath the Fang. Rather than finishing at the notch south of the pass and contouring to the South Face, this line stays lower and further left (west), working past the Southwest Face along the base of the west-facing wall. The Fang is the formation that catches people out. A boot path around its back side leads up into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth; from there, getting to the Tooth Fairy means backtracking down and picking a way through rough climbers' paths in the trees and across the rock fields.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: moat between snow and rock at the base in early season
loose talus in Great Scott Bowl
rockfall from parties on the South Face and Southwest Face above and right
the boot path behind the Fang leads to the wrong gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Tooth Fairy is a bolted line on the west-facing wall, and the bolts are the test. Traverse left along the base past the Southwest Face until you are under a wall with a line of fixed protection running up it — if the rock above you is blocky and takes only gear, you are still on the Southwest Face or have drifted round toward the South Face.

If you are standing in a narrow gully with the Fang on one side and the Tooth on the other, you are on the wrong side of the Fang: go back down rather than up.

In early season a moat between the snow of the bowl and the rock at the base can force extra scrambling to reach the first bolt; that moat is normal here, not a sign you are in the wrong place.

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.notes: Note the access before anything else: the road up to the historic trailhead has a permanent washout, so the day starts with a long bike or walk past the vehicle gate before the trail proper begins. From the trailhead, the trail climbs through forest to the small lake at about two and a half miles — last easy water, and no fires or camping within two hundred feet of it. Continue up into the open meadows of the flats at about four and a half miles, the best camping on the route, then a further couple of miles to the GAP at roughly six miles, where the maintained tread ends and most parties bivy. The gap gives the first real view of the three summits and of the glacier below them.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Crevasses open on the glacier by midsummer and bare ice with a moat appears late in the season; an axe is a year-round item on this peak.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the col
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season, with bare ice by late summer
Loose rock in the chimney and ramp system
No established trail or cairned route above the gap — route-finding is entirely on you
The descent is a committing series of rappels, and some stations are fixed slings of unknown age
Fog on the glacier traverse has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the gap, drop about four hundred feet off-trail down snow and talus onto the glacier, cross it, and climb back up roughly a thousand feet on the far side to the col between the middle and north towers. That col is the base of the climbing, and the thousand-foot re-ascent is the discriminator: this is the only one of the three summits whose route requires you to gain a col before you touch its rock. From the col the line is a ramp that leads left and then angles right into a shallow chimney — the chimney is the check, being the one chimney breaching the block from this col, and it is fourth class with a move or two of low fifth. Above it an exposed fourth-class ridge leads to a grassy ramp and the summit. Negative markers: if you are standing under three stacked wooden ladders bolted into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the southern end of the ridge, two towers away; if you have climbed a short face straight off the glacier with no col gained, you are on the middle tower's south face.

approach_variants.name: Surprise Creek past Surprise and Glacier lakes
approach_variants.notes: The more popular way in, from a trailhead that is easy to find near Scenic on US 2. Climb the Surprise Creek trail to Surprise Lake, join the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it north to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south from the pass to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin under the north face.
hazards: Rarely repeated 600 ft class 5 line, first climbed 1972; rock quality and protection unconfirmed
Loose or lichen-covered alpine granite likely on an infrequently climbed face
Unofficial, unmarked path south of Trap Pass to the lakes basin under the face
Remote setting with sparse modern beta

approach_variants.name: Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Thunder Mountain Lakes
bivy.notes: Lake basin under the granite of Slippery Slab Tower and Thunder Mountain, reached by the unofficial trail south from Trap Pass. The closest camp to the north face. Fragile ground; camp only on rock or bare sites.
bivy.water: The lakes
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few small sites on durable ground

approach_variants.notes: From the Tunnel Creek trailhead off US 2, climb about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south a couple of miles over meadowy ground and up the switchbacks to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin.
hazards: Snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer
Rarely repeated 600 ft class 5 line, first climbed 1972; rock quality and protection unconfirmed
Loose or lichen-covered alpine granite likely on an infrequently climbed face
Unofficial path south of Trap Pass to the lakes basin; fragile ground at the lakes
Remote setting with sparse modern beta

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the middle line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, take the maintained Snow Lake Trail about a mile and a quarter and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Skirt the west and north shore; the tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus.

Work up and right toward the obvious talus and dirt gully on the peak's northwest side; a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow it into the basin, then climb moraine along the left side of the small permanent snow patch to Unicorn Col just west of the summit. A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs — easier travel than the scree either side — and leads east around the south side to the base of the summit horn.

The climb itself is a single pitch of blocky low-fifth-class climbing, about 40-50 ft, on the south and southeast face, with one fixed piton mid-pitch.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose blocks on the approach scramble to the base of the horn
A short exposed pitch above broken ground where a fall has real consequence
A rappel that may not reach the ground on a 30 m rope, particularly with an open moat late season
An old bleached snag at the top that is no longer a sound anchor
Two different rappel lines off the same block landing in different places
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right along the foot of the horn: the roof, the classic route, Open Book. All three start within about 70 ft of each other and all three finish at the same slung block, so the bottom is the only place this can be got right.

The classic route is the middle one, and it takes the south and southeast face direct — blocky low-fifth climbing straight up, one pitch of about 40-50 ft, with one fixed piton mid-pitch. A piton at half height on open face is the positive confirmation.

The distance test is the practical one and it works by feel rather than by sight:
  — The roof starts about 20 ft to your left, at the point where the ridgeline meets the block.
  — Open Book starts about 50 ft to your right, at two wide, left-leaning cracks.

So the two negatives are tactile, which is what you want when the horn is in cloud: if you are fighting a wide awkward crack that wants big cams, you have walked past this route to the right and you are on Open Book. If there is a roof over your head and you are in a gully or chimney, you have gone left past it and you are on the roof, at 5.6.

Character test: this is blocky face and crack climbing on the open face. Not inside a chimney, not in a wide crack. If you are inside anything, you are on a neighbour.

Why it matters: this is the middle grade of the three — 5.4, against Open Book's easy fifth and The Roof's 5.6. Being one line out changes the grade in whichever direction you drifted, on a short pitch above broken ground.

Descent detail worth settling at the top rather than over the edge: there are effectively two rappel lines off the summit block, one dropping to the notch and the ground below the horn, the other landing on the snow patch side. A 30 m rope has been reported as just short depending on which one you use and on how open the moat is late season; 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the rock horn — the old bleached snag some older reports mention is no longer sound.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the rightmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Identical approach to the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded rise; work up and right into the talus and dirt gully on the northwest side, where a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn.

This route takes the right-hand end of the south face rather than the face direct, and it is the easiest of the three summit-block lines — a step down from the Classic Route and well below The Roof.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Wide-crack climbing that is awkward and poorly protected without large cams
Loose rock in the gully and chimney terrain around the summit tower
Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out
An exposed step near the top of the horn with real air below on the east side
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right along the foot of the horn: the roof, the classic route, open book. Open book is the rightmost and the easiest.

The positive test is unmistakable and it is a count: two wide, left-leaning cracks, about 50 ft right of the classic route's base. Two of them, wide, leaning left. From there the line climbs up and left toward the anchor shared with the other routes.

The negative is about crack width and you feel it in the first few moves, which is exactly when you want to know: if the crack takes your fingers and hands comfortably, you are on the classic route, 50 ft to your left, at 5.4. Open Book's cracks are wide and awkward and want large cams — that awkwardness is the route, not a sign you are off it.

The second negative is overhead: if there is a roof above you, you have walked the entire width of the block and you are on the roof at 5.6 — the hardest of the three and the far left end of the list.

Orientation test: this line is at the right-hand end of the south face. The Classic Route goes straight up the middle of the same face. If you are directly beneath the south face looking up at blocky ground with a piton visible at half height, you are one line to the left of here.

Descent: the same shared anchor as the other two — the large rock horn on the south side, about 40-50 ft above the notch. Avoid the old dead snag some older reports mention; it is no longer trustworthy. A 30 m rope has been found marginal or short depending on which of the two rappel lines you take off the horn, so 40 m removes the doubt. Downclimbing this line is viable given the grade, but it is still exposed near the top.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) leaves the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 27-28 miles east of Granite Falls; about 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel end at the Sunrise Mine trailhead, around 2,400 ft, with a pit toilet and a Northwest Forest Pass requirement.

Trail #707 starts in second-growth and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs — a genuine obstacle in high runoff. It then climbs through Wirtz Basin and out onto open cairned talus to Headlee Pass, about 4,720 ft at 2.7 miles: a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Beyond the pass the trail drops through trees and crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, following it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 5,000 ft and 3.5 miles. That is the last dependable running water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Allow three hours or more from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
hazards: Rockfall from parties above in the Headlee Pass couloir
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish in high runoff
Steep exposed heather on the ledge traverse — treacherous when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into mid-to-late summer; axe worth carrying early season
approach_variants.baseFinding: The confirmation that you are in the right place to start traversing is two large cairns on a saddle at about 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake visible below to the northwest. Do not drop into the saddle. The heather-covered ledge system starts about 30 ft above the cairns on third-class slabs and runs west across the north face for roughly 800 ft, with a goat trail worn through it; there is one exposed step down off the saddle before it widens. This is the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, the small summit just northeast of Vesper; the two cairns and the view of Copper Lake are the reliable test. At the far end of the traverse, where the ledge runs out, the original start goes up and then right on about 60 ft of low fifth to third-class slabs and an obvious flaky gully. The cleaner and now more common variation is reached by backtracking slightly and making an exposed third-class traverse down and around the toe of a buttress to a clean 5.6 layback flake. Negative marker: Ragged Edge jogs hard right within the first pitch or two. A first pitch that runs straight up the face and stays there is True Grit, not this route.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Creek rib to Burgundy Col
approach_variants.notes: From the unsigned roadside pullout, find the faint boot path dropping east through loose talus into the trees past a trail register, then cross Early Winters Creek on a log. The path climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply, to a basin bench around 6,400 to 6,500 ft where there is good camping and a late-season spring, then continues up scree and snow to Burgundy Col.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn. This face takes sun through the day, so it comes into condition earlier and holds later than the shaded sides of the group
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to the col
Early Winters Creek log crossing can be awkward at high flow
Nothing on the approach is signed or marked
approach_variants.baseFinding: Burgundy Col is the reference and the tower's position at the col is the test. Coming up the timbered rib and scree from Burgundy Creek, Vasiliki Tower is the formation standing on your left as you arrive at the col; the Wine Spires proper are the group on the right, and the crest running away beyond the tower on the left is Vasiliki Ridge. The route starts from the col itself: scramble up broken ground to a system of dihedrals that trend rightwards across the face above you. Those right-trending corners are the proof — the ordinary line simply follows them, and the harder direct variation on this face is the one that steps left out of them onto cracks. If the corners above you lean the other way, or the wall you are under is in shade for most of the day, you are on the wrong side of the tower: this is the sunny side, which is why it is climbed early and late in the season.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the leftmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as the other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake for the last reliable water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded hump; contour up and right into the obvious northwest talus and dirt gully, where a heather-bench climbers' path reappears near the top and drops you into the basin under the peak. Climb the moraine beside the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the summit cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn — roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.

This is the hardest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, following a steeper and more sustained line than either neighbour, with an old piton at about half height.

Carry a double-length runner or a cordelette. The top anchor for this line sits set back from the edge, so the rappel power-point has to be extended out to the lip to keep the rope running cleanly over the roof feature.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose rock reported in the gully and chimney section
The steepest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, and awkward to reverse
A top anchor set back from the edge, which drags the rope over the roof unless extended
An old piton at half height that should not be treated as protection
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left to right along the foot of the horn: the roof, the Classic Route, Open Book. The roof is the leftmost and the hardest.

The positive test is a junction rather than a crack, which is why it is easy to find in poor light: it starts about 20 ft left of the Classic Route, at the point where the ridgeline meets the summit block. Ridge into block — that meeting point is the marker.

The feature itself is the second confirmation and it is overhead: a wide gully or chimney running beneath a roof. You climb the gully, then step right under the roof onto a ledge, then up to the belay. If there is no roof above you, you are not on this route. There is an old piton at about half height.

The two negatives, both to your right:
  — 20 ft right, blocky climbing straight up the open south face with a piton mid-pitch, and no roof: that is the Classic Route at 5.4.
  — 70 ft right, two wide left-leaning cracks: that is Open Book at easy fifth.
So every way of being wrong here makes the climbing easier, not harder — which is the safer direction, but it also means nothing about the ground will warn you that you missed the route you came for.

Grade as a check: 5.6, noticeably burlier than the Classic Route's corner and well above Open Book. If it feels like the easiest thing on the block, you are not on it.

And the one piece of descent planning that has to happen before you leave the ground: the top anchor for this line is set back from the edge. Extend it with a cordelette or long sling so the rope runs over the lip rather than dragging on the roof. Most parties rappel this line even if they downclimbed elsewhere on the peak, because reversing it is considerably more exposed than reversing its neighbours. A single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft; 30 m has been reported marginal depending on which of the two lines off the horn you use, so 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the rock horn, not the retired snag.

approach_variants.name: Yellow Aster Butte Trail, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead, around 3,600-3,700 ft, on Twin Lakes Road (FR-3065), start on Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686. It climbs through forest switchbacks with a couple of seasonal creek crossings in the first mile.

At roughly 1.5 miles the signed Tomyhoi Lake Trail splits off right toward Gold Run Pass near 5,400 ft. Stay left, then contour into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns at about 5,200-5,600 ft — roughly two hours and four miles from the car, and the last dependable water.

From the basin leave maintained trail: head north-northwest over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm.

As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the north — right — side rather than staying on the crest. The path fades into scree and talus near the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. The moat below the false summit opens as the season goes on and is the crux either way
hazards: A rock-and-ice moat at the notch that is the crux of the outing and widens through the season
Glacier-polished slick rock at the snow margin
Minor crevasse hazard traversing the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier
Loose, exposed, non-obvious route-finding on scree and rock benches approaching the notch
The descent through the V-slot is the most exposed step of the day and is where parties rope up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a moat, not a ledge — the climbing starts where the glacier meets the rock at about 7,200-7,250 ft, at a notch in the jagged ridge below the false summit. Traverse along the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid several rock pinnacles, and aim for that notch. Getting into it means a traverse on hard snow around a small moat, and in many years that shallow rock-and-ice moat is the crux of the entire outing.

The rock by the glacier is glacier-polished and slick, and that is a tactile confirmation you are in the right place as well as a warning. Smooth, scoured rock at the snow margin means you are at the moat.

There is a documented alternative and it is worth knowing before you commit: drop 100 to 200 ft lower and climb a rock finger to reach the same notch. A party that arrives at an open moat it does not like has a published option other than retreat.

Gear is genuinely disputed here and the honest statement is that reports differ: some parties manage the moat traverse with an ice axe alone on firm snow, others want crampons. It opens as the season goes on. Carry for the worse case.

Above the notch, the sequence is the check: an exposed traverse around a rib gains the climbable side of the summit block, then roughly 160 ft along the left edge of the ridge, then a ledge crossed west to a wide corner where the crux is a short V-shaped slot. Third class throughout with that one slot harder. The block looks far worse from the false summit than it climbs — repeatedly, in every account — so an intimidating view from the false summit is not evidence you are off route.

Old ring pitons on the route are a reminder this is not a maintained line, not a sign you are on the right one.

approach_variants.name: Green Ridge and Charlie Brown Lake
approach_variants.notes: The trailhead is an unsigned climbers' and fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the Middle Fork road, roughly 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek trailhead at about 1,350 ft — no sign, no formal parking, and easy to drive straight past. Climb Green Ridge steeply, staying left where a fork drops northeast to Green Ridge Lake, over the ridge high point near 4,840 ft, past a small tarn, then down about 800 ft into the Upper Garfield lake basin and north through steep forest to Charlie Brown Lake. That mid-route descent has to be re-climbed on the way out, so it costs far more than the raw mileage suggests.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Unsigned roadside start that is easy to miss
Broken cliff bands and loose duff on the slopes above the lake
800 ft of elevation loss and regain in the middle of the route
A steep gully walled by rock that holds snow and ice into summer
A corniced summit ridge on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding: Charlie Brown Lake at about 4,390 ft is where the walking stops and the scramble begins, and it is the right place to stop because the whole remaining route is visible from its shore. From the outlet, work onto the peak's southeast slopes and thread up through broken cliff bands and duff to a broad talus field at roughly 4,850 ft — that talus field is the marker that you are on the correct line rather than one of the several plausible-looking weaknesses below it. From the top of the talus, angle left into an obvious gully with grassy slopes at its head. The gully is walled by rock on both sides and tops out near 5,400 ft at a notch beside a protruding rock on the south ridge, and it shoots you straight out onto the more south-facing slopes of the mountain. If you are traversing across the face rather than gaining height in a defined gully, you have gone past it. Above the notch the last few hundred feet are easy but steep heather to the summit ridge. Carry an axe and traction if snow is still sitting in that gully.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek, Borealis Lake and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the large lot above the boat ramp at Colonial Creek, follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south to McAllister Camp; the old bridge near mile 6.6 is gone and the crossing is now on logs a short way upstream of the old site. Across the creek pick up the unmaintained boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and blowdown up the north ridge past a viewpoint that gives the first look at the peaks. Continue through forest and heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the base camp. From camp rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle; it has retreated into an upper and a lower tier separated by slabs and cliffs, to the col.
approach_variants.season: July and August are best; earlier ascents need ice technique, and the south-facing snow above the col softens dangerously through the day
hazards: Crevasses on the Borealis Glacier, worse late in the season
Brushy, poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp
Afternoon softening of the south-facing snow finger — start early
Class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges above the snow
approach_variants.baseFinding: Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and this peak, is the base, and which way you turn on it is the whole test. Standing on the col, Primus is the peak to the west and this one is to the east; the route turns east. Above the pass on that side a single steep snow finger runs up roughly 200 ft. It is unmistakable from the col and there is no second candidate, and it is the entry to the climb. Above the snow the ground becomes rock ramps and ledges, class 3 to 4, following the west ridge to a bouldery summit. If you have left the col heading west onto a broad class 2-3 ridge, you are climbing Primus instead. If you are still threading crevasses on slabby, tiered ice below the col, you have not reached the pass at all — the glacier here is split into two tiers by slabs and cliffs and it is the upper tier that runs to the col.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then north along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the unsigned Wine Spires pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass, roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff near milepost 166, at about 4,300 ft. A boot path drops down loose scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700-plus ft to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. A flat bench campsite, the Bench, at about 6,460 ft sits about halfway up and is the more common camp for this objective than the col itself.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A class 4 ridge traverse with real exposure to reach the tower
Loose scree-covered talus on the initial drop from the highway
A log crossing of Early Winters Creek
The whole approach shares a trail with the Wine Spires objectives and then deliberately departs from it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Vasiliki Ridge and Ares Tower rise directly north of Burgundy Col and the Wine Spires camp area. So the test is directional and it is the opposite of every other route from this trailhead: from the bench or the col, go north.

Every Wine Spires objective, Burgundy, Chianti, Pernod, Chablis, is reached by going to Burgundy Col and then south or east from it. Ares Tower is the one you reach by contouring and scrambling north along the ridge crest. If you have dropped onto snow beneath an east-facing wall, you have gone south and you are under the Wine Spires.

Arrival: Ares Tower is the high point of Vasiliki Ridge at about 8,190 ft. Following the crest north, you are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambleable and rises into a tower. The climbing is a 4th-class scramble to a notch, then one short low-5th-class step to the true summit; Grade II-III.

Confirm by the hardware, and on this ridge it is the one piece of fixed gear worth knowing about: there is a fixed anchor at the Ares Tower summit, and the standard descent is a single rappel from it down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then a reversal of the fourth-class ridge scramble.

So the pattern of the day is: stash gear at a notch below the tower, climb the short summit step, rappel back to your gear. If there is nowhere sensible to leave a pack, you are not at the tower yet.

Camp choice as a planning fact: the Bench at about 6,460 ft is the more common camp for this objective than Burgundy Col, which is 1,300 ft higher and in the wrong direction.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.notes:
Darrington to the end of Squire Creek Road (Madison Ave south, T, right on Darrington Street). The road is gated by a washout.

On foot: old roadbed, flagged landslide crossing at about five minutes, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes more to the wide dry streambed full of white boulders. That is the turn-off, and it is the last one before the trail heads south out of the valley.

Descend the bed roughly 200 feet, trend left into the alders to find the informal path, follow it about 30 minutes to the ford of Squire Creek, then keep on as the trail fades along the underground creek bed until the basin opens, about two hours from the car. That is only the basin: Salish Peak's base is higher still, reached by scrambling up the left side of Roan Wall, and the full approach to this route runs about six hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford drops and the basin snow has gone
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Path fades entirely in the basin
Residual avalanche snow at the base early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding: All the Waterfall Basin lines are found from the same reference: follow the creek bed until the thin boulder-filled watercourse comes down directly from the wall, scramble it, and you are at the base with Martha's Place — the huge overhung boulder — beside you. From there pick the line off the wall. Note the route name is a bird reference, not a closure: there is no known raptor closure for this basin, so do not read the name as a seasonal restriction.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington turn south on Madison Ave, follow it to a T, turn right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and follow it to where a washout gates it off.

Walk the old roadbed. A landslide crossing comes about five minutes in and is flagged. The original road end is about 30-40 minutes from the car. Carry on along the old trail for another 20-30 minutes.

The turn-off is a landmark, not a sign: a large dry streambed roughly 50 feet wide and full of white boulders. This is the last turnoff before the Squire Creek trail swings south out of the valley toward Squire Creek Pass — if the trail starts climbing away southward, you walked past it.

Drop about 200 feet down the streambed, trending left into alders, where an informal path becomes visible. Follow that upvalley for roughly 30 minutes to a ford of Squire Creek. Past a small creek channel the trail fades; keep following the underground creek bed and it opens into the basin, about two hours from the car. Allow 3 to 3.5 hours in all to reach the base of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the Roan Wall base commonly holds residual avalanche snow well into the climbing season
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek — difficult in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the season
Faint informal path through alder; the trail fades entirely in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In the basin, keep following the creek bed until a thin, boulder-filled watercourse comes down directly out of the wall above you. That watercourse is obvious once it appears, and scrambling up it puts you at the base of Roan Wall — the big red slab split by a prominent corner system.

The overhung boulder called Martha's Place, which carries sport routes on its underside, sits near the base and is the bivy; if you can see it you are in the right place.

Critical: the first two pitches are approach pitches, not the route. An obvious bolted 80-foot 5.8 slab, then a low-fifth 150-foot groove, come before the climbing proper. Easy bolted slab at the bottom of a 5.11 route is correct here, not evidence you are on the wrong line. Center Stage takes the middle of the wall; the harder crux slab pitch is high (P7), not low.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway via Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065). Trail #707 crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on a log almost immediately — a real obstacle in high runoff — then climbs through Wirtz Basin, breaks into cairned talus and boulder fields, and reaches Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles. The pass is a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from above is a genuine hazard.

Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek and follows it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft, 3.5 miles and 2,700 ft from the car — last reliable water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Three hours or more car to base.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier needs axe and crampons for the ledge traverse
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep exposed heather benches, slick when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into early-to-mid summer
Loose rock on the face — treat as alpine despite the bolted belays
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the two large cairns on the saddle at about 5,700 ft (near 48.01375 -121.51451), with Copper Lake below to the northwest; the heather ledge system starts about 30 ft above the cairns on third-class slabs, not from the saddle floor. Traverse west on the goat trail through the heather.

True Grit itself is identified by its first anchor, not by its first moves. Pitch 1 is about 200 ft of easy, clean granite and finishes by stepping left to a bolted belay sitting directly beneath an obvious narrow chimney. If there is no chimney above the anchor you have reached, you are not on True Grit. It is the more direct of the two lines here — Ragged Edge jogs sharply right in its first pitch or two, so a line that keeps going straight up is this one.

approach_variants.name: Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from Twin Lakes to the 1935 lookout
approach_variants.notes:
From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft — the parking area between the two lakes, with a vault toilet — pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. It starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather.

At roughly a quarter to half a mile there is a signed junction with High Pass Trail #676, which goes on toward the Gargett Mine and Mount Larrabee. Stay left or straight to remain on #685.

Beyond the junction the trail leaves the last trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs by tight switchbacks. Around 0.9 mile an unmarked climbers' path splits off offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow and scree; the standard trail continues by switchbacks and is the preferred line.

At about 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit; a short final push along the open ridge reaches the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521 ft. About 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300 ft of gain.

There is no water on route or at the lookout.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct, and the limiting factor is the last two and a half miles of FS-3065 rather than the trail
hazards: The last two and a half miles of FS-3065, rough and one-lane in places, high-clearance recommended
Hard lingering snow on the upper switchbacks into August in heavy-snow years, over consequential runout
A signed junction at 0.25-0.5 mile that serves five much larger objectives
An unmarked climbers' path at 0.9 mile up snow and scree
No water on route or at the lookout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no climbing on this route and saying so is the honest answer — what there is, is one junction you can get wrong and one slope that can hurt you. The route is a maintained trail from the car to the lookout, so 'the base' is the trailhead between the two lakes.

The junction at a quarter to half a mile is the only real decision. #685 for Winchester goes left or straight; #676 for High Pass, the Gargett Mine, Mount Larrabee, American Border Peak and the Pleiades goes right. It is signed, but it is the branch point for five different objectives in this basin and taking it by accident sends you toward a very much bigger day. If you find yourself contouring around the west side of Winchester Mountain and losing height toward a pass, you are on #676.

The second one is unmarked, at about 0.9 mile: a climbers' path splits off up snow and scree as a direct alternative to the switchbacks. It is rougher and it is not the standard line. In cloud, a path that stops switchbacking and goes straight up is the wrong one.

Arrival at the ridge: at roughly 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit, with only a few hundred feet of open ridge left. Cresting a ridge with the lookout to your northeast is the confirmation.

The real hazard is the upper switchbacks, and it is worth reading as a base finding of a different kind: steep snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and the southeast slopes into August in heavy-snow years, it hardens overnight, and the runout below is consequential. An ice axe is a reasonable thing to be carrying on a lookout trail in early season.

name: Windy Peak via Iron Gate Trailhead (Boundary Trail / Sunny Pass Approach)

approach_variants.name: Trail 342 from Long Swamp
approach_variants.notes: This is the easternmost of the high peaks here and by far the least technical, being a trail walk with a very short scramble stapled on the end, so the real work is the drive. Long gravel forest roads out of Loomis reach Long Swamp Campground, where Trail 342 starts and climbs steadily through burned lodgepole and recovering meadow to a camp with water partway up and then out onto open, treeless ridge. A shorter trail comes in from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead a few miles further west but is overgrown in stretches from lack of use, and a third start at Iron Gate involves the roughest driving of the three. Water on the upper trail is limited and seasonal, so carry enough for a long day.
approach_variants.season: Late June to early October
hazards: Long trail mileage with limited seasonal water on the upper half
Fully exposed, treeless ridge and summit in wind and lightning
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the true summit
Standing fire-killed snags along the burned lower trail in wind
Long gravel forest road driving far from any town, no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The trail does not go to the top, which is the single most useful thing to know here.
