Tread climbs to a junction and high point below and south of the summit at roughly 8,100 ft and then begins contouring and descending onward toward Horseshoe Basin and the Boundary Trail. The base of the scramble is exactly where the trail stops climbing. Standing on the plateau at that point, the summit rocks are obvious: they stand up as a small blocky pyramid of about three hundred feet, and there is nothing else nearby that looks like it. Leave the constructed tread and take the cairned, braided path up open talus on the south side of that pyramid; it is easy blocky scrambling and takes only a few minutes. The confirmations at the top are physical and worth checking, because the plateau carries other rises. Benchmark nails are set in the summit rock at the site of the old lookout, and remnants of the lookout's telephone line still run down the northwest slope toward the saddle, so if you can find the wire you are on the right high point. The way to know you have overshot is comfort: if you are walking downhill on good graded tread with the summit rocks behind your shoulder, you have passed the turn and should come back to the trail's high point.

approach_variants.name: Windy Creek trail from Cathedral Driveway
approach_variants.notes: The shortest way up. From the Cathedral Driveway trailhead, a few miles west of Long Swamp on the same road, climb the Windy Creek trail about five miles to its junction with the Windy Peak trail, then go a short distance more to the summit. Some maps wrongly show the trail starting from the Cathedral Driveway trail about half a mile west of the trailhead.
hazards: Trail reported overgrown in stretches from lack of use
Long gravel forest road driving far from any town, no cell coverage
Fully exposed, treeless ridge and summit in wind and lightning
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the true summit
Limited seasonal water on the upper trail
Standing fire-killed timber in wind

approach_variants.name: Boundary Trail from Iron Gate

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Windy Peak and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. Expect burn. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a free self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

approach_variants.notes: The roughest drive of the three. From FR-39, turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about six miles to the Iron Gate trailhead; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended and passenger cars are not advised. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass and Horseshoe Basin, then take the Windy Peak trail west to the summit scramble.
hazards: Roughest drive of the three, high clearance advised on the last six miles of road
Fire-killed standing timber comes down in wind; blowdown changes yearly
Water is scarce on the climb and worsens through the season; dependable only at lakes in the basin
Fully exposed alpine tundra and ridge with no shelter when weather arrives from the border
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the summit
Remote, no cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the col southwest of the tower
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path along the lake's west shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.

From the col the climbing is short: about 100 ft up the sharp ridge, a few feet right onto the south face at Class 4, a 5.5 step-up, a short face, and a scramble to the summit slot.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
Exposure on the sharp ridge above the col
Hard-to-find protection on the 5.5 crux
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter
Downclimbing the south face back to the col is the usual descent and is Class 2-3 with one harder step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the col southwest of the tower, this line goes straight up the sharp ridge above the col for about 100 ft. That ridge crest is the route.

So the arrival test is the col, and it has three parts:
  1. You reached it by ascending snow or class 2 rock from the basin — not by crossing a steep snowfield, which is the west-side approach, and not by traversing across light rock under Dragontail's south ridge, which is the east face.
  2. Above you the ground rises as a defined, narrow crest rather than as an open face.
  3. The tower's summit block is directly above that crest, with the four-foot summit slot the last obstacle.

If the crest feels wrong: the ridge is sharp and exposed, and the recorded warning about this line is that placements on the crux are tricky to find. That is a route-finding statement as much as a protection one — a leader who cannot find gear may be a few feet off the correct line, on ground with fewer features.

And the common mistake: parties heading for the tower from Aasgard Pass drift too far east, toward Dragontail. If Dragontail's bulk is directly ahead of you rather than off to your right, you have gone past the tower.

approach_variants.name: Boundary Trail from Tungsten Mine Camp
approach_variants.notes: The scramble here is trivial and the approach is not, so treat this as a multi-day backpack with a short walk-up at the end of it. From the road end at Thirtymile the Chewuch River trail runs north for eight or nine miles, passing a waterfall a couple of miles in and crossing a burn where standing snags are a real concern in wind, to a signed junction where the Tungsten Creek trail turns off. That trail climbs a further six miles and about two thousand feet to the old mine camp on the mountain's south side, where the Boundary Trail comes in. The creek the trail follows on its last stretch is the final dependable water; in dry years everything above it can be dry streambed and stagnant pools. Most parties camp near the mine and climb the peak the following morning.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Extremely long remote approach with no cell coverage
Early or late season snow squalls above 7,000 ft arriving with little warning
Higher, more difficult fords of Tungsten Creek and the Chewuch in early season
Standing fire-killed snags through the burned section in wind
Unstable historic mine debris and equipment near the camp
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Bear, cougar and wolf country - proper food storage required
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a bend in a trail, and it is about a mile beyond the place most people mistake for it. The Tungsten Creek trail ends at its junction with the Boundary Trail at roughly 6,750 ft at the old mine camp, and that camp is conspicuous, with iron pipe, timbers and collapsed structures scattered across the slope on the mountain's south side. That is not the start. From the camp, follow the Boundary Trail west for about a mile, climbing gently to around 6,900 ft, to the point where the trail stops running west along the flank and turns to head south toward Apex Pass. That turn is the marker; leave the trail there and go northeast, straight up. The confirmation is what you can see from the bend: the whole west slope of the mountain is laid out above you in one uninterrupted piece, broad and gentle, heather and talus with no cliff band anywhere across it. If you are looking at broken rock steps or a wall, you have left the trail at the wrong place. The way to know you have overshot is direction: once past the bend the Boundary Trail heads south and climbs toward Apex Pass, away from the mountain, so if the trail has turned south under you, turn round. Lines further round to the north or south of this slope break into short sections of low class 3 and are not the recommended way; the west slope is the least steep and the one to use.
